The two lower branches are different reductions but share the same counting
bridge. The degree, deletion, monotonicity, and block laws then use only
finite combinatorics and polynomial algebra.

\subsection{Three easy ways to state a false variant (manuscript~01)}
\paragraph{Using only covering relations.}
For the chain $1<2<3$, the relation $1<3$ must appear in the matching graph.
Using just the two Hasse edges would give $\gamma_1=2$, whereas the correct
value is $3$ and $h=1+6t+6t^2+t^3$. The lower ideals are unchanged by taking
transitive closure, but the compatible-pair formula is not unchanged unless
the closure is taken as well. The second proof of
Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:cancel} explains why: paths must be compressible to
edges of the relation.

\paragraph{Testing only principal ideals.}
For the poset $a<b$ and $a<c$, the vector $(x_a,x_b,x_c)=(0,2,2)$ satisfies
the inequalities for the three principal ideals. It violates the inequality
for the full ideal, because its total is four while the ground set has size
three. The polytope in \eqref{gam:eq:Q} uses \emph{all} lower ideals.

\paragraph{Counting witnesses rather than supports.}
With two sources and two targets and every source below every target,
there are two compatible bijections but only one ordered support pair with
those specified sources and targets. That pair contributes one, not two.
This distinction is the reason the gamma polynomial is not in general the
ordinary matching generating polynomial.

\subsection{Real-rootedness and flagness remain separate}
The universal theorem does not imply real-rootedness. Part~II's height-two
analysis already contains counterexamples, with the earlier small example
credited to Shivam Patel~\cite{Patel}. To see the distinction in an exact
instance (manuscript~01), let $\Theta_3$ be the bipartite graph consisting
of three internally disjoint paths of length three with common endpoints.
Its height-two poset has gamma polynomial
\[
 p(u)=1+9u+24u^2+16u^3+u^4,
\]
as counted in Part~II (the case $m=3$ of~\eqref{htwo:eq:thetapoly}). The
identity
\[
 p(-x)=(1-x)(1-4x)^2+x^4
\]
shows that $p$ is positive on $[-1,0]$. Its nonnegative coefficients exclude
nonnegative roots. If all its roots were real, all four would therefore be
strictly below $-1$, contradicting the fact that their product is one.
A nonreal zero $u_0$ of $p$ lifts through $t=u_0(1+t)^2$ to nonreal
zeros of $h_\tau(t)=(1+t)^8p(t/(1+t)^2)$: the quotient is real for real
$t\ne-1$, and $t=-1$ cannot solve this equation. Thus $h_\tau$ is not
real-rooted. This example and its discovery are not claimed anew. [Merge
note: this is a short second proof that $P_{\Theta_3}$ is not real-rooted;
Part~II's Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:thetaintro} counts its real roots exactly,
and Proposition~\ref{htwo:prop:roottransfer} is the lifting argument.]

Similarly, Boolean orbits of an auxiliary finite set are not a flag
simplicial sphere. Theorem~\ref{gam:gv:thm:orbits} supplies a nonnegative gamma
expansion, not the face-incidence structure demanded by
Conjecture~5.1(d). The root-polytope formula in
\eqref{gam:gv:eq:rootrecovered} does not remove that distinction.

\subsection{Suggested Lean development order (manuscript~06)}
A useful first module would treat finite relations, disjoint pairs of finite
sets, and relation-respecting bijections. It should prove the near-perfect
support/reachability lemma and the coefficient defect before introducing
any geometry. A second module would establish the ideal Hall criterion and
common-support cancellation, then perform the finite-sum reindexing that
gives the gamma expansion of $p_\tau$.

A third module can express the demand/support identity as an explicit
hypothesis and prove the support-fibre reduction and
Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:main} conditional on that hypothesis. Such a theorem must
be labeled conditional; it would not be a completed formal proof of the
conjecture. Discharging the hypothesis requires formalizing the classical
root-polytope route or developing a direct finite combinatorial proof.
The quotient-block and deficiency formulas can then be proved by finite
counting and elementary polynomial algebra.

The elementary graph classification is therefore a realistic independent
formalization target, while the main theorem has one substantial library
boundary. No Lean source or successful Lean compilation is claimed in this
package. Likewise, the external mathematical theorems used in the paper
are ordinary cited inputs, not assertions that they already exist in the
repository's trusted kernel boundary.

\subsection{A staged proof-assistant project (manuscript~01)}
A practical formalization can separate the new order-theoretic work from
the existing geometric input. First define finite preorders, lower ideals,
and the support-fiber excess map. The equivalence in
Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:fibre} is a finite-sum inequality argument and should be a
small, independent target. Next prove the Boolean summation: this gives a
formal implication from the explicit counting-bridge statement to the
universal gamma theorem.

A second finite target is overlap cancellation. One may formalize the
partial-permutation graph and its path decomposition, or iterate a
bijection from a source until it reaches a target. Finiteness and injectivity
exclude entry into a cycle. The resulting compatible core supports the
commuting toggles and every restriction-counting identity.

To obtain a fully closed formal proof, the counting bridge must itself be
proved rather than silently postulated. The supplied ordinary proof reduces
it to Hall's theorem and the two published root-polytope results; a natural
bijective proof of the bridge could yield a substantially smaller formal
library dependency. A Lean theorem with an unproved bridge hypothesis is a
valuable intermediate artifact, but is not a complete formal verification
of Conjecture~5.2. No uncompiled Lean file or such conditional proof is
presented as verified in this package.

[Merge note: neither plan has been started. No Lean or Rocq declaration in
ProveIt formalizes any statement of Part~IV.]

\section{Further research questions and topics}\label{gam:sec:questions}
The following questions are proposed research directions. Except where an
existing conjecture is named, no claim is made that the formulation is new
or that the literature has never addressed a related version (manuscript~06).
Manuscript~01 adds: the flag question is the remaining named conjecture in
the cited source; the others are proposed directions arising from the proof,
whose worldwide open status has not been exhaustively surveyed, and they
should be viewed as specific research tasks, not as assertions that the
literature contains no related results. Research
questions~\ref{gam:q:first}--\ref{gam:q:review} are manuscript~06's, in its
order, with manuscript~01's formulation added where it asks the same
question; Research questions~\ref{gam:gv:q:faces}--36 are the rest of
manuscript~01's.

\begin{question}[A direct demand/support bijection; manuscripts~06 and~01]\label{gam:q:first}\label{gam:q:bijection}
Construct an explicit bijection in Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:count} that is compatible
with right-support restriction as in Proposition~\ref{gam:prop:gradedinput}.
A mere lexicographic matching of two equally sized lists is not the target.
Can an augmenting-path or activity construction explain the correspondence
without importing Ehrhart theory? This would remove the largest
formalization dependency of the main theorem. (Manuscript~01: construct an
explicit bijection from $\mathcal R_H$ to perfectly matchable support pairs
that preserves the exact receiver support. Can it respect induced subgraphs
or a controlled choice of vertex ordering?)
\end{question}
Proposition~\ref{gam:prop:gradedinput} proves the required cardinality
identities, but the geometric proof does not identify a natural map. Such a
construction would make the Boolean action on actual preorder lattice points
explicit and would simplify a complete formalization (manuscript~01).
[Merge note: this is Part~II's Research question~\ref{gam:q:bridge}, asked
again with the receiver support preserved.]
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: answered in Part~IX. The two-flow
maps of Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:main} are explicit, polynomial-time and
support-preserving, and their proof imports no Ehrhart theory
(Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:count} and the merge note after it). The
ordering sub-question is answered in part: the maps depend only on the
chamber of a cost order (Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:chambers}) and obey
deletion laws outside the selected sets; full automorphism-equivariance is
impossible (Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:symmetry}), and the rest is Research
question~\ref{tf:q:functoriality}.]

\begin{question}[Boolean orbits on actual lattice points]\label{gam:q:orbits}
Can one realize the terms in \eqref{gam:eq:main} as orbits of a natural system
of involutions on $\Qt\cap\Z^E$, with a $k$th orbit containing one point
for every subset of $n-2k$ free labels? Compatibility with relabeling and
restriction is desirable. The present support-count identity does not
supply such an action.
\end{question}
[Merge note: manuscript~01's Theorem~\ref{gam:gv:thm:orbits} realizes such
orbits on the support-pair model $\mathscr M_\tau$, not on $\Qt\cap\Z^E$;
the question stays open as stated.]

\begin{question}[Flag-polytopal realization; manuscripts~06 and~01]\label{gam:q:flag}
Does every $h_\tau$ occur as the $h$-polynomial of an $n$-dimensional flag
simplicial polytope, as asked in \cite[Conjecture~5.1(d)]{AC}? The gamma
formula gives nonnegative coefficients but no flag face complex. A useful
intermediate objective is a simplicial model whose face numbers are the
transport-support counts; it must account for the fact that deleting an
arbitrary single signed endpoint need not preserve balance. (Manuscript~01:
can the disjoint-support model be used to construct a flag simplicial
$n$-polytope whose $h$-polynomial is $h_\tau$?)
\end{question}
The existing Boolean families provide ranks but no face-gluing rules.
A successful construction must address intersections and sphere topology,
not merely reproduce the gamma coefficients. It need not use the same
canonical lattice triangulation considered in Part~I (manuscript~01).
[Merge note: compare Part~II's Research questions~6 and~7 and its crown
obstruction, Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:crownintro}.]

\begin{question}[Classification beyond a perfect matching]\label{lor:hq:beyondpm}% label added in batch 55 (Part V)
Extend Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:balanced} to arbitrary bipartite graphs, including
unequal shores and graphs whose maximum matching does not saturate either
shore. Is there a useful decomposition of the palindromic cases into
balanced preorder blocks and residual components? Palindromicity is to be
measured in the actual polynomial degree. The endpoint argument here does
not directly apply when that degree is smaller than a shore size.
\end{question}
[Added 29 September 2026, batch 55: answered in Part~V. Apart from isolated
vertices there are no residual components: the palindromic cases are

\begin{question}[Coefficient shape beyond gamma-positivity]\label{lor:hq:shape}% label added in batch 55 (Part V)
Which preorders have log-concave, unimodal, or real-rooted gamma polynomials?
The general theorem answers none of these stronger questions for
$\Gamma_\tau$. For real-rootedness, the already documented height-two
counterexamples rule out an unrestricted assertion. Relations to quotient
width and induced comparability configurations are concrete targets.
\end{question}
[Added 29 September 2026, batch 55: for every poset of height two the
log-concavity and unimodality parts are answered: $\gamma_k/\binom{\min(m,n)}k$
is log-concave with no internal zeros (Part~V,
Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:gammaULC}). For arbitrary preorders Part~V proves only
that $h_\tau$ is ultra-log-concave; log-concavity of $\Gamma_\tau$ remains

\begin{question}[Extremal profiles with prescribed structure]
Determine the maximal and minimal $\gamma_k$ when block sizes, quotient
width, or matching number are fixed. Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:bounds} gives sharp
unrestricted bounds, but fixing these structural parameters may make the
extremizers quite different from chains or universal equivalence classes.
The positive block formula offers a way to separate local multiplicities
from quotient feasibility.
\end{question}

cover-graph parameter is a separate question because transitive closure
can enlarge neighborhoods and graph width. Establish precise arithmetic
and bit-complexity bounds, and determine the counting complexity without

\end{question}
[Added 29 September 2026, batch 55: without parameter restrictions,

[Added 30 September 2026, batch 68: Part~XI computes every weighted

\begin{question}[A geometric interpretation of the gamma coefficients]
The signed-vector formula counts balanced points of the cube
$\{-1,0,1\}^E$ satisfying ideal inequalities. Can these points be realized
as a natural collection of faces, lattice points in a canonical section,
or standard monomials of a graded algebra? Such an interpretation might
connect positivity to Part~I's root-polytope model, but would
require more than the enumerative identity established here.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Limit laws for support size]\label{lor:hq:limit}% label added in batch 55 (Part V)
For growing families of preorders, what conditions on $\Gamma_\tau$ or the

mixing variable and the conditional binomial size. Can the variance and
tail bounds be sharpened using comparability density or matching

\end{question}
[Added 29 September 2026, batch 55: Part~V proves same-mean binomial

Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:statistics} has it at uniform weight), and a

\begin{question}[Independent formal and mathematical review; manuscripts~06 and~01]\label{gam:q:review}
Formalize first the elementary endpoint-defect and cancellation theorems,
and independently review the support-fibre equivalence. Then discharge the

balanced-graph characterization with existing Gorenstein and
matching-decomposition criteria to determine which parts are already

(Manuscript~01: formalize the universal theorem with no unproved
assumptions, and develop an independent proof of the counting bridge that
avoids the root-polytope machinery.)
\end{question}
The finite-order part is short enough to audit separately. Closing the
bridge dependency, while retaining the multivariate support interpretation,

\begin{question}[Which gamma vectors are face vectors?; manuscript~01]\label{gam:gv:q:faces}
Do the numbers $\gamma_k(\tau)$ arise as the face numbers of a useful simplicial
or balanced complex, with a construction natural under induced restriction?
\end{question}
Simply treating compatible pairs as faces is inadequate: removing one
source without a receiver destroys equal cardinality. The locality formula
\eqref{gam:gv:eq:deckgamma} suggests studying endpoint-supported structures or
quotients of matching complexes with carefully controlled identifications.

\begin{question}[The even-cardinality reconstruction defect; manuscript~01]
What additional deletion, marking, or contraction data determines the top
gamma coefficient when $n$ is even? Can one reconstruct it from a suitably
enriched polynomial deck without reconstructing the entire preorder?
\end{question}
Equation~\eqref{gam:gv:eq:deletiondifferential} reconstructs every other
coefficient but annihilates the middle monomial.
Corollary~\ref{gam:gv:cor:derivative} identifies the missing scalar as a
signed value at $-1$, counted by full endpoint cores. This gives a precise
target for richer reconstruction data.

A single pair's feasibility is a matching problem; counting distinct pairs

but does not supply a general efficient counting algorithm or a hardness

\begin{question}[Local changes of the relation; manuscript~01]
Find effective formulas for the gamma increment when one adds a relation
and then takes transitive closure. Can the newly compatible cores be

Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:monotone} already proves nonnegativity of every increment.
An exact local rule would be stronger and could lead to constructive

Identify structural classes of preorders for which $\Gamma_\tau$ is

\begin{question}[Refining the lattice-point statistic; manuscript~01]
What counterpart of the Boolean expansion survives if one records both

\end{question}

\begin{question}[Beyond unit ideal budgets; manuscript~01]\label{gam:gv:q:last}
Which integral budget functions $b(I)$ admit an analogue for

The excess substitution changes the right-hand side to

\section{Conclusion}\label{gam:sec:conclusion}
The main formula treats the gamma coefficients of a preorder not as
mysterious alternating combinations of lattice-point counts, but as counts
of disjoint feasible transport supports. Fixing a lattice point's zeros
exposes a bipartite demand problem; summing those problems exposes Boolean
intervals. This proves gamma-positivity for every finite preorder, including
all equivalence-class blowups and all heights.

The matching viewpoint also gives a structural converse. In a balanced
bipartite graph with a perfect matching, a palindromic support polynomial
forces the relation obtained from that matching to be transitive. The
failure is measured exactly by missing reachability pairs. Positive block
formulas, coefficientwise monotonicity, sharp bounds, and the exact root
multiplicity at $-1$ then follow from the same finite support model.

The unresolved step toward a more conceptual and more readily formalized
proof is not another positivity inequality. It is a natural combinatorial
realization of the inherited demand/support equinumeracy. The proofs and
checks supplied here isolate that issue while giving an explicit answer to
the stated gamma-positivity conjecture.

Manuscript~01 concludes in the same sense. The general preorder problem
admits a uniform solution once zero coordinates are allowed on the entire
ground set. The ideal inequalities then become a bipartite supply--demand
system, and the classical counting bridge turns each support fiber into a
family of matchable pairs. Summing over the free coordinates produces the
gamma basis with no cancellation of signs. The resulting coefficients count
ordered disjoint compatible source and receiver sets. This proves the full
gamma-positivity conjecture, explains why arbitrary height and arbitrary
equivalence blocks cause no exception, and supplies an exact
matching-theoretic meaning for the vanishing at $-1$. The same finite model
gives relation-monotonicity, complement-duality, induced-deck identities,
and a block-capacity formula. The remaining work is not to infer positivity
from more examples, but to understand natural bijections, geometric
realizations, stronger root properties, and complete formal verification of
the classical bridge and its new consequences.

\section{Normalization and independent-review checklist}\label{gam:sec:normalization}
\noindent\emph{(Appendix~A of manuscript~06.)}

\subsection{The three different cardinalities}
A perfect matching is a set of edges. A matchable support pair $(U,V)$ is a
pair of vertex sets admitting at least one perfect matching. A hypertree is
a degree-minus-one vector admitting at least one realizing spanning tree.
The proofs count the latter two without realization multiplicity. The
$K_{2,2}$ example in Remark~\ref{gam:rem:K22} is a minimal check against
conflating these notions.

\subsection{Three polynomial models, with different dimensions}
The original preorder polytope $\Qt$ lies in $\R^n$, and $h_\tau$ counts
its points by support. The doubled graph $G_\tau$ has $2n$ vertices and
$p_{G_\tau}$ has degree $n$. The augmented edge polytope
$B_{\widehat{G_\tau}}$ has dimension $2n$ and its Ehrhart numerator is the
same polynomial, with higher coefficients zero. These dimension statements
are consistent because the degree of an Ehrhart numerator can be strictly
smaller than the polytope dimension.

For a general graph $H$ with shores of sizes $p,q$, its augmented graph has
$p+q+2$ vertices, is connected and bipartite, and its edge polytope has
dimension $p+q$. The two affine equations say that the coordinate sum on
each augmented shore is one. The natural affine lattice is the intersection
of that affine space with the ambient integer lattice. No factor of a
lattice index is inserted in \eqref{htwo:eq:KPinput}.

\subsection{Orientation and equality cases}
A relation edge is always directed from a source in the lower direction to
a target in the upper direction. Hence a matching must satisfy
$|A\cap I|\ge|B\cap I|$ for ideals $I$, not the reverse inequality. In the
near-perfect-support lemma, omitting $a$ on the source side and $b$ on the
target side detects a path from $b$ to $a$. The count $|\overline R|$ is
invariant under swapping their dummy names, but the proof is not.

The signed-vector formula uses signs on individual elements, not just
blocks. Once block differences are fixed, the multinomial coefficients in
\eqref{gam:eq:localB} recover precisely the lost labeling information. The
formula would be wrong without these factors.

\subsection{A short audit path}
An independent reviewer can check the main theorem by verifying the two
implications of Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:fibre}, the normalization in the established
input Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:count}, and the finite sum in
\eqref{gam:eq:fixedsupport}. The second principal theorem can be checked
separately from the directed-path construction in Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:reach} and
the cancellation counterexample in Proposition~\ref{gam:prop:canceliff}.
None of those steps depends on the finite verification data.

\section{A compact proof certificate}\label{gam:gv:sec:certificate}
\noindent\emph{(Appendix~A of manuscript~01.)}
This section records the complete logical skeleton for a reader checking
the generalization rather than its consequences.

Let $S\subseteq E$, $Z=E\setminus S$, and $H_{Z,S}$ have edge $zs$ when
$z\le_\tau s$. Write $x=\one_S+c$ on $S$, with zero coordinates on $Z$.
For $T\subseteq S$,
\[
 x\in\Qt
 \ \Longrightarrow\
 c(T)\le c(S\cap\down T)
 \le |Z\cap\down T|=|N_{H_{Z,S}}(T)|.
\]
Conversely, for a lower ideal $I$,
\[
 c(I\cap S)\le |Z\cap\down(I\cap S)|\le |Z\cap I|
 \ \Longrightarrow\ x(I)\le|I|.
\]
Thus the exact-support fiber has size $|\mathcal R_{H_{Z,S}}|$.
The classical bridge says that this is
\[
 \#\{(U,V):U\subseteq Z,\ V\subseteq S,\ U\match_\tau V\}.
\]
For any fixed disjoint compatible $(U,V)$, its allowed supports are exactly
$S=V\sqcup C$, $C\subseteq E\setminus(U\cup V)$. Hence
\[
 H_\tau(\zv)
 =\sum_{(U,V)}\sum_C z_{V\cup C}
 =\sum_{(U,V)}z_V\prod_{w\notin U\cup V}(1+z_w).
\]
This proves the theorem. The only imported count is justified by the
explicit demand-to-hypertree-vector correspondence and the published
identities \eqref{htwo:eq:KPinput}--\eqref{htwo:eq:OTinput}. No statement about
preorder gamma-positivity is used in those inputs.

\phantomsection\part*{Part V.\quad Ultra-log-concave support polynomials: palindromic cores, approximate and exact counting}
\addcontentsline{toc}{part}{Part V.\texorpdfstring{\quad}{ } Ultra-log-concave support polynomials}

\noindent\emph{Part~V was added on 29 September 2026 in batch~55 of
ProveIt's incoming-report intake, from two manuscripts that prove the same
main theorem independently: for every finite bipartite graph, the
demand-support enumerator divided by $\binom rk$, $r$ the smaller shore, is
log-concave with no internal zeros, so every preorder support polynomial
$h_\tau$ is ultra-log-concave of order $n$. The unweighted inequality is the
case of Example~2.4 of Theorem~A of R\"ohrle and Ulirsch~\cite{RU}, composed
with the published support-counting bridge; what is new here is that
composition and its consequences. Part~V also classifies the palindromic
support polynomials of all bipartite graphs, answering Research
question~\ref{lor:hq:beyondpm}, gives approximation schemes for partition
functions and single coefficients, and shows exact counting
$\#\mathrm P$-complete already for posets of height two. Parts~I--IV are
unchanged except for dated pointers to this addition.
Section~\ref{lor:sec:prov} records the provenance, fixes the notation and
states what is answered.}

\section{Provenance, conventions and what Part~V answers}
\label{lor:sec:prov}

\subsection{Two manuscripts, one addition}
\label{lor:sec:source}
Part~V merges two batch-55 manuscripts. Both are AI-assisted research
manuscripts dated 29 September 2026, both are 23 A4 pages as delivered, and
the title page of each names ChatGPT (``ChatGPT --- AI-assisted mathematical
research''). Neither saw the other. They are called \emph{source~06} and
\emph{source~07} below, after the file prefixes that continue this report's
local sequence (Part~I's unprefixed files count as~01, Parts~II--IV used
\texttt{02-} to \texttt{05-}). Part~IV's ``manuscript~06'' and
``manuscript~01'' are different documents, batch-44 manuscripts; the
source numbers avoid reusing their names.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item \textbf{Source~06 (the base):} batch-55 manuscript~01, \emph{Beyond
Real-Rootedness: Ultra-Log-Concavity and Approximate Counting for Preorder
Support Polynomials} (subtitle \emph{Transversal-matroid lifts, external
fields, and coefficient recovery}), archive
\nolinkurl{ProveIt_Lorentzian_Support.zip}. It arrived in ProveIt commit
\texttt{08985ea78} and was held over from batch~54 to be merged with
source~07. It is pinned to commit \texttt{e9a57d735} (full hash in
Section~\ref{lor:sec:pins}), at which this report's \texttt{article.tex} was
the Git blob \texttt{d52a2633b58e74aa653e\allowbreak 967eb56adc1aa41bc8ae}:
Parts~I--IV exactly as printed above. Its verifier, sampler, unit tests,
recorded outputs, build script and source notes are shipped with the prefix
\texttt{06-lorentzian-support-}.
\item \textbf{Source~07:} batch-55 manuscript~02, \emph{Beyond Real Roots:
Ultra-Log-Concavity, Palindromic Cores, and Efficient Counting for Preorder
Support Polynomials} (subtitle \emph{A bimatroid bridge resolving two
components of the bipartite support-enumerator problem}), archive
\nolinkurl{ProveIt_Support_Polynomials_Research.zip} (inner directory
\nolinkurl{ProveIt_Support_Polynomials/}, main file
\nolinkurl{support_polynomials.tex}). It arrived in \texttt{23dd71d2d} and is
pinned to commit \texttt{de2f8fa8c}, with the same article blob
\texttt{d52a2633} and this report's README as blob
\texttt{846d9f19fadac9cd933b\allowbreak 74370cdb8fafa2211c5d}. Its three
programs, recorded outputs, build script and two notes are shipped with the
prefix \texttt{07-support-polynomials-}.
\end{itemize}
Both were placed in commit \texttt{26473dfa0}. This report did not change
between the two pins and the placement, so every statement of either source
about ``the repository'' or ``the report'' concerns Parts~I--IV exactly as
printed. The manuscripts, delivery READMEs and PDFs are not shipped; they
survive in the arrival commits. Source~06's checksum list
\texttt{SHA256SUMS.txt} was verified (13/13) at placement and retired;
source~07 shipped none. Sections~\ref{lor:sec:verification}
and~\ref{lor:sp:sec:verification} name the shipped files.

\emph{Why 06 is the base.} The two manuscripts prove the same main theorem
with the same transversal matroid, the same hypotheses (a finite bipartite
graph, positive vertex weights) and essentially the same Lorentzian
argument. Source~06 was held first and already carried the prefix
\texttt{06-}; it states the corollaries that bear on this report's open
questions (ultra-log-concave height-two $\gamma$-vectors, a single-coefficient
approximation scheme, a covariance bound), and its probabilistic and
algorithmic layers are the larger. Source~07 contributes whole sections
source~06 lacks: palindromic cores (Section~\ref{lor:sp:sec:pal}), an
intersection realization (Section~\ref{lor:sp:sec:geometry}), convex-order
domination with an exact equality classification
(Section~\ref{lor:sec:probability}), exact-counting hardness
(Section~\ref{lor:sp:sec:hardness}), several examples, and the correct
attribution to R\"ohrle--Ulirsch. Proofs taken from source~07 were re-read
for hidden uses of stronger hypotheses. The only difference of setting is
that source~07 deletes isolated vertices before choosing the normalizing
shore; this leaves the polynomial unchanged, so source~06's theorem applied
to the nonisolated core gives source~07's order~$d$.

\emph{A third proof.} Batch-55 manuscript~05 (source~09, printed as
Part~VII, with its stability sections in Part~VI) proves the same
ultra-log-concavity theorem with the same matroid and the same Lorentzian
proof, and credits R\"ohrle--Ulirsch correctly. Its coefficient sections are
not reprinted; Section~\ref{lor:sec:merge} lists what of them is used here.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~06 (as delivered).}
For a bipartite graph $H=(X\sqcup Y,E)$, consider the nonnegative integral
vectors $c$ satisfying $c(S)\le |N_H(S)|$ for all $S\subseteq Y$, and count
these vectors by the number of positive coordinates. We prove that the
resulting coefficient sequence is ultra-log-concave, with binomial
normalization of order $\min(|X|,|Y|)$, even after positive vertex weights
are introduced. The proof joins a published support-counting identity to
the classical transversal-matroid model for perfectly matchable sets and
the Lorentzian theory of matroid bases.

The application gives an affirmative answer to the unimodality component
of Dai--Hou--Liu--Thawinrak--Wang's Problem~5.3 for \emph{every} bipartite
graph. In particular, every finite preorder has an ultra-log-concave support
polynomial. For height-two posets, the gamma polynomial is ultra-log-concave
as well, answering the coefficient-shape question from ProveIt's preorder
report on that entire class. These conclusions do not require real roots.

We establish multivariate complete log-concavity, a covariance-matrix bound,
and binomial moment-generating-function domination under external fields.
A matching oracle and the matroid basis walk yield fully polynomial-time
randomized approximation schemes for partition functions, specified
support fibres, and individual ordinary coefficients. The latter assertion
is justified by an explicit log-concave tilting reduction, not by unstable
interpolation. Integer capacities and all positive integral dilates of
preorder polytopes are included, with the input-encoding limitation stated.
Exact finite verification accompanies the proofs.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~07 (as delivered).}
The failure of real-rootedness does not prevent strong coefficient inequalities
for preorder support polynomials. We identify perfectly matchable vertex
supports of a bipartite graph with the bases of an explicit fundamental
transversal matroid. Together with the existing support-enumerator/root-polytope
identities and R\"ohrle--Ulirsch's bimatroid theorem, this proves ultra-log-concavity
for every bipartite demand-support enumerator, and therefore for every finite
preorder, including arbitrary equivalence classes. In particular, the unimodality
component of Dai--Hou--Liu--Thawinrak--Wang's Problem 5.3 needs no graph
restriction. We also give a complete palindromicity criterion: after isolated
vertices are deleted, the graph must be a doubled preorder, with its two copies
identified along a perfect matching. This extends the repository's balanced
criterion to all bipartite graphs. The resulting theory supplies binomial
convex-order domination under every positive fugacity, an exact weighted-star
classification of equality in the variance bound, a geometric intersection
realization, a rapidly mixing support sampler, and an FPRAS for the corresponding
partition functions. A leaf-extension interpolation gives exact-counting
hardness even for height-two preorder lattice-point counts. Written proofs are
accompanied by exact finite checks on 69,632 bipartite graphs and all 390 labelled
preorders through size four. The general bimatroid and mixing theorems are
credited inputs, not discoveries of this manuscript.
\end{tcolorbox}
\noindent The two abstracts are reproduced as delivered. Their ``the
repository'' and ``ProveIt's preorder report'' mean Parts~I--IV of this
report; source~07's ``the repository's balanced criterion'' is Part~IV's
Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:balanced}.

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Status and attribution (source~06, as delivered).}
The matroid construction, the geometric
counting bridge, and the general Lorentzian and mixing theorems are
\emph{prior results}, credited at their points of use. The contribution is
an explicit application and extension to the current support-polynomial
questions, with complete reductions and additional consequences. This is
an unrefereed research article, not a Lean-verified development. No claim of
worldwide priority, or of solving flag realizability or general gamma
log-concavity, is made.
\end{statusbox}

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Status and scope (source~07, as delivered).}
This manuscript is not refereed or formalized in Lean.
It contains conventional proofs and executable finite regression tests. Global
priority of the applications is not established. It does not solve flag
realizability, classify real-rooted graphs, or construct a direct demand-to-support
bijection. These boundaries are kept explicit throughout.
\end{statusbox}

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Priority and prior work (merge).} The unweighted inequality
of Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:main} is \emph{not new}: it is Theorem~A of
F.~R\"ohrle and M.~Ulirsch, \emph{Logarithmic Concavity of
Bimatroids}~\cite{RU}, for the bimatroid of a relation (their
Example~2.4, whose regular minors are the pairs $(I,J)$ joined by a
matching), with the same normalization $\binom{\min(m,n)}k$; their
Proposition~2.2 is the extended-matroid construction of
Section~\ref{lor:sec:lift}, and their Theorem~E, for realizable bimatroids,
contains the intersection realization of
Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:geometry}. Source~07 credits this; source~06
does not cite R\"ohrle--Ulirsch, and its Section~\ref{lor:sec:intro} is
printed with a merge note to that effect. What Part~V adds is the
composition with the published support-counting bridge (Ohsugi--Tsuchiya
and Oh~\cite{OT20,Oh}; Dai--Hou--Liu--Thawinrak--Wang and
Davis--Kohl~\cite{DHLTW,DK}), hence the transfer to demand enumerators and
to every preorder, the weighted two-shore form, and the consequences. The
transversal-matroid model of perfectly matchable sets is classical
(Balas--Pulleyblank~\cite{BP}, as identified by Mori~\cite{Mori}); the
Lorentzian theory is Br\"and\'en--Huh's~\cite{BH}; the basis-walk mixing and
approximate-counting machinery is Anari--Liu--Oveis Gharan--Vinzant's~\cite{ALOV};
the $\#\mathrm P$-completeness input is Colbourn--Provan--Vertigan's~\cite{CPV}.
The palindromicity criterion extends and re-proves Part~IV's
Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:graphintro} and Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:balanced}; the
height-two identity is Part~II's Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:main}; the
nonreal-rooted example $\Theta_3$ is Part~II's, with priority credited to
Shivam Patel~\cite{Patel}. Three manuscripts of batch~55 (sources~06, 07
and~09) proved the ultra-log-concavity transfer independently on the same
day. The Röhrle--Ulirsch record was checked for this merge on
29 September 2026 against the arXiv abstract page and the HTML of
\arxiv{2402.15317v3}: Theorem~A states
$R_k^2/\binom{m\wedge n}k^2\ge R_{k+1}R_{k-1}/(\binom{m\wedge n}{k+1}\binom{m\wedge n}{k-1})$
for the numbers $R_k$ of regular $k\times k$ minors, and Example~2.4 is the
bimatroid of a relation. No worldwide publication priority is claimed for
any result of Part~V.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{Notation of Part~V}
\label{lor:sec:notation}
Part~V works with a finite bipartite graph $H=(X\sqcup Y,E)$, with $|X|=m$
and $|Y|=n$, and with a finite preorder $\tau$ on $[n]$, using Part~I's
$\Qt$, $\J$ and $h_\tau$ and Part~IV's $\gamma_k(\tau)$ and $\Gamma_\tau$.
Table~\ref{lor:tab:notation} lists what Part~V adds or uses differently.
Three symbols were changed from the sources; no normalization was changed:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item the transversal matroid of $H$, $M_H$ in both sources, is printed
$\mathsf M_H$, because $M_G(u)$ is Part~II's matching polynomial, and
because Part~VII's $M_G$ is the \emph{dual} convention
(Section~\ref{mat:sec:lift});
\item the random support size, $K$ in both sources, is printed $L$, as in
Part~IV's Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:statistics}, where $K$ is the mixing variable;
source~07's bit length $L$ is printed $L_{\mathrm{bit}}$;
\item the preorder polytope, $Q_\tau$ in both sources, is printed
$\Qt=\mathcal Q_\tau$, and source~06's $\mathcal J(\tau)$ is printed $\J$, as
in Part~I.
\end{itemize}
Source~07's macros for $\mathbb E$, $\mathbb P$, $\mathcal B$, $\mathcal D$ are
typeset as the host's. The letters $r$ and $d$ are \emph{not} renamed; their
meaning depends on the source and is fixed in the table.

\subsection{What Part~V answers}
\label{lor:sec:answers}
Status after Part~V, as of 29 September 2026:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item \textbf{Every preorder support polynomial is ultra-log-concave}
(Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:preorderintro}), with the sharp constant, and
positive integral dilations are included (Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:dilation}).
This is stronger than the unimodality of Conjecture~5.1(b) of~\cite{AC},
proved in Part~IV (and by Part~I's proposed geometric route), and it does not follow from $\gamma$-positivity.
\item \textbf{The unimodality part of Problem~5.3 of~\cite{DHLTW}} holds for
every bipartite graph (Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:DHLTW}), and its
\textbf{palindromicity part} is classified
(Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:headline-pal}): after isolated vertices are
deleted, the graph must be a doubled preorder.
\item \textbf{Part~IV's Research question~\ref{lor:hq:beyondpm}
(``Classification beyond a perfect matching'') is answered}: there are no
residual components beyond isolated vertices, and recognition takes a
matching and a transitive closure.
\item \textbf{Research question~\ref{lor:hq:shape} (``Coefficient shape
beyond gamma-positivity'')} is answered in its log-concavity and unimodality
parts for every poset of height two (Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:gammaULC}); for
arbitrary preorders log-concavity of $\Gamma_\tau$ remains open, and
real-rootedness of $\Gamma_\tau$ is untouched.
\item \textbf{Research question~\ref{lor:hq:param} (``Parameterized exact
algorithms'')}: its last sentence is answered. Without parameter
restrictions, $|\Qt\cap\Z^n|$ is $\#\mathrm P$-complete under Turing
reductions, already in height two (Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:preorderhard}),
and it has an FPRAS (Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:FPRASpartition}). The
parameterized question remains open.
\item \textbf{Research question~\ref{lor:hq:countcx} (``Exact counting
complexity'')}: computing a specified $\gamma_k$ for unrestricted preorders
is $\#\mathrm P$-hard, already in height two (merge consequence after
Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:preorderhard}); in height two each $\gamma_k$ has an
FPRAS (Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:coefficients}). Efficient classes remain open.
\item \textbf{Research question~\ref{lor:hq:limit} (``Limit laws for support
size'')} gains same-mean binomial convex-order domination under every
positive external field, with equality exactly for antichains
(Corollary~\ref{lor:sp:cor:preorderprob}), and a covariance-matrix bound
(Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:covariance}); no central limit theorem is proved.
\item \textbf{Conjecture~5.3 and flag realization} are unchanged: Part~V
proves no real-rootedness and constructs no flag polytope. $\Theta_3$ shows
that the Lorentzian conclusions do not upgrade to real stability
(Section~\ref{lor:sec:examples}).
\end{itemize}
Part~V refutes no statement of Parts~I--IV, and nothing in them is
retracted. Parts~I--IV gain dated pointers: the title block, abstract,
scope box and reading route; Section~\ref{sec:problem}; Part~IV's remark
after Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:balanced}, Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:statistics},
Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:unimodal} and Research questions~\ref{lor:hq:beyondpm},
\ref{lor:hq:shape}, \ref{lor:hq:param}, \ref{lor:hq:limit},
\ref{lor:hq:countcx} and~\ref{lor:hq:rootgeom}, which received labels for
this purpose.

\section{The questions and the answer}
\label{lor:sec:intro}
A failed real-rootedness conjecture need not mark the end of a coefficient
inequality program. Real-rootedness is a sufficient mechanism for many
inequalities, but it is stronger than the inequalities themselves. This
article isolates a different mechanism for the preorder support polynomials
studied in ProveIt: a homogeneous polynomial on a larger ground set whose
coefficients are those of a matroid basis enumerator.

The relevant repository is Vladimir Reshetnikov's \emph{ProveIt}, specifically
this report, Parts~I--IV above. Its four parts develop a root-polytope realization,
height-two matching-support formulas and nonreal-rooted examples, cactus
determinant models, and gamma-positivity for every finite preorder. Its
current research questions include the shape of the gamma coefficients and
the complexity of computing them. Those earlier results are not claimed
again here.

The external research target is also precise. Dai, Hou, Liu, Thawinrak and
Wang ask in Problem~5.3 of \cite{DHLTW} which bipartite support enumerators
have the properties conjectured for preorders by Athanasiadis and Chapoton
\cite{AC}. We settle the \emph{unimodality part} uniformly, and strengthen it
to ultra-log-concavity. This does not classify palindromicity or
real-rootedness; the three demands have different answers.

\subsection{Main theorem in finite combinatorial form}
Let $H=(X\sqcup Y,E)$ be a finite bipartite graph, with $|X|=m$ and $|Y|=n$.
Parallel edges have no effect and are discarded. Write $N_H(S)\subseteq X$
for the neighbors of $S\subseteq Y$, and put
\begin{equation}
 \cD_H=\left\{c\in\Z_{\ge0}^{Y}:
        \sum_{y\in S}c_y\le |N_H(S)|\quad(S\subseteq Y)\right\}.
 \label{lor:eq:demand}
\end{equation}
The support polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 F_H(z)=\sum_{c\in\cD_H}\prod_{y:c_y>0}z_y,
 \qquad F_H(t,\ldots,t)=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k(H)t^k.
 \label{lor:eq:F}
\end{equation}
The exponent of a coordinate in this polynomial is its \emph{presence
indicator}, not its value $c_y$. Thus $F_H$ is multiaffine even though
$c_y$ may exceed one.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform coefficient theorem; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:thm:main}
Set $r=\min(m,n)$. The support coefficients satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \frac{a_k(H)^2}{\binom r k^2}
 \ \ge\
 \frac{a_{k-1}(H)}{\binom r{k-1}}
 \frac{a_{k+1}(H)}{\binom r{k+1}}
 \qquad(1\le k<r).
 \label{lor:eq:mainULC}
\end{equation}
Their nonzero indices are exactly $0,1,\ldots,\nu(H)$, where $\nu(H)$ is
the maximum matching size. In particular they are log-concave and unimodal.
The polynomial $F_H(z)$ is completely log-concave on the positive orthant.
The same coefficient inequality holds after positive product weights are
placed on the two vertex supports of each perfectly matchable set.
\end{theorem}
The precise meaning of the weighted statement appears in
Section~\ref{lor:sec:weighted}. If $r\le1$, the inequalities are vacuous but the
conclusions about support and unimodality retain their usual meaning. Zero
coefficients beyond the actual degree are included in the normalization.

For a preorder $\tau$ on $[n]$, let $\J$ denote its lower
ideals and define
\begin{equation}
 \Qt=\{x\in\R_{\ge0}^{n}:x(I)\le |I|\quad(I\in\J)\},
 \qquad h_\tau(t)=\sum_{x\in \Qt\cap\Z^n}t^{|\supp(x)|}.
 \label{lor:eq:preorderQ}
\end{equation}
Reflexivity and transitivity, but not antisymmetry, are required.

\begin{corollary}[All finite preorders; sources~06, 07 and~09]\label{lor:cor:preorderintro}
For every finite preorder on $n$ labels, $h_\tau(t)=\sum_{k=0}^nh_kt^k$
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 h_k^2\ge
 \frac{(k+1)(n-k+1)}{k(n-k)}\,h_{k-1}h_{k+1}
 \qquad(1\le k<n).
 \label{lor:eq:preorderULC}
\end{equation}
Every coefficient is positive. Consequently the ordinary coefficients are
strictly log-concave at every interior index. The binomial normalization
is universally sharp: the antichain has $h_\tau=(1+t)^n$.
\end{corollary}
This is a statement about $h_\tau$, not about its gamma transform. The
latter distinction is essential throughout the article.

[Merge note: the unweighted inequality~\eqref{lor:eq:mainULC} is
Theorem~A of R\"ohrle and Ulirsch~\cite{RU} for the relation bimatroid of
their Example~2.4, whose regular $k\times k$ minors are exactly the pairs
$U\sim_HS$ with $|S|=k$; their normalization is the same $\binom{\min(m,n)}k$.
Source~06 does not cite them; the statements of this section that are new
relative to~\cite{RU} are the transfer through
Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge} to demand vectors and preorders, the
weighted two-shore form, and the consequences.]

\subsection{The same theorems as stated by source~07}
\label{lor:sec:sp:headline}

The relevant part of ProveIt is the four-part report
\emph{A Reflexive Root-Polytope Model for Preorder $h$-Polynomials}
(this report, Parts~I--IV). Its later parts distinguish three questions which must not be
conflated: real-rootedness, $\gamma$-positivity, and flag-polytopal realization.
The report proves a transport-support formula for $\gamma$-positivity, records
nonreal-root examples, and leaves flag realization open. Its determinant
construction is deliberately restricted: a support-exact unit-modulus matrix
exists precisely for bipartite cacti. None of those facts implies that the
coefficient sequence loses all strong concavity outside the cactus class.

There is a second, broader target. Dai, Hou, Liu, Thawinrak, and Wang
\cite[Problem 5.3]{DHLTW} ask which bipartite graphs have demand-support
enumerators satisfying the unimodality, palindromicity, and real-rootedness
properties suggested by preorder polynomials. We separate these properties.
The answer for \emph{unimodality is every bipartite graph}. The answer for
\emph{palindromicity is an explicit, polynomial-time recognizable class}.
Real-rootedness is strictly stronger and is not classified here.

Let $H=(X\sqcup Y,E)$ be a finite simple bipartite graph. A pair
$(I,J)$, with $I\subseteq X$, $J\subseteq Y$, is a \emph{matchable support}
if $H[I\sqcup J]$ has a perfect matching; the empty pair is allowed. Define
\[
 p_H(t)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(H)}t^{|I|}=\sum_{k=0}^{r}p_k t^k,
 \qquad r=\nu(H).
\]
Here $\nu(H)$ is the maximum matching size. Each support is counted once,
not once per perfect matching. Delete isolated vertices and let $a,b$ be the
remaining shore sizes. Set $d=\min(a,b)$; an edgeless graph has $d=r=0$.

\begin{theorem}[Universal coefficient inequality; Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC} on the nonisolated core]
\label{lor:sp:thm:headline-ulc}
For every bipartite graph, the sequence
\[
 \left(\frac{p_k}{\binom d k}\right)_{k=0}^{d},
 \qquad p_k=0\quad(k>r),
\]
is log-concave and has no internal zeros. Thus $p_H$ is unimodal and its
positive coefficients are strictly log-concave at all internal indices.
The same assertions hold after each support $(I,J)$ receives any positive
vertex-product weight $\prod_{x\in I}\alpha_x\prod_{y\in J}\beta_y$.
\end{theorem}

The unweighted graph inequality is a direct specialization of the established
bimatroid inequality of R\"ohrle and Ulirsch \cite[Theorem A]{RU}, not a new
bimatroid theorem. The important transfer is to the newer support-enumerator
and preorder questions. The weighted formulation follows from positive
specialization of the same matroid basis polynomial.

\begin{theorem}[Complete palindromicity criterion]
\label{lor:sp:thm:headline-pal}
For every bipartite graph $H$, the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item $p_H(t)$ is palindromic with respect to its actual degree $r$.
\item Its nonisolated core has two shores of size $r$, has a perfect matching,
and, after identifying matched vertices, its edge relation is a preorder.
\item $p_H(t)$ is $\gamma$-positive with respect to degree $r$.
\end{enumerate}
If the criterion holds for one perfect matching, it holds for every perfect
matching of the core. It can be decided without computing $p_H$.
\end{theorem}

The balanced, perfect-matching case and its transport-pair proof already occur
in Part~IV (Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:graphintro}, Corollary~\ref{gam:cor:balanced}). The passage to arbitrary graphs is supplied here by
an extremal-support argument, with a quantitative obstruction in
Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:top}. A complete proof is included so that the classification does
not depend on accepting an unrefereed repository proof.

For a preorder $\tau$ on $[n]$, let $h_\tau(t)=\sum h_k t^k$ count lattice
points of its preorder polytope by the number of positive coordinates. The
precise definition is in Section~\ref{lor:sec:bridge}.
Source~07's Corollary~1.3 (``Every finite preorder'') is
Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:preorderintro}, with the added remark that the
normalized inequality is strictly stronger than
$h_k^2>h_{k-1}h_{k+1}$ and that all equivalence-class sizes and heights are
allowed; it is not printed again.

\subsection{What is new here, and what is imported}
There are three substantial external ingredients. First, the number of
vectors in \eqref{lor:eq:demand} with a prescribed support is the number of
opposite-shore subsets matchable to that support. We use the established
geometric counting theorem in the form appearing in the proof of
Ohsugi--Tsuchiya's Proposition~3.4 \cite{OT20}, based on Oh's work \cite{Oh}.
Second, every matroid basis polynomial is Lorentzian, and nonnegative linear
substitutions preserve that property \cite{BH}. Third, the weighted
matroid basis down-up walk has a rank-controlled mixing bound \cite{ALOV}.
These are cited theorems, not discoveries or formalizations in this article.

The transversal-matroid representation of bipartite perfectly matchable
sets is also classical. Balas and Pulleyblank's work \cite{BP} is explicitly
identified as the source of this observation by Mori \cite{Mori}. We give
the short construction in full because it makes the coefficient,
probabilistic and algorithmic consequences transparent.

The principal contribution is the resulting package of statements for the
current preorder and bipartite support problems: both-shore weighted
normalizations, conditional support laws, external-field covariance and
tail bounds, and a rigorous reduction for approximating individual
coefficients. The inspected sources do not establish a worldwide priority
claim for these consequences; some may be implicit in earlier work. The
article asserts the proved implications, not the absence of all precedents.

\section{The support-counting bridge}
\label{lor:sec:bridge}
For $U\subseteq X$ and $S\subseteq Y$, write $U\sim_H S$ when $|U|=|S|$
and $H[U\sqcup S]$ has a perfect matching. Equivalently, there exists a
bijection $f:S\to U$ with $f(y)y\in E$. Each pair $(U,S)$ is counted once, not once per matching.

\subsection{The geometric theorem in the needed form}
For $S\subseteq Y$, define
\begin{equation}
 P_{H,S}=\sum_{x\in X}
       \conv\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{e_y:y\in S,\ xy\in E\}\bigr)
       \ \subseteq\R^S.
 \label{lor:eq:minkowski}
\end{equation}
An empty neighborhood contributes the single point $0$.

\begin{lemma}[Published positive-coordinate count]\label{lor:lem:externalbridge}
The number of integer points of $P_{H,S}$ whose coordinates indexed by
$S$ are all strictly positive is
\begin{equation}
 \#\{U\subseteq X: U\sim_H S\}.
 \label{lor:eq:positivecount}
\end{equation}
For $S=\varnothing$, both sides are one.
\end{lemma}
\noindent\emph{Source and normalization.}
This is the fixed-receiver-support count in the proof of
\cite[Proposition~3.4]{OT20}. In that proof the summands are
$\Delta_{\{0\}\cup N(x)}$ in one extra coordinate, and their total coordinate
sum is $m$. Eliminating the zeroth coordinate gives
\eqref{lor:eq:minkowski}. The relevant positive-coordinate lattice-point
identity is attributed there to \cite[Lemma~22 and Proposition~26]{Oh}.
We import this counting theorem; in particular, we do not replace its
geometric proof by an unproved claim of a canonical bijection.

\begin{lemma}[The integral feasibility model]\label{lor:lem:hallmodel}
The integer points of $P_{H,Y}$ are precisely $\cD_H$.
For a prescribed support $S$, the points of $\cD_H$ supported exactly on
$S$ are precisely the positive-coordinate integer points of $P_{H,S}$,
extended by zero outside $S$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every point of the Minkowski sum is obtained by distributing at most one
unit from each $x\in X$ among its neighboring receiver coordinates.
Therefore its sum on $T\subseteq Y$ is at most $|N_H(T)|$.

Conversely, let $c$ be an integer vector satisfying those inequalities.
Replace each receiver $y$ by $c_y$ labeled copies, each with the same
neighbors as $y$. For any set of these copies, let $T$ be the original
receivers it uses. The number of selected copies is at most
$c(T)\le |N_H(T)|$. Hall's theorem therefore matches every copy to a
distinct donor. Each donor contributes either $0$ or one coordinate vector
to \eqref{lor:eq:minkowski}, and their sum is $c$.

If $c$ is zero outside $S$, the matching uses only the receiver copies in
$S$. The same construction is thus valid in $P_{H,S}$. Conversely any
point of that smaller sum extends by zero to the larger sum. Requiring
strict positivity on $S$ gives exactly the claimed support fibre.
\end{proof}
This proof needs only the integer version of the polytope correspondence.
It does not assert that an integer vector has a unique donor allocation.
Such allocations usually have multiplicity, which is why counting all
allocations would give the wrong polynomial.

\begin{proposition}[Exact multivariate bridge; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:prop:bridge}
For every $S\subseteq Y$,
\begin{equation}
 [z_S]F_H(z)=\#\{U\subseteq X:U\sim_H S\},
 \qquad z_S:=\prod_{y\in S}z_y.
 \label{lor:eq:supportbridge}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 F_H(z)=\sum_{U\sim_H S}z_S,
 \qquad F_H(t,\ldots,t)=p_H(t):=\sum_{U\sim_H S}t^{|S|}.
 \label{lor:eq:FHmatching}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:hallmodel} identifies the coefficient with the left-hand
side of Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:externalbridge}. Apply that lemma separately to each
$S$, then sum the resulting finite identities.
\end{proof}
The last polynomial is the perfectly matchable set polynomial of a
bipartite graph, with the exponent equal to half the number of selected
vertices; this terminology is used in \cite{DK}. For example, $K_{2,2}$
has $p_H(t)=1+4t+t^2$, not $1+4t+2t^2$.

\subsection{The bridge in source~07's formulation, and a second proof}
\label{lor:sec:sp:bridge}
For $S\subseteq Y$, write $N_H(S)\subseteq X$ for its neighborhood. Define
\begin{equation}
 \cD_H=\{c\in\Z_{\ge0}^{Y}:c(S)\le |N_H(S)|\text{ for every }S\subseteq Y\},
 \qquad c(S)=\sum_{y\in S}c_y.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:hall}
\end{equation}
The bound $c(Y)\le |X|$ makes this set finite. Its support enumerator is
\[
 D_H(t)=\sum_{c\in\cD_H}t^{|\supp(c)|},
 \qquad D_H(\mathbf z)=\sum_{c\in\cD_H}\prod_{y:c_y>0}z_y.
\]
The variables mark whether a coordinate is positive, not its numerical value.
For example, one receiver with $s$ suppliers has demands $0,1,\ldots,s$;
its polynomial is $1+st$, not $1+t+\cdots+t^s$.

Source~07's Lemma~2.1 (``Established counting bridge and its refinement'')
states $D_H(\mathbf z)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(H)}\prod_{y\in J}z_y$, hence
$D_H(t)=p_H(t)$: this is Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge} in source~07's
notation ($D_H=F_H$). Its proof is a different import route.

\begin{proof}[Second proof of Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge} (source~07)]
We first state exactly the imported enumerative input. Augment $H$ by
$x_0,y_0$, join $x_0$ to all of $Y\cup\{y_0\}$ and $y_0$ to all of $X$, and
form
\[
 B_{\widehat H}=\conv\{e_x+f_y:xy\in E(\widehat H)\}.
\]
Use the full affine integer lattice. The two root-polytope results
\cite[Theorem 1.2]{DHLTW} and \cite[Theorem 3.10]{DK} identify its $h^*$-polynomial
with $D_H(t)$ and $p_H(t)$, respectively. The first source puts its demand
coordinates on the left shore; apply its theorem to the shore-swapped graph.
Swapping shores preserves the augmented root polytope up to an integral
coordinate permutation. In particular
$|\cD_H|=p_H(1)$. These equalities, not a conjectural positivity assertion, are
the imported boundary.

For the refinement, let $u_J$ count demands of exact support $J$ and let $v_J$
count pairs $(I,J)$ which are matchable. Applying the total-count identity to
$H[X\sqcup T]$, for every $T\subseteq Y$, gives
\[
 \sum_{J\subseteq T}u_J=\sum_{J\subseteq T}v_J.
\]
Induction on $|T|$, subtracting all proper subsets, gives $u_T=v_T$. This is
precisely the multivariate identity. Isolated vertices and empty shores cause
no exception.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the bridge does not give]
A polynomial identity is not a direct algorithmic bijection. The proof does not
tell us which demand vector should correspond to a given matchable pair.
Consequently a uniform support sampler is not, by itself, a uniform sampler
of the actual demand vectors. It does sample their support set $J$ with the
correct multiplicity distribution, by Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge}.
\end{remark}
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: Part~IX supplies the missing
algorithmic bijection (Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:main}) and a second proof of
Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge} that imports no lattice-point theorem
(Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:count}).]


\subsection{A consistency check with the recent geometric formulation}
Augment $H$ by adding one vertex on each shore, adjacent to every vertex
of the opposite shore, including each other. Denote the result by
$\widehat H$. Its bipartite root polytope can be written
\[
 R_{\widehat H}=\conv\{e_x-e_y:xy\in E(\widehat H)\}.
\]
The equivalent plus-sign convention differs by a lattice coordinate
reflection. The identities in \cite{OT20,DHLTW} give
\begin{equation}
 h^*(R_{\widehat H},t)=p_H(t)=F_H(t,\ldots,t).
 \label{lor:eq:rootpoly}
\end{equation}
Here $h^*$ is the numerator of the Ehrhart series with its dimensionally
correct denominator. Thus our inequalities also apply to this entire
class of \emph{augmented} bipartite root polytopes. Nothing here asserts
ultra-log-concavity for every lattice polytope or every unaugmented root
polytope.

\section{The classical matroid lift}
\label{lor:sec:lift}
We now explain why counting matchable \emph{supports} rather than matching
\emph{witnesses} is exactly the right convention.

Make a disjoint private copy $X^\circ=\{x^\circ:x\in X\}$ of $X$. The ground
set of a transversal matroid $\mathsf M_H$ is
\[
 \Omega=X^\circ\sqcup Y,
\]
and its matching slots are the original elements of $X$. The element
$x^\circ$ is adjacent only to slot $x$, whereas $y\in Y$ is adjacent to the
slots in $N_H(y)$. A subset of $\Omega$ is independent when it can be
matched injectively into the slots.

This family is hereditary. Its augmentation property is the usual
alternating-path augmentation between matchings of two independent sets
of unequal size. Thus it is a transversal matroid. The private elements
form a basis, so its rank is exactly $m$, even when $H$ has isolated
vertices. This is the concrete version of the classical connection
credited in Section~\ref{lor:sec:intro}.

\begin{proposition}[Basis correspondence; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:prop:bases}
The bases of $\mathsf M_H$ are exactly
\begin{equation}
 B(U,S)=(X^\circ\setminus U^\circ)\sqcup S,
 \qquad U\sim_H S.
 \label{lor:eq:bases}
\end{equation}
In particular this is a bijection between support pairs and bases.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every basis has size $m$. If its receiver part is $S$, write its private
part as $X^\circ\setminus U^\circ$. The size equation gives $|U|=|S|$.
The selected private elements occupy precisely their own slots in
$X\setminus U$. Therefore the remaining elements $S$ must be matched to
$U$, and a basis is possible exactly when $U\sim_H S$.

Conversely, choose one matching between $S$ and $U$. Together with the
forced private-slot edges it matches all of $B(U,S)$ into $X$. The resulting
basis set does not depend on which matching was chosen. Recovering $S$
as $B\cap Y$ and $U$ as the missing private elements gives the inverse.
\end{proof}

Source~07 proves the same bijection (its Proposition~3.1, ``Complement one
shore'', with the private elements identified with $X$ itself) by the same
forced-slot argument, and adds:
This is the fundamental-transversal/extended-matroid construction, not a new
kind of matroid. Its role here is to make the support model compatible with
existing matroid geometry and algorithms.

\subsection{Generic minors, without a unit-determinant requirement}
Let $A_H$ be the $m\times n$ matrix whose entry on edge $xy$ is an independent
indeterminate $q_{xy}$, with zero elsewhere. Work over
$\mathbb Q(q_{xy}:xy\in E)$. The determinant of $A_H[I,J]$ is a signed sum indexed
by perfect matchings of $H[I\sqcup J]$. Different matchings use different
edge monomials, so no two terms cancel. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \det A_H[I,J]\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(I,J)\in\PM(H).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:generic}
\end{equation}
Expanding along identity columns shows that $[I_m\mid A_H]$ represents
$\mathsf M_H$. Thus matchable supports are precisely the regular minors of a realizable
bimatroid, in the terminology of \cite{RU}.

The entries need not have modulus one, and the nonzero determinants need not
have equal magnitudes. This is why the construction works beyond the cactus
class in the repository. Substituting an all-ones adjacency matrix would be
wrong: a $2\times2$ all-ones minor vanishes although its support is matchable.
Generic \emph{nonvanishing} and faithful \emph{unit modulus} are different
requirements.

Write $a_A=\prod_{x\in A}a_x$. The basis generating polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal B_H(a,z)=\sum_{B\text{ basis of }\mathsf M_H}\prod_{e\in B}w_e
   =\sum_{U\sim_H S}a_{X\setminus U}z_S,
 \label{lor:eq:basispoly}
\end{equation}
where $w_{x^\circ}=a_x$ and $w_y=z_y$. It is multiaffine and homogeneous of
degree $m$. Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge} now gives the key equality
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{F_H(z)=\mathcal B_H(\mathbf1,z).}
 \label{lor:eq:dehom}
\end{equation}
Thus a nonhomogeneous support polynomial is an affine slice of a
homogeneous matroid polynomial. No determinant representation is required.


\subsection{The homogeneous lift and conditioning in source~07's notation}
\label{lor:sec:sp:lift}
The basis polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 \cB_H(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)
 =\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(H)}\prod_{x\in X\setminus I}x_x
                              \prod_{y\in J}y_y.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:basis}
\end{equation}
It is homogeneous of degree $m$ and multiaffine. The original occupied-vertex
polynomial, whose terms have varying degree $2|I|$, is not this polynomial.
Complementing one shore is essential.

For positive activities $\alpha_x,\beta_y$, write
\[
 p_H^{\alpha,\beta}(t)
 =\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(H)}\alpha_I\beta_J t^{|J|}
 =\sum_k c_k t^k.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left(\prod_{x\in X}\alpha_x\right)
 \cB_H\bigl((s/\alpha_x)_{x\in X},(t\beta_y)_{y\in Y}\bigr)
 =\sum_k c_k s^{m-k}t^k.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:weightlift}
\end{equation}
Supplier activities on the right side are inverse activities for private
matroid elements on the left. Confusing these two conventions would sample
the wrong probability distribution.

\begin{proposition}[Conditioning]
\label{lor:sp:prop:conditioning}
Fix any collection of vertices required to be covered or uncovered. If at least
one support satisfies the requirements, the corresponding conditional weighted
basis distribution is the positive-activity basis distribution of a matroid
minor of $\mathsf M_H$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $x\in X$, being covered means the private element $x$ is absent from the
basis; being uncovered means it is present. For $y\in Y$ these meanings are
reversed. Required present elements are contracted and required absent elements
are deleted. A feasible set of required present elements is independent.
The bases of the minor correspond bijectively to the surviving bases after
removing the required elements. Their common weight factor cancels on
normalization.
\end{proof}
This fact does not assert that every minor has a presentation by a graph of
exactly the same form. The ordinary minor oracle is enough.
[Merge note: Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:conditioning} conditions vertices
of both shores; source~06's Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:conditional} below
conditions receivers and adds complete log-concavity of the conditioned
polynomial.]

\subsection{Exactly which analytic theorem is used}
A polynomial with nonnegative coefficients is \emph{completely
log-concave} if every iterated directional derivative in nonnegative
directions is either zero or log-concave on the positive orthant. For a
homogeneous polynomial, this agrees with being Lorentzian.

We use the following parts of \cite{BH}: matroid basis polynomials are
Lorentzian (Theorem~3.10); nonnegative linear substitutions preserve
Lorentzian polynomials (Theorem~2.10); and Lorentzian and complete
log-concavity are equivalent in the homogeneous case (Theorem~2.30).
A bivariate degree-$d$ homogeneous polynomial
$\sum b_ks^{d-k}t^k$ is Lorentzian exactly when its nonnegative coefficient
sequence has no internal zeros and $b_k/\binom d k$ is log-concave
(Example~2.26).

\begin{theorem}[Multivariate completion]\label{lor:thm:CLC}
For $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde F_H(s,z):=s^mF_H(z/s)
       =\mathcal B_H(s\mathbf1,z)
 \label{lor:eq:homogenization}
\end{equation}
is Lorentzian. The polynomial $F_H(z)$ is completely log-concave.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion follows from the nonnegative linear substitution
$a_x=s$ in \eqref{lor:eq:basispoly}. For the second, extend each nonnegative
direction on the $z$ coordinates by zeros on the $a$ coordinates.
Differentiation in those directions commutes with restriction to
$a=\mathbf1$. Each resulting derivative of $\mathcal B_H$ is log-concave
or zero. A log-concave function restricted to an affine convex slice remains
log-concave. This proves the required assertion for every sequence of
directions. If $m=0$, $F_H=1$ and the conclusion is immediate.
\end{proof}
The homogenizing degree in \eqref{lor:eq:homogenization} is $m$, not necessarily
the actual degree $\nu(H)$. Dividing a Lorentzian polynomial by a power of
a homogenizing variable does not automatically preserve the property.
We therefore do not silently replace $m$ by $\nu(H)$.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 68: with positive weights on both shores
the replacement is false. Part~XI's Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:division} is a
Lorentzian polynomial of the form~\eqref{lor:eq:weightedhom}, of degree
15, whose quotient by the seventh power of the homogenizing variable is
not Lorentzian (Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness}).]

\section{Weighted inequalities on both shores}
\label{lor:sec:weighted}
For positive real weights $u=(u_x)_{x\in X}$ and $v=(v_y)_{y\in Y}$, define
\begin{equation}
 A_H(t;u,v)=\sum_{U\sim_H S}u_Uv_St^{|S|}
          =\sum_{k=0}^{\nu(H)}a_k(u,v)t^k.
 \label{lor:eq:weighted}
\end{equation}
When $u=\mathbf1$, this is the original support enumerator with the
external field $z_y=t v_y$. General $u$ weights a donor \emph{support}; it
is not an unspecified weighting of individual demand vectors.

\begin{theorem}[Two-shore ultra-log-concavity; sources~06, 07 and~09]\label{lor:thm:weightedULC}
For $r=\min(m,n)$, the sequence
\[
 \left(\frac{a_k(u,v)}{\binom r k}\right)_{k=0}^{r}
\]
is log-concave and has no internal zeros, with zero padding after
$\nu(H)$. In particular Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:main} holds.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First group all private variables and all receiver variables in the
basis polynomial, but use the inverse donor weights:
\begin{align}
 \left(\prod_{x\in X}u_x\right)
 \mathcal B_H\bigl((s/u_x)_{x\in X},(t v_y)_{y\in Y}\bigr)
 &=\sum_{U\sim_H S}u_Uv_Ss^{m-|S|}t^{|S|}\notag\\
 &=\sum_k a_k(u,v)s^{m-k}t^k.
 \label{lor:eq:weightedhom}
\end{align}
This is a nonnegative linear substitution in a Lorentzian polynomial,
followed by positive scalar multiplication. The bivariate criterion gives
ultra-log-concavity with normalization $\binom m k$.

Now interchange $X$ and $Y$. A support pair $(U,S)$ in $H$ becomes $(S,U)$
in the transposed graph, with the weights interchanged. It has the same
weight $u_Uv_S$ and the same cardinality. The identical construction
therefore gives normalization $\binom n k$. Choose the smaller shore to
obtain the displayed conclusion.

Every matching of size $k$ supplies a support pair, and every such pair
has a witnessing matching of size $k$. Submatchings show that all indices
from $0$ to $\nu(H)$ occur. All weights are positive, so no cancellation
or internal zero is possible. Finally, for $0<k<r$, the binomial factor in
\eqref{lor:eq:mainULC} is greater than one; this implies ordinary log-concavity,
and a nonnegative log-concave sequence without internal zeros is unimodal.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The published unimodality question; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:cor:DHLTW}
Every bipartite graph in \cite[Problem~5.3]{DHLTW} has a unimodal
support-enumerator. More strongly, it satisfies \eqref{lor:eq:mainULC}, and so
does the corresponding augmented-root-polytope $h^*$-polynomial in
\eqref{lor:eq:rootpoly}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Up to interchanging the shore names, their support-enumerator is
\eqref{lor:eq:F}; the neighborhood inequalities specify the same integer
vectors. Apply Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC} with unit weights and use
\eqref{lor:eq:rootpoly} for the Ehrhart formulation.
\end{proof}
This is an answer to one component of that problem. For example,
$K_{1,2}$ gives $1+2t$, which is not palindromic in its actual degree.
Section~\ref{lor:sec:examples} gives an example with nonreal roots.

Source~07 proves the same corollary (its Corollary~4.1, ``The unimodality
component of Problem 5.3'') by Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge} and, for
preorders, by~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:preorderbridge}, noting that for the doubled
preorder graph both active shores have size $n$ and all coefficients are
positive.
\subsection{Sharpness and elementary extremal checks}
If $H$ consists of $r$ disjoint edges, with any number of isolated vertices
added, then
\[
 p_H(t)=(1+t)^r.
\]
When the smaller shore has size $r$, equality holds in every normalized
inequality. Thus the normalization cannot be universally strengthened
beyond the binomial one at the stated shore sizes.

If $H=K_{m,n}$, every equal-size pair is matchable, so
\begin{equation}
 p_H(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(m,n)}\binom m k\binom n k t^k.
 \label{lor:eq:completebip}
\end{equation}
For an arbitrary $H$,
$0\le a_k(H)\le\binom m k\binom n k$. The upper bound is a count of
possible pairs, not of edge matchings.


\subsection{The Lorentzian step made explicit (source~07)}
\label{lor:sec:sp:ulc}
We use the following established facts from \cite[Theorems 2.10, 2.30,
3.10]{BH}. Every matroid basis polynomial is Lorentzian. Nonnegative linear
substitutions and nonnegative directional derivatives preserve this property.
A nonzero homogeneous Lorentzian polynomial, and each of its nonzero partial
derivatives, is log-concave on the positive orthant. For a quadratic
polynomial, the relevant Hessian has at most one positive eigenvalue.
R\"ohrle--Ulirsch \cite[Theorem A]{RU} already apply this mechanism to
regular-minor counts. We give the graph specialization explicitly, including
the normalization constant.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:headline-ulc}, a second route to Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC} (source~07)]
Delete isolated vertices and orient the shores so that $|X|=d\le |Y|$.
They do not change $p_H^{\alpha,\beta}$. By Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bases} and the imported
matroid theorem, equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:weightlift} is a Lorentzian polynomial
\[
 F(s,t)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}c_j s^{d-j}t^j.
\]
Fix $1\le k<d$. The derivative
$\partial_s^{d-k-1}\partial_t^{k-1}F$ is $As^2+Bst+Ct^2$, where
\begin{align*}
 A&=\tfrac12c_{k-1}(d-k+1)!(k-1)!,\\
 B&=c_k(d-k)!k!,\\
 C&=\tfrac12c_{k+1}(d-k-1)!(k+1)!.
\end{align*}
Its Hessian has at most one positive eigenvalue, so $B^2\ge4AC$. Dividing
factorials gives
\begin{equation}
 c_k^2\ge
 \frac{(k+1)(d-k+1)}{k(d-k)}c_{k-1}c_{k+1}.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:ulc}
\end{equation}
This is exactly log-concavity of $c_k/\binom d k$. A maximum matching supplies
a support of each size $0,\ldots,r$ by taking submatchings; all its weights
are positive. Hence there are no internal zeros. Since the multiplier in
equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:ulc} is greater than one, ordinary log-concavity is strict whenever
both neighboring coefficients are positive. The usual decreasing-ratio
criterion then gives unimodality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Bounds from the first and last coefficients}
\begin{proposition}
\label{lor:sp:prop:bounds}
For a positive vertex-weighted support polynomial $p(t)=\sum c_k t^k$, with
$c_0=1$ and active-shore parameter $d\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 c_k\le\binom d k(c_1/d)^k,
 \qquad
 p(z)\le(1+c_1z/d)^d\quad(z\ge0).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:upper}
\end{equation}
If $c_d>0$, then also
\begin{equation}
 c_k\ge\binom d k c_d^{k/d},
 \qquad
 p(z)\ge(1+c_d^{1/d}z)^d.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:lower}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Set $b_k=c_k/\binom d k$. On the positive interval, the ratios $b_k/b_{k-1}$
are nonincreasing, with $b_0=1$ and $b_1=c_1/d$. Their product gives the
upper bound, including any trailing zeros. When $b_d>0$, concavity of
$\log b_k$ puts it above the chord between $(0,0)$ and $(d,\log c_d)$,
which gives the lower bound. Summing the coefficient bounds proves the
polynomial inequalities.
\end{proof}

For unweighted graphs, $c_1=|E|$. For a preorder, $c_d=1$ and $c_1=|\tau|$.
Consequently
\[
 (1+z)^n\le h_\tau(z)\le(1+|\tau|z/n)^n.
\]
The right bound is often weaker than bounds using the entire relation; it is
useful because it uses only one coefficient. We do not call it an optimal
fixed-size preorder bound. For graphs with $d$ disjoint equal-degree stars,
equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:upper} is attained exactly.

\subsection{Why the order is the smaller active shore}
The theorem permits removal of isolated vertices before normalization. It does
not silently replace $d$ by the maximum matching size $r$. That would be a
stronger assertion when $r<d$; no such strengthening is proved here.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 68: with positive weights on both shores
it is false (Part~XI, Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness}); with unit weights it
is open (Research question~\ref{hb:q:unit}).]
Nor may one divide by both shore binomial coefficients. The latter plausible
variant is false even for forests; see Example~\ref{lor:sp:ex:bad-normalization}.

The coefficient bound is sharp uniformly in $d$ and $k$: a graph consisting
of $d$ independent edges has $p_H(t)=(1+t)^d$. For preorders, the same
example is the antichain. Sharpness concerns the displayed universal constant,
not the classification of equality at an individual index in an arbitrary
graph.

\subsection{Two-sided normalization fails even for a forest}
\begin{example}
\label{lor:sp:ex:bad-normalization}
Take three suppliers with neighborhoods
\[
 N(x_1)=\{y_1,y_2,y_4\},\quad N(x_2)=\{y_3\},\quad N(x_3)=\{y_1\}.
\]
This graph is a forest, and
\[
 p_H(t)=1+5t+6t^2+2t^3=(1+t)(1+4t+2t^2).
\]
Its zeros are real, but the sequence obtained by division by
$\binom3k\binom4k$ is
\[
 1,\quad\frac5{12},\quad\frac13,\quad\frac12.
\]
At index two, $1/9<5/24$. Thus real-rootedness, let alone our theorem, does
not justify simultaneous division by both shore binomial coefficients.
\end{example}

\subsection{Integer capacities and dilations}
Let each donor $x$ have capacity $b_x\in\Z_{\ge0}$ and replace the
right-hand side of \eqref{lor:eq:demand} by
$\sum_{x\in N_H(S)}b_x$. Put $B=\sum_xb_x$. Construct $H^{(b)}$ by replacing
$x$ with $b_x$ distinct copies of the same neighborhood.

\begin{corollary}[Capacity extension]\label{lor:cor:capacity}
The capacity support polynomial is $F_{H^{(b)}}$. Its ordinary coefficients
are ultra-log-concave with normalization
$\binom{\min(B,n)}k$, including arbitrary positive receiver external
fields. Its multivariate polynomial is completely log-concave, with the
Lorentzian completion of degree $B$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The neighborhood size in the cloned graph is exactly the capacity sum in
the original inequalities. Thus the feasible integer vectors, not merely
their counts, coincide. Apply Theorems~\ref{lor:thm:CLC} and
\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC} to the cloned graph.
\end{proof}
The distinction between actual degree, receiver count, and homogenizing
degree matters here. A capacity of one million is not a single unit donor.
Algorithmic consequences of cloning are polynomial in $B$, hence only
\emph{pseudopolynomial} when capacities are encoded in binary.

\section{Consequences for preorders and gamma coefficients}
\label{lor:sec:preorders}
\subsection{The direct reduction uses the full relation}
Let $H_\tau$ have a donor copy and a receiver copy of $[n]$, with an edge
$i\to j$ exactly when $i\le_\tau j$. Diagonal edges are included.

\begin{lemma}\label{lor:lem:preorderreduction}
$\Qt\cap\Z^n=\cD_{H_\tau}$, and therefore
$h_\tau(t)=F_{H_\tau}(t,\ldots,t)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The predecessor set of $S$ is $\down S$, which is a lower ideal. The ideal
inequalities and nonnegativity give
$x(S)\le x(\down S)\le |\down S|=|N_{H_\tau}(S)|$.
Conversely, if $I$ is a lower ideal, reflexivity and downward closure give
$N_{H_\tau}(I)=I$. The neighborhood inequality for $I$ is exactly the
required ideal inequality. The argument works for real nonnegative vectors
as well as for integral ones.
\end{proof}
Using only the Hasse edges would invalidate this identification. Likewise,
checking only principal ideals is not sufficient in general. Neither
shortcut is used here.

Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:preorderintro} follows immediately from this lemma and
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC}. Positivity follows because $\{0,1\}^n$
is contained in $\Qt$. We also obtain, for all $k$,
\begin{equation}
 \binom n k\le h_k\le\binom n k^2.
 \label{lor:eq:preorderbounds}
\end{equation}
The first bound counts binary vectors; the second counts all possible
matchable support pairs in the doubled graph.
[Merge note: both bounds are also in Part~IV's Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:bounds}.]

\begin{remark}[Source~07's form of the reduction]
Source~07 proves Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:preorderreduction} by the same
ideal-to-neighbourhood argument and records the following facts, printed as
delivered.
\end{remark}
A preorder is a reflexive, transitive relation, not necessarily antisymmetric.
An ideal $A\subseteq[n]$ satisfies $j\in A$, $i\le_\tau j\Rightarrow i\in A$.
Following Athanasiadis and Chapoton \cite{AC}, define
\begin{equation}
 \Qt=\{c\in\R_{\ge0}^n:c(A)\le |A|\text{ for every ideal }A\},
 \qquad
 h_\tau(t)=\sum_{c\in \Qt\cap\Z^n}t^{|\supp(c)|}.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:preorder}
\end{equation}
This support polynomial is \emph{not, by definition, the Ehrhart numerator of
$\Qt$}. The augmented root polytope is a different polytope.

Let $G_\tau$ have suppliers $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and receivers
$y_1,\ldots,y_n$, with $x_i y_j$ an edge exactly when $i\le_\tau j$.
For $S\subseteq[n]$, its supplier neighborhood is the ideal $\downarrow S$.
If $c\in \Qt$, then
$c(S)\le c(\downarrow S)\le |\downarrow S|$.
Conversely, the Hall inequality for an ideal $A$ is exactly
$c(A)\le |A|$, because $N(A)=A$. Therefore
