\begin{equation}
 \Qt\cap\Z^n=\cD_{G_\tau},\qquad h_\tau(t)=p_{G_\tau}(t).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:preorderbridge}
\end{equation}
The first equality is elementary; the second uses Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge}.
The diagonal matching is perfect. Thus $h_0=h_n=1$, $h_k>0$ for all
$0\le k\le n$, and $h_1=|\tau|$, where $|\tau|$ counts ordered related pairs,
including all $n$ reflexive pairs.

\begin{corollary}[Every positive integral dilation]\label{lor:cor:dilation}
For an integer $q\ge1$, let
\[
 h_{\tau,q}(t)=\sum_{x\in q\Qt\cap\Z^n}t^{|\supp(x)|}.
\]
Its coefficients are ultra-log-concave with normalization $\binom n k$,
also under arbitrary positive support weights. Its multivariate version
is completely log-concave.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The scaled inequalities are $x(I)\le q|I|$. The proof of
Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:preorderreduction} identifies these with capacity $q$ on
each of the $n$ donors. In Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:capacity}, $B=qn$, so
$\min(B,n)=n$.
\end{proof}
Palindromicity is special to the original normalization and is not asserted
for $q>1$. For instance, one isolated label has support polynomial
$1+qt$ in the $q$th dilation.

\subsection{Palindromicity by an elementary support-pair involution}
The following known preorder facts are included to specify how our stronger
inequality fits the earlier theory, not as additional novelty claims.

[Merge note: Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:idealhall} and the involution below re-prove
Part~IV's ideal Hall criterion (Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:idealhall}) and
complement-duality (Theorem~\ref{gam:gv:thm:duality}); the palindromicity it
gives is part of Part~IV's Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:graphintro} for
preorders. Source~07's Section~\ref{lor:sp:sec:pal} extends the
palindromicity classification to every bipartite graph.]
\begin{lemma}[Ideal Hall criterion]\label{lor:lem:idealhall}
For $A,B\subseteq[n]$ of equal size, there is a bijection
$f:A\to B$ satisfying $a\le_\tau f(a)$ exactly when
\begin{equation}
 |A\cap I|\ge |B\cap I|\quad(I\in\J).
 \label{lor:eq:idealHall}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows because every predecessor matched to a point of an ideal
lies in that ideal. Conversely, for $T\subseteq B$, use the ideal
$\down T$. Its inequality gives
$|A\cap\down T|\ge|B\cap\down T|\ge|T|$, which is Hall's condition for
a matching of $B$ into $A$.
\end{proof}
The transformation
\begin{equation}
 (A,B)\longmapsto([n]\setminus B,[n]\setminus A)
 \label{lor:eq:complement}
\end{equation}
preserves \eqref{lor:eq:idealHall}, exchanges size $k$ with size $n-k$, and
is its own inverse. By Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge}, it proves
$h_k=h_{n-k}$. Interchanging the two supports also proves invariance under
reversal of the preorder.

\begin{proposition}[Equality throughout the normalized inequalities; sources~06 and~09]
For $n\ge2$, equality holds in all $n-1$ inequalities in
\eqref{lor:eq:preorderULC} if and only if $\tau$ is the antichain preorder.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $b_k=h_k/\binom n k>0$. Equality throughout forces consecutive ratios
$b_k/b_{k-1}$ to be constant. Since $h_0=h_n=1$, all $b_k$ equal one.
In particular $h_1=n$. But the support fibre on a single receiver $j$
contains exactly the values $1,\ldots,|\down j|$, so
$h_1=\sum_j|\down j|$. Reflexivity contributes $n$, and any non-diagonal
relation contributes a further term. Hence $h_1=n$ precisely for the
antichain. The converse follows from $h=(1+t)^n$.
\end{proof}
This classifies simultaneous equality, not equality in one specified
inequality for a general graph or a weighted model.

[Merge note: source~09 proves the same equality clause, as part of its
Theorem~4.2, by the same argument ($q_k=h_k/\binom nk$ with constant ratios
and $h_1$ counting related ordered pairs). Source~07's
Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:equality} classifies equality in the variance bound
for weighted graphs, which contains the simultaneous case for preorders
(Corollary~\ref{lor:sp:cor:preorderprob}).]

\subsection{The height-two gamma question has a uniform answer}
Write the palindromic support polynomial as
\begin{equation}
 h_\tau(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}
               \gamma_k(\tau)t^k(1+t)^{n-2k},
 \qquad \Gamma_\tau(u)=\sum_k\gamma_k(\tau)u^k.
 \label{lor:eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
Part~IV already establishes the disjoint transport-support
interpretation of these coefficients (Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:main}). In height two,
its specialization is particularly simple.

Let $P_H$ be the height-two poset on $X\sqcup Y$ whose strict relations are
$x<y$ for the edges $xy$ of $H$. Then
\begin{equation}
 h_{P_H}(t)=(1+t)^{m+n}
        p_H\!\left(\frac{t}{(1+t)^2}\right),
 \qquad \Gamma_{P_H}(u)=p_H(u).
 \label{lor:eq:heighttwo}
\end{equation}
For completeness, the support-pair proof takes any compatible pair in the
doubled preorder graph and cancels its common intersection. Cancellation
preserves all the differences in \eqref{lor:eq:idealHall}; conversely one can
restore the intersection by diagonal edges. A disjoint nonempty pair in
height two has its sources in $X$ and receivers in $Y$. A pair of size $k$
leaves $m+n-2k$ labels that may be placed independently in the common
intersection. Summing $t^{k+|W|}$ over that intersection $W$ gives
$t^k(1+t)^{m+n-2k}$, proving \eqref{lor:eq:heighttwo}.

\begin{corollary}[All height-two gamma sequences]\label{lor:cor:gammaULC}
For every height-two poset $P_H$, the sequence
$\gamma_k(P_H)/\binom r k$, $r=\min(m,n)$, is log-concave with no internal
zeros. Thus every such gamma polynomial has log-concave, unimodal
coefficients, even when it is not real-rooted.
\end{corollary}
This answers Part~IV's ``Coefficient shape beyond gamma-positivity''
question (Research question~\ref{lor:hq:shape}) for all height-two posets. It does not answer it for arbitrary
preorders or even for all posets of height three. In particular, applying
\eqref{lor:eq:preorderULC} to $h_\tau$ is not a proof of a corresponding
inequality for $\Gamma_\tau$.

[Merge note: source~07 states the height-two identity as its
equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:heighttwo} and remarks that it identifies the
height-two $\gamma$-polynomial with $p_H$, but does not state
Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:gammaULC}; source~09 remarks the same identity.]

\section{Palindromic cores: an exact structural classification}
\label{lor:sp:sec:pal}

All polynomials in this section are unweighted. Palindromicity refers to actual
degree: $p(t)=t^r p(t^{-1})$, where $r=\deg p$. Arbitrary external fields
need not preserve it.

\subsection{A maximum-support factorization}
\begin{proposition}[Top coefficient and a defect bound]
\label{lor:sp:prop:top}
Let the nonisolated shores have sizes $a,b$, and let $r=\nu(H)$. Let
$\mathcal L$ be the collection of left $r$-sets which occur in a maximum
matching, and let $\mathcal R$ be the analogous right collection. Then
\begin{equation}
 \PM_r(H)=\mathcal L\times\mathcal R,
 \qquad
 p_r=|\mathcal L|\,|\mathcal R|
 \ge(a-r+1)(b-r+1).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:topfactor}
\end{equation}
In particular, $p_r=1$ precisely when $a=b=r$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The generic matrix $A_H$ has rank $r$ by equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:generic}. The row bases are
exactly $\mathcal L$ and the column bases exactly $\mathcal R$. If $I$ is a
row basis, restriction to coordinates $I$ is an isomorphism from the column
space to the coordinate space of dimension $r$: a vector vanishing on $I$
vanishes on all rows because the rows in $I$ span. Applying this isomorphism
to any column basis $J$ shows that $A_H[I,J]$ is invertible. This proves the
Cartesian-product statement.

Fix one row basis. Every other active row is nonzero and can replace at least
one of its members, yielding a different basis containing that row. Hence
there are at least $1+(a-r)$ row bases. The column argument is identical.
If $p_r=1$, the bound forces $a=b=r$. Conversely, when $a=b=r$, the full
pair of shores is the sole support of size $r$.
\end{proof}

There is also a graph-only proof of the qualitative conclusion. Every
nonisolated vertex is covered by some maximum matching: if a maximum matching
leaves it uncovered, swap in an incident edge, removing the edge currently
covering its neighbor. A unique maximum support must therefore contain every
nonisolated vertex. The generic-matrix proof additionally supplies the product
formula and the quantitative lower bound.

\subsection{The balanced reachability calculation}
Suppose now that the active core has $r$ vertices on each shore and has a
perfect matching. Label the matched pairs $(x_i,y_i)$, and define
$iRj$ when $x_i y_j$ is an edge. The relation $R$ is reflexive. Let $\overline R$
be its reflexive transitive closure.

[Merge note: Lemmas~\ref{lor:sp:lem:defect} and~\ref{lor:sp:lem:cancel} re-prove
Part~IV's endpoint theorem (Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:graphintro}) and overlap
cancellation (Proposition~\ref{gam:prop:canceliff}) for a balanced core;
source~07 credits this. The new content of this section is
Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:top} and the extension of the classification to
all bipartite graphs, including unequal shores and deficient matchings.]
\begin{lemma}[First and penultimate coefficients]
\label{lor:sp:lem:defect}
For $r\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 p_1=|R|,\qquad p_{r-1}=|\overline R|.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:defect}
\end{equation}
Thus $p_{r-1}-p_1$ is exactly the number of missing transitive pairs.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first equality counts edges. A support of size $r-1$ deletes one supplier
$x_a$ and one receiver $y_b$. If the remaining graph has a perfect matching,
its directed assignment on $[r]$ has one vertex without an outgoing edge
($a$) and one without an incoming edge ($b$). For $a\ne b$, following its
edges from $b$ produces a directed path ending at $a$: it cannot enter a cycle,
since that would give a vertex two incoming edges. Therefore $b\,\overline R\,a$.
For $a=b$, use the reflexive path.

Conversely, choose a simple directed path from $b$ to $a$. Match along this
path and use diagonal edges at all vertices off the path. This covers every
supplier except $x_a$ and every receiver except $y_b$. Thus deletion pairs
are in bijection with ordered reachability pairs. The assertion remains valid
when $r=1$; then both sides of the second equality equal one.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transitive complement cancellation]
\label{lor:sp:lem:cancel}
Let $R$ be reflexive and transitive on $[r]$. A pair $(I,J)$ of equal-size
subsets is matchable exactly when $(I\setminus J,J\setminus I)$ is matchable.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 (I,J)\longmapsto([r]\setminus J,[r]\setminus I)
 \label{lor:sp:eq:palmap}
\end{equation}
is an involution on matchable pairs, reversing their size from $k$ to $r-k$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Represent a matching $I\to J$ as a directed graph on $[r]$. Each vertex has
indegree and outdegree at most one, so its nontrivial components are directed
paths or cycles. A path starts in $I\setminus J$ and ends in $J\setminus I$.
Transitivity shortcuts each path to a permitted edge from its start to its end.
The cycles require no surviving edge. This proves the forward cancellation.
Conversely, a matching between the differences extends by diagonal edges on
$I\cap J$.

For the complement pair, use the shortcut edges just constructed and add
identity edges at vertices outside $I\cup J$. Its source is
$[r]\setminus J$ and its target $[r]\setminus I$. Applying the same set
transformation twice returns $(I,J)$, proving the involution.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:headline-pal}]
If $p_H$ is palindromic then $p_r=p_0=1$, so Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:top} forces a balanced
core with a perfect matching. By Lemma~\ref{lor:sp:lem:defect}, palindromicity also gives
$|R|=|\overline R|$. Since $R\subseteq\overline R$, the relation is transitive.
This proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii), including the edgeless case separately.

Assume (ii). For each matchable pair $(I,J)$, write
$U=I\setminus J$, $V=J\setminus I$, and $C=I\cap J$.
By Lemma~\ref{lor:sp:lem:cancel}, $U,V$ are disjoint and matchable, and $C$ may be
\emph{any} subset of $[r]\setminus(U\cup V)$. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 p_H(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}\gamma_k t^k(1+t)^{r-2k},
 \quad
 \gamma_k=\#\{(U,V):U\cap V=\varnothing,\ |U|=|V|=k,\ U\to_R V\}.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
This proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii), with the already-known transport-pair
interpretation from Part~IV (Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:main}). Each basis polynomial
$t^k(1+t)^{r-2k}$ is palindromic of degree $r$, proving (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i).
Finally, starting with any perfect matching in the same graph, the necessity
argument applies again and proves transitivity of its associated relation.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Recognition without enumerating the polynomial}
Delete isolated vertices. If the remaining shore sizes differ, return ``not
palindromic.'' Otherwise find a maximum matching. If it is not perfect, return
``not palindromic.'' Use a perfect matching to label both shores and test
transitivity of $R$, for example by computing its Boolean transitive closure.
Return ``palindromic'' exactly when the closure adds no pair. Matching and
closure are polynomial-time operations; a straightforward closure takes
$O(r^3)$ Boolean operations. In particular this is not an algorithm which
first computes exponentially many coefficients and then compares them.

This proves the palindromicity component of the bipartite support-enumerator
problem as well, using Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge}. For a preorder, the criterion always
holds. Combining symmetry with strict log-concavity yields strict increase
toward the middle, except for the unavoidable two equal middle coefficients
when the degree is odd.

\section{An intersection-theoretic realization}
\label{lor:sp:sec:geometry}

The general geometric statement below is a special case of the realizable
bimatroid theory in \cite[Theorem E]{RU}. We include the construction to fix the
factorials and explain what it does \emph{not} imply about flag polytopes.

\begin{proposition}[Normalized intersection realization]
\label{lor:sp:prop:geometry}
For a graph with $m$ suppliers, there is a projective variety $Z_H$ of dimension
$m$ and nef divisor classes $L_v$, indexed by $X\sqcup Y$, such that
\begin{equation}
 \cB_H(\mathbf w)=\frac1{m!}\int_{Z_H}\left(\sum_v w_v L_v\right)^m.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:intersection}
\end{equation}
In particular, with $U=\sum_{x\in X}L_x$ and $V=\sum_{y\in Y}L_y$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_k p_k s^{m-k}t^k
 =\frac1{m!}\int_{Z_H}(sU+tV)^m,
 \qquad
 \frac{p_k}{\binom m k}=\frac1{m!}\int_{Z_H}U^{m-k}V^k.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:mixed}
\end{equation}
The same construction applies to $s^n h_\tau(t/s)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
There is a complex specialization of the edge variables for which exactly the
structurally nonzero minors stay nonzero: their finite product is a nonzero
polynomial, so its nonvanishing set is nonempty. Let $C=[I_m\mid A_H]$ be
such a specialization. Its columns give linear coordinate functions on
$\C^m$. Take the closure of the resulting affine linear space in
$(\mathbb P^1)^{X\sqcup Y}$; normalizing, or passing to a smooth projective
resolution, does not change the intersection calculation below. Let $L_v$
be the pullback of the point/hyperplane class of the $v$th projective line.
These classes are nef and satisfy $L_v^2=0$.

For a set $B$ of $m$ coordinates, the associated coordinate projection has
generic degree one if those columns form a basis, because its restriction to
the affine linear space is an invertible linear map. If the columns are
dependent, its image has dimension less than $m$, so its top intersection is
zero. The boundary of the affine space has smaller dimension and does not
contribute over a general target point. Thus
\[
 \int_{Z_H}\prod_{v\in B}L_v=
 \begin{cases}1,&B\text{ a basis of }\mathsf M_H,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
Expanding the $m$th power, square terms vanish and every basis monomial occurs
$m!$ times. This proves equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:intersection}; grouping the two shores gives
equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:mixed}.
\end{proof}

This construction is compatible with the Hodge-theoretic source of
ultra-log-concavity. It is an intersection realization, not a construction of
a simplicial flag polytope with the prescribed $h$-vector. Nor does it require
the repository's proposed equality with the Ehrhart numerator of its
lower-dimensional directed root polytope. The normalizing factor $1/m!$ is
explicit to avoid different conventions for ``volume polynomial.''

\section{Conditional laws, covariance, and concentration}
\label{lor:sec:probability}
\subsection{Conditioning on present and absent coordinates}
For a positive external field $z\in\R_{>0}^{Y}$, give $c\in\cD_H$
probability proportional to $z_{\supp(c)}$. Equivalently, its support law is
\begin{equation}
 \PP_z(S)=\frac{[z_S]F_H\,z_S}{F_H(z)}.
 \label{lor:eq:law}
\end{equation}
Fix disjoint $T,A\subseteq Y$ and condition on $T\subseteq S$ and
$S\cap A=\varnothing$, assuming this event has positive probability. Once
the forced variables are removed, its generating polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 G_{T,A}(z)=
 \left.\left(\prod_{y\in T}\partial_{z_y}\right)F_H(z)
                          \right|_{z_a=0\ (a\in A)}.
 \label{lor:eq:conditional}
\end{equation}
The external-field factor on $T$ is constant and disappears upon
normalization.

\begin{proposition}[Hereditary complete log-concavity]\label{lor:prop:conditional}
The nonzero polynomial $G_{T,A}$ is completely log-concave. It is an affine
slice of the basis polynomial of a minor of $\mathsf M_H$ of rank $m-|T|$.
Consequently its extra-support-size coefficients, under positive external
fields, are ultra-log-concave with normalization
$\binom{m-|T|}k$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Differentiating a multiaffine basis polynomial in the variables of an
independent set $T$ gives the basis polynomial of the contraction $\mathsf M_H/T$.
Setting the variables of $A$ to zero then retains exactly the bases avoiding
$A$. Since the conditioning event is nonempty, deleting $A$ does not lower
the rank of that contracted matroid. Its rank is $m-|T|$.
Setting the surviving private variables to one gives
\eqref{lor:eq:conditional}. Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:CLC}'s argument and the bivariate
Lorentzian criterion apply without alteration. A rank-zero case is a
nonzero constant.
\end{proof}
The specified normalization is the rank of the displayed minor. No
unjustified replacement by the number of unforced receiver coordinates is
made.

\subsection{A homogeneous concavity inequality}
We record the standard homogeneous concavity equivalence
\cite[Proposition~2.33]{BH}, with a proof fixing the covariance constant.

\begin{lemma}\label{lor:lem:rootconcavity}
If $B$ is a positive log-concave homogeneous polynomial of degree $d\ge1$
on the positive orthant, then $B^{1/d}$ is concave there. Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \nabla^2\log B\preceq
           -\frac1d(\nabla\log B)(\nabla\log B)^{\mathsf T}.
 \label{lor:eq:rootconcavity}
\end{equation}
The inequality remains valid on any affine slice, with the restricted
gradient and Hessian.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $d=1$ the polynomial is linear and direct differentiation proves the
claim. For general $d$, let $x$ be a positive point and write any direction
$v$ as $v=w+\alpha x$, where
$\alpha=(\nabla B\cdot v)/(dB)$ and $\nabla B\cdot w=0$.
Log-concavity implies $w^{\mathsf T}(\nabla^2B)w\le0$.
Euler's identities give
$\nabla^2B\,x=(d-1)\nabla B$ and
$x^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2B\,x=d(d-1)B$.
The cross term vanishes, and hence
\[
 v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2B\,v
 \le\frac{d-1}{dB}(\nabla B\cdot v)^2.
\]
Subtract the gradient-square term in the Hessian of $\log B$ to obtain
\eqref{lor:eq:rootconcavity}. The Hessian of $B^{1/d}$ has the same required
sign. Restriction amounts to applying the inequality only to directions
tangent to the affine slice.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[External-field covariance bound]\label{lor:thm:covariance}
For $m\ge1$, let $I_y=\ind_{\{y\in S\}}$ under \eqref{lor:eq:law}, let
$p_y=\EE I_y$, and write $p=(p_y)_{y\in Y}$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\Cov(I)\preceq\diag(p)-\frac1m pp^{\mathsf T}.}
 \label{lor:eq:covariance}
\end{equation}
In particular, for every real vector $b$,
\begin{equation}
 \Var\!\left(\sum_yb_yI_y\right)
 \le\sum_yp_yb_y^2-\frac1m\left(\sum_yp_yb_y\right)^2.
 \label{lor:eq:linearvariance}
\end{equation}
The same statement holds for the remaining indicators after the
conditioning above, with $m$ replaced by $m-|T|$ when that rank is positive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:rootconcavity} to $\mathcal B_H$ of degree $m$ and
restrict its private variables to one. Let $D=\diag(z_y)$.
Logarithmic differentiation of the probability generating function gives
\begin{equation}
 D\nabla\log F_H=p,
 \qquad
 D(\nabla^2\log F_H)D=\Cov(I)-\diag(p).
 \label{lor:eq:covhessian}
\end{equation}
For distinct indices this is the usual covariance identity. On the
diagonal, multiaffineness gives
$z_y^2\partial_{yy}\log F_H=-p_y^2$, which is exactly
$\Var(I_y)-p_y$. Conjugate \eqref{lor:eq:rootconcavity} by $D$ and rearrange.
The conditioned claim uses the minor polynomial from
Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:conditional}.
\end{proof}
This is a positive-semidefinite matrix comparison, not a claim that each
off-diagonal covariance is nonpositive. Complete log-concavity is weaker
than real stability and does not justify importing every negative
dependence property of determinantal models.


\subsection{Binomial convex-order domination (source~07)}
\label{lor:sec:sp:probability}
Let $p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k t^k$ be a positive vertex-weighted support polynomial,
where $d$ is the smaller active shore. For fugacity $z>0$, define
\begin{equation}
 \PP_z(L=k)=\frac{c_kz^k}{p(z)},\qquad
 \mu=\EE_zL=\frac{zp'(z)}{p(z)}.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:law}
\end{equation}
The random variable counts matched pairs, or equivalently half the number of
covered vertices. Under the demand interpretation it counts positive
coordinates when the activities are attached to receiver support. If both
shores carry activities, the graph measure remains well defined, but no
unspecified weight on individual demand vectors is being asserted.

\subsection{A finite convex-order lemma}
\begin{lemma}[Binomial domination from ultra-log-concavity]
\label{lor:sp:lem:convexorder}
Suppose a distribution $\pi$ on $\{0,\ldots,d\}$ is ultra-log-concave of order
$d$ and has mean $\mu$. If $B\sim\operatorname{Bin}(d,\mu/d)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \EE_\pi\phi(L)\le\EE\phi(B)
 \label{lor:sp:eq:cx}
\end{equation}
for every convex function $\phi$ on $[0,d]$. Equality for $\phi(k)=k^2$
holds if and only if the two distributions are identical.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The endpoint means $0,d$ are deterministic. Otherwise let $q_k$ be the
binomial mass function, which is positive everywhere. The ratios
$\pi_k/q_k$ form a log-concave sequence: division by $q_k$ differs from division
by $\binom d k$ only by a positive geometric factor and a constant. Therefore
the set where $\pi_k-q_k$ is positive is an interval, allowing zeros between
its endpoints.

If the two laws differ, their equal mass and equal mean force negative
differences on both sides of the positive interval. Otherwise one distribution
would have strictly larger mean. Choose real cutpoints $u<v$, between the
sign regions, so that differences are nonnegative inside $(u,v)$ and
nonpositive outside it. Let $\ell$ be the affine line joining
$(u,\phi(u))$ to $(v,\phi(v))$. Convexity gives $\phi\le\ell$ between the
cutpoints and $\phi\ge\ell$ outside. Hence
\[
 \sum_k(\pi_k-q_k)(\phi(k)-\ell(k))\le0.
\]
The affine part sums to zero by equal mass and mean, proving equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:cx}.
For $\phi(k)=k^2$, choose the cutpoints between integer sign regions. The
quadratic-minus-secant is strictly negative inside and strictly positive
outside, so some nonzero difference gives a strict inequality. The converse
when the laws coincide is immediate.
\end{proof}

This lemma is a general consequence of ultra-log-concavity, not a new theorem
specific to preorders. Its short proof is included because it exposes exactly
the equality condition used below.

\begin{theorem}[All-fugacity binomial bounds]
\label{lor:sp:thm:probability}
For every bipartite support model with at least one edge, positive vertex
activities, and every $z>0$,
\begin{align}
 \Var_z L&\le\mu(1-\mu/d),\label{lor:sp:eq:variance}\\
 \EE_z e^{\lambda(L-\mu)}
 &\le e^{-\lambda\mu}
       (1-\mu/d+(\mu/d)e^\lambda)^d
       \qquad(\lambda\in\R).\label{lor:sp:eq:mgf}
\end{align}
For $\mu/d<q\le1$,
\begin{equation}
 \PP_z(L\ge dq)\le
 \exp\{-d\,\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert\mu/d)\},
 \label{lor:sp:eq:chernoff}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p)=q\log(q/p)+(1-q)\log((1-q)/(1-p))$.
There is an analogous lower-tail inequality for $0\le q<\mu/d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Exponential tilting preserves ultra-log-concavity. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lor:sp:lem:convexorder} to $k^2$ and $e^{\lambda k}$. The usual exponential
Markov bound, minimized at
$e^\lambda=q(1-p)/(p(1-q))$, gives equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:chernoff}. Endpoint probabilities
are interpreted by limits. An edgeless graph has $L=0$ and is treated separately.
\end{proof}

One can also derive the variance bound directly from the two-variable Hessian.
For $F(s,t)=s^dp(t/s)$, nonpositivity of its Hessian determinant gives
\[
 dp(z)p''(z)\le(d-1)p'(z)^2.
\]
Substitution in
$\Var L=\mu+z^2p''(z)/p(z)-\mu^2$
recovers equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:variance}. The convex-order argument is stronger and is
needed for the clean equality statement.


\subsection{The same bound at the actual weighted mean (source~06)}
Let $L=|S|$ in the positive weighted-pair distribution associated to
\eqref{lor:eq:weighted}, and let $\mu=\EE L$. Let $r=\min(m,n)>0$.

\begin{theorem}[Binomial moment bound; sources~06, 07 and~09]\label{lor:thm:binomial}
For every real $s$,
\begin{equation}
 \EE e^{sK}\le
       \left(1-\frac\mu r+\frac\mu r e^s\right)^r,
 \qquad
 \Var L\le\mu\left(1-\frac\mu r\right).
 \label{lor:eq:binomial}
\end{equation}
Thus the moment-generating function is dominated by that of a binomial
random variable with $r$ trials and the same mean.
\end{theorem}
This is Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:probability} for the weighted pair law
at unit fugacity, and Lemma~\ref{lor:sp:lem:convexorder} proves it, with all
convex test functions in place of $e^{sL}$. Source~06's own proof is a
different, analytic route.
\begin{proof}[Second proof (source~06)]
Write $A(t)=A_H(t;u,v)$, absorbing the initial activity into $v$ if
necessary. Choose the smaller-shore lift in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC}. Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:rootconcavity} gives
\[
 A A''\le(1-1/r)(A')^2.
\]
Under a scalar tilt $t>0$, the mean is $\mu(t)=tA'(t)/A(t)$. Therefore
\begin{equation}
 \Var_tK=t\mu'(t)
 \le\mu(t)-\frac{\mu(t)^2}{r}.
 \label{lor:eq:logisticvariance}
\end{equation}
Put $\psi(s)=\log(A(e^s)/A(1))$ and $v(s)=\psi'(s)$. Then
$v'(s)\le v(s)(1-v(s)/r)$, and $v(0)=\mu$.
The zero-mean case is constant; otherwise $0<v(s)<r$ at every finite $s$
unless the law is deterministic, which can be handled directly.
The derivative of $\log(v/(r-v))$ is at most one. Hence for $s\ge0$,
$v(s)$ is at most the logistic solution with initial value $\mu$; for
$s\le0$ it is at least that solution. Integrating from zero in the
appropriate direction gives, for both signs of $s$,
\[
 \psi(s)\le r\log(1-p+pe^s),\qquad p=\mu/r.
\]
Exponentiating proves the first assertion. Equation
\eqref{lor:eq:logisticvariance} at $t=1$ proves the second.
\end{proof}

For $0<p<1$ and $q\in[0,1]$, put
\[
 D(q\Vert p)=q\log\frac qp+(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p},
\]
with the continuous endpoint conventions. Chernoff's argument applied to
\eqref{lor:eq:binomial} gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \PP(L\ge rq)&\le e^{-rD(q\Vert p)} &&(q\ge p),\\
 \PP(L\le rq)&\le e^{-rD(q\Vert p)} &&(q\le p).
 \end{aligned}
 \label{lor:eq:chernoff}
\end{equation}
For a uniformly chosen lattice point of $\Qt$, symmetry gives
$\mu=n/2$, recovering $\Var L\le n/4$ and
$\PP(|L-n/2|\ge a)\le2e^{-2a^2/n}$. Part~IV already obtains these
unweighted estimates by its gamma-binomial mixture (Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:statistics}). The additional content
here is the arbitrary external field, the actual weighted mean, and the
multivariate conditional covariance bound.

\begin{remark}[The Hoeffding form for every ultra-log-concave law; source~09]
\label{lor:rem:hoeffding}
Source~09 proves Lemma~\ref{lor:sp:lem:convexorder} and the bounds of
Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:probability} again, for any nonzero ultra-log-concave
sequence of order $d$ tilted by $t>0$, by the same single-crossing and
chord argument, and adds the two-sided bound
\[
 \PP(|L-\mu|\ge s)\le2e^{-2s^2/d}\qquad(s\ge0).
\]
Its proof, as delivered: the logarithm of the centered Bernoulli moment
function has value and first derivative zero at $\theta=0$, and its second
derivative is the variance of a tilted Bernoulli variable, at most $1/4$.
Integrating twice gives the upper bound $\theta^2/8$. The
moment-generating-function bound~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:mgf} consequently implies
$\EE e^{\theta(L-\mu)}\le e^{d\theta^2/8}$. Markov's inequality, optimized
at $\theta=4s/d$, bounds the upper tail by $e^{-2s^2/d}$; using negative
$\theta$ bounds the lower tail. Add the two bounds. Source~09 adds: for
$h_{\tau,w}$ at $t=1$, palindromicity gives $\mu=n/2$, so
$\Var(L)\le n/4$; the argument works for all positive transport activities
(Part~VII's Theorem~\ref{mat:thm:weighted-preorder}), all size tilts and all
bipartite support models, and it is a consequence of ultra-log-concavity,
not a new general theorem about log-concave measures.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Equality is exactly an equal-strength star forest}
Orient the active core so that $|X|=d\le|Y|$. Define the weighted strength
of a supplier by
\[
 s_x=\alpha_x\sum_{y\in N_H(x)}\beta_y.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Sharp equality classification]
\label{lor:sp:thm:equality}
Assume $H$ has at least one edge and all vertex activities are positive. The
following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item Equality holds in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:variance} for one $z>0$.
\item $p_H^{\alpha,\beta}(t)=(1+at)^d$ for some $a>0$.
\item The neighborhoods of the smaller-shore vertices are pairwise disjoint,
and all strengths $s_x$ are equal.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, equality holds for every $z>0$. In the unweighted
case, the active graph is a disjoint union of $d$ stars of the same degree,
centered on the smaller shore.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By the equality clause of Lemma~\ref{lor:sp:lem:convexorder}, (i) makes the tilted
coefficient law exactly binomial. Dividing its masses by $z^k$ and using
$c_0=1$ gives $c_k=\binom d k a^k$ for a positive $a$. Thus (i) implies (ii).

Suppose (ii). Then $c_1=da=\sum_xs_x$ and $c_d=a^d>0$. The total weight of
supports covering every supplier is at most the total weight of matchings
covering every supplier, which is at most the weight of all independent
choices of one neighboring receiver for each supplier. Hence
\begin{equation}
 c_d\le\sum_{\substack{\text{matchings covering }X}}\wt(M)
 \le\prod_{x\in X}s_x
 \le\left(\frac1d\sum_{x\in X}s_x\right)^d=a^d=c_d.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:equalitychain}
\end{equation}
All inequalities are equalities. The arithmetic--geometric mean equality
forces equal strengths. If two suppliers share a receiver, there is a
positive-weight choice assigning that receiver to both, and arbitrary neighbors
to the other suppliers. This is counted in the product but is not a matching,
contradicting equality in the second inequality. Thus neighborhoods are disjoint.

Conversely, under (iii) every support chooses independently whether to use each
star and, when it does, which receiver to use. Therefore
$p(t)=\prod_x(1+s_xt)=(1+at)^d$. The tilted law is binomial, completing all
implications. Positivity is essential for the strict collision argument;
zero activities should first be handled by deleting their forbidden vertices.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Preorder support fluctuations]
\label{lor:sp:cor:preorderprob}
For $n\ge1$, choose a lattice point of $\Qt$ with probability proportional to
$z^{|\supp(c)|}$. Its support size obeys equations~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:variance}, \eqref{lor:sp:eq:mgf} and~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:chernoff}
with $d=n$. Equality in the variance bound at one $z>0$ holds precisely when
$\tau$ is an antichain. In particular, for the uniform law,
\[
 \EE L=n/2,\qquad \Var L\le n/4,
 \qquad
 \PP(|L-n/2|\ge s)\le2e^{-2s^2/n},
\]
with strict variance inequality for every non-antichain preorder.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:preorderbridge}. In the balanced graph $G_\tau$, pairwise disjoint
nonempty neighborhoods force exactly one receiver per supplier. Since all
diagonal edges are present, these are precisely the diagonal edges; there
are no nontrivial comparisons. Palindromicity gives the mean at $z=1$.
The tail follows from equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:chernoff} and the elementary bound
$\mathrm{KL}(1/2+u\Vert1/2)\ge2u^2$, obtained by differentiating twice.
\end{proof}

Part~IV already obtains the uniform mean, variance formula,
and a Hoeffding-type bound from its centered-binomial mixture (Theorem~\ref{gam:thm:statistics}). The additional
content here is domination by the same-mean binomial for every positive
fugacity, the graph-wide weighted theorem, and its exact equality classification.

\section{Polynomial-time approximation and support sampling}
\label{lor:sec:algorithms}
We distinguish exact counting, approximate counting, sampling supports,
and sampling actual integer vectors. They are not interchangeable tasks.
The input graph is given explicitly. A positive rational weight has a
standard binary encoding. An approximation scheme is fully polynomial if
its running time is polynomial in the input bit length, $\varepsilon^{-1}$,
and $\log(\delta^{-1})$, and its relative error is at most $\varepsilon$
with probability at least $1-\delta$.

\subsection{A matching oracle and the basis walk}
Independence in $\mathsf M_H$ is decided by a bipartite matching from the selected
ground elements to the $m$ slots. The presentation has $m+n$ ground
elements and $m+|E|$ incidence edges. A basic augmenting-path algorithm
already gives a polynomial-time oracle. A starting basis is $X^\circ$.

At a basis $B$ of rank $d$, the down-up step first removes a uniformly
chosen element $e\in B$. It then chooses a feasible extension
$B-e+f$ with probability proportional to its product weight. Since the
weight of the retained set is common, the extension probabilities are
proportional simply to the weight of $f$. There are at most $m+n$
candidates, each testable by the matching oracle.

Theorem~1.1 of \cite{ALOV} gives a spectral gap at least $1/d$ for this walk
and the mixing estimate
\begin{equation}
 t_{B_0}(\eta)\le d\log\frac1{\eta\pi(B_0)},
 \label{lor:eq:mixing}
\end{equation}
where $\pi$ is the normalized weighted basis measure. Our product weights
preserve the required log-concavity by a positive variable scaling.
The same theorem applies after contractions and deletions.

For clarity about bit complexity, suppose there are $N$ ground elements,
rank $d$, and all positive element weights lie between $2^{-b}$ and $2^b$.
Every basis weight lies between $2^{-db}$ and $2^{db}$, and there are at
most $2^N$ bases. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \pi(B_0)\ge2^{-N-2db}.
 \label{lor:eq:startingmass}
\end{equation}
Thus the logarithm in \eqref{lor:eq:mixing} is polynomially bounded in the
input bit length. Exact rational extension probabilities are computable
with polynomial bit length; no exponentially small probability has to be
estimated directly just to run a step.


\subsection{The chain in explicit form (source~07)}
\label{lor:sec:sp:chain}
For $S\subseteq X\sqcup Y$, let $S_X=S\cap X$ and $S_Y=S\cap Y$.
The private elements $S_X$ reserve their own slots. Thus
\begin{equation}
 S\text{ is independent in }\mathsf M_H
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S_Y\text{ can be matched into }X\setminus S_X.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:oracle}
\end{equation}
This is a bipartite maximum-matching query; no symbolic determinant is computed.
For a size-$m$ set it is a basis query. The supplied implementation uses
augmenting paths and exact integer bitmasks. It is a reference implementation,
not a claim of optimal matching complexity.

\subsection{The correct local chain}
Give matroid elements positive activities
\[
 \lambda_x=\alpha_x^{-1}\quad(x\in X),\qquad
 \lambda_y=z\beta_y\quad(y\in Y).
\]
The product weight of $B_{I,J}$ differs from $\alpha_I\beta_Jz^{|J|}$ by the
constant $\prod_x\alpha_x^{-1}$. Starting at a basis $B$, perform one step:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.8em]
\item Remove a uniformly chosen element $b\in B$ and set $S=B\setminus\{b\}$.
\item Enumerate $C(S)=\{e\notin S:S\cup\{e\}\text{ is a basis}\}$.
\item Choose $e\in C(S)$ with probability
$\lambda_e/\sum_{f\in C(S)}\lambda_f$, and move to $S\cup\{e\}$.
\end{enumerate}
The old element is an allowed completion, so the chain has self-loops.
Detailed balance follows because for adjacent bases $B=S+b$, $B'=S+e$,
\[
 \pi(B)P(B,B')=
 \frac{\lambda_S\lambda_b\lambda_e}
 {Z_M\,m\sum_{f\in C(S)}\lambda_f}
 =\pi(B')P(B',B).
\]
Basis exchange ensures irreducibility.

In support coordinates, an exchange can replace a supplier, replace a receiver,
add a supplier--receiver pair, or remove such a pair. An added pair need not be
an edge in a fixed previously chosen matching: global rematching may be needed.
The chain acts on supports, not on chosen perfect matchings.

\begin{theorem}[Rapid mixing, by the general matroid theorem]
\label{lor:sp:thm:mixing}
For a nonzero rank-$m$ model, this chain has spectral gap at least $1/m$.
If $B_0$ is its starting basis, the conservative bound
\begin{equation}
 t\ge m\log\frac1{\varepsilon\pi(B_0)}
 \label{lor:sp:eq:mixing}
\end{equation}
is sufficient for total variation error at most $\varepsilon$.
In the uniform case, starting at $B_0=X$, it is enough to take
\begin{equation}
 t\ge m\left(\log\binom{m+n}{m}+\log\frac1\varepsilon\right).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:uniformmixing}
\end{equation}
The shores can first be exchanged and isolated vertices removed to lower the
rank used in this bound.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The positively rescaled basis polynomial is strongly log-concave by the
Lorentzian theorem. The chain is exactly the down-up chain in
\cite[Theorem 1.1]{ALOV}, which supplies the gap and equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:mixing}.
In the uniform case $\pi(X)=1/p_H(1)$ and the number of bases is at most
$\binom{m+n}{m}$. The rank-zero model is deterministic.
\end{proof}

The bound is not advertised as the latest or sharpest possible mixing bound.
Its advantage is that the exact chain, oracle, and imported theorem match
without an unproved transfer. For rational positive activities of bit length
$L_{\mathrm{bit}}$, a crude starting-mass bound is
\[
 \log\pi(B_0)^{-1}\le\log\binom{m+n}{m}
       +m\log(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}),
\]
which is polynomial in the input bit size. Conditional models use
Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:conditioning} and the same theorem on a matroid minor.

\begin{theorem}[Partition functions and support laws; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:thm:FPRASpartition}
For every explicit bipartite graph, $F_H(z)$ at positive rational $z$ has
an FPRAS. So does $A_H(1;u,v)$ at positive rational vertex weights. There
is a polynomial-time sampler arbitrarily close in total variation to the
support law of the corresponding weighted integer vectors when
$u=\mathbf1$. In particular, $|\Qt\cap\Z^n|$ has an FPRAS for every
explicit finite preorder.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The polynomial identities reduce each partition function to a positive
known scalar times a weighted matroid basis partition function. Sampling
bases using \eqref{lor:eq:mixing} and retaining $B\cap Y$ gives the support
law, because Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bases} supplies exactly the multiplicity
in \eqref{lor:eq:supportbridge}. Taking an image cannot increase total
variation distance.

Here is the counting self-reduction, to make the algorithmic implication
explicit. In any weighted rank-$d$ matroid on at most $N$ elements, the sum
of element inclusion probabilities is $d$. Some element therefore has
probability at least $1/N$. Approximate all inclusion probabilities to
additive error $1/(4N)$, using independent sufficiently mixed samples, and
choose a largest empirical marginal. On the simultaneous success event,
the chosen element has true inclusion probability at least $1/(2N)$.
Estimate that probability $p_e$ to relative accuracy
$\varepsilon/(10N)$ and contract $e$. For the partition functions,
\begin{equation}
 Z(M)=\frac{w_eZ(M/e)}{p_e}.
 \label{lor:eq:selfreduction}
\end{equation}
Repeat until rank zero, where $Z=1$. There are at most $N$ stages. Allocate
failure probability over all stages and estimate all marginals and chosen
probabilities with standard bounded-variable concentration. The lower
bound $p_e\ge1/(2N)$ makes all sample counts polynomial; the product of the
relative errors in \eqref{lor:eq:selfreduction}, including their reciprocals,
is at most $\varepsilon$ with the displayed conservative accuracy.

Every contracted set is independent, so its oracle can be implemented by
adjoining that set before querying the original matching presentation.
A greedy extension supplies a starting basis in each minor. The weight
bound \eqref{lor:eq:startingmass} remains valid. Fresh randomness and mixing
accuracy small enough for a union bound complete the claimed FPRAS.
Finally apply Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:preorderreduction} for $\Qt$.
\end{proof}
The general basis mixing theorem and its use in approximate counting are
established results \cite{ALOV}; the proof above spells out their concrete
application rather than presenting a new universal matroid-counting
algorithm.

Source~07 states the same result as its Corollary~8.2 (``Counting
consequences''): given a bipartite graph and positive rational vertex
activities and fugacity, $p_H^{\alpha,\beta}(z)$ has an FPRAS, and consequently
so do $|\cD_H|$, $h_\tau(1)$ and $h_\tau(z)$ for positive rational $z$, by the
positive-activity matroid-base counting theorem~\cite{ALOV} applied
through~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:oracle} and~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:weightlift}, whose oracle
calls are polynomial-time matching calls. It then makes the self-reduction
concrete with explicit constants:

For clarity, the self-reduction underlying the imported algorithm can be
made concrete. In a rank-$q$ conditional minor on at most $N$ elements,
\(\sum_e\pi(e\in B)=q\). Therefore some element has marginal at least
$q/N\ge1/N$. Estimate all marginals by independent, sufficiently mixed samples,
choose an element whose estimate is largest, and contract it. Repeat until the
rank is zero. If $p_i$ is the successive inclusion marginal and $e_i$ the chosen
element, then
\begin{equation}
 Z_M=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\lambda_{e_i}}{p_i}.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:telescoping}
\end{equation}
The conditional rank-zero partition function is one.

Here is a deliberately conservative error allocation. Set
$\rho=\varepsilon/(4m)$ and $\eta=\rho/(4N)$ for $m>0$. At each stage use
\[
 T\ge\frac{1}{2\eta^2}\log\frac{4Nm}{\delta}
\]
independent runs, each within $\delta/(4mT)$ of its exact conditional law.
Hoeffding's inequality and a union bound ensure that all empirical marginals
are within $\eta$ of their true values, except with probability at most
$\delta$ after also accounting for sampling error. The selected element has
true marginal at least $1/N-2\eta\ge1/(2N)$, and its relative estimation error
is at most $2N\eta\le\rho$. The product in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:telescoping} then has
multiplicative error bounded by $(1\pm\rho)^{\mp m}$, contained in
$[1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]$ for $0<\varepsilon<1$ with these constants.
This proves polynomial sample complexity; it is not a practical optimization.

The shipped program implements the oracle, exact enumeration, the rational
weighted down-up sampler, and the finite verifier. It does \emph{not} claim to
be a production implementation of this full FPRAS wrapper. Sampling and counting
individual coefficients at a prescribed internal index are also not silently
included in Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:FPRASpartition}.

\subsection{Precisely what is sampled for a preorder}
A sample from $\mathsf M_{G_\tau}$ gives a pair $(I,J)$ with the desired support-model
law. Its $J$-marginal equals the distribution of the positive-coordinate set
of a correspondingly weighted lattice point, by Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bridge}. Its
cardinality has exactly the $h_\tau$ distribution. The algorithm does not
output the positive \emph{values} of that lattice point. A direct or efficiently
invertible demand/support bijection would close this remaining algorithmic gap.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: Part~IX closes it; see
Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:preordersampler}.]

\subsection{A specified exact support fibre}
\begin{corollary}\label{lor:cor:fibreFPRAS}
For a specified $S\subseteq Y$, the number of points of $\cD_H$ with
support exactly $S$ is either detectably zero or has an FPRAS.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Its count is the number of $|S|$-subsets $U\subseteq X$ matchable to $S$.
Use the transversal matroid on ground set $X$ with slots $S$. If its rank
is smaller than $|S|$, the count is zero, which a maximum matching detects.
Otherwise the desired sets are exactly its bases. Apply the same basis
counting algorithm.
\end{proof}
This is a count of integer vectors in a fibre. The proof does not produce
a vector from a sampled opposite-shore basis.

\subsection{Why coefficient approximation needs another argument}
A partition-function approximation does not justify numerical interpolation
of the coefficient vector. Interpolation can amplify relative errors
severely. Nor should one simply restrict the basis walk to bases with
exactly $k$ receivers and assume its mixing theorem still applies: that
slice need not be the bases of a matroid.

Instead we use log-concavity to tilt the full distribution until the
requested coefficient has polynomially large probability.

\begin{lemma}[Mass at an index between substantial tails]\label{lor:lem:mass}
Let $(p_0,\ldots,p_d)$ be a probability sequence, log-concave with no
internal zeros. If
\[
 \sum_{i<k}p_i\ge\tfrac14,
 \qquad \sum_{i\ge k}p_i\ge\tfrac14,
\]
then $p_k\ge1/(4(d+1))$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There is an $i<k$ with $p_i\ge1/(4(d+1))$, and a $j\ge k$ with the same
bound. Log-concavity and absence of internal zeros imply that every entry
between $i$ and $j$ is at least the smaller endpoint entry: interpolate
linearly in the concave sequence $\log p_\ell$. Apply this at $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Individual coefficient FPRAS]\label{lor:thm:coefficients}
For an explicit bipartite graph $H$ and an index $k$, $a_k(H)$ is either
detectably zero or has an FPRAS. Consequently every ordinary coefficient
$[t^k]h_\tau(t)$ and every height-two gamma coefficient
$\gamma_k(P_H)$ has an FPRAS. The entire vector can be approximated to
simultaneous relative accuracy in fully polynomial time.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $N=m+n$ and $A(t)=p_H(t)=\sum_{j=0}^da_jt^j$, where $d=\nu(H)$ is
computable by maximum matching. Then $a_0=1$, every $a_j$ for $0\le j\le d$
is a positive integer, and
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j=0}^d a_j\le2^N
 \label{lor:eq:coefbound}
\end{equation}
by the basis correspondence. Indices outside this interval have zero
coefficient, and $a_0$ needs no approximation. Assume $1\le k\le d$.

For an activity $t>0$, define
$p_j(t)=a_jt^j/A(t)$ and $q(t)=\PP_t(L<k)$.
The sequence $p_j(t)$ is log-concave. Differentiating with respect to
$\log t$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \frac{d}{d\log t}q(t)=\Cov_t(\ind_{\{L<k\}},L)\le0,
 \qquad \left|\frac{d}{d\log t}q(t)\right|\le d.
 \label{lor:eq:CDFderivative}
\end{equation}
For the sign, values of $L$ in the indicated event are smaller than values
in its complement; condition on the event and its complement. The absolute
bound follows since both conditional expectations lie in $[0,d]$.

Put $T=2^{N+5}$. By \eqref{lor:eq:coefbound},
\[
 q(T^{-1})\ge\PP_{T^{-1}}(L=0)\ge31/32,
 \qquad q(T)\le\PP_T(L<d)\le1/32.
\]
The first estimate bounds the total positive-degree weight by $2^N/T$;
the second compares the lower-degree weight with $a_dT^d$, using $a_d\ge1$.

Consider the rational grid
\begin{equation}
 t_j=\left(1+\frac1{32d}\right)^j,
 \qquad -J\le j\le J,
 \qquad J=64d(N+5).
 \label{lor:eq:grid}
\end{equation}
Since $\log(1+1/(32d))\ge1/(64d)$, the endpoints bracket $T^{-1}$ and $T$.
The change of $q$ between neighboring grid points is at most $1/32$ by
\eqref{lor:eq:CDFderivative}. Each grid activity is a rational with
$O(dN\log(d+1))$ bits.

Use binary search on this grid, estimating $q(t_j)$ to additive error
$1/64$ by the weighted basis sampler. Accept a point when its estimate
belongs to $[3/8,5/8]$. Otherwise move the lower endpoint to the point if
the estimate exceeds $5/8$, and move the upper endpoint to it if the
estimate is below $3/8$. Allocate the failure probabilities over
$O(\log(J+1))$ tests. On their simultaneous success event, an unaccepted
lower endpoint has $q>39/64$ and an unaccepted upper endpoint has
$q<25/64$. They cannot become adjacent, because their difference would
exceed the adjacent-grid bound $1/32$. Thus the search accepts a point.
At that point $q\in[23/64,41/64]\subseteq[1/4,3/4]$.
Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:mass} now gives
\begin{equation}
 p_k(t)\ge\frac1{4(d+1)}.
 \label{lor:eq:pkbound}
\end{equation}

Estimate $A(t)$ using Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:FPRASpartition} and estimate $p_k(t)$
by independent samples. The latter relative estimate takes
$O(d\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ ideal samples by
\eqref{lor:eq:pkbound}. Choose each approximate sampler's total-variation
error small enough that a coupling and union bound cover the entire
sample batch. Equation~\eqref{lor:eq:mixing} depends only logarithmically on
this extra accuracy. Finally use the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 a_k=\frac{A(t)\,p_k(t)}{t^k}.
 \label{lor:eq:coefficientrecovery}
\end{equation}
Relative accuracy $\varepsilon/4$ in both factors is more than sufficient
for relative accuracy $\varepsilon$ in the product. All activity bit
lengths, sample counts, oracle costs and mixing times are polynomial.

The preorder case uses $H_\tau$, and the height-two gamma case uses
\eqref{lor:eq:heighttwo}. Run the scheme for all at most $N+1$ coefficients and
divide the permitted failure probability among them to get the final
assertion.
\end{proof}
The same argument applies to positive rational product weights after
replacing \eqref{lor:eq:coefbound} and the lower coefficient bound by the
bounds obtained from their input bit lengths. The unweighted theorem
already covers the integer counts asked about above.

\subsection{Sampling after fixing the support size}
At the accepted activity in the preceding proof, rejection until $L=k$
takes at most $4(d+1)$ trials in expectation for the ideal sampler.
Conditional on acceptance, the factor $t^k$ is constant. Thus the accepted
bases are uniform among bases with $k$ receivers in the unit-weight case.
Taking their receiver supports gives the support distribution of a uniform
integer vector conditioned to have support size $k$.

To obtain a high-probability running-time bound, truncate after
$O(d\log(1/\delta))$ trials. For approximate samples, choose the
unconditioned total-variation accuracy smaller than the desired
conditional accuracy times the lower bound in \eqref{lor:eq:pkbound}.
Conditioning can amplify errors by the reciprocal of the acceptance
probability, but that reciprocal is polynomially bounded here.

\begin{statusbox}
\textbf{Sampling boundary.} All samplers above return a support set, or an
auxiliary matchable support pair. They do \emph{not} yet return a uniform
integer vector in $\cD_H$ or $\Qt$. Equal fibre cardinalities do not
by themselves provide an efficient fibrewise bijection. The direct,
restriction-compatible demand/support bijection remains a separate
research task.
\end{statusbox}
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: Part~IX answers this.
Theorems~\ref{tf:thm:main} and~\ref{tf:thm:sampler} return actual demand
vectors, and Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:preordersampler} actual lattice points
of $\Qt$, with the total-variation error transferred exactly
(Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:tv}); the bijection is restriction-compatible for
receivers outside the support and suppliers outside the selected set, not
for arbitrary minors. See Section~\ref{tf:sec:answers}.]
Similarly, these are randomized approximation results, not polynomial-time
exact counting algorithms. No \#P-hardness classification is asserted.
[Merge note: source~07 supplies one; see Section~\ref{lor:sp:sec:hardness}.]

\section{Exact counting remains hard}
\label{lor:sp:sec:hardness}

Fast randomized approximation is compatible with exact counting being
$\#\mathrm P$-complete. We give an explicit reduction rather than infer hardness
from a superficial resemblance to counting matchings.

\subsection{The leaf-extension identity}
For an integer $\ell\ge0$, form $H^{(\ell)}$ by attaching $\ell$ private leaves
to every original vertex of $H$. Leaves are placed on the opposite shore.
Let $N=|X|+|Y|$ count the original vertices.

\begin{lemma}[Leaf transform]
\label{lor:sp:lem:leaf}
\begin{equation}
 p_{H^{(\ell)}}(u)
 =(1+\ell u)^N\,
 p_H\left(\frac{u}{(1+\ell u)^2}\right).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:leaf}
\end{equation}
The right side is a polynomial after cancellation.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In a matchable support, an included leaf forces its original neighbor to be
included and matched to it. No original vertex can have two included leaves.
Delete these forced pairs. The remaining support $W$ lies in $H$ and is
perfectly matchable there. Conversely, choose any such $W$, and at each
original vertex outside $W$ either add nothing or add that vertex together
with one of its $\ell$ leaves. These choices are uniquely recoverable from
the resulting support.

If $|W|=2k$, its contribution is
$u^k(1+\ell u)^{N-2k}$. Summing over $W$ gives equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:leaf}. This proof
counts supports rather than matchings, so it survives multiple matchings on $W$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Hardness for graph supports}
The standard input is that counting bases of a transversal matroid, presented
by a bipartite graph, is $\#\mathrm P$-complete
\cite{CPV}. One can assume a presentation with $r$ slots, all saturable, where
$r$ is the rank. To see the reduction to such a presentation, choose $r$
independent rows of the generic presentation matrix using a maximum matching.
They span its row space, so restriction to them preserves independence of every
set of columns. This is again a graph presentation and can be obtained in
polynomial time.

For that graph, with exactly $r$ vertices on one shore, the top coefficient
$p_r$ is the number of transversal bases on the other shore. By
equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:leaf} at $u=1$,
\begin{equation}
 p_{H^{(\ell)}}(1)=(1+\ell)^N
       p_H((1+\ell)^{-2}).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:interpolate}
\end{equation}
The $r+1$ values $\ell=0,\ldots,r$ give distinct rational arguments.
Exact interpolation recovers $p_r$. Each enlarged graph has at most
$N(r+1)$ vertices, and the interpolation data have polynomial bit length.

\begin{theorem}[Exact graph-counting complexity]
\label{lor:sp:thm:graphhard}
Computing $p_H(1)=|\cD_H|$ is $\#\mathrm P$-complete under polynomial-time
Turing reductions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The reduction above proves hardness using \cite{CPV}. Membership in
$\#\mathrm P$ is immediate by guessing a vertex subset and testing, in
polynomial time, whether its induced bipartite graph has a perfect matching.
Each subset is one witness regardless of how many matchings it has.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Hardness even for height-two preorder lattice counts}
Orient the edges of an arbitrary bipartite graph $H$ from its lower shore to
its upper shore, obtaining a height-two poset $P_H$ on $N$ elements. The
height-two identity of Part~II (Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:main}) is
\begin{equation}
 h_{P_H}(t)=(1+t)^N p_H\left(\frac{t}{(1+t)^2}\right).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:heighttwo}
\end{equation}
For completeness, partition lattice points by the zero set $Z$ on the lower
shore and the positive-coordinate set $S$ on the upper shore. The excess
above one on $S$ is a demand vector of $H[Z\sqcup S]$. The total-count bridge
replaces it by a matchable pair $(I,J)$ with $I\subseteq Z$, $J\subseteq S$.
For a fixed size-$k$ pair, summing all allowed $Z,S$ contributes
$t^k(1+t)^{N-2k}$, which proves equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:heighttwo}. This also identifies the
height-two $\gamma$-polynomial with $p_H$.

Apply equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:heighttwo} to $H^{(\ell)}$, which has $N_\ell=N(1+\ell)$
vertices. At $t=1$, the leaf transform gives
\begin{equation}
 h_{P_{H^{(\ell)}}}(1)=
 2^{N_\ell}(1+\ell/4)^N
 p_H\left(\frac{4}{(\ell+4)^2}\right).
 \label{lor:sp:eq:heighthard}
\end{equation}
Once again $r+1$ oracle values interpolate $p_H$ and recover its hard top
coefficient.

\begin{theorem}[Exact preorder-counting complexity]
\label{lor:sp:thm:preorderhard}
The number $|\Qt\cap\Z^n|=h_\tau(1)$ is $\#\mathrm P$-complete under
polynomial-time Turing reductions, even when $\tau$ is an ordinary poset of
height at most two. Nevertheless it has an FPRAS.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Equation \eqref{lor:sp:eq:heighthard} and the preceding transversal-base reduction
prove hardness. Membership in $\#\mathrm P$ follows from
$h_\tau(1)=p_{G_\tau}(1)$, with a guessed support and a deterministic matching
test. Alternatively, one may guess the bounded integer coordinates and verify
their Hall feasibility by a flow computation. The FPRAS is
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:FPRASpartition}. This is a Turing reduction, not a parsimonious reduction.
\end{proof}

The hardness input and general approximation machinery are established
results. The displayed graph transforms make their application to these
particular support and preorder quantities explicit. No deterministic
polynomial-time exact counter is claimed.

\begin{corollary}[A specified height-two $\gamma_k$; merge consequence]
\label{lor:cor:gammahard}
Computing a specified coefficient $\gamma_k(\tau)$ of an unrestricted finite
preorder is $\#\mathrm P$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions,
already for posets of height two. For posets of height two every
$\gamma_k(P_H)$ has an FPRAS.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:heighttwo}, $\Gamma_{P_H}=p_H$, so
$\gamma_k(P_H)=p_k(H)$. In the reduction above, the graph presentation has
exactly $r$ vertices on one shore, and $p_r$ is the number of transversal
bases, which is $\#\mathrm P$-hard to compute~\cite{CPV}; an oracle for
$\gamma_r(P_H)$ therefore returns this number. The FPRAS is
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:coefficients}.
\end{proof}
[Merge note: this corollary is stated by neither source; it combines
source~07's reduction with the height-two identity, which both sources
state. It answers the ``specified $\gamma_k$'' part of Research
question~\ref{lor:hq:countcx}.]

\section{Examples that separate the properties}
\label{lor:sec:examples}
\noindent\emph{(Source~06's Section~8, with source~07's examples.)}
\subsection{A four-cycle and the danger of multiplicities}
Let $H=K_{2,2}$ with receivers $y_1,y_2$. The demand set consists of the
nonnegative pairs with $c_1+c_2\le2$. Its multivariate polynomial is
\[
 F_H(z_1,z_2)=1+2z_1+2z_2+z_1z_2.
\]
The corresponding matroid on $x_1^\circ,x_2^\circ,y_1,y_2$ is uniform of
rank two: every two-element subset is a basis. Setting the private
variables to one yields exactly the displayed polynomial. There are six
lattice points and six bases, but seven edge matchings if both perfect
matching witnesses are counted separately.

At unit fields, the mean receiver support size is one and its variance is
$1/3$. This is below the binomial upper bound $2(1/2)(1-1/2)=1/2$.
The model is a simple check that bases must be counted as sets.

\subsection{The eight-element nonreal example}
Let $\Theta_3$ be the graph with three internally disjoint paths of length
three joining common endpoints. Choose shores
\[
 X=(a,c_1,c_2,c_3),\qquad Y=(b,d_1,d_2,d_3)
\]
and edges $a d_i$, $d_i c_i$, $c_i b$ for $i=1,2,3$. Its perfectly
matchable set polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 p_{\Theta_3}(u)=1+9u+24u^2+16u^3+u^4.
 \label{lor:eq:theta}
\end{equation}
This is the previously documented example in Parts~II and~IV
(Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:thetaintro}),
where the earlier small preorder counterexample is credited to Shivam
Patel. We use the example and independently check its coefficients; we do
not claim to have discovered it.

Its order-four normalized sequence is
\[
 1,\quad\frac94,\quad4,\quad4,\quad1,
\]
which is log-concave. Yet the polynomial does not have all real roots.
Indeed,
\[
 p_{\Theta_3}(-x)=(1-x)(1-4x)^2+x^4>0\qquad(0\le x\le1).
\]
Positive coefficients exclude nonnegative roots. If all four roots were
real, all would be less than $-1$, contradicting their product being one.
Thus ultra-log-concavity is genuinely weaker than real-rootedness in the
class covered by the theorem.

The height-two preorder on these eight vertices has
\begin{align}
 h_{P_{\Theta_3}}(t)
 ={}&1+17t+106t^2+303t^3+427t^4\notag\\
    &\hspace{11mm}+303t^5+106t^6+17t^7+t^8.
 \label{lor:eq:thetah}
\end{align}
It has $1281$ lattice points. Both its ordinary coefficient sequence,
normalized by $\binom8k$, and its gamma sequence, normalized by $\binom4k$,
are log-concave. Its ordinary polynomial is nevertheless not real-rooted:
a nonreal root $u$ of \eqref{lor:eq:theta} lifts through
$t=u(1+t)^2$, and real $t\ne-1$ would give real $u$.

The completion $s^4p_{\Theta_3}(t/s)$ is Lorentzian but not real stable.
If it were stable, setting $s=1$ would give a univariate stable polynomial
with real coefficients, hence a real-rooted one. This example prevents an
incorrect upgrade from the Lorentzian conclusion to real stability.

\subsection{A numerical view of the improvement}
For \eqref{lor:eq:thetah}, the unweighted support law is symmetric about four.
Its variance, computed exactly from the coefficients, is
\[
 \frac{2\bigl(16+17\cdot9+106\cdot4+303\bigr)}{1281}
 =\frac{1792}{1281}<2.
\]
The bound $2$ is $n/4$. More importantly, after changing the positive
coordinate fields, symmetry disappears but the covariance estimate and
the same-mean binomial comparison remain valid. They require neither a
symmetric law nor a real-root factorization.

\subsection{The same example as delivered by source~07}
\label{lor:sp:ex:theta}
Let $\Theta_3$ have suppliers $u,b_1,b_2,b_3$ and receivers $v,a_1,a_2,a_3$,
with edges $u a_i$, $b_i a_i$, and $b_i v$ for $i=1,2,3$. It consists of
three internally disjoint length-three paths from $u$ to $v$. Its polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 p_{\Theta_3}(t)=1+9t+24t^2+16t^3+t^4.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:theta}
\end{equation}
The height-two preorder on these eight vertices has
\begin{align}
 h(t)={}&1+17t+106t^2+303t^3+427t^4\notag\\
       &\quad+303t^5+106t^6+17t^7+t^8.
 \label{lor:sp:eq:theta-h}
\end{align}
This is the existing counterexample credited to Shivam Patel by
Part~II and~\cite{Patel}; neither its discovery nor its minimality is claimed here.
It has $h(1)=1281$.

The quartic in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:theta} has discriminant $-5243<0$, hence exactly
two real roots and one nonreal conjugate pair. Indeed a real square-free
quartic has negative discriminant exactly when it has one conjugate pair.
The quadratic substitution in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:heighttwo} then gives nonreal roots of
$h$: a nonreal value of $t/(1+t)^2$ cannot arise from real $t$.
Nevertheless both polynomials satisfy the appropriate ultra-log-concavity
inequalities. A real-stable homogeneous lift would force its univariate
specialization to be real-rooted, so the Lorentzian lift here is genuinely
weaker than stability.
\subsection{Complete bipartite graphs and antichains}
For $K_{m,n}$ with $m,n\ge1$, every equally sized pair is matchable, so
\[
 p_{K_{m,n}}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(m,n)}\binom m k\binom n k t^k.
\]
When $m=n$, the active graph is the doubled indiscrete preorder and is
palindromic. When $m\ne n$, its top coefficient exceeds one, so it is not
palindromic. Both cases satisfy ultra-log-concavity. For $d$ disjoint edges,
$p=(1+t)^d$, corresponding to the antichain and equality in the sharp universal
coefficient bound.

\subsection{A reflexive but nontransitive core}
Take the relation on $[3]$ with all diagonal pairs and the additional pairs
$(1,2),(2,3)$, but not $(1,3)$. Direct counting gives
\[
 p(t)=1+5t+6t^2+t^3.
\]
Its penultimate coefficient exceeds its first coefficient by one, exactly the
one missing transitive pair. It is not palindromic, although its normalized
coefficients $1,5/3,2,1$ are log-concave. This separates the two components
of the support-enumerator problem.

\subsection{Cardinality conditioning is not a matroid minor}
\label{lor:sp:ex:layer}
Even for two disjoint edges, restricting to supports of size exactly one
selects two basis monomials
$x_2y_1+x_1y_2$. Their supports do not satisfy basis exchange: replacing
$x_2$ from $\{x_2,y_1\}$ by either element of $\{x_1,y_2\}$ gives neither
allowed basis. Thus fixed-cardinality support sampling does not follow by
pretending that the selected layer is a matroid minor. Conditioning individual
vertices, as in Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:conditioning}, is a different operation.

\section{Finite verification and reproducibility}
\label{lor:sec:verification}
The accompanying standard-library Python verifier checks distinct
representations, using exact integer and rational arithmetic. The proofs
remain those in the preceding sections.

For a bipartite graph it enumerates demand vectors by all neighborhood
inequalities, counts support pairs by a recursive perfect-matching test,
and independently enumerates bases using an augmenting-path oracle on
the private-copy presentation. It compares the resulting coefficient
\emph{for every receiver support}, not merely the diagonal specialization.
It then checks the binomially normalized inequalities by integer
cross-multiplication. A second pass assigns positive integer weights to
both shores and checks the weighted inequalities.

On every bipartite graph with both shores of size at most three, the
program also checks every nonempty conditioning event that specifies each
receiver as forced present, forced absent, or free. For covariance, it
computes the matrix on the right of \eqref{lor:eq:covariance} minus the actual
covariance using rational arithmetic and checks all principal minors.
This is an exact positive-semidefiniteness test in those finite instances.

For preorders, a separate enumerator tests \emph{all lower-ideal
inequalities} on nonnegative integer vectors of total at most $n$, then
compares with the doubled-graph support counts. Every reflexive labeled
relation is considered and exactly the transitive ones are retained.

For demand vectors, the second route enumerates all nonnegative coordinate

\section{Proof audit and limits of the conclusions}
\label{lor:sec:audit}
\subsection{The imported boundary is small and explicit}
The general graph conclusions rely on the positive-coordinate count in
Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:externalbridge} and the matroid Lorentzian theorem. The
counting and sampling complexity statements additionally rely on the
basis-walk theorem. These are ordinary mathematical theorem citations;
none is being claimed as a checked declaration in ProveIt.

The ordinary preorder inequalities have a route independent of the
repository's unrefereed gamma and simplicial-polytope arguments:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\text{ideal inequalities}
 \Longrightarrow \text{bipartite demand vectors}\\
 &\qquad\Longrightarrow \text{matroid bases}
 \Longrightarrow \text{Lorentzian inequalities}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The height-two gamma corollary additionally uses the finite cancellation
identity, whose proof was supplied above. It therefore does not require
assuming the full unrefereed geometric realization of the preorder
polynomial.

\subsection{Claims deliberately not made}
The article does not solve flag-polytopal realization, classify all
palindromic bipartite support polynomials, or restore real-rootedness.
It does not prove log-concavity of the gamma polynomial for arbitrary
preorders. It does not assert pairwise negative correlation merely from
complete log-concavity. It does not count matchings with their witness
multiplicities. It does not give a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm
or a polynomial-in-binary-capacity algorithm by expanding exponentially
many donor copies. Finally, support sampling is not silently promoted to
sampling actual lattice points.

\subsection{Proof dependencies and a formalization route (source~07)}
\label{lor:sp:sec:formal}
The logical structure is short enough to audit without reading every
application. The support-counting identity is the only geometric enumeration
input needed to move from graph supports to demand vectors. The matroid basis
bijection is elementary. The coefficient inequality then uses the established
Lorentzian theorem, while the complete palindromic-core characterization has
an independent finite graph proof. Probability and algorithmic consequences
branch from those two mechanisms rather than depend on the repository's
unrefereed flag or root-polytope claims.

A realistic formalization should be divided into the following layers.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.8em]
\item \textbf{Finite combinatorics.} Formalize matchable support pairs, the
private-slot matroid, the complement-one-shore equivalence, path cancellation,
and reachability of deletion pairs. These statements do not need analysis.
\item \textbf{Coefficient algebra.} Formalize the bivariate derivative
calculation and the factorial/binomial conversion. It can initially be stated
with the relevant quadratic Hessian inequality as an explicit hypothesis.
\item \textbf{Imported mathematics.} Prove or instantiate the general
Lorentzian basis theorem and the two root-polytope counting identities. Until
these are formalized, they remain visible theorem dependencies, not hidden
axioms labelled as completed proofs.
\item \textbf{Probability and algorithms.} Formalize the finite convex-order
lemma, the star equality chain, and detailed balance. The full spectral mixing
theorem is a separate major dependency; implementation tests do not discharge it.
\end{enumerate}

No Lean file is shipped as if it had been checked. The value of the present
separation is that the finite structural classification can be formalized
independently of the much larger Hodge-theoretic and mixing libraries.
