\section{Further research questions and topics}
\label{lor:sec:future}
The following are specific research targets, not assertions that their
worldwide status has been exhaustively surveyed. They separate statements
settled here from stronger statements that would require new arguments.

\begin{question}[Normalization by the matching number; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:q:first}
Can $\binom{\nu(H)}k$ replace $\binom{\min(m,n)}k$ for all bipartite graphs,
or under a useful structural hypothesis? The present proof supplies the
shore-size normalization only. The question is nontrivial when no maximum
matching saturates either shore.
(Source~07: can $\binom d k$ in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:ulc} be replaced by $\binom r k$ for
$r=\nu(H)<d$, either for all graphs or for a meaningful subclass? Prove the
stronger claim or find a smallest counterexample, including positive vertex
weights as a separate version.)
\end{question}
Deleting isolated vertices can sharpen a displayed bound, but does not
remove a general Hall deficiency. The obstruction to dividing a
Lorentzian completion by a homogenizing monomial must be addressed rather
than ignored.

The present proof cannot simply cancel the factor $s^{d-r}$ from a Lorentzian
homogenization: division by a monomial is not, in general, a Lorentzian
preserving operation. For example $s(s^2+4st+5t^2)$ satisfies the degree-three
bivariate criterion, while $s^2+4st+5t^2$ fails the degree-two criterion.

[Merge note: the batch-55 placement dossier searched for a counterexample
(evidence only): among all 4,160 bipartite graphs on shores $(4,4)$ with
$2\le\nu(H)<d$, and 264 seeded random graphs with shores up to $(6,6)$, none
violates log-concavity of $a_k/\binom{\nu(H)}k$. The question stays open.]

[Added 30 September 2026, batch 68: answered negatively for positive
vertex weights on both shores. Part~XI's Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness}
gives a graph with 30 vertices, 104 edges and $\nu(H)=8<15=\min(m,n)$,
with weight $500$ on eight core vertices and $1$ on the others, whose
weighted support polynomial violates the last inequality of order eight;
a family of matching number six fails as well
(Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:rank6phase}), and any normalization depending on
$\nu(H)$ alone must be at least about $\frac43\nu(H)$ along even ranks
(Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:universalorder}). Every positively weighted graph
satisfies the first rank-normalized inequality
(Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:firstidentity}), hence all of them when
$\nu(H)\le2$. The unit-weight version (the finite search above concerns
it) and the version with weights on one shore remain open (Research
questions~\ref{hb:q:unit} and~\ref{hb:q:oneshore}); no smallest
counterexample is determined (Research question~\ref{hb:q:rank}). The
division example of the preceding paragraph has an instance inside the
class: Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:division}.]

\begin{question}[Equality, rigidity, and sharper covariance bounds; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:q:equality}
Characterize equality at a single ultra-log-concavity index under positive
weights, and characterize the null directions of
$\diag(p)-pp^{\mathsf T}/m-\Cov(I)$. Can neighborhood redundancy or a
canonical decomposition replace the ambient rank in part of this bound?
(Source~07: classify equality at one internal coefficient in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:ulc}, not merely
simultaneous binomial equality. Quantify how a shared neighbor or unequal
weighted star strengths forces a positive gap in equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:variance}.)
\end{question}
The antichain classification above concerns simultaneous equality only.
A complete answer is likely to require equality information in the
Lorentzian Hessian inequalities, not just the coefficient count.

The exact equality theorem suggests using collision mass in
equation~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:equalitychain}. Converting that endpoint deficit into a uniform
positive-fugacity variance gap is the missing step; it is not supplied by
qualitative compactness when activities approach zero.

[Merge note: simultaneous equality in the variance bound, for every
positive weighting, is settled by source~07's
Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:equality}; source~06's antichain proposition is its
preorder case.]
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 68: equality at the first index is
classified for the normalization by $\nu(H)$, under positive weights:
exactly the disjoint unions of $\nu(H)$ stars with equal edge-weight sums
(Part~XI, Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:equality}). For a larger normalization,
including $\min(m,n)>\nu(H)$, the first inequality is strict
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:answers}). Other indices remain open.]

\begin{question}[Binary capacities and approximation complexity]\label{tf:hq:capacities}% label added in batch 64 (Part IX)
Can partition functions or individual support coefficients for large
binary-encoded capacities be approximated in time polynomial in the
encoding length, without explicitly cloning donors? A compressed
transversal-polymatroid walk, or another representation of the same
support counts, would be needed.
\end{question}
This is the correct next step after Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:capacity}; the
pseudo-polynomial cloned presentation is not already an answer.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: still open. Part~IX's bijection and
sampler also reach dilations only by cloning, and its Research
question~\ref{tf:q:capacities} asks the same for them.]

\begin{question}[Deterministic and practical coefficient algorithms]\label{hb:hq:algorithms}% label added in batch 68 (Part XI)
Develop a deterministic approximation method for these special
transversal-matroid partition functions, or a practically competitive
implementation of the tilting FPRAS. Analyze dependence on graph width,
repeated neighborhoods, and sparse presentations. Compare with exact
algorithms for the same classes.
\end{question}
The rational-grid construction is designed to prove polynomial complexity,
not to be the fastest numerical tuning rule. Its probability lower bound
provides a useful correctness target for faster implementations.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 68: Part~XI gives an exact algorithm whose
cost is governed by the matching number and by the neighbourhood types of
the vertices outside a minimum cover (Theorems~\ref{hb:thm:algorithmformula}
and~\ref{hb:thm:FPT}); approximation is not treated there.]

\begin{question}[Algorithmic use of the preorder quotient]
Exploit equivalence classes and the quotient poset to accelerate the independence
oracle or aggregate the Markov chain without losing its stationary law.
Can the running time depend primarily on the number of equivalence classes or
on a structural width parameter?
\end{question}
Any aggregation must count supports, not matchings or orbit representatives
with uniform weight. The general rank-$n$ sampler gives a correctness baseline
against which compressed implementations can be tested.

\begin{question}[Distributional comparison under relation extension]
When a preorder is enlarged by adding comparisons, does its support-size law
become smaller in convex order after the appropriate mean normalization?
Determine which order extensions preserve such a comparison.
\end{question}
Coefficientwise growth of transport counts is not enough by itself: the
partition function also changes. A proof would need a likelihood-ratio or
coupling argument, and could yield sharper variance bounds than the universal
binomial comparison.

\begin{question}[Formalization in layers; sources~06 and~07]\label{lor:q:last}
Formalize the private-copy basis correspondence and preorder reduction
first, then the finite support-fibre count, and finally the analytic and
probabilistic implications. State imported results explicitly until they
are discharged. Can the elementary coefficient-recovery reduction be
verified independently of the implementation of the matching oracle?
(Source~07, ``A small independently checked formal core'': formalize the complete palindromic-core theorem, including isolated vertices
and the actual-degree convention, and verify the recognition algorithm against
that theorem. Then formalize the weighted-star equality theorem assuming the
ULC inequality.)
\end{question}
A conditional Lean theorem about a supplied support-counting identity is a
useful intermediate object, but should not be labeled an unconditional
formal proof of the present theorem.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: the finite support-fibre count now
has an elementary proof (Part~IX, Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:count}), a
natural target for this layer; Research question~\ref{tf:q:formal} asks
for a certified checker of its certificates.]

These two projects isolate finite and elementary arguments from the large
imported theories. They would substantially increase confidence in the new
applications without pretending that a few computational examples formalize
Lorentzian Hodge theory.


\subsection{Questions of sources~06 and~07 already posed in Parts~II--IV}
\label{lor:sec:oldquestions}
These questions of the sources repeat earlier questions of this report, or
are answered inside Part~V. They are printed as delivered, without new
numbers, each after a pointer to the question it repeats.

\noindent\emph{Repeats Research question~\ref{lor:hq:shape}} (coefficient
shape beyond gamma-positivity):
\paragraph{Gamma log-concavity beyond height two (source~06).}
Is $\Gamma_\tau$ log-concave for every finite preorder? If not, determine a
minimal counterexample and structural restrictions that recover it.
Height-three posets and chains of nontrivial equivalence classes are useful
first test families. Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:gammaULC} settles height two, but the
ordinary $h$-inequalities do not settle this question.
A productive approach would identify a homogeneous completion of the
\emph{disjoint} transport-support polynomial, rather than reusing the
completion for all doubled support pairs.


\noindent\emph{Repeat Research questions~\ref{gam:q:bijection}
and~\ref{gam:q:bridge}} (a bijective demand/support bridge):
\paragraph{An effective demand/support bijection (source~06).}
Construct a support-preserving bijection that is compatible with a
controlled ordering or restriction of the receiver set and can be
evaluated and inverted in polynomial time. Such a construction would
upgrade the support samplers to actual integer-vector samplers and might
substantially reduce the proof-assistant dependency on geometry.
The existing geometric counting theorem is the starting point, and Oh's
bijections must be compared carefully before claiming a genuinely new
construction. Compatibility and computational complexity are part of the
target, not consequences of a cardinality identity.

\paragraph{A direct demand/support bijection (source~07).}
Construct a natural, efficiently invertible map from $\cD_H$ to matchable
supports, preferably preserving the exact receiver support. The equality of
these refined counts is proved above, but an arbitrary ranking-and-unranking
bijection would not explain the combinatorics. Such a map would turn the
support sampler into an actual demand-vector sampler.
A first test should reject any rule depending on a noncanonical chosen
matching. Lexicographically selecting allocations and retaining one extreme
supplier from each allocation can merge different demand vectors. A successful
construction must control this loss of information.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 64: both paragraphs are answered by
Part~IX. Its maps are evaluated and inverted in polynomial time, preserve
the exact receiver support, and read the demand vector off a spanning
tree extracted from an optimum, with no chosen matching; they turn the
support sampler into an actual demand-vector sampler
(Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:sampler}). Section~\ref{tf:sec:target} compares
them with Oh's bijection, whose existence they realize.]


\noindent\emph{Repeat Research questions~\ref{ade:hq:preserve},
\ref{ade:hq:classify} and~\ref{lor:hq:rootgeom}, and bear on Part~VI}
(real stability and real roots):
\paragraph{Real stability of the multivariate support polynomial (source~06).}
Which bipartite graphs have a real-stable $F_H(z)$, or a real-stable
private-copy basis polynomial? The two formulations should not be assumed
equivalent. The repository's cactus models give a natural comparison
class, while $\Theta_3$ shows that the unrestricted real-stability claim
fails.
A stable affine slice may arise from a nonstable completion. Conversely,
a stable completion gives a stable slice. This directionality should be
retained in any classification.

\paragraph{Real-rootedness inside the Lorentzian class (source~07).}
Classify graph operations which preserve real-rootedness of $p_H$, and seek a
structural recognition theorem broader than cacti. The nonreal-root family of
Part~II (Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:thetaintro}) shows that low treewidth alone is insufficient.
The aim should be a criterion for the univariate polynomial, not an unnecessary
unit-modulus determinant representation. The latter is a strictly stronger
requirement in the existing repository results.

[Merge note: Part~VI classifies stability for two treewidth-two families
and proves that stability of $\Phi_G$ is strictly stronger than
real-rootedness of $p_G$.]

\noindent\emph{Answered in Part~V:}
\paragraph{Efficient sampling of a fixed coefficient layer (source~07).}
For prescribed $k$, construct a polynomial-time approximate sampler of
$\PM_k(H)$, or determine the approximation complexity of $p_k$. Separate
$k=\nu(H)$, where Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:top} factors the problem into two transversal-base
counts, from internal layers.
The example in Section~\ref{lor:sp:ex:layer} blocks the most direct matroid-minor argument.
A fugacity method would need a proved lower bound on the mass of the desired
layer and an effective way to choose a suitable fugacity.

[Merge note: answered by source~06's Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:coefficients}
and its fixed-size sampler (Section~\ref{lor:sec:algorithms}): every $a_k$ has
an FPRAS, and at the tilted activity found there the layer $k$ has mass at
least $1/(4(d+1))$, so rejection sampling gives the layer. The fugacity method
the delivered text asks for is exactly that argument.]

\noindent\emph{Repeat Research questions~\ref{gam:q:flag} and~\ref{gam:gv:q:faces}}
(flags and face numbers):
\paragraph{Flags and the preorder $\gamma$-vector (source~07).}
Does every preorder support polynomial occur as the $h$-polynomial of a flag
simplicial polytope? Does the transport-pair $\gamma$-vector satisfy stronger
face-number inequalities or admit a canonical simplicial-complex model?
Neither the intersection realization nor ultra-log-concavity supplies a flag
triangulation. The repository's induced-crown obstruction concerns its canonical
lattice model and must not be promoted into a disproof of all flag realization.


\noindent\emph{Repeats Research question~\ref{lor:hq:limit}} (limit laws):
\paragraph{Limit laws without real-rootedness (source~06).}
Which growing graph or preorder families have asymptotically normal
support size? The same-mean binomial upper bound gives concentration but
not a central limit theorem. Seek hypotheses phrased in terms of
component structure, correlation decay, or the growing matroid lift,
including sequences whose polynomials have many nonreal zeros.


\section{Conclusion}
\label{lor:sec:conclusion}
The failure of real-rootedness leaves a substantial uniform theorem intact.
Every bipartite demand support enumerator admits a classical
transversal-matroid completion, and that completion imports the full
Lorentzian coefficient mechanism. The resulting theorem is stronger than
unimodality, applies to all finite preorders and their positive integral
dilations, and settles the gamma coefficient-shape question throughout
height two.

The same structure has algorithmic content. Matching feasibility supplies
a basis oracle; the matroid walk supplies approximate sampling; and
log-concave tilting makes a requested coefficient visible with
polynomially large probability. This gives approximation schemes without
confusing support sets with their matching witnesses or with actual
integer vectors. The remaining questions concern genuinely stronger
structures: general gamma inequalities, effective lattice-point
bijections, sharper normalizations, and compressed-capacity algorithms.

Source~07 concludes in the same sense:

The useful replacement for universal real-rootedness is not merely
unimodality. Bipartite matchable supports have a homogeneous matroid lift,
which imports the full binomially normalized log-concavity inequality. The
existing demand/root-polytope identities then transfer this structure to every
preorder support polynomial and to the general bipartite support-enumerator
problem. Palindromicity has a different explanation: uniqueness of the largest
support forces a balanced core, and its first/penultimate coefficient defect
measures failure of transitivity exactly.

Together these mechanisms answer the unimodality and palindromicity components
of the stated research target, while preserving the distinction from the still
unclassified real-rooted case. They also expose a useful computational
dichotomy: exact counts are hard even in height two, yet uniform or positively
weighted support measures admit rapid sampling and randomized approximation.
The mathematical advance claimed here is this explicit transfer, classification,
and set of consequences relative to the inspected repository, not a rediscovery
of general matroid concavity or a claim to have solved every remaining preorder
conjecture.

\section{Compact proof certificates}
\label{lor:sec:certificates}
\noindent\emph{(Appendix~A of source~06, and Appendix~A of source~07 as Section~\ref{lor:sp:app:certificate}.)}
\subsection{The coefficient inequality in four steps}
For an ordinary unweighted graph, a reader can check the central argument
through the following equalities and one imported theorem:
\begin{align*}
 F_H(z)&=\sum_{U\sim_H S}z_S
       &&\text{(published support-counting bridge)},\\
 \mathcal B_H(a,z)&=\sum_{U\sim_H S}a_{X\setminus U}z_S
       &&\text{(private-slot basis correspondence)},\\
 \mathcal B_H(s\mathbf1,t\mathbf1)&=\sum_ka_ks^{m-k}t^k
       &&\text{(homogeneous grouping)},\\
 \frac{a_k^2}{\binom m k^2}&\ge
 \frac{a_{k-1}}{\binom m{k-1}}\frac{a_{k+1}}{\binom m{k+1}}
       &&\text{(Lorentzian bivariate criterion)}.
\end{align*}
Transpose the graph to obtain the other shore normalization. For
preorders, neighborhood sets are lower closures, giving the direct
identification of the integer inequalities.

\subsection{The coefficient-recovery algorithm}
The theoretical algorithm of Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:coefficients} is summarized
below. Its probability budgets are specified in the proof.
\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
Input: graph H, coefficient index k, relative error eps, failure delta.\\
Compute d = maximum-matching size.\\
Return 0 for k outside [0,d]; return 1 for k = 0.\\
Form the rational activity grid of equation (\ref{lor:eq:grid}).\\
Binary-search using samples to estimate Pr(L < k).\\
Stop when both sides of the threshold have substantial mass.\\
Approximate Z = p\_H(t) by weighted basis self-reduction.\\
Estimate q = Pr(L = k) by repeated weighted basis samples.\\
Return Z * q / t\^{}k.
\end{quote}
The lower bound $q\ge1/(4(d+1))$ is the reason the final empirical step is
fully polynomial. This bound is proved; it is not an assumption about the
shape of a numerically observed histogram.

\subsection{The example discriminant and exact normalization checks (source~07)}
\label{lor:sp:app:certificate}
For $q(t)=t^4+16t^3+24t^2+9t+1$, direct integer resultant computation gives
\[
 \operatorname{disc}(q)=\operatorname{Res}(q,q')=-5243.
\]
The monic quartic sign factor is $(-1)^{4\cdot3/2}=1$.
The supplementary script \nolinkurl{code/example_certificate.py} [shipped as
\nolinkurl{code/07-support-polynomials-example_certificate.py}] computes this
resultant using fraction-free integer elimination, independently counts two real
roots by Sturm's rule, and constructs the height-two transform. The existence
of nonreal roots does not depend on a numerical root plot.

For the eight-element support polynomial, the binomial-normalized sequence is
\[
 1,\quad \frac{17}{8},\quad \frac{53}{14},\quad
 \frac{303}{56},\quad \frac{61}{10},\quad
 \frac{303}{56},\quad\frac{53}{14},\quad\frac{17}{8},\quad1.
\]
Each internal log-concavity inequality holds exactly. These numbers are an
illustration of the theorem, not a substitute for its all-graph proof.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~08 (as delivered).}
A matching-support polynomial counts an endpoint set once whenever it admits
at least one perfect matching.  Replacing matching multiplicities by this
Boolean existence condition destroys the usual determinantal construction.
We study the resulting multivariate stability problem, left open beyond
special graph classes in the inspected ProveIt research corpus.
For a tree $T$, form a bipartite graph whose left vertices are $V(T)$, whose
right vertices are $E(T)$ together with one apex, and whose apex is adjacent
to every left vertex.  We prove that its signed matching-support polynomial
is real stable if and only if
$C_T=I-\tfrac12 A_T$ is positive semidefinite, equivalently
$\rho(A_T)\le2$.  Thus its stable members are exactly the trees of finite
$A,D,E$ and affine $D,E$ type.  The mechanism is the exact identity
$F_T=\det L+s\tr(\adj(L)C_T)$; failure of the spectral condition produces an
explicit rational negative Rayleigh certificate.  The criterion survives
arbitrary subdivisions between the original apex neighbors.
For quadrilateral books, the threshold is exactly four pages, although the
univariate support polynomial is real-rooted for every number of pages.
At five pages, two elements of the associated uniformly random matroid
basis have covariance $1/576$.  An independent expected-determinant argument
proves stability for every even-path multi-theta graph.  Combined with the
tree criterion and a credited earlier nonreal-root example, this gives a
complete stability classification of simple bipartite multi-theta graphs.
Proofs, explicit examples, exact finite verifiers, provenance boundaries,
and a further research program are included.
\end{tcolorbox}
\noindent The abstract is reproduced as delivered; its $\Theta(3,3,3)$ is
printed $\vartheta(3,3,3)$ below (Section~\ref{ade:sec:notation}), and its
``inspected ProveIt research corpus'' is Parts~I--IV of this report.

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Status and scope (source~08, as delivered).}
This is an unrefereed, AI-assisted mathematical
research draft.  Its general claims rest on the written proofs, not on the
finite tests.  No Lean or Rocq verification is claimed.  The results are
presented as developments beyond the inspected repository material;
worldwide priority has not been established.  The classical ADE
classification and the earlier eight-vertex nonreal-root example are
explicitly credited, not claimed as discoveries of this article.
\end{statusbox}

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Priority and prior work (merge).} The ADE list of trees with
spectral radius at most two is classical (McKee--Smyth~\cite{McKeeSmyth}
recall the context); the half-plane-property framework is Choe--Oxley--Sokal--Wagner's
and Br\"and\'en's~\cite{COSW,Branden}, and Br\"and\'en's Theorem~5.6 is the
multiaffine Rayleigh criterion, whose necessary direction is reproved here.
The nonreal-root obstruction $\vartheta(3,3,3)=\Theta_3$ is Part~II's, with
priority credited to Shivam Patel~\cite{Patel}; even-cycle stability is
contained in Part~II's cactus theorem (Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:stability}) and
in Ohsugi--Tsuchiya's univariate result~\cite{OT21}. Part~III already proved
that $\Phi_{K_{2,3}}$ and its tree attachments are stable without a faithful
matrix (Theorem~\ref{cac:thm:stable23}, Corollary~\ref{cac:cor:trees}); source~09's
complete bipartite blocks extend that example, and its vertex-sum theorem
generalizes Part~III's leaf lemmas (Lemmas~\ref{cac:lem:leaf}
and~\ref{cac:lem:leafstable}). Source~09 does not cite these Part~III
results; merge notes add the credit. The one-vertex gluing theorem was
proved independently by both sources on the same day. Source~08's focused
literature search found no earlier statement of the tree incidence--apex
equivalence; that is not a priority certificate, and no worldwide priority
is claimed for any result of Part~VI.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{Notation of Part~VI}
\label{ade:sec:notation}
Part~VI uses Part~III's signed support polynomial $\Phi_G$
(equation~\eqref{cac:eq:Phi}) and Part~II's $p_G$; source~08's shores are
written $U\sqcup V$ where Parts~II--III write $A\sqcup B$.
Table~\ref{ade:tab:notation} lists what Part~VI adds or uses differently.
Two symbols of the sources were changed; no normalization was changed:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item source~08's theta graphs $\Theta(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_q)$ are printed
$\vartheta(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_q)$, extending Part~III's rule
(Section~\ref{cac:sec:prov}), because Part~II's $\Theta_m$ has $m$ paths of
length three; only $\vartheta(3,3,3)=\Theta_3$ is both;
\item source~08's canonical transversal matroid $M_G$ is printed
$\mathsf M_G$, because $M_G(u)$ is Part~II's matching polynomial and because
source~09's matroid, printed $M_G$ as delivered, is its dual.
\end{itemize}
Source~08's set of matchable pairs $\mathcal M(G)$ is typeset with the
host's macro and is Part~IV's $\mathcal M(H)$.
\emph{The two matroid conventions.} With the same shores $A=U$ (left) and
$B=V$ (right), source~08's $\mathsf M_G$ has one slot per left vertex and the
bases $(U\setminus I)\sqcup J$, rank $|U|$; source~09's $M_G$ has one slot per
right vertex and the bases $I\sqcup(V\setminus J)$, rank $|V|$. Each basis of
one is the complement of a basis of the other, so $M_G=(\mathsf M_G)^*$ on the
same ground set, and the two basis polynomials are $F_G$ of source~08 and
$F_G$ of source~09, different polynomials under one letter
(Table~\ref{ade:tab:notation}). Stability of a basis polynomial is invariant
under duality, so the two bridges (Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge} and
Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:stable-bridge}) say the same thing. Part~V's
$\mathsf M_H$ is source~08's convention, with the private copies relabelled.

 & a Laplacian.\\

 deck operator.\\

\subsection{What Part~VI answers}

Status after Part~VI, as of 29 September 2026:

\item \textbf{Stability of $\Phi_G$ is strictly stronger than

\section{Research target and main conclusions}
\label{ade:sec:intro}

\subsection{What is counted, and why stability is difficult}

Let $G=(U\sqcup V,E)$ be a finite simple bipartite graph.  A pair
$(I,J)$, with $I\subseteq U$, $J\subseteq V$ and $|I|=|J|$, is
\emph{matchable} when the induced graph on $I\sqcup J$ has a perfect
matching.  The empty pair is matchable.  Write $\PM(G)$ for these pairs.
The univariate polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 p_G(t)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(G)}t^{|I|}.
 \label{ade:eq:pdef}
\end{equation}
A pair with seven different perfect matchings still contributes only one
monomial.  This distinction from the ordinary matching-generating
polynomial is essential throughout.

The multivariate polynomial naturally used in the repository is
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_G(z)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(G)}(-1)^{|I|}
       \prod_{u\in U\setminus I}z_u
       \prod_{v\in V\setminus J}z_v.
 \label{ade:eq:Phidef}
\end{equation}
A real polynomial is \emph{real stable} if it is nonzero whenever every
variable lies in the open upper half-plane
$\HH=\{z\in\C:\im z>0\}$.  Thus stability is a zero-exclusion statement
in many complex variables, not just a statement about one diagonal.

For a matrix $K$ supported on the edges of $G$, Cauchy--Binet assigns the
weight $|\det K_{I,J}|^2$ to a matchable endpoint pair.  Usually that weight
is neither zero nor one.  The issue is to recover the Boolean support
coefficients without losing the analytic zero-exclusion property.
The principal construction here accomplishes this by a second-moment
identity, rather than by a single faithful edge-phase matrix.

\subsection{The exact tree criterion}

For a nonempty tree $T$, let $\calA(T)$ have left vertex set $V(T)$ and
right vertex set $E(T)\sqcup\{\star\}$.  A right vertex $e=\{i,j\}$ is
adjacent to $i,j$, and $\star$ is adjacent to every vertex of $T$.
There are $2r$ vertices when $r=|V(T)|$.

\begin{theorem}[Main criterion]
\label{ade:thm:intromain}
For every finite nonempty tree $T$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \Phi_{\calA(T)}\text{ is real stable}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 I-\tfrac12 A_T\succeq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho(A_T)\le2.
 \quad}
 \label{ade:eq:intromain}
\end{equation}
Here $A_T$ is the adjacency matrix.  The same criterion holds after
subdividing the edges of $T$ arbitrarily before forming incidence vertices,
provided that the apex remains adjacent only to the original vertices.
\end{theorem}
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 63: Part~VIII removes the terminal
convention for a single apex over a tree: for an arbitrary apex
neighbourhood $S\subseteq V(T)$, stability holds exactly when every
branching vertex of the subtree spanned by $S$ is marked and the
suppressed skeleton is an ADE tree (Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main}).]

The list of trees with adjacency spectral radius at most two is classical:
the finite simply-laced Dynkin trees $A,D,E$ and the affine simply-laced
Dynkin trees $\widetilde D,\widetilde E$; affine $A$ diagrams are cycles,
not trees.  We give an elementary proof of the tree list in
Section~\ref{ade:sec:ADE}.  The contribution at issue is the equivalence with
matching-support stability, not the spectral classification by itself.

The proof supplies more information than a yes/no test.  Let
\begin{equation}
 L=\diag(x_i)+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}y_{ij}(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^T,
 \qquad C_T=I-\tfrac12 A_T.
 \label{ade:eq:LCintro}
\end{equation}
The homogeneous support polynomial $F_T$, defined precisely in
Section~\ref{ade:sec:bridge}, satisfies
\begin{equation}
 F_T(x;y,s)=\det L+s\tr\bigl(\adj(L)C_T\bigr).
 \label{ade:eq:identityintro}
\end{equation}
This is a polynomial identity for \emph{every} tree, including those for
which $C_T$ is indefinite.  Positivity of $C_T$ is exactly what turns the
identity into a stability proof.  When $C_T$ is not positive semidefinite,
Section~\ref{ade:sec:criterion} gives real rational variable values at which a
Rayleigh difference is negative.

\subsection{Two sharp consequences}

Let $B_m$ be the quadrilateral book with a common edge and $m$ internally
disjoint three-edge paths between its endpoints.  Then
$B_m=\calA(K_{1,m})$.

\begin{theorem}[The book transition]
\label{ade:thm:introbook}
The polynomial $\Phi_{B_m}$ is real stable exactly when $m\le4$.
Nevertheless, $p_{B_m}$ has only negative real zeros for every $m\ge0$.
For $m\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 p_{B_m}(t)=(1+t)^{m-2}
 \bigl(1+(2m+3)t+(m^2+m+3)t^2+t^3\bigr).
 \label{ade:eq:introbook}
\end{equation}
At $m=5$, the associated basis polynomial has a Rayleigh difference
$-256$ at the all-ones point.
\end{theorem}

The threshold persists if the $m$ paths are lengthened by even numbers of
edges while the common edge is retained.  The last assertion is stronger
than failure of stability: it violates the ordinary positive-weight
Rayleigh inequality and yields a positively correlated pair under the
uniform basis measure.

A \emph{multi-theta graph} consists of $q\ge2$ internally vertex-disjoint
paths with the same two endpoints.  Simplicity permits at most one
one-edge path.  Bipartiteness says that all path lengths have the same
parity.

\begin{theorem}[Multi-theta classification]
\label{ade:thm:introtheta}
For a finite simple bipartite multi-theta graph $G$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 \item if all path lengths are even, $\Phi_G$ is real stable;
 \item if all path lengths are odd and no path has length one,
       $\Phi_G$ is real stable exactly when there are two paths;
 \item if one path has length one and there are $m$ other paths,
       $\Phi_G$ is real stable exactly when $m\le4$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Part (i) uses a separate independent-column expected-determinant method.
Part (ii) uses a matroid-minor reduction to the earlier
$\vartheta(3,3,3)$ obstruction, not a claim of a new first counterexample to
real-rootedness.

\subsection{Source~09's stability statement}
\label{ade:sec:mat:intro}
Source~09 states, in its introduction (as delivered):
For a finite simple graph $G$, let $\Phi_G$ be its signed matching-support
polynomial, defined in Section~\ref{ade:mat:sec:stability}. We also prove
\begin{equation}
\boxed{\quad \Phi_G\text{ is real stable}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Phi_B\text{ is real stable for every block }B\text{ of }G.\quad}
\label{ade:mat:eq:intro-block}
\end{equation}
For bipartite $G$, this connects directly to the half-plane property of the
matching-support matroid. Complete bipartite graphs and even cycles supply
stable blocks of arbitrary size.

\subsection{Relation to ProveIt and the literature}
\label{ade:sec:prior}

The inspected ProveIt report (this report's Parts~II--IV) gives a faithful-matrix
classification for bipartite cacti, a stable noncactus example $K_{2,3}$
and its tree attachments, and further questions about stability and
real-rootedness.  It also develops the height-two preorder identity
\begin{equation}
 h_{P_G}(t)=(1+t)^{|U|+|V|}\,
             p_G\!\left(\frac{t}{(1+t)^2}\right).
 \label{ade:eq:preorderimport}
\end{equation}
Its discussion credits Shivam Patel for the eight-element nonreal-root
example corresponding to $\vartheta(3,3,3)$.  We preserve that attribution.
The general gamma-positivity developments in that report are not targets
of the present article.

The half-plane-property theory of matroid basis polynomials is classical
\cite{COSW,Branden}.  We use its language, while proving the special
closure and determinant facts needed here.  Cactus real-rootedness has
prior literature \cite{OT21}.  The ADE spectral classification is likewise
classical, and the account of McKee and Smyth \cite{McKeeSmyth} provides
an inspected primary source for its context.  The root-polytope
identifications and duality in the surrounding preorder literature also
have prior work \cite{DHLTW}; none is claimed here.

The scope is specific.  The article resolves the
\emph{restricted classification problems} in
Theorems~\ref{ade:thm:intromain} and~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta}, gives sharp new
consequences within that development, and offers proofs for checking.  It
does not classify stability for all bipartite graphs; it does not solve the
flag-polytope question; and it does not establish that no earlier matroid
paper contains an equivalent formulation of these restricted results.

\section{A homogeneous bridge to matroids and stability}
\label{ade:sec:bridge}

\subsection{The canonical basis polynomial}

Put $r=|U|$.  For a subset $S$, use $x^S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i$.
Define
\begin{equation}
 F_G(x;y)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(G)}x^{U\setminus I}y^J.
 \label{ade:eq:Fdef}
\end{equation}
This is homogeneous of degree $r$, multiaffine, and has coefficients in
$\{0,1\}$.  The coefficient of $x^U$ is one.

\begin{lemma}[Canonical transversal matroid]
\label{ade:lem:matroid}
The sets $(U\setminus I)\sqcup J$, for $(I,J)\in\PM(G)$, are the
bases of a rank-$r$ transversal matroid $\mathsf M_G$.  They are also the bases of
$[I_r\ K]$, where $K$ has an independent indeterminate in every edge
position and zero elsewhere, over the field of rational functions in
those indeterminates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Present a transversal matroid by one set
$\{u\}\cup N_G(u)$ for each $u\in U$, on the ground set $U\sqcup V$.
A chosen left element $u$ can represent only its own row.  After choosing
the left elements $U\setminus I$, representing the remaining rows is
exactly a perfect matching from $I$ to $J$.  This proves the first claim.
For the matrix claim, expand the minor on columns
$(U\setminus I)\sqcup J$ along the identity columns.  The remaining minor
is $\det K_{I,J}$.  In its Leibniz expansion, different perfect matchings
produce different monomials in independent indeterminates, so cancellation
cannot make a structurally nonzero minor vanish.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Inversion bridge]
\label{ade:prop:bridge}
The polynomials $F_G$ and $\Phi_G$ are real stable simultaneously.
Moreover, stability implies that $p_G$ has only negative real zeros.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Directly from the definitions,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_G(x,z_V)=z^V F_G\bigl(x;-z_V^{-1}\bigr).
 \label{ade:eq:bridge}
\end{equation}
The transformation $z\mapsto-1/z$ maps $\HH$ bijectively onto itself.
The factor $z^V$ does not vanish there, giving equivalence.
For the last assertion,
$p_G(t)=F_G(\one;t\one)$.  Specialization of the $x$ variables to the
real number one preserves stability or gives the zero polynomial; the
latter is excluded by the constant coefficient one.  Diagonalization of
the $y$ variables preserves stability.  A univariate real stable real
polynomial has no nonreal zeros, since a nonreal zero and its conjugate
would put one zero in $\HH$.  Finally, the nonnegative coefficients and
constant coefficient one exclude nonnegative real zeros.
\end{proof}


\subsection{The dual bridge for all simple graphs (source~09)}
\label{ade:mat:sec:stability}
For a finite simple graph $G$ on $V$, a subset $S$ is perfectly matchable
when the induced graph $G[S]$ has a perfect matching. Define
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_G(z)=\sum_{S\text{ perfectly matchable}}
                     (-1)^{|S|/2}z^{V\setminus S}.
\label{ade:mat:eq:Phi}
\end{equation}
This is multi-affine, real, and has leading monomial $z^V$.
A real polynomial is \emph{real stable} if it is nonzero whenever all
variables lie in $\HH=\{z\in\C:\im z>0\}$. For a homogeneous matroid
basis polynomial this is the usual half-plane property, after a common
rotation of variables if another half-plane convention is used
\cite{Branden}.

\begin{theorem}[Exact stability bridge]\label{ade:mat:thm:stable-bridge}
For bipartite $G=(A\sqcup B,\mathcal E)$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_G(z_A,z_B)=
 \left(\prod_{a\in A}z_a\right)
 F_G\bigl((-1/z_a)_{a\in A},(z_b)_{b\in B}\bigr).
\label{ade:mat:eq:reciprocal}
\end{equation}
Consequently $\Phi_G$ is real stable if and only if the basis polynomial of
$M_G$ is real stable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The term belonging to $(I,J)$ on the right is
$(-1)^{|I|}z^{A\setminus I}z^{B\setminus J}$, exactly the term in
\eqref{ade:mat:eq:Phi}. The map $z\mapsto-1/z$ is a bijection of $\HH$ to itself,
and none of the prefactors vanishes there. Applying the same reciprocal
substitution again, or using its inverse, proves both implications.
\end{proof}

Thus the stability problem is a half-plane-property problem for a concrete
class of transversal matroids. Lorentzianity holds for every $M_G$, but
stability is stronger and can fail. The partial reciprocal substitution is
important: the positive support polynomial in the matched variables is not
being asserted stable.

[Merge note: source~09's $M_G$ is the dual of source~08's $\mathsf M_G$
(Section~\ref{ade:sec:notation}); Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:stable-bridge} is
Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge} read through that duality. Source~09's
$\Phi_G$ agrees with Part~III's~\eqref{cac:eq:Phi} on bipartite graphs and is
defined for every simple graph.]

\subsection{The analytic facts used below}

We record details to make the proof boundary transparent.  The standard
specialization statement follows by substituting $a+i\ep$ and letting
$\ep\downarrow0$, using Hurwitz's theorem on the product of upper
half-planes.  A limit is zero-free or identically zero.  Differentiation
also preserves stability or gives zero: for fixed remaining variables,
logarithmic derivatives in one variable have nonpositive imaginary part,
and the derivative is obtained as a stable limit.  These are standard
closure facts in \cite{COSW,Branden}.

For a real multiaffine polynomial $f$, set
\begin{equation}
 \del_{ij}f=(\partial_i f)(\partial_j f)-f\,\partial_i\partial_j f.
 \label{ade:eq:Rayleigh}
\end{equation}
The expression does not depend on the two variables $z_i,z_j$.

\begin{lemma}[Necessary Rayleigh inequality]
\label{ade:lem:rayleigh}
If a nonzero real multiaffine polynomial $f$ is real stable, then
$\del_{ij}f(a)\ge0$ for every real assignment $a$ and every pair $i,j$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Specialize all other variables to real values.  The resulting polynomial
is zero or a stable bivariate polynomial
$g(z,w)=A+Bz+Cw+Dzw$ with real coefficients.
If $AD-BC>0$, the zero of $g$ in the $z$ variable is
\[
 z=-\frac{A+Cw}{B+Dw},\qquad
 \im z=\frac{(AD-BC)\im w}{|B+Dw|^2}>0
\]
for $w\in\HH$ away from the possible denominator zero.  This contradicts
stability.  Thus $BC-AD\ge0$, which is the required Rayleigh difference.
The identically zero specialization has difference zero.
\end{proof}

Br\"and\'en's Theorem 5.6 \cite{Branden} gives the converse too.  The
main necessity proof in this article only needs the elementary direction
just proved.  In particular, no numerical root-finding is part of that
proof.

\begin{lemma}[Matroid and induced-graph minors]
\label{ade:lem:minors}
Real stability of a matroid basis polynomial is preserved under matroid
deletion and contraction, apart from the harmless zero-polynomial case
for deleting a coloop or contracting a loop in the direct formulas.
Also, if $\Phi_G$ is stable and $H$ is an induced subgraph, then $\Phi_H$
is stable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a noncoloop, deletion is specialization of its variable to zero;
for a nonloop, contraction is differentiation.  Loop and coloop cases
reduce by a constant or linear factor.  For induced graph deletion there
is an even more direct formula:
$\partial_{z_v}\Phi_G=\Phi_{G-v}$, because differentiation selects exactly
the supports that leave $v$ unmatched.  Its leading monomial is nonzero.
Iterate this identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Induced-subgraph inheritance]\label{ade:mat:lem:induced}
For $W\subseteq V(G)$,
\begin{equation}
 \left(\prod_{v\notin W}\partial_{z_v}\right)\Phi_G=\Phi_{G[W]}.
\label{ade:mat:eq:induced-derivative}
\end{equation}
Hence signed-support stability passes to induced subgraphs.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Differentiation retains exactly the terms for which the matching support
avoids every deleted vertex, and removes those vertices from the unmatched
monomial. Real stability is preserved by differentiation, with zero as the
only possible exception; here the full remaining monomial has coefficient
one, so the derivative is not zero. The differentiation property follows
from univariate Gauss--Lucas and limits, or from the standard stable
polynomial closure properties \cite{Branden}.
\end{proof}

[Merge note: Lemma~\ref{ade:mat:lem:induced} is the second half of
Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:minors}, for every simple graph.]

\section{Forest cofactors recover Boolean matching supports}
\label{ade:sec:cofactor}

\subsection{Incidence matrices and the single unrooted component}

Fix a tree $T$ on $U=[r]$.  For every edge $e=\{i,j\}$, choose the
column $b_e=e_i-e_j$; reversing a column has no effect on
$b_eb_e^T$.  Let $B$ be the matrix of these columns.
The right apex variable will be denoted by $s$.

Consider $I\subseteq U$, $J\subseteq E(T)$ with $|I|=|J|+1$ and the
rectangular matrix $B_{I,J}$.  A selected edge with both endpoints in $I$
is an \emph{internal edge}.  A selected edge with exactly one endpoint in
$I$ is a \emph{half-edge}.  A selected edge disjoint from $I$ gives a zero
column.  Components below mean components of the internal-edge forest on
$I$, including isolated vertices.

\begin{lemma}[Cofactor support lemma]
\label{ade:lem:forestcofactor}
The pair $(I,J\sqcup\{\star\})$ is matchable in $\calA(T)$ if and only if
there is no zero column, every internal component has at most one
half-edge, and exactly one component $W$ has no half-edge.
In this case
\begin{equation}
 \det[B_{I,J}\ \ w_I]=\pm\sum_{i\in W}w_i.
 \label{ade:eq:cofactor}
\end{equation}
The sign depends on the ordering of rows and columns, not on $w$.
If the pair is not matchable, the determinant vanishes identically.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A component with $k$ rows has $k-1$ internal columns, because the
underlying graph is a forest.  If it has $h$ half-edges, it has
$k-1+h$ selected columns other than the apex.  More than $k$ such columns
cannot all be matched to its rows, so $h\le1$ is necessary.  The apex can
supply a missing column to only one component, so exactly one component
must have $h=0$ and all others must have $h=1$.

Conversely, a component with one half-edge has a square incidence matrix
with determinant $\pm1$.  This follows by peeling off a leaf, or by
rooting the component at that half-edge and matching edges toward their
unique available child rows.  For an unrooted component $W$, the
incidence matrix has rank $|W|-1$.  Deleting any one row gives determinant
$\pm1$, and its left kernel is spanned by $\one_W$.  Appending $w_W$
therefore gives determinant $\pm\sum_{i\in W}w_i$.
Combining the rooted components with this last component proves
\eqref{ade:eq:cofactor} and also constructs a perfect matching when a chosen
apex entry on $W$ is nonzero.
If there is no matching, every term in the Leibniz expansion vanishes,
which proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

The set $W$ is a connected vertex set in $T$, and the induced graph
$T[W]$ contains exactly $|W|-1$ edges.  This uses the uniqueness of paths
in a tree: an omitted tree edge between two vertices of $W$ could not be
replaced by another path in the selected forest.

\subsection{The uniquely determined covariance}

For every connected nonempty vertex set $W\subseteq U$,
\begin{equation}
 \one_W^T C_T\one_W
 =|W|-|E(T[W])|=1,
 \qquad C_T=I-\tfrac12 A_T.
 \label{ade:eq:connectedenergy}
\end{equation}
This simple Euler characteristic is the source of the spectral threshold.

\begin{proposition}[Covariance rigidity]
\label{ade:prop:uniqueC}
If a real symmetric matrix $C$ satisfies
$\one_W^TC\one_W=1$ for every nonempty connected vertex set $W$ of $T$,
then $C=C_T$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Singletons give $C_{ii}=1$.  An adjacent pair gives
$2+2C_{ij}=1$, hence $C_{ij}=-1/2$.
Proceed by induction on the distance between two nonadjacent vertices
$i,j$.  Apply the hypothesis to the vertex set of their unique path.
All entries between closer nonadjacent pairs are zero by induction, and
the diagonal and adjacent-pair contributions already sum to one.
The only remaining contribution is $2C_{ij}$, so it is zero.
\end{proof}

Thus the covariance is not selected merely because it is convenient.
The coefficients corresponding to connected subtrees force it.  In
particular, testing positive semidefiniteness of this specific matrix has
a structural reason.

\subsection{The determinant--adjugate identity}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Boolean coefficient identity]
\label{ade:thm:detidentity}
For every nonempty tree $T$, with $L$ as in \eqref{ade:eq:LCintro},
\begin{equation}
 F_{\calA(T)}(x;y,s)
 =\det L+s\tr\bigl(\adj(L)C_T\bigr).
 \label{ade:eq:detidentity}
\end{equation}
No definiteness assumption is required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Introduce an auxiliary real vector $w$ of indeterminates and use
Cauchy--Binet:
\begin{align}
 \det(L+sww^T)
 &=\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq U,
                   J\subseteq E(T)\\|I|=|J|}}
      x^{U\setminus I}y^J\det(B_{I,J})^2 \notag\\
 &\quad+s\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq U,
                   J\subseteq E(T)\\|I|=|J|+1}}
      x^{U\setminus I}y^J\det[B_{I,J}\ \ w_I]^2.
 \label{ade:eq:CB}
\end{align}
The square minors in the first line are $0$ or $\pm1$ and are nonzero
exactly on matchable supports of the subdivided tree.  Indeed, a forest
has at most one perfect matching on any fixed induced vertex set, so
there is at most one nonzero Leibniz term.

Apply to the coefficients in the second line the linear functional on
quadratic polynomials in $w$ defined by
$w_iw_j\mapsto(C_T)_{ij}$.  By Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:forestcofactor}, a feasible
coefficient becomes $\one_W^TC_T\one_W=1$; an infeasible coefficient stays
zero.  The result is exactly \eqref{ade:eq:Fdef} for $\calA(T)$.
On the other hand, the rank-one determinant identity gives
\[
 \det(L+sww^T)=\det L+s\,w^T\adj(L)w.
\]
Applying the same functional gives \eqref{ade:eq:detidentity}.
This argument takes place in a polynomial ring, so it remains valid when
$L$ is singular and when $C_T$ is indefinite.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the formula is not]
In general \eqref{ade:eq:detidentity} is \emph{not}
$\det(L+sC_T)$.  The latter would include higher powers of $s$ and count
more than one apex column.  Nor does the formula supply a faithful
unit-phase matrix on the edges of $\calA(T)$.  It therefore does not
contradict the repository's much more restrictive cactus classification.
\end{remark}

\section{The spectral criterion and explicit failure certificates}
\label{ade:sec:criterion}

\subsection{Sufficiency, including the affine boundary}

\begin{lemma}[A positive covariance gives stability]
\label{ade:lem:covstable}
Let
$L=\diag(x_i)+\sum_e y_e b_eb_e^T$ with real vectors $b_e$ and let
$0\ne C\succeq0$ be real symmetric.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \det L+s\tr(\adj(L)C)
 \label{ade:eq:resolventstable}
\end{equation}
is nonzero when all $x_i,y_e,s\in\HH$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For these assignments, $\im L\succ0$, because the diagonal imaginary
part is already positive definite and every other summand has
nonnegative imaginary part.  In particular, $L$ is invertible.  Write
\[
 q=\tr(CL^{-1}).
\]
The exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \im L^{-1}=-L^{-*}(\im L)L^{-1}\prec0
 \label{ade:eq:imaginaryinverse}
\end{equation}
implies $\im q<0$, since $C$ is nonzero and positive semidefinite.
Expression~\eqref{ade:eq:resolventstable} equals
$\det L(1+sq)$.  Its vanishing would give $s=-1/q$, whose imaginary part
is negative.  This contradicts $s\in\HH$.
\end{proof}

By Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:detidentity}, $C_T\succeq0$ implies stability of
$F_{\calA(T)}$, and Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge} transfers it to $\Phi$.
The proof includes singular positive semidefinite matrices.  There is no
missing limiting argument at the affine Dynkin diagrams, where $C_T$ has
a one-dimensional kernel.

\subsection{Necessity by a rank-one adjugate}

\begin{theorem}[Rational negative Rayleigh certificate]
\label{ade:thm:negative}
Suppose $\rho(A_T)>2$.  There is a vector $v\in\mathbb Q_{>0}^{r}$ with
$v^TC_Tv<0$.  For any such vector, make the real rational assignments
\begin{align}
 y_{ij}&=\frac1{v_iv_j}\quad(ij\in E(T)),\label{ade:eq:certy}\\
 x_i&=\frac{\deg_T(i)}{v_i^2}
         -\sum_{j\sim i}\frac1{v_iv_j},\qquad s=0.
 \label{ade:eq:certx}
\end{align}
Put $c=\prod_i v_i^{-2}$.  Then, for every $i$,
\begin{equation}
 \del_{s,x_i}F_{\calA(T)}
 =c^2v_i^2(v^TC_Tv)<0.
 \label{ade:eq:explicitRayleigh}
\end{equation}
Consequently neither $F_{\calA(T)}$ nor $\Phi_{\calA(T)}$ is real stable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A connected tree has a strictly positive Perron eigenvector for $A_T$.
Its quadratic form under $C_T$ is negative when the eigenvalue is greater
than two.  Strict inequalities and density of rational vectors give a
positive rational $v$ with the same property.

At \eqref{ade:eq:certy}--\eqref{ade:eq:certx},
\begin{equation}
 L_0=D_v^{-1}\Lap(T)D_v^{-1},\qquad D_v=\diag(v_i).
 \label{ade:eq:rankdeficient}
\end{equation}
The ordinary tree Laplacian has kernel $\R\one$, rank $r-1$, and
adjugate $\one\one^T$.  The last fact follows either from the elementary
incidence cofactors of a tree or from the matrix-tree theorem with its
single spanning tree.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 \det L_0=0,\qquad \adj(L_0)=c\,vv^T.
 \label{ade:eq:adjrankone}
\end{equation}
At $s=0$, Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:detidentity} now gives
\[
 F=0,\qquad F_s=c\,v^TC_Tv,\qquad F_{x_i}=c\,v_i^2.
\]
In the Rayleigh difference, the term $FF_{s,x_i}$ vanishes, leaving
\eqref{ade:eq:explicitRayleigh}.  Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:rayleigh} excludes stability.
\end{proof}

Combining sufficiency and necessity proves the first equivalence in
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:intromain}.  The second follows because a tree is
bipartite, so the adjacency spectrum is symmetric about zero, and the
largest eigenvalue is the spectral radius.  In fact, positive
semidefiniteness of $I-A_T/2$ already says that the largest eigenvalue is
at most two.

\begin{example}[An entirely rational excluded case]
For $T=K_{1,5}$, order the center first and take
$v=(2,1,1,1,1,1)^T$.  Then $v^TC_Tv=-1$, all edge variables are $1/2$,
the center variable is $-5/4$, and the five leaf variables are $1/2$.
With $s=0$, $c=1/4$, so
$\del_{s,x_0}F=-1/4$.
This certificate uses a negative center variable.  Section~\ref{ade:sec:books}
gives a stronger certificate at the all-positive all-ones point for the
same graph.
\end{example}

\subsection{An algorithmic form}

The theorem admits exact certificates on both sides.  A positive result
can be certified by the ADE shape description in the next section or by
an exact rational positive-semidefinite decomposition of $C_T$.
A negative result can be certified by a positive rational vector with
$v^TC_Tv<0$, followed by the explicit formulas above.  Finding the vector
numerically and rationalizing it is legitimate only when the final
quadratic inequality is checked exactly.  No estimated eigenvalue is
needed in the final certificate.

The role of positivity is also sharp at the level of the construction:
Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:uniqueC} shows that no different real symmetric
covariance on the same oriented tree-incidence columns can repair an
indefinite $C_T$ while keeping every connected-support coefficient equal
to one.  The Rayleigh certificate then proves that the failure is not
merely a defect of that particular representation.

\section{Why the stable trees are exactly of ADE type}
\label{ade:sec:ADE}

We now classify the trees with $2I-A_T\succeq0$.  This is a classical
spectral classification, included here with proof to make the main
criterion usable without an external classification theorem.  Its
historical context and the finite/affine diagrams are discussed in
\cite{McKeeSmyth}.

\subsection{The explicit list}

For a tree with one trivalent vertex, its \emph{arm lengths} are the
numbers of edges from that vertex to each of its three leaves.  Sort them
as $a\le b\le c$.

\begin{theorem}[Classical tree list, in explicit form]
\label{ade:thm:ADElist}
A nonempty finite tree $T$ satisfies $\rho(A_T)\le2$ exactly in the
following cases:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
 \item a path $A_r$, $r\ge1$;
 \item one trivalent vertex with arms $(1,1,c)$, $c\ge1$
       (the finite diagram $D_{c+3}$);
 \item one trivalent vertex with arms
       $(1,2,2),(1,2,3),(1,2,4)$
       (respectively $E_6,E_7,E_8$);
 \item one trivalent vertex with arms
       $(2,2,2),(1,3,3),(1,2,5)$
       (respectively $\widetilde E_6,\widetilde E_7,\widetilde E_8$);
 \item the four-leaf star $K_{1,4}=\widetilde D_4$;
 \item two trivalent vertices joined by a path of length $d\ge1$,
       with exactly two additional leaves at each end
       (the diagram $\widetilde D_{d+4}$).
\end{enumerate}
The matrices $2I-A_T$ are positive definite in (a)--(c) and positive
semidefinite of corank one in (d)--(f).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, a proper connected tree extension of a subtree with a strictly
positive adjacency eigenvector of eigenvalue two has spectral radius
greater than two.  To see this directly, extend the eigenvector by zero
outside the smaller graph and then put a small positive value $\ep$ at
one neighboring new vertex.  The quadratic form gains a term linear in
$\ep$, while the squared norm gains only $\ep^2$.  Its Rayleigh quotient
is therefore greater than two for sufficiently small $\ep>0$.

A vertex of degree at least five contains $K_{1,5}$ as a subtree, whose
spectral radius is $\sqrt5>2$.  A vertex of degree four contains
$K_{1,4}$, whose positive eigenvector of eigenvalue two is two at the
center and one at each leaf.  The extension observation forces the whole
tree to equal that star.

Suppose there are at least two trivalent vertices and none of larger
degree.  Choose two with no other trivalent vertex on their connecting
path, and include the two neighbors off the path at each end.  This gives
a double-fork subtree: the connecting path with four attached leaves.
The vector that is two on the path and one on the four leaves is a
positive eigenvector of eigenvalue two.  Again, the tree must equal that
subtree.  This proves (f) and excludes further branching.

With no branching the tree is a path, and $2I-A_T$ is positive definite.
One elementary verification uses successive Schur pivots
$2,3/2,4/3,\ldots,(r+1)/r$, all positive.
With one trivalent vertex, eliminate each of the three path arms.
For an arm of length $a$, the endpoint entry of the inverse of its
path matrix $2I-A_{A_a}$ is $a/(a+1)$; the same Schur recursion proves
this.  The remaining center pivot is nonnegative exactly when
\begin{equation}
 2-\frac a{a+1}-\frac b{b+1}-\frac c{c+1}\ge0,
 \quad\text{or equivalently}\quad
 \frac1{a+1}+\frac1{b+1}+\frac1{c+1}\ge1.
 \label{ade:eq:arms}
\end{equation}
If $a\ge3$, this is impossible.  If $a=2$, it forces $b=c=2$.
If $a=1$, then $b=1$ permits every $c\ge1$; $b=2$ permits
$c=2,3,4,5$; $b=3$ permits only $c=3$; and $b\ge4$ is impossible.
These are exactly (b)--(d).  The strict and equality cases of the center
pivot give the stated ranks.  The positive eigenvectors already displayed
handle (e)--(f), or one may eliminate their four leaves and use a path
Schur calculation.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
$r$ & 1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8&9\\
\midrule
All unlabeled trees &1&1&1&2&3&6&11&23&47\\
Stable incidence--apex types &1&1&1&2&3&4&5&5&4\\

The stable count for every $r\ge10$ is three, by the classification:
