\end{table}

\subsection{Consequences for the graph family}

The restriction is on the \emph{auxiliary tree} $T$, not on the number of
cycles of $\calA(T)$.  Even a path $T=A_r$ gives arbitrarily large graphs
with overlapping cycles and stable support polynomials.  Thus the theorem
goes well beyond cactus graphs in a controlled family.

On the other hand, the first excluded auxiliary trees occur at six
vertices.  There are six unlabeled trees on six vertices; only
$A_6,D_6,E_6,\widetilde D_5$ qualify.  One excluded type is $K_{1,5}$,
which produces the five-page book.  The other is a proper extension of
$K_{1,4}$.  Their exclusion follows from explicit certificates, not from
an extrapolation of Table~\ref{ade:tab:ADEcounts}.

The equivalence also distinguishes three logically different statements.
A tree may fail the spectral test and hence multivariate stability;
its univariate diagonal may nevertheless remain real-rooted.  The book
family proves this separation exactly.  Finally, even on the stable
side, the polynomial need not admit the repository's faithful
vertex-indexed determinant.  Stability is the broad analytic property;
a faithful determinant is a much narrower representation.

\section{Subdividing between apex neighbors}
\label{ade:sec:subdivision}

\subsection{The terminal-skeleton construction}

Let $T$ be a tree, whose vertices will be called \emph{terminals}.
Replace each edge of $T$ by a path of positive length, using internally
disjoint paths, to obtain a tree $\widehat T$.  The terminal set is still
$V(T)\subseteq V(\widehat T)$.  Define $\calA(\widehat T;T)$ to have left
vertices $V(\widehat T)$, right vertices $E(\widehat T)\sqcup\{\star\}$,
and the usual incidence edges.  The apex is adjacent to terminals only.
In particular, inserting a new left vertex does \emph{not} make it a new
apex neighbor.

Embed $C_T$ into a matrix $\widehat C_T$ on $V(\widehat T)$ by putting
zeros in every row and column belonging to a nonterminal.  Use the
incidence vectors of $\widehat T$ to define $\widehat L$.

\begin{theorem}[Subdivision invariance of the criterion]
\label{ade:thm:subdivision}
For every terminal-skeleton construction above,
\begin{equation}
 F_{\calA(\widehat T;T)}
 =\det\widehat L+s\tr\bigl(\adj(\widehat L)\widehat C_T\bigr).
 \label{ade:eq:subdivisionidentity}
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{\calA(\widehat T;T)}\text{ is real stable}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \rho(A_T)\le2.
 \label{ade:eq:subdivisioncriterion}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the identity and sufficiency]
Use the same forest-cofactor argument as before.  A potentially nonzero
apex minor has a unique unrooted component $W$ of selected rows.  Because
the apex vector is supported only on terminals, its cofactor expression
is $\pm\sum_{i\in W\cap V(T)}w_i$.

If $S=W\cap V(T)$ is empty, the endpoint pair is not matchable using the
apex and the quadratic functional gives zero.  If $S$ is nonempty, it is
a connected vertex set in the skeleton $T$.  Indeed, a connected set in
$\widehat T$ containing two terminals contains their entire unique path,
including every intervening terminal.  Therefore
\[
 \one_W^T\widehat C_T\one_W
 =\one_S^TC_T\one_S=1.
\]
This proves \eqref{ade:eq:subdivisionidentity} coefficient by coefficient.
If $C_T\succeq0$, its zero extension is positive semidefinite and nonzero,
so Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:covstable} proves stability.
\end{proof}

For necessity we record the precise minor operation.  It is important not
to assume that arbitrary graph edge contraction preserves the support
polynomial.

\begin{lemma}[Generic path shortening]
\label{ade:lem:shorten}
Suppose a bipartite graph contains a path
$a-c-b-d$, where $a,b$ are left vertices and $c,d$ are right vertices.
Assume $b$ has only neighbors $c,d$, $c$ has only neighbors $a,b$, and
there is no edge $a-d$.  In the canonical matroid, contract the right
element $c$ and delete the left identity element $b$.  The resulting
matroid is the canonical matroid of the graph obtained by removing $b,c$
and replacing the path by the edge $a-d$, leaving all other incidences
unchanged.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the generic representation $[I\ K]$ of
Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:matroid}.  The column for $c$ is
$\alpha e_a+\beta e_b$, with independent nonzero indeterminates.
In the quotient by this column,
$e_b=-(\alpha/\beta)e_a$.  Deleting the identity element $b$ leaves the
other identity elements as a basis of the quotient.  The only other
column affected is $d$, where its $b$ entry $\gamma$ becomes the new
$a$ entry $-\alpha\gamma/\beta$.

There is no preexisting $a-d$ entry to combine with it.  The new entry is
algebraically independent of all remaining edge entries: the variable
$\gamma$ occurred nowhere else and can be solved from the new entry after
adjoining the discarded nonzero parameters $\alpha,\beta$.
Thus the resulting zero pattern has a generic representation of exactly
the shortened graph, as claimed.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:subdivision}]
Apply Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:shorten} repeatedly to every inserted nonterminal of
$\widehat T$.  Such a vertex has degree two and is not adjacent to the
apex, and the tree condition ensures there is no preexisting shortcut
edge.  We obtain $\mathsf M_{\calA(T)}$ as a matroid minor.  If the subdivided
polynomial were stable, Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:minors} and the inversion bridge
would force stability of $\Phi_{\calA(T)}$.  Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:negative}
then forces $\rho(A_T)\le2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the terminal convention matters}

Subdividing and then joining the apex to \emph{all} new left vertices is
a different construction: it replaces the skeleton itself by
$\widehat T$ and tests $\rho(A_{\widehat T})$.  The theorem does not say
that this modified operation is neutral.  The invariant is the tree
connecting the designated apex neighbors after suppressing the new
nonterminals.  This distinction is particularly visible for books: the
common spine endpoints stay fixed, while a page path can be lengthened
without adding new apex edges.

[Added 30 September 2026, batch 63: when the apex neighbourhood is not the
terminal set, an unmarked vertex of degree at least three in the subtree
spanned by the neighbours forbids stability (Part~VIII,
Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:branch}), and otherwise the suppressed skeleton decides
(Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main}).]

\section{Quadrilateral books: four stable pages, all-real diagonals}
\label{ade:sec:books}

\subsection{The graph and its spectral threshold}

The graph $B_m$ has left vertices $u,b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and right vertices
$v,a_1,\ldots,a_m$.  Its edges are
\begin{equation}
 uv,\qquad ua_i,\quad a_ib_i,\quad b_iv\quad(1\le i\le m).
 \label{ade:eq:bookedges}
\end{equation}
For $m=0$ it is a single edge.  For $m=1$ it is a four-cycle.  For
$m\ge2$ the pages overlap in the edge $uv$, so it is not a cactus.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.05,
 leftv/.style={circle,draw=Ink,fill=Ink,inner sep=2.8pt},
 rightv/.style={circle,draw=Ink,fill=white,inner sep=2.8pt}]
 \node[leftv,label={left:{$u$}}] (u) at (0,0) {};
 \node[rightv,label={right:{$v=\star$}}] (v) at (5,0) {};
 \foreach \i/\y in {1/1.3,2/0,3/-1.3}{
   \node[rightv,label={above:{$a_{\i}$}}] (a\i) at (1.6,\y) {};
   \node[leftv,label={above:{$b_{\i}$}}] (b\i) at (3.4,\y) {};
   \draw[Ink] (u)--(a\i)--(b\i)--(v);
 }
 \draw[Ink] (u) .. controls (0.9,-2.3) and (4.1,-2.3) ..
   node[midway,below=3pt] {\small common edge} (v);
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{The three-page book $B_3=\calA(K_{1,3})$.
Filled and open vertices indicate the two bipartition classes.
Each displayed three-edge path, together with the common edge, is a page.}
\label{ade:fig:book}
\end{figure}

The matrix forced by the cofactor identity is
\begin{equation}
 C_{K_{1,m}}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&-\tfrac12\one^T\\
  -\tfrac12\one&I_m
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \label{ade:eq:starC}
\end{equation}
Its Schur complement is $1-m/4$.  Hence the matrix is positive
semidefinite exactly when $m\le4$, proving the stability threshold in
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introbook}.  By Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:subdivision}, the same
threshold holds for a common edge together with $m$ odd paths of any
length at least three.

[Merge note: in Part~II's labelling, $B_m$ is $\Theta_m$ plus the edge
$d\,b_0$ joining its endpoints: source~08's $u,v,a_i,b_i$ are Part~II's
$d,b_0,b_i,a_i$, with the letters $a_i$, $b_i$ exchanged
(Section~\ref{htwo:sec:theta} draws $\Theta_m$). The formula of
Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bookp} is Part~II's~\eqref{htwo:eq:thetapoly} plus
$u$: $p_{B_m}(u)=p_{\Theta_m}(u)+u$, the single extra support being the edge
$d\,b_0$ itself.]

\subsection{A closed form for the entire univariate family}

\begin{proposition}[Book support polynomial]
\label{ade:prop:bookp}
For $m\ge2$, formula \eqref{ade:eq:introbook} holds.  The two smaller cases are
$p_{B_0}(t)=1+t$ and $p_{B_1}(t)=1+4t+t^2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In the identity of Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:detidentity}, put every left variable
equal to one and every right variable, including the apex, equal to $t$.
With the center first, the matrix $L$ is
\begin{equation}
 L=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1+mt&-t\one^T\\
 -t\one&(1+t)I_m
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \label{ade:eq:bookL}
\end{equation}
Let $d=1+t$ and $S=1+mt/d$.  Its determinant is $d^mS$, and block
inversion gives
\begin{equation}
 \tr(C_{K_{1,m}}L^{-1})
 =\frac m d+\frac{1-mt/d^2}{S}.
 \label{ade:eq:bookresolvent}
\end{equation}
For example, the center diagonal contributes $1/S$, the leaf diagonals
contribute $m/d+mt^2/(d^2S)$, and the two off-diagonal blocks of $C$
together subtract $mt/(dS)$, which combine to
\eqref{ade:eq:bookresolvent}.  Thus
\begin{align*}
 p_{B_m}(t)
 &=d^m\left[S+t\left(\frac{mS}{d}+1-\frac{mt}{d^2}\right)\right]\\
 &=d^{m-2}\bigl(1+(2m+3)t+(m^2+m+3)t^2+t^3\bigr).
\end{align*}
The calculation is an identity of rational functions that simplifies to
a polynomial, and therefore holds at the values initially excluded by
block inversion.  At $m=0,1$ the apparent negative powers of $d$ cancel,
giving the two separately stated polynomials.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Every book diagonal is real-rooted]
\label{ade:thm:bookreal}
For every $m\ge0$, all zeros of $p_{B_m}$ are real and negative.
For $m\ge2$, its three cubic-factor zeros are distinct, and the
multiplicity of $-1$ is exactly $m-2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put
\[
 Q_m(t)=1+(2m+3)t+(m^2+m+3)t^2+t^3.
\]
The cubic discriminant is the exact expression
\begin{equation}
 \disc_t Q_m=m^2(8m^3+13m^2+54m-27)>0
 \quad(m\ge2).
 \label{ade:eq:cubicdisc}
\end{equation}
For a transparent positivity check, put $m=k+2$; the factor in parentheses
becomes $8k^3+61k^2+202k+197$.
A real cubic with positive discriminant has three distinct real roots.
Its positive coefficients and constant coefficient one exclude zero and
positive roots, so all three are negative.
Since $Q_m(-1)=m(m-1)>0$, none equals $-1$.
The cases $m=0,1$ follow directly from their displayed formulas.
\end{proof}

Every $B_m$ is chordal bipartite: a cycle using the common edge is a
four-cycle, while a cycle using two page paths has the common edge as a
chord.  For $m\ge1$ it has treewidth two, as seen by gluing the
width-two decompositions of the four-cycle pages along the common edge.
Consequently this is an infinite connected, chordal-bipartite,
treewidth-two family in which the diagonal is real-rooted for every size
but multivariate stability fails from $m=5$ onward.  No general first
separation between real-rootedness and stability is claimed; the result
here is this explicit sharp family and its exact threshold.

\subsection{A positive-weight Rayleigh failure and its probability law}

Let $a$ be the left center variable and $b$ the right apex variable, and
set all other variables of $F_{B_m}$ equal to one.  The same block
calculation, now with edge variables one, gives
\begin{equation}
 F_{B_m}(a,b)=2^m\left[
 a+\frac m2+b\left(\frac m2\left(a+\frac m2\right)
                       +1-\frac m4\right)\right].
 \label{ade:eq:bookbivariate}
\end{equation}
Its Rayleigh difference is independent of $a,b$:
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad\del_{a,b}F_{B_m}=4^{m-1}(4-m).\quad}
 \label{ade:eq:bookdelta}
\end{equation}
This also holds for $m=0$, with the expression interpreted as the rational
number $4^{-1}\cdot4=1$.

For a homogeneous multiaffine basis polynomial $F$ with nonnegative
coefficients, the uniform basis measure has
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(\one_{i\in B},\one_{j\in B})
 =\frac{F(\one)F_{ij}(\one)-F_i(\one)F_j(\one)}{F(\one)^2}
 =-\frac{\del_{ij}F(\one)}{F(\one)^2}.
 \label{ade:eq:covrayleigh}
\end{equation}
For books,
\begin{equation}
 Z_m=F_{B_m}(\one)=2^{m-2}(m^2+3m+8),
 \label{ade:eq:bookZ}
\end{equation}
and hence
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(\one_{u\in B},\one_{\star\in B})
 =\frac{4(m-4)}{(m^2+3m+8)^2}.
 \label{ade:eq:bookcov}
\end{equation}

\begin{example}[Five pages, with all counts exposed]
For $B_5$ there are $384$ bases.  The numbers containing the center, the
apex, and both are respectively $112,272,80$.  Thus
\[
 \del_{u,\star}F=112\cdot272-384\cdot80=-256,
 \qquad
 \Cov(\one_{u\in B},\one_{\star\in B})=\frac1{576}>0.
\]
The univariate polynomial is nevertheless
\[
 p_{B_5}(t)=1+16t+75t^2+140t^3+115t^4+36t^5+t^6
           =(1+t)^3(1+13t+33t^2+t^3).
\]
The random objects here are bases of $\mathsf M_{B_5}$, not uniformly random
perfect matchings.  In the support correspondence, the left center is
in the basis when it is \emph{not} in the matched left endpoint set,
whereas the apex is in the basis when it \emph{is} in the matched right
endpoint set.  This distinction prevents an incorrect interpretation of
the covariance as a matching-multiplicity statement.
\end{example}

\section{Independent columns and all even-path multi-theta graphs}
\label{ade:sec:even}

The tree covariance construction does not include all stable multi-theta
graphs.  When the two endpoints are in the same bipartition class, a
separate expected-determinant argument works for arbitrarily many paths.
We give the analytic closure lemma first, because an arbitrary average of
stable polynomials need not be stable.

\subsection{A squarefree expected-determinant lemma}

\begin{lemma}[A differential stability operation]
\label{ade:lem:operator}
If $f$ is stable, then $f+y\partial_z f$, with $y$ a new variable, is
stable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix all original variables other than $z$ in $\HH$.  The resulting
nonzero polynomial in $z$ has roots outside $\HH$.  At $z\in\HH$, its
logarithmic derivative is a sum of terms $1/(z-\alpha)$, each of negative
imaginary part.  It is either zero because the polynomial is constant, or
has negative imaginary part.  In the nonconstant case,
$f+yf_z=f(1+y f_z/f)$ could vanish only at
$y=-1/(f_z/f)$, which is in the lower half-plane.  The constant case is
immediate.  This applies at every upper-half-plane assignment.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Independent-column expectation]
\label{ade:thm:expected}
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_c$ be independent real random column vectors in
$\R^r$, with finite second moments.  Then
\begin{equation}
 P(x;y)=\EE\det\left(\diag(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^c y_j a_ja_j^T\right)
 \label{ade:eq:expected}
\end{equation}
is real stable.  It has coefficient one on $\prod_i x_i$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $C_j=\EE(a_ja_j^T)\succeq0$.  The polynomial
\[
 H(x;z)=\det\left(\diag(x_i)+\sum_j z_j C_j\right)
\]
is stable, because the imaginary part of its matrix is positive definite
at upper-half-plane assignments.
Apply Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:operator} once for each variable $z_j$, then
specialize all $z_j$ to zero.  The resulting polynomial is stable or zero,
and is
\begin{equation}
 \left.
 \prod_{j=1}^c(1+y_j\partial_{z_j})H(x;z)
 \right|_{z_1=\cdots=z_c=0}.
 \label{ade:eq:squarefreeoperator}
\end{equation}
Its $x_1\cdots x_r$ coefficient is one, so it is not zero.

It remains to identify it with \eqref{ade:eq:expected}.  A rank-one update
$a_ja_j^T$ appears at most linearly in the determinant as a function of
$y_j$.  For a squarefree set of selected columns, the coefficient is
multilinear in their outer products.  Independence permits replacing each
outer product by its expectation.  This is exactly the squarefree
coefficient of $\prod z_j$ selected by \eqref{ade:eq:squarefreeoperator}.
Equivalently, expand squared minors by Cauchy--Binet and take the
expectation of the product of the two entries contributed by each column.
Only that column's second moment is used.
\end{proof}

This lemma is an elementary instance of the established stability
machinery around positive-semidefinite determinants and differential
operators \cite{COSW,Branden}.  Its use here is to realize Boolean support
coefficients for a particular graph family.  Independence of the columns
and the squarefree truncation are essential; the proof is not a claim
that all convex combinations preserve stability.

\subsection{The random incidence construction}

Let $G$ consist of $q\ge2$ internally disjoint paths of lengths
$2\ell_1,\ldots,2\ell_q$, each joining the left endpoint $u$ to the left
endpoint $v$.  Every right vertex lies between two consecutive left
vertices along a path.  Orient each path from $u$ to $v$.

Create a random matrix $K$ with rows indexed by left vertices and columns
by right vertices.  On an ordinary path column between consecutive left
vertices $a,b$, use $e_a-e_b$.  On the \emph{first} right column of path
$i$, instead use
\begin{equation}
 e_u+\ep_i e_b,
 \qquad
 \Pr(\ep_i=1)=\frac{1-1/\sqrt2}{2},\quad
 \Pr(\ep_i=-1)=\frac{1+1/\sqrt2}{2}.
 \label{ade:eq:signlaw}
\end{equation}
The signs are independent, so $\EE\ep_i=-1/\sqrt2$ and
$\ep_i^2=1$.  When $\ell_i=1$, the first column is also the only column
on the path; the construction still applies.

\begin{lemma}[Expected minor weights are exactly Boolean]
\label{ade:lem:evenminors}
For every pair of equally sized row and column sets $I,J$,
\begin{equation}
 \EE\det(K_{I,J})^2
 =\begin{cases}
   1,&(I,J)\in\PM(G),\\
   0,&(I,J)\notin\PM(G).
  \end{cases}
 \label{ade:eq:evenweights}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An unsupported minor vanishes structurally.  Suppose the support is
matchable.  It cannot contain three complete endpoint-to-endpoint paths.
Indeed, for $k\ge3$ complete paths, the right vertices on those paths
number $\sum\ell_i$, while their left neighbors number
\[
 2+\sum(\ell_i-1)=\sum\ell_i+2-k<\sum\ell_i.
\]
Hall's condition for matching those columns fails.  Every cycle of a
multi-theta graph uses two complete paths, so a matchable selected support
has at most one cycle.

A forest support has at most one perfect matching.  The corresponding
determinant then has one term of magnitude one, giving expectation one.
A support with one cycle has either one perfect matching, covered by the
same argument, or two.  In the two-matching case, the matchings agree off
the cycle and alternate on it.  The cycle consists of two complete paths,
say $i,j$.  The squared magnitudes of the two determinant terms are both
one.  Their product depends on the two random first-column signs
$\ep_i,\ep_j$ and on no other random sign with odd exponent.

If both special columns were ordinary oriented-incidence columns
($\ep_i=\ep_j=-1$), the two terms would cancel: they are the two terms
of a cycle-incidence determinant.  Therefore their product, as a function
of the actual signs, is $-\ep_i\ep_j$.  Its expectation is $-1/2$.
The expected squared sum is consequently $1+1+2(-1/2)=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Even multi-theta stability]
\label{ade:thm:eventheta}
Every simple multi-theta graph whose paths all have even length has real
stable signed matching-support polynomial.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Cauchy--Binet and Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:evenminors} give
\[
 F_G(x;y)=\EE\det(\diag(x)+K\diag(y)K^T).
\]
The random columns of $K$ are independent, with the nonspecial columns
viewed as constant random variables.  Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:expected} proves
stability of $F_G$, and Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge} transfers it to
$\Phi_G$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Arbitrarily many even paths]
The graph $K_{2,q}$ has $q$ paths of length two. [Merge note: it is also the case $\ell=2$ of source~09's Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:biclique}, which proves every $K_{\ell,r}$ stable.]  Its support polynomial is
\[
 p_{K_{2,q}}(t)=1+2qt+\binom q2t^2.
\]
The theorem strengthens real-rootedness of this quadratic to multivariate
stability, for every $q$.  More generally, it permits any positive even
length on each path, not only length two.  Exact examples are
\[
 p_{\vartheta(2,2,4)}=1+8t+16t^2+4t^3,
 \qquad
 p_{\vartheta(4,4,4)}=1+12t+51t^2+92t^3+63t^4+6t^5.
\]
The examples illustrate the theorem, but their finite verification is not
its proof.
\end{example}

\section{The full simple bipartite multi-theta classification}
\label{ade:sec:theta}

\subsection{The single-cycle case}

\begin{lemma}[Even cycles are stable]
\label{ade:lem:cycle}
If $G$ is a simple even cycle, then $\Phi_G$ is real stable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Index the cycle so that each right column lies between two consecutive
left vertices.  Use oriented-incidence columns except at one right
vertex, where the two entries are $1,\ep$ with
$\Pr(\ep=1)=1/4$ and $\Pr(\ep=-1)=3/4$.
Every proper matchable square support is a forest and has a unique
matching, hence squared determinant one.  The full support has two
alternating matchings.  Their product is $\ep$: at $\ep=-1$ the oriented
incidence determinant cancels.  Its expected squared determinant is
$2+2\EE\ep=1$.
Thus the expected determinant is $F_G$, and
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:expected} proves stability.  This is an alternative
short proof of a special case already included in the cactus results
of the repository and the surrounding literature.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Second proof of Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:cycle}, source~09]
Source~09's Proposition~\ref{ade:mat:prop:cycles} (Section~\ref{ade:mat:sec:stable-families})
proves the same statement with a Hermitian adjacency matrix whose cycle phase
has real part $(-1)^r/2$, so that $\Phi_{C_{2r}}$ is a vertex determinant;
it is Part~II's cactus construction for one cycle, as source~09 says.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The credited three-odd-path obstruction}

The graph $\vartheta(3,3,3)$ has left vertices $u,b_1,b_2,b_3$, right
vertices $v,a_1,a_2,a_3$, and edges $ua_i,a_ib_i,b_iv$ for $1\le i\le3$.
It is the three-page book \emph{with its common edge removed}.
Its polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 p_{\vartheta(3,3,3)}(t)=1+9t+24t^2+16t^3+t^4.
 \label{ade:eq:thetaobstruction}
\end{equation}
For completeness, its coefficients can be checked without numerical
search.  There are nine edges.  For a two-element left set containing
$u$, there are five matchable two-element right sets, giving $3\cdot5$;
for a left set $\{b_i,b_j\}$ there are three, giving $3\cdot3$.
Every three-element left set can be matched to every three-element right
set, giving $4\cdot4=16$.  The full set is matchable and contributes one.

The exact discriminant is
\begin{equation}
 \disc_t(1+9t+24t^2+16t^3+t^4)=-5243<0.
 \label{ade:eq:thetadisc}
\end{equation}
A real polynomial all of whose roots are real has nonnegative
discriminant, so this is a nonreal-root obstruction.  It follows from
Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge} that $\Phi_{\vartheta(3,3,3)}$ is not stable.
The repository credits the corresponding earlier preorder counterexample
to Shivam Patel.  Equation~\eqref{ade:eq:thetaobstruction} is reproduced as
an exact input to the classification, not as a new first disproof.

\paragraph{Source~09's certificates for the same graph.}
Source~09 prints the same obstruction in Part~II's labelling
(Section~\ref{ade:mat:sec:examples}), with a Sturm chain for the diagonal
and an exact Rayleigh certificate for the multivariate polynomial. As
delivered:
Let $\Theta_3$ have endpoints $0,1$ and three internally disjoint
length-three paths
\[
 0-2-3-1,\qquad0-4-5-1,\qquad0-6-7-1.
\]
The repository credits the first preorder real-rootedness counterexample
based on this graph to Shivam Patel, not to its own later report
(Part~II, Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:thetaintro}; \cite{Patel}). We do not claim the counterexample as new.
Direct support enumeration gives
\begin{equation}
 p_{\Theta_3}(u)=1+9u+24u^2+16u^3+u^4.
\label{ade:mat:eq:theta-p}
\end{equation}
A positively rescaled Sturm chain is
\begin{align*}
 q_0&=u^4+16u^3+24u^2+9u+1,\\
 q_1&=4u^3+48u^2+48u+9,\\
 q_2&=144u^2+165u+32,\\
 q_3&=4557u+1120,\\
 q_4&=-1.
\end{align*}
At $-\infty$ the signs are $+,-,+,-,-$, giving three variations; at
$+\infty$ they are $+,+,+,+,-$, giving one. Hence the quartic has exactly
two real roots. The other two are nonreal.

[Merge note: source~09 then derives $h_{P_{\Theta_3}}$ and checks its
ultra-log-concavity at $k=1$; that display is Part~V's~\eqref{lor:eq:thetah}
and is not repeated.]
\subsection{A small exact failure of multivariate stability}
For a multi-affine polynomial $f$, its Rayleigh difference is
\[
 \Delta_{ij}f=(\partial_i f)(\partial_j f)-f\,\partial_i\partial_j f.
\]
If $f$ is real stable, this expression is nonnegative at every real
assignment of the other variables. One can see the necessity directly:
a real bivariate specialization has the form
$a xy+b x+c y+d$, and its potential root
$y=-(bx+d)/(ax+c)$ has imaginary part
$(ad-bc)\im(x)/|ax+c|^2$. Stability therefore forces
$bc-ad\geq0$. Real specializations follow by a limit; if the specialization
is zero the Rayleigh difference is zero. This is the necessary direction
of the multi-affine criterion of \cite{Branden}.

For $f=\Phi_{\Theta_3}$ and the endpoints $i=0,j=1$, set
\begin{equation}
 (z_2,z_3,z_4,z_5,z_6,z_7)=(3,2,-2,-2,2,2).
\label{ade:mat:eq:ray-assignment}
\end{equation}
The resulting bivariate polynomial is
\[
 f(z_0,z_1)=45z_0z_1-27z_0-18z_1+11,
\]
so $\Delta_{01}f=(-27)(-18)-45\cdot11=-9$.
The included standard-library
program recomputes this integer directly from feasible vertex subsets.
Thus the corresponding matroid polynomial is Lorentzian but not stable.
Negative coordinates in this certificate are legitimate: real stability
requires the Rayleigh inequalities at \emph{all} real assignments, not only
positive activities.

\subsection{Proof of the classification}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta}]
If the common endpoints belong to the same bipartition class, all paths
are even, and Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:eventheta} applies.

Suppose all paths are odd and none has length one.  With two paths the
graph is an even cycle, so Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:cycle} applies.
With at least three paths, choose three and delete all internal vertices
of the others.  This is an induced subgraph.  Each remaining odd path
has length at least three.  While a path has length at least five, apply
Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:shorten} at its first two internal vertices, starting at
the left common endpoint.  Those two vertices have degree two and there
is no existing shortcut edge.  The operation decreases its length by
two.  Repeating gives the canonical matroid of $\vartheta(3,3,3)$ as a
minor.  A stable original basis polynomial would force a stable basis
polynomial on that minor, contradicting \eqref{ade:eq:thetadisc}.

Finally, suppose there is one one-edge path and $m$ other paths.
Every other path is odd of length at least three.  This graph is exactly
the terminal-skeleton construction of a star with $m$ leaves: the star
center is the left spine endpoint, its leaves are the last left vertices
on the page paths, and the right apex is the other spine endpoint.
Lengths greater than three come from nonterminal subdivisions of the
star arms.  Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:subdivision} and the Schur complement
$1-m/4$ prove the criterion $m\le4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{p{0.46\textwidth}p{0.40\textwidth}}
\toprule
Path pattern & Exact stability condition\\
\midrule
All paths even & Always stable, with any number of paths\\
All paths odd, no direct edge & Stable exactly for two paths\\
One direct edge and $m$ other odd paths & Stable exactly for $m\le4$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Classification of simple bipartite multi-theta graphs.
The distinction between a direct edge and a lengthened path is essential.}
\label{ade:tab:thetas}
\end{table}

\subsection{Subdivision can hide a diagonal obstruction}

The minor proof cannot be replaced by a blanket claim that all odd
three-path diagonals are nonreal-rooted.  For example,
\begin{equation}
 p_{\vartheta(3,3,5)}(t)
 =1+11t+41t^2+59t^3+25t^4+t^5
 \label{ade:eq:theta335}
\end{equation}
has five negative real roots, although its multivariate polynomial is
not stable by the classification.
A completely rational root certificate is obtained from the following
five disjoint open intervals:
\begin{equation}
 (-23,-22),\quad(-2,-1),\quad(-1/2,-2/5),\quad
 (-1/3,-1/4),\quad(-1/4,-1/5).
 \label{ade:eq:theta335intervals}
\end{equation}
The signs at their endpoints alternate within each interval.  More
explicitly, the values at
$-23,-22,-2,-1,-1/2,-2/5,-1/3,-1/4,-1/5$ are respectively
\[
 -136734,\ 94139,\ 39,\ -4,\ -3/32,\ 43/3125,\
 2/243,\ -13/1024,\ 24/3125.
\]
The intermediate value theorem gives five distinct roots, exhausting the
degree.  Thus even an odd-path graph whose obstruction becomes visible
through a matroid minor can have an entirely real-rooted diagonal.
This is a second reason to formulate the classification genuinely
multivariately.


\subsection{Infinitely many induced-minimal obstructions (merge observation)}
\label{ade:sec:inducedminimal}
Source~09 asks (Research question~\ref{ade:q:last}) whether the unstable
bipartite graphs have a finite set of induced-minimal obstructions within a
fixed treewidth or maximum-degree class. Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta}(ii)
answers this negatively, although neither source says so. Every
$\vartheta(a,b,c)$ with $a,b,c$ odd and at least three is bipartite,
subcubic, of treewidth two, and unstable. Every proper induced subgraph of
it is a cactus: deleting an internal vertex of one path leaves a cycle with
a pendant path, deleting an endpoint leaves a tree, and induced subgraphs of
cacti are cacti. Bipartite cacti have stable $\Phi$ by Part~II's
Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:stability}. Hence each such $\vartheta(a,b,c)$ is an
induced-minimal unstable graph, and there are infinitely many of them in the
class of subcubic graphs of treewidth two. Source~09's same question also
names subdivisions of theta graphs as ``a useful first target'' of its first
question; Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta} is exactly that classification.

\section{Closure, weights, and preorder consequences}
\label{ade:sec:consequences}

\subsection{Articulation gluing and tree attachments}

\noindent\emph{Source~08 proves the one-vertex gluing theorem for two
bipartite graphs with aligned bipartitions (its Proposition~10.1). Source~09
proves the same theorem for all simple graphs, with the same formula and
argument, and adds block localization. It is printed once, in source~09's
form (as delivered, its Section~12).}

\label{ade:mat:sec:blocks}
Suppose $G_1,G_2$ have exactly one common vertex $v$, and no edges run
between their other vertices. Write $G=G_1\vee_vG_2$ and
\[
 \Phi_{G_i}=z_v A_i+B_i,\qquad A_i=\Phi_{G_i-v}.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Support-exact vertex sum]\label{ade:mat:lem:vertex-sum}
For arbitrary finite simple graphs in this configuration,
\begin{align}
 \Phi_G&=z_vA_1A_2+B_1A_2+A_1B_2 \label{ade:mat:eq:vertex-sum}\\
       &=\Phi_{G_1}A_2+A_1\Phi_{G_2}-z_vA_1A_2.\notag
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A support avoiding $v$ is matchable exactly when its restrictions to the two
pieces are matchable; this gives the first term. A support containing $v$
must match $v$ to a vertex in exactly one piece. In that piece the number
of selected vertices other than $v$ is odd; in the other it is even.
These parities identify the piece uniquely from the support, irrespective
of the matching witness. Therefore the two remaining cases are disjoint
and contribute $B_1A_2$ and $A_1B_2$. The sign exponents add and the
unmatched monomials multiply, establishing the formula without counting
any support twice.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Stability under a one-vertex sum]\label{ade:mat:thm:vertex-stable}
The polynomial $\Phi_{G_1\vee_vG_2}$ is real stable if and only if both
$\Phi_{G_1}$ and $\Phi_{G_2}$ are real stable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows from induced-subgraph inheritance. For sufficiency,
fix every variable other than $z_v$ in $\HH$. Each $A_i$ is a nonzero
stable polynomial, so $A_i\ne0$ at the chosen values. Since
$z_vA_i+B_i$ has no zero with $z_v\in\HH$, its sole zero
$-B_i/A_i$ lies outside $\HH$. Thus
\[
 \im(B_i/A_i)\geq0.
\]
By \eqref{ade:mat:eq:vertex-sum},
\[
 \frac{\Phi_G}{A_1A_2}=z_v+B_1/A_1+B_2/A_2.
\]
The right-hand side has strictly positive imaginary part for $z_v\in\HH$.
It cannot vanish. This proves stability.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact block localization]\label{ade:mat:cor:blocks}
A finite simple graph has stable signed-support polynomial if and only if
every block does. Here bridges are two-vertex blocks and isolated vertices
may be treated separately as one-vertex blocks.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For disjoint unions, $\Phi$ is a product. A connected graph is assembled
from its blocks by successive one-vertex sums, along its block-cut tree.
Use Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:vertex-stable} repeatedly. Conversely every block is
an induced subgraph on its vertex set, so Lemma~\ref{ade:mat:lem:induced} applies.
\end{proof}

This answers the articulation-gluing problem completely. It reduces, but
does not solve, the classification of stable bipartite graphs to their
2-connected blocks. Ordinary univariate real-rootedness alone is not the
hypothesis of the gluing theorem.

On the diagonal, \eqref{ade:mat:eq:vertex-sum} gives the useful recurrence
\begin{equation}
 p_{G_1\vee_vG_2}
 =p_{G_1}p_{G_2-v}+p_{G_1-v}p_{G_2}-p_{G_1-v}p_{G_2-v}.
\label{ade:mat:eq:p-vertex}
\end{equation}
Its stability consequence requires the multivariate argument, not merely
inspection of this subtraction formula.

In particular, attaching arbitrary trees at any vertices preserves
stability, and cannot repair a nonstable core.  Thus every stable family
in this article yields a larger family by tree attachments.  This closure
principle is routine stability machinery, included with proof to specify
what is and is not preserved.  It is not a replacement for the
classification of the two-connected core.

\subsection{Positive vertex weights}

For positive real weights $w_v$, define the weighted support polynomial
\begin{equation}
 p_{G,w}(t)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(G)}
       t^{|I|}\prod_{u\in I}w_u\prod_{v\in J}w_v.
 \label{ade:eq:weightedp}
\end{equation}
The inversion bridge gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 p_{G,w}(t)=\left(\prod_{u\in U}w_u\right)
 F_G\bigl((w_u^{-1})_{u\in U};(tw_v)_{v\in V}\bigr).
 \label{ade:eq:weightbridge}
\end{equation}
Consequently every stable graph proved here has a real-rooted weighted
support polynomial for \emph{every} positive vertex-weight assignment.
This is stronger than the unweighted statement.
For books with more than four pages we have proved the unweighted
real-rootedness theorem, not this full weighted assertion.  The negative
Rayleigh certificate must not be read as a proof that every weighted
diagonal fails, or even as an exhibited nonreal-root weighted diagonal.

Source~09 proves the same consequence in its own normalization (as
delivered, its Section~13.1):
For positive vertex activities $w_v$, put
\[
 p_{G,w}(u)=\sum_{S\text{ perfectly matchable}}w^S u^{|S|/2}.
\]
Positive scaling and diagonalization of a stable $\Phi_G$ show that
\begin{equation}
 \left(\prod_vw_v\right)\Phi_G((x/w_v)_v)
   =x^{|V|}p_{G,w}(-x^{-2})
\label{ade:mat:eq:weighted-diag}
\end{equation}
is a real-rooted polynomial in $x$. The expression on the right is
understood after expansion, so no value at $x=0$ is required. A nonzero
root $u$ of $p_{G,w}$ would give roots of $x^2=-1/u$ on the left; all of
those roots are real, forcing $u<0$. Thus all roots of $p_{G,w}$ are real
and negative. This applies to the entire block family above.

\subsection{Height-two preorder polynomials}

Part~II's height-two matching-support formula (Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:main})
\eqref{ade:eq:preorderimport} immediately transfers the univariate results.
This subsection imports that identity; the preceding graph and matroid
theorems do not depend on it.

If $p_G(t)=\prod_{j=1}^d(1+\lambda_jt)$ with $\lambda_j>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 h_{P_G}(t)=(1+t)^{n-2d}
       \prod_{j=1}^d\bigl((1+t)^2+\lambda_jt\bigr),
 \qquad n=|U|+|V|.
 \label{ade:eq:hfactor}
\end{equation}
Each quadratic is $t^2+(2+\lambda_j)t+1$ and has two negative real roots.
Thus $h_{P_G}$ is real-rooted.  Its reciprocal pairing of roots is visible
directly in this factorization.

For $B_m$, $m\ge2$, the formula becomes
\begin{align}
 h_{P_{B_m}}(t)
 &=(1+3t+t^2)^{m-2}R_m(t),\label{ade:eq:bookh}\\
 R_m(t)
 &=(1+t)^6+(2m+3)t(1+t)^4\notag\\
 &\qquad +(m^2+m+3)t^2(1+t)^2+t^3.
 \label{ade:eq:booksextic}
\end{align}
This proves real-rootedness of the entire associated height-two preorder
family, even though the stronger signed support stability fails for all
$m\ge5$.  The underlying preorder gamma-positivity and its general
transport-pair interpretation are prior repository results, not claims
of this article.

\subsection{What these results do not imply}

A stable signed support polynomial is not itself a construction of a flag
simplicial polytope with a prescribed $h$-vector.  Conversely, the failure
of stability shown here is not a disproof of such a flag realization.
The lattice-triangulation obstructions in the repository concern a
different geometric requirement.

Similarly, the ADE criterion classifies only incidence--apex graphs over
a tree, with the stated terminal convention.  It does not classify all
fundamental transversal matroids with the half-plane property, all
bipartite graphs with stable support polynomial, or all real-rooted
support diagonals.  These remaining distinctions motivate the research
questions below.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 63: Part~VIII removes the terminal
convention for a single apex over a tree (Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main});
within one-apex tree hosts the criterion now classifies every apex
neighbourhood. The other limitations of this paragraph stand.]


\section{Stable blocks beyond cactus determinants (source~09)}
\label{ade:mat:sec:stable-families}
\begin{theorem}[Every complete bipartite block is stable]\label{ade:mat:thm:biclique}
For all $\ell,r\geq1$, $\Phi_{K_{\ell,r}}$ is real stable and
\begin{equation}
 p_{K_{\ell,r}}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(\ell,r)}
                              \binom\ell k\binom r k t^k.
\label{ade:mat:eq:biclique}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every balanced pair $(I,J)$ is matchable, proving the coefficient formula.
Proposition~\ref{mat:prop:lift} says that every $r$-element subset of
$A\sqcup B$ is a basis: the lift is the uniform matroid $U_{r,\ell+r}$.
Thus $F_G=e_r$, the elementary symmetric polynomial in all vertex variables.
It is stable, since it is, up to a positive factorial, the specialization
at $s=0$ of
\[
 \partial_s^{\ell}\prod_{v\in A\sqcup B}(s+z_v).
\]
The product is stable, differentiation preserves stability, and real
specialization preserves stability or gives zero; the resulting elementary
symmetric polynomial is not zero. The reciprocal bridge proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Even cycles, with an explicit certificate]
\label{ade:mat:prop:cycles}
For each $r\geq2$, $\Phi_{C_{2r}}$ is real stable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $H$ be a Hermitian adjacency matrix of the cycle, with all edge entries
of modulus one. Choose one edge phase so that the product around the
oriented cycle, $\eta$, has real part $(-1)^r/2$; set the other phases to
one and reverse phases to their conjugates. Every proper induced subgraph
is a forest, so every perfectly matchable proper support has a unique
perfect matching. Its contribution to $\det(\operatorname{diag}(z)-H)$ is
therefore exactly $(-1)^{|S|/2}$.

For the full vertex set, the two perfect matchings contribute $2(-1)^r$.
The two oriented cycle permutations contribute $-2\Re(\eta)$. Their sum
is $(-1)^r$, the coefficient required for counting the full support once.
Hence this determinant equals $\Phi_{C_{2r}}$.

If all $z_v\in\HH$, then for nonzero $u\in\C^{2r}$,
\[
 \im\bigl(u^*(\operatorname{diag}(z)-H)u\bigr)
       =\sum_v\im(z_v)|u_v|^2>0.
\]
The matrix has no nonzero null vector and its determinant does not vanish.
\end{proof}

The cycle certificate is a restatement of the determinant method already
used in the repository; it is included so the block-family theorem has a
complete proof within this article.

\begin{corollary}[Biclique--cycle block family]\label{ade:mat:cor:block-family}
Every graph whose blocks are complete bipartite graphs or even cycles has
a real-stable signed-support polynomial. The conclusion allows arbitrary
articulation patterns, arbitrary biclique sizes, bridges, and isolated
vertices.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:biclique}, Proposition~\ref{ade:mat:prop:cycles}, and
Corollary~\ref{ade:mat:cor:blocks}; an isolated vertex contributes $z_v$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why this is genuinely beyond faithful matrices}
A faithful unit-phase matrix for a bipartite graph has zeros off the edges,
unit-modulus entries on them, and each matchable square minor has squared
modulus one. The inspected report proves that such matrices exist exactly
on cacti (Part~III, Theorem~\ref{cac:thm:classification}). Here is the elementary obstruction already visible
inside $K_{2,3}$. Normalize its first row to $(1,1,1)$ by column phases.
The second row consists of unit complex numbers $u_1,u_2,u_3$. Faithfulness
would require $|u_i-u_j|=1$ for each distinct pair. Three such points form
an equilateral triangle of side one, whose circumradius is $1/\sqrt3$, not
one. They cannot all lie on the unit circle.

Yet Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:biclique} proves signed stability for every
$K_{\ell,r}$. In particular, stable blocks with $\min(\ell,r)\geq2$ and
$\max(\ell,r)\geq3$ contain a $K_{2,3}$ obstruction and admit no faithful
matrix. Stability is therefore not merely the old determinant construction
with different phases.

[Merge note: Part~III already separated stability from faithful
matrices with the block $K_{2,3}$ (Theorem~\ref{cac:thm:stable23},
Corollary~\ref{cac:cor:trees}), including the equilateral-triangle
obstruction for faithful phases on $K_{2,3}$; source~09 does not cite it.
Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:biclique} extends that example to every $K_{\ell,r}$,
and its abstract's ``strictly extending cactus-based constructions'' should
be read with that credit.]

\subsection{A stable noncactus with two different block types}
\label{ade:mat:sec:examples}
Glue $K_{3,3}$ and $C_6$ at one vertex. The resulting graph has eleven
vertices and is not a cactus. The relevant polynomials are
\begin{align*}
 p_{K_{3,3}}&=1+9u+9u^2+u^3,& p_{K_{3,3}-v}&=1+6u+3u^2,\\
 p_{C_6}&=1+6u+9u^2+u^3,&p_{C_6-v}&=1+4u+3u^2.
\end{align*}
Equation~\eqref{ade:mat:eq:p-vertex} gives
\begin{equation}
 p_G(u)=1+15u+66u^2+107u^3+55u^4+6u^5.
\label{ade:mat:eq:glued-example}
\end{equation}
Its roots are all negative by the proved multivariate theorem, not by a
numerical root plot. Arbitrary trees or additional stable blocks may be
attached while retaining the conclusion.

\section{Exact verification and reproducibility}
\label{ade:sec:verification}

\subsection{The finite checks that were actually run}

The included program \texttt{code/verify.py} uses exact integer and
rational arithmetic in SymPy, plus NetworkX to generate nonisomorphic
trees.  Its complete machine-readable output is in
\texttt{data/verification\_results.json} [shipped as
\nolinkurl{data/08-ade-stability-verification_results.json}; the program is
\nolinkurl{code/08-ade-stability-verify.py}].  The delivered run records
Python 3.13.5, SymPy 1.14.0, and NetworkX 3.6.1.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{p{0.64\textwidth}r}
\toprule
Check & Count\\
\midrule
Unlabeled trees on one through nine vertices &95\\
Exact weighted determinant-identity evaluations on these trees &190\\
All apex-containing coefficient checks, trees through five vertices &462\\
Book sizes checked, $m=0,\ldots,8$ &9\\

For each of the 95 trees, the program independently compares an exact
Schur-complement positive-semidefiniteness test with a combinatorial ADE
shape classifier.  It then enumerates matchable endpoint pairs and checks
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:detidentity} at two deterministic positive integral
weight assignments.  Those evaluations alone are not an identity proof;
the coefficient argument in Section~\ref{ade:sec:cofactor} supplies that.
For every tree through five vertices, every apex-containing coefficient
is also checked directly using integer incidence cofactors and the exact
quadratic form $q^TC_Tq$.

For books, the program verifies every coefficient of the displayed
univariate formula through eight pages, the all-ones Rayleigh formula,
and the uniform covariance counts.  It symbolically verifies the cubic
discriminant and the quartic obstruction discriminant.  It checks the
rational rank-one-adjugate certificate for $K_{1,5}$.
For $\vartheta(2,2,2)$, $\vartheta(2,2,4)$ and $\vartheta(4,4,4)$, it enumerates
all sign assignments in \eqref{ade:eq:signlaw} and every square minor,
retaining $\sqrt2$ symbolically.  The numbers of checked minors are
respectively $10,35,462$, totaling $507$.
Four additional checks compare the complete basis sets before and after
path contraction/deletion with the predicted shortened graph.  Six
weighted evaluations test the zero-extended covariance identity for
three subdivided stars, including a nonstable five-leaf skeleton.

\subsection{The support enumerator deliberately removes multiplicities}

A dynamic program enumerates pairs $(I,J)$ as follows.  Set
$D(\varnothing)=\{\varnothing\}$.  For a nonempty row set $I$, choose its
least element $i$ and put
\begin{equation}
 D(I)=\{J\cup\{j\}:J\in D(I\setminus\{i\}),\ j\in N(i)\setminus J\}.
 \label{ade:eq:dp}
\end{equation}
The braces denote a \emph{set}; repeated ways to produce the same $J$
are removed.  Induction on $|I|$ shows that $D(I)$ consists precisely of
the column sets matchable to $I$.  This avoids the most dangerous
computational error in this subject: accidentally checking the ordinary
matching polynomial instead of the matching-support polynomial.

The exact PSD checker uses symmetric Schur complements.  A negative
diagonal excludes positive semidefiniteness.  A zero diagonal must have a
zero row in a positive semidefinite matrix; otherwise the checker rejects.
Positive pivots reduce the dimension by an exact rational Schur
complement.  Thus the test does not classify borderline affine diagrams
using floating-point tolerances.

\subsection{A proposed formalization boundary}

A future Lean or Rocq development could keep the main proof modular.
The finite combinatorial layer defines matchability, the support
polynomial and the unique-unrooted-component decomposition.  A linear
algebra layer proves the incidence-cofactor identity and the exact
adjugate formula.  An analytic layer proves the upper-half-plane
resolvent lemma and the necessary Rayleigh inequality.  The spectral
layer then supplies Perron positivity and the elementary ADE tree list.

The negative certificates are particularly suitable for a small exact
checker: the checker need only verify positive rational entries in $v$
and $v^TC_Tv<0$, after a general theorem has connected those data to
\eqref{ade:eq:explicitRayleigh}.  Evaluating a rational inequality without
that connecting theorem would not by itself certify the original
stability claim.  No part of this planned formalization is represented
as already completed in the delivered package.

\paragraph{Source~09's checks of its stability sections.}
Source~09's single verifier (Part~VII, Section~\ref{mat:sec:verification})
also checks the sixteen exact signed vertex-sum identities, the $\Theta_3$
support polynomial and the Rayleigh value $-9$ from vertex-subset
feasibility.

\section{Further research questions and topics}
\label{ade:sec:questions}

The following questions are proposed directions, not theorems asserted by
this article.  Their purpose is to separate the next genuinely missing
steps from what the present results already settle.

\begin{question}[Beyond the classified graph families; sources~08 and~09]\label{ade:q:first}
Characterize the bipartite graphs $G$ for which the canonical transversal
matroid $\mathsf M_G$ has stable basis polynomial.  Can a useful class of
forbidden \emph{canonical matroid minors}, rather than merely induced
graphs, organize the answer?
(Source~09, ``Which 2-connected bipartite graphs are stable?'': classify the bipartite blocks $B$ for which $\Phi_B$ is real stable.
Theorem~\ref{ade:mat:thm:stable-bridge} reformulates this as the half-plane property
for the concrete matroid $M_B$, and Corollary~\ref{ade:mat:cor:blocks} removes all
articulation complications. A useful first target is the exact
classification for subdivisions of theta graphs. A proof must distinguish
univariate real-rootedness from full multivariate stability.)
\end{question}
The path-shortening proof shows why induced-graph obstructions alone can
miss a persistent failure.  The five-page book and the three-odd-path
obstruction give different mechanisms and should be treated separately.
A general classification is not supplied by the ADE or multi-theta
results.

[Merge note: by Corollary~\ref{ade:mat:cor:blocks} the two formulations are
equivalent; source~09's ``useful first target'', the subdivisions of theta
graphs, is Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta}. The question overlaps Part~III's
Research question~\ref{ade:hq:classify}.]

\begin{question}[All tree incidence--apex diagonals]\label{mts:hq:diagonals}
For which trees $T$ is the univariate polynomial
\begin{equation}
 p_{\calA(T)}(t)
 =\det(I+t\Lap(T))
   +t\tr\bigl(\adj(I+t\Lap(T))C_T\bigr)
 \label{ade:eq:treeunivariatequestion}
\end{equation}
real-rooted?  In particular, is it real-rooted for every tree?
\end{question}
The spectral stability criterion settles the ADE cases, while the book
formula settles every star, including non-ADE stars.  These facts do not
settle the question for arbitrary trees.  A plausible route is to analyze
the residues of
$\tr(C_T(I+t\Lap(T))^{-1})$ in Laplacian eigenspaces; positivity of those
residues would require a separate proof and is not assumed here.

[Merge note: evidence only. For this merge the diagonal was checked
exactly for every unlabelled tree with $2\le r\le12$ (986 trees; $r=1$ is
immediate): all are real-rooted.]
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 63: source~10 poses the same question for
arbitrary markings (Part~VIII, Research question~\ref{mts:q:diagonal}).]

\begin{question}[Positive-weight Rayleigh versus full stability]
Within the incidence--apex tree family, characterize the trees for which
all Rayleigh differences are nonnegative on the \emph{positive} orthant.
Does this condition have a spectral description different from ADE?
\end{question}
The universal failure certificate uses arbitrary real left variables.
The book certificate is stronger and already fails at positive weights.
Equating these two levels without proof would be a mistake.

\begin{question}[Several apex columns]\label{mts:hq:apices}
Replace one apex by two or more independently selectable apex vertices,
with prescribed terminal neighborhoods.  Is there an exact Boolean
coefficient formula involving mixed covariances or higher exterior
moments that yields a tractable stability criterion?
\end{question}
The single-apex case only sees one unrooted component.  Several apex
columns must resolve simultaneous components and remove the
multiplicities of their assignments.  A product of single-apex formulas
would generally overcount.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 63: source~10 poses the same question
(Part~VIII, Research question~\ref{mts:q:apices}).]

\begin{question}[Base graphs with cycles]\label{mts:hq:cycles}
Which parts of the covariance method survive if the auxiliary incidence
graph is not a tree?  Can cycle-space corrections replace the identity
$|W|-|E(T[W])|=1$ without destroying positive semidefiniteness?
\end{question}
The tree proof exploits both unique paths and unimodular incidence
cofactors.  The even-theta construction suggests that independent random
columns can sometimes correct cycle multiplicities, but it does not
yet provide a general replacement for the connected-subtree energy law.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 63: source~10 poses the same question for
unicyclic, cactus and bounded-cycle-rank hosts (Part~VIII, Research
question~\ref{mts:q:cycles}).]

\begin{question}[Boundary Rayleigh certificates]
Find compact sums-of-squares expressions for the Rayleigh differences
of the affine $\widetilde D,\widetilde E$ incidence--apex polynomials.
Can their one-dimensional covariance kernel yield a uniform formula?
\end{question}
The analytic proof already establishes nonnegativity.  A transparent
algebraic certificate would be valuable for formalization, exact
optimization and a comparison with the repository's explicit $K_{2,3}$
certificates.

\begin{question}[Weighted and perturbed covariance models]
For which deformations of the support coefficients can the forced matrix
$C_T$ be replaced by a weighted adjacency expression while preserving
nonnegative coefficients and a useful combinatorial meaning?
\end{question}
Merely replacing $A_T$ by a weighted matrix no longer leaves every
connected-support coefficient equal to one.  A successful generalization
must state exactly what the new coefficients count.

\begin{question}[Sampling and computational certificates]
Can the determinant--adjugate and independent-column representations be
turned into exact samplers for the Boolean endpoint-support measure, or
into polynomial-time symbolic stability certificates for the classified
families?
\end{question}
The formulas provide compact partition functions on the stable side,
but sampling a determinant mixture and forgetting its auxiliary vector
need not automatically give a simple uniform-support sampler.  The
conditional distributions and normalization must be analyzed.

\begin{question}[Formal integration into ProveIt]\label{mts:hq:formal}
Formalize the cofactor support lemma, the covariance rigidity theorem,
and the rational Rayleigh certificate compiler, then connect them to the
repository's existing matching-support and preorder semantics.
\end{question}
This route would turn the written argument into a machine-checked
extension without importing the whole surrounding unrefereed research
corpus.  The separate expected-determinant proof could then be added as a
second, independently useful stability module.

[Merge note: compare Part~III's Research question~19 (kernel-checked
certificate theory).]

\begin{question}[Minimal induced obstructions; source~09]\label{ade:q:last}
Describe the induced-minimal bipartite graphs with unstable $\Phi_G$.
The eight-vertex theta graph gives one obstruction, but the present
manuscript does not claim a minimality classification. Is there a finite
obstruction set within a fixed treewidth or fixed maximum-degree class?
Any proposed list can be tested using exact Rayleigh certificates.
\end{question}

[Merge note: the finite-obstruction part has a negative answer,
Section~\ref{ade:sec:inducedminimal}; describing all induced-minimal
unstable graphs remains open.]

\section{Conclusion}

The central obstruction in matching-support enumeration is that several
perfect matchings must contribute only once.  For tree incidence--apex
graphs, an oriented forest cofactor identifies exactly one unrooted
component, and the matrix $I-A_T/2$ assigns that component the required
weight one.  This matrix is forced by the coefficients.  Its positive
semidefiniteness proves stability through a resolvent, while its failure
produces a rank-one-adjugate Rayleigh obstruction.  The resulting exact
criterion is therefore both constructive and sharp.

The classical ADE tree list becomes a stability classification through
this mechanism.  The book family exhibits a four-page boundary that
cannot be detected from its univariate roots, and the independent-column
method gives the complementary even-path family.  Together with exact
minor reduction, these arguments classify the simple bipartite
multi-theta graphs while preserving the distinction between new
restricted results, classical inputs, earlier counterexamples, and the
still-open general questions.

Source~09 concludes on stability (as delivered):

The stability question is correspondingly sharper. The reciprocal bridge
places it inside half-plane-property theory, while the block theorem
isolates the genuinely difficult 2-connected cases. Complete bipartite
blocks show that stability extends far beyond faithful cactus matrices.
Together these results provide a concrete continuation of the repository's
program without reviving a false real-rootedness conjecture or relabeling
its existing gamma-positivity theorem as a new discovery.

\section{Compact certificates for readers and proof checkers}
\label{ade:app:certificates}

\subsection{The main theorem in six equations}

The mathematical core can be reduced to the following chain, with each
step justified in the main text:
\begin{align*}
 \det[B_{I,J}\ \ w_I]&=\pm\one_W^T w,
     &&\text{unique unrooted component;}\\
 \one_W^T(I-A_T/2)\one_W&=1,
     &&\text{connected subtree;}\\
 F_T&=\det L+s\tr(\adj L\,C_T),
     &&\text{coefficient identity;}\\
 \im\tr(C_TL^{-1})&<0\quad(C_T\succeq0),
     &&\text{upper-half-plane nonvanishing;}\\
 \adj(D_v^{-1}\Lap(T)D_v^{-1})&=
        \left(\prod_i v_i^{-2}\right)vv^T,
     &&\text{tree cofactors;}\\
 \del_{s,x_i}F_T&=c^2v_i^2(v^TC_Tv)<0\quad(v^TC_Tv<0),
     &&\text{explicit obstruction.}
\end{align*}
The last line is evaluated at the rational assignment in
\eqref{ade:eq:certy}--\eqref{ade:eq:certx}; it is not an identity at arbitrary
variables.  The first line applies to feasible apex minors and is zero
on infeasible ones.

\subsection{A simple exact PSD checker}

For a rational symmetric matrix $M$, repeat the following operations.
A negative diagonal entry rejects $M$.  A zero diagonal with a nonzero
entry in its row also rejects it; a zero row and column can be removed.
Otherwise choose a positive pivot $a$ and write
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b^T\\b&D\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
 M\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D-bb^T/a\succeq0.
\]
The dimension decreases, so the procedure terminates and uses exact
rational operations.  The implementation in the verifier is independent
of its ADE shape classifier.  The comparison of these two finite
procedures is a regression check on the explicit diagram list, not a

\phantomsection\part*{Part VII.\quad The transversal matroid of a preorder: reconstruction, duality and gammoids}
\addcontentsline{toc}{part}{Part VII.\texorpdfstring{\quad}{ } The transversal matroid of a preorder}

\noindent\emph{Part~VII was added on 29 September 2026 in batch~55 of
ProveIt's incoming-report intake, from one manuscript. It studies the
transversal matroid $M_\tau$ on two copies of the ground set of a finite
preorder, whose bases are the matchable support pairs of Part~IV: $M_\tau$
determines $\tau$ up to isomorphism, its automorphism group is computed,
order reversal is matroid duality, its rank function is an upset minimum,
and height-two preorder matroids generate exactly the finite gammoids under
minors. The manuscript's ultra-log-concavity sections are the third proof
of Part~V's main theorem and are credited there; its stability sections are
in Part~VI. Parts~I--VI are unchanged except for dated pointers.
Section~\ref{mat:sec:prov} records the provenance, fixes the notation and
states what is answered.}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~09 (as delivered).}
A matching support remembers the vertices covered by a matching, but not the
choice of matching. We use its classical transversal-matroid lift to develop
new structural consequences for the preorder-polynomial program in
ProveIt. For a reflexive relation $R$, we prove that transitivity is equivalent
to the two copies of each element being clones in the associated matroid.
For a preorder, we give an upset formula for every matroid rank, identify all
intrinsic clone classes, reconstruct the entire weighted quotient poset from
the unlabeled matroid, and determine its full automorphism group. Order
reversal becomes matroid duality. Every transversal matroid is an explicit
minor of the matroid of a height-two poset; consequently these height-two
matroids generate exactly the finite gammoids under minors.

Combining established matching-support identities with the
Br\"and\'en--Huh and R\"ohrle--Ulirsch theory proves ultra-log-concavity of
\emph{every} finite preorder $h$-polynomial, including a positive
transport-weighted version. This retains Newton-type coefficient
inequalities even though real-rootedness fails. We distinguish this
application from the already published general bimatroid inequality.
Finally, a partial reciprocal substitution identifies stability of a signed
matching-support polynomial with the half-plane property of its matroid.
We prove that signed-support stability is local to the blocks of a graph,
and obtain stable families with arbitrary complete-bipartite blocks,
strictly extending cactus-based constructions. All new structural arguments
are supplied in full. Exact finite checks and a negative Rayleigh
certificate are included as supplementary evidence, not as substitutes for
proof.
\end{tcolorbox}
\noindent The abstract describes the whole manuscript. Its stability claims
are Part~VI's Theorems~\ref{ade:mat:thm:vertex-stable}
and~\ref{ade:mat:thm:biclique}; ``strictly extending cactus-based
constructions'' is to be read with Part~III's $K_{2,3}$ example
(Theorem~\ref{cac:thm:stable23}), which source~09 does not cite.

Part~VII answers no numbered question of Parts~I--VI; its matroid strand

(Corollary~\ref{mat:cor:gammoids}). Part~IV's
Proposition~\ref{gam:prop:canceliff} and Theorem~\ref{gam:gv:thm:orbits}
gain dated pointers. Part~VII refutes nothing, and nothing is retracted.

\section{The question left after real-rootedness fails}
\label{mat:sec:overview}
The preorder program of Athanasiadis and Chapoton associates a polynomial
$h_\tau(t)$ with a finite preorder $\tau$ by counting lattice points according
to support size \cite{AC}. The inspected ProveIt\ report (this report, Parts~I--IV) develops
root-polytope realizations, gamma expansions, counterexamples to
real-rootedness, and matrix constructions for matching supports. In particular, its recent Parts II--IV already establish
many conclusions that must not be presented again as new: the height-two
matching-support formula, gamma-positivity for every preorder, and the
classification of faithful unit-phase matrices by bipartite cacti.

The useful next question is therefore not whether every $h_\tau$ has only
real roots. It is what robust structure survives the counterexamples, and
whether the support model retains more information than its univariate
polynomial. This manuscript gives two answers. The coefficient sequence
always satisfies ultra-log-concavity. More surprisingly, an associated
unlabeled matroid retains the entire preorder, including the sizes of its
equivalence classes.

\subsection{Principal conclusions}
Let $E$ be an $n$-element set. A preorder is a reflexive, transitive relation
on $E$; antisymmetry is not assumed. Let $E^+$ and $E^-$ be disjoint labeled
copies. We construct a rank-$n$ transversal matroid $M_\tau$ on
$E^+\sqcup E^-$. Write $\overline\tau$ for the quotient poset of equivalence
classes, and let $m_C$ be the size of a class $C$.

The main structural results are
\begin{align}
M_\tau\cong M_\sigma&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tau\cong\sigma,
\label{mat:eq:intro-reconstruction}\\
\Aut(M_\tau)&\cong
 \left(\prod_{C\in\overline\tau}\mathfrak S_{2m_C}\right)
 \rtimes\Aut(\overline\tau,m),
\label{mat:eq:intro-aut}\\
M_\tau^*&=M_{\tau^{\mathrm{op}}},
\label{mat:eq:intro-dual}
\end{align}
where the duality identity uses the fixed labels on the two copies.
The semidirect-product isomorphism depends on choices of identifications
inside the clone classes; its kernel and quotient have intrinsic meanings.

The coefficient conclusion is the following: if
$h_\tau(t)=\sum_{k=0}^n h_k t^k$, then
\begin{equation}
\boxed{\quad
 h_k^2\geq
 \frac{(k+1)(n-k+1)}{k(n-k)}h_{k-1}h_{k+1}
 \qquad(1\leq k<n).
\quad}\label{mat:eq:intro-ulc}
\end{equation}
The same inequalities hold for the transport-weighted coefficients defined
in Section~\ref{mat:sec:weighted}. In particular, the ordinary coefficient
sequence is strictly log-concave at every interior index when $n\geq2$.
This statement does not assert strictness after binomial normalization.
