\section{The support--matroid bridge and elementary analytic facts}\label{mts:sec:bridge}

\noindent\emph{Merge note. The four lemmas of this section are Part~VI's,
in source~10's formulation; source~10 proves them by the same arguments as
Part~VI, and its proofs are replaced by pointers. Its statements are kept
because later sections cite them.}

\begin{lemma}[Canonical transversal matroid]\label{mts:lem:matroid}
For a bipartite graph with shores $U$ and $B$, the sets
$(U\setminus I)\sqcup J$, with $I\sim J$, are the bases of a rank-$|U|$
transversal matroid. Its basis polynomial is
$F_G(x;y)=\sum_{I\sim J}x^{U\setminus I}y^J$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:matroid} (the matroid $\mathsf M_G$ and its basis
polynomial~\eqref{ade:eq:Fdef}), proved there by the same one-slot-per-left-vertex
presentation.
\end{proof}

Source~10 also recalls the generic linear representation $[I\ K]$ of
Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:matroid}, with an independent indeterminate $K_{ub}$ on
each graph edge; a basis minor is nonzero precisely when $I\sim J$.

\begin{lemma}[Inversion bridge and induced subgraphs]\label{mts:lem:bridge}
For a bipartite graph $G$ with shores $U,B$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_G(x,z_B)=\left(\prod_{b\in B}z_b\right)
                F_G\bigl(x;(-1/z_b)_{b\in B}\bigr).
 \label{mts:eq:inversion}
\end{equation}
Thus $F_G$ and $\Phi_G$ are stable simultaneously. Stability of $\Phi_G$
passes to every induced subgraph.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Identity~\eqref{mts:eq:inversion} and the first conclusion are
Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge}, equation~\eqref{ade:eq:bridge}. The
second is Lemmas~\ref{ade:lem:minors} and~\ref{ade:mat:lem:induced}, by the
identity
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{z_v}\Phi_G=\Phi_{G-v},
 \label{mts:eq:induced}
\end{equation}
iterated; its leading unmatched monomial excludes the zero polynomial.
\end{proof}

We use the standard closure properties under differentiation and real
specialization \cite{COSW,Branden}. Real specialization follows by
approaching the real point from $\HH$ and applying Hurwitz's theorem; the
limit is zero-free or identically zero. For a matroid basis polynomial,
deletion and contraction are respectively specialization at zero and
differentiation, with the usual loop/coloop factors treated separately.
Hence matroid minors inherit stability.

\begin{lemma}[Necessary Rayleigh inequality]\label{mts:lem:rayleigh}
If a real multiaffine polynomial $f$ is stable, then, for all distinct
variables $z_i,z_j$ and every real assignment $a$,
\begin{equation}
 \del_{ij}f(a):=f_i(a)f_j(a)-f(a)f_{ij}(a)\ge0.
 \label{mts:eq:rayleigh}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:rayleigh}, with the same bivariate
specialization argument.
\end{proof}

The converse is Br\"and\'en's general theorem \cite{Branden}; our negative
certificates require only the elementary direction just proved.

\begin{lemma}[A stable polynomial has real-rooted support diagonal]\label{mts:lem:diagonal}
If $F_G$ is stable, then
\begin{equation}
 p_G(t)=F_G(\one;t\one)=\sum_{I\sim J}t^{|I|}
 \label{mts:eq:p}
\end{equation}
has only negative real zeros, or is constant.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is the last assertion of Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:bridge}, with the
same specialization and diagonalization argument.
\end{proof}

The converse is false; the repository's books provide examples
(Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introbook}). This distinction will also matter when we introduce
a second enumerator, counting \emph{which markings} are stable.

\section{The unmarked-branch obstruction}\label{mts:sec:branch}

\subsection{A small obstruction, with its original credit}

Let $\vartheta(3,3,3)$ consist of three internally disjoint paths of length three
between a left endpoint and a right endpoint. It is $\calA(K_{1,3};S)$ when
$S$ consists of the three leaves and excludes the center. Its support
polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 p_{\vartheta(3,3,3)}(t)=1+9t+24t^2+16t^3+t^4.
 \label{mts:eq:theta}
\end{equation}
This is an existing obstruction in this report, which attributes the earlier
counterexample to Shivam Patel~\cite{Patel}. We reproduce the small certificate rather
than claim a new example.
[Merge note: \eqref{mts:eq:theta} is Part~VI's~\eqref{ade:eq:thetaobstruction}
and Part~II's $p_{\Theta_3}$ (Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:thetaintro}). The
coefficient count below differs from Part~VI's (which counts matchable
right sets per left set) and is kept as a second route.]

Here is a direct coefficient count (source~10's route). The graph has nine edges and degree
sequence $(3,3,2,2,2,2,2,2)$. Its number of two-edge matchings is
\[
 \binom92-2\binom32-6\binom22=24.
\]
There is no four-cycle, so two matchings cannot share a four-vertex
support. Each shore has four vertices, and every choice of three vertices
from each shore is matchable. To verify this last assertion, label the
left vertices $u,b_1,b_2,b_3$ and the right vertices $a_1,a_2,a_3,\star$,
with edges $ua_i,b_ia_i,b_i\star$. If $u$ is omitted, match the leaves to
their private $a_i$ columns, using $\star$ for the unique missing private
column when necessary. If $u$ is retained and $\star$ is omitted, match
the two retained leaves privately and give $u$ the third column. Finally,
if both $u$ and $\star$ are retained, either an available private column
belongs to the omitted leaf, in which case give it to $u$, or both
available private columns belong to retained leaves. In the latter case
give one to $u$, its leaf to $\star$, and match the other leaf privately.
Thus the size-three coefficient is $\binom43^2=16$. The full graph has a
perfect matching, giving final coefficient one.

For an exact nonreal-root certificate,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{disc}(t^4+16t^3+24t^2+9t+1)=-5243.
 \label{mts:eq:thetadisc}
\end{equation}
If all four roots were real and distinct, the discriminant would be
positive; repeated roots would give zero. Thus the polynomial has a
nonreal root. The included program independently enumerates the supports
and computes the discriminant over the integers. By
Lemma~\ref{mts:lem:diagonal}, $F_{\vartheta(3,3,3)}$ is not stable.
[Merge note: \eqref{mts:eq:thetadisc} is Part~VI's~\eqref{ade:eq:thetadisc};
Part~VI also prints source~09's Sturm chain and Rayleigh certificate for
the same graph. The ``included program'' is shipped as
\nolinkurl{code/10-marked-trees-verify.py}; its recorded output
\nolinkurl{data/10-marked-trees-verification.json} lists the coefficients
$1,9,24,16,1$ and the discriminant $-5243$.]

\subsection{Shortening odd paths by legitimate matroid minors}

It is not correct to assume that arbitrary graph contractions preserve
matching-support stability. We use the following specific operation,
already present in the repository's terminal-subdivision argument.

\begin{lemma}[Path shortening]\label{mts:lem:shorten}
Suppose a bipartite graph has a path $a-c-b-d$, where $a,b$ are on the
left and $c,d$ on the right. Suppose $N(b)=\{c,d\}$,
$N(c)=\{a,b\}$, and $a$ is not adjacent to $d$. In its canonical matroid,
contract the right element $c$ and delete the left private element $b$.
The result is the canonical matroid of the graph obtained by removing
$b,c$ and replacing this path by the edge $a-d$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
This is Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:shorten}; source~10's proof, in the generic
representation $[I\ K]$, is the same argument almost word for word and is
not reprinted.
\end{proof}

Consequently, a graph consisting of three internally disjoint odd paths,
each of length at least three, is nonstable. Shorten each path by pairs of
edges until all three have length three. The intermediate internal vertices
satisfy the degree conditions in Lemma~\ref{mts:lem:shorten}. Stability of the
original canonical matroid would imply stability of the resulting
$\vartheta(3,3,3)$ minor, a contradiction.
[Merge note: this is Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta}(ii) for three paths,
with the same proof (Section~\ref{ade:sec:theta}).]

\begin{theorem}[An unmarked hull branch forbids stability]\label{mts:thm:branch}
If $S\ne\varnothing$ and $K=\Hull_T(S)$ has a vertex $v\notin S$ of degree
at least three, then $F_{T,S}$ and $\Phi_{\calA(T;S)}$ are not stable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose three components of $K-v$. Each contains a mark. In each choose a
mark $a_i$ at minimum distance from $v$, and take the path from $v$ to
$a_i$. Its internal vertices are unmarked. The three paths meet only at
$v$. In $\calA(T;S)$ their incidence subdivisions, followed by the three
edges $a_i\star$, form three paths from $v$ to $\star$ of lengths
$2d_T(v,a_i)+1\ge3$.

The graph induced on precisely these path vertices is exactly this odd
theta graph. There are no cross-edges, because $T$ is a tree; there are
no extra apex edges, because there are no internal marks on the chosen
paths. The preceding minor argument proves it nonstable. Induced-subgraph
inheritance in Lemma~\ref{mts:lem:bridge} excludes stability of the original graph,
and the inversion bridge transfers the conclusion to $F_{T,S}$.
\end{proof}

[Merge note: Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:branch} is new as a statement; its
proof applies Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introtheta}(ii) and induced
inheritance (Lemma~\ref{ade:mat:lem:induced}) to the induced multi-theta
graph $\vartheta(2d_1+1,2d_2+1,2d_3+1)$ between $v$ and $\star$. It is the
case that Part~VI's terminal convention excludes
(Section~\ref{ade:sec:subdivision}, ``Why the terminal convention
matters'').]

\section{Exactly when a supported covariance exists}\label{mts:sec:covariance}

The geometric obstruction also has a precise algebraic interpretation.
A matrix is \emph{supported on $S$} if all its rows and columns outside
$S$ are zero. Consider the connected-set interpolation conditions
\begin{equation}
 \one_W^T C\one_W=\ind_{\{W\cap S\ne\varnothing\}}
 \qquad\text{for every nonempty connected vertex set }W\subseteq V(T).
 \label{mts:eq:energy}
\end{equation}
They ask that the quadratic form turn the number of usable apex entries
in a connected component into the Boolean assertion that at least one is
present.

\begin{theorem}[Existence and uniqueness of the supported covariance]\label{mts:thm:covariance}
For $S\ne\varnothing$, a real symmetric matrix supported on $S$ satisfying
\eqref{mts:eq:energy} exists if and only if $S$ is branch-complete. When it
exists it is unique and equals the zero extension of
\begin{equation}
 C_H=I-\tfrac12 A_{H(T,S)}.
 \label{mts:eq:C}
\end{equation}
For $S=\varnothing$, the unique supported matrix is zero and it satisfies
\eqref{mts:eq:energy}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First suppose the marking is branch-complete. For connected $W$, the set
$R=W\cap S$ is either empty or connected in the skeleton $H$. Indeed, the
unique path in $T$ between two elements of $R$ belongs to $W$, and contains
every intervening mark on their skeleton path. Consequently
\[
 \one_W^T C\one_W=|R|-|E(H[R])|
 =\begin{cases}0,&R=\varnothing,\\1,&R\ne\varnothing.\end{cases}
\]
This proves existence even when $C_H$ is indefinite.

For uniqueness, singleton marks give $C_{aa}=1$. For adjacent marks in
$H$, their connecting path contains exactly those two marks, so its
energy is $2+2C_{ab}=1$ and $C_{ab}=-1/2$. Induct on distance in $H$ for a
nonadjacent pair $a,b$. On their connecting path, diagonal and adjacent-pair
contributions already sum to one. All other pairs of smaller distance
have zero entry by induction. The remaining term $2C_{ab}$ must vanish.
This determines every entry supported on $S$.

Conversely, suppose an unmarked branch $v$ exists. Choose three first
marks $a,b,c$ in distinct directions as in Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:branch}. The path
between any two of them contains no other mark. Singleton and two-mark
path energies force
\[
 C_{aa}=C_{bb}=C_{cc}=1,\qquad
 C_{ab}=C_{ac}=C_{bc}=-\tfrac12.
\]
The connected union of the three paths contains exactly these three marks,
so its energy is $3+2(-3/2)=0$, contradicting its required energy one.
The empty case is immediate from the support requirement.
\end{proof}

[Merge note: for $S=V(T)$ the uniqueness half is Part~VI's covariance
rigidity, Proposition~\ref{ade:prop:uniqueC}, with the same induction on
distance, and the existence half is~\eqref{ade:eq:connectedenergy}. The
support restriction, the branch-complete generality and the nonexistence
half at an unmarked branch are new.]

\begin{remark}[The support restriction is part of the theorem]
We have classified matrices supported on the apex neighborhood and
satisfying every connected-set equation. We have not ruled out unrelated
determinantal models, indefinite matrices with additional off-neighborhood
entries, or higher-moment constructions. On the positive-semidefinite
side, zero rows outside $S$ follow automatically from the zero diagonal
entries forced by singleton equations.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The coefficient identity, including unmarked fringe}

Choose an orientation of $T$. For $e=uv$, let $b_e=e_u-e_v$, with the sign
chosen according to the orientation, and put
\begin{equation}
 L(x,y)=\diag(x_v)_{v\in V}+\sum_{e\in E}y_e b_eb_e^T.
 \label{mts:eq:L}
\end{equation}
Changing an orientation does not change $L$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact Boolean determinant--adjugate identity]\label{mts:thm:identity}
Suppose $S$ is branch-complete, or empty, and let $C$ be the matrix in
Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:covariance}. Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{F_{T,S}(x;y,s)=\det L+s\,\tr\bigl(\adj(L)C\bigr).}
 \label{mts:eq:identity}
\end{equation}
This is a polynomial identity, with no invertibility or definiteness
assumption. It holds on the original host tree, including every unmarked
subdivision vertex and every unmarked attached subtree.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $B$ be the oriented incidence matrix. By Cauchy--Binet,
\begin{align}
 \det(L+sww^T)
 &=\sum_{|I|=|J|}x^{V\setminus I}y^J\det(B_{I,J})^2\notag\\
 &\quad+s\sum_{|I|=|J|+1}x^{V\setminus I}y^J
                      \det[B_{I,J}\ \ w_I]^2,
 \label{mts:eq:CB}
\end{align}
where $I\subseteq V$, $J\subseteq E$, and $w$ is an auxiliary vector.
The first-line minor is zero or $\pm1$ and is nonzero exactly on a
matchable support. One can see this by leaf elimination; alternatively,
the underlying incidence graph is a tree, so a fixed support has at most
one perfect matching and hence at most one nonzero determinant term.

For the second line, consider the internal-edge forest on the chosen rows
$I$. A selected edge with one endpoint in $I$ is a half-edge; an edge
with no endpoint in $I$ gives a zero column. A component with $k$ vertices
and $h$ half-edges has $k-1+h$ selected columns. If $h>1$, those columns
cannot be assigned distinct rows. When there is no zero column and every
component has at most one half-edge, the equality $|I|=|J|+1$ forces exactly
one component $W$ to have no half-edge; every other component has one.

A component with one half-edge gives a square incidence block of
determinant $\pm1$. In the component $W$, the internal incidence block
has left kernel spanned by $\one_W$, and each maximal cofactor has modulus
one. Thus
\begin{equation}
 \det[B_{I,J}\ \ w_I]=\pm\sum_{v\in W}w_v.
 \label{mts:eq:cofactor}
\end{equation}
In every other component configuration the augmented determinant vanishes
identically. If $w$ is supported on $S$, an apex matching exists exactly
when this unique unrooted component meets $S$.

Apply the linear functional $w_uw_v\mapsto C_{uv}$ to the quadratic
coefficients of \eqref{mts:eq:CB}. By \eqref{mts:eq:energy}, the square in
\eqref{mts:eq:cofactor} becomes one when $W\cap S\ne\varnothing$ and zero
otherwise. Each feasible apex support is therefore counted exactly once.
The first line is unchanged. On the left, the rank-one determinant
identity gives
\[
 \det(L+sww^T)=\det L+s\,w^T\adj(L)w.
\]
The same functional produces \eqref{mts:eq:identity}. Everything takes place
in a polynomial ring, so singular substitutions are allowed.
\end{proof}

[Merge note: Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:identity} generalizes Part~VI's
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:detidentity} ($S=V(T)$) and the terminal-subdivision
identity~\eqref{ade:eq:subdivisionidentity} ($K=T$) to hosts with unmarked
fringe; its cofactor analysis is Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:forestcofactor}. Part~VI
reaches fringe only through the vertex-sum theorem, not by an identity.]

\begin{remark}
The right side is generally \emph{not} $\det(L+sC)$: that determinant
would introduce higher powers of $s$ and represent several apex choices.
Nor is the coefficient identity the assertion that every matching has the
same weight. The connected-component quadratic functional is precisely
what removes the matching multiplicity.
\end{remark}

\section{Stability, rational certificates, and the ADE list}\label{mts:sec:spectral}

\subsection{Positive covariance gives stability}

The following resolvent argument is the analytic mechanism already used
for full-apex trees in Part~VI. The extended identity allows the
same argument on every branch-complete marking.

\begin{lemma}[Resolvent positivity]\label{mts:lem:resolvent}
Let $L=\diag(x_i)+\sum_e y_e b_eb_e^T$, with real vectors $b_e$. If
$C\succeq0$, then $\det L+s\tr(\adj(L)C)$ is stable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $C\ne0$ this is Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:covstable}, with the same
argument through
\begin{equation}
 \im L^{-1}=-L^{-*}(\im L)L^{-1}\prec0,
 \label{mts:eq:im-inverse}
\end{equation}
which gives $\im\tr(CL^{-1})<0$; source~10 notes that this follows also by
factoring $C=RR^*$ and taking the trace of the negative definite form on
the nonzero columns of $R$. If $C=0$, the polynomial is $\det L$, which
does not vanish because $\im L\succ0$ for $x_i,y_e\in\HH$.
\end{proof}

Singular positive-semidefinite matrices cause no difficulty; in particular,
the affine ADE boundary is included without an extra approximation step.

\subsection{A negative certificate directly on the original tree}

\begin{theorem}[Rational Rayleigh certificate with subdivisions and fringe]\label{mts:thm:certificate}
Suppose $S$ is nonempty and branch-complete, but $C_H$ is not positive
semidefinite. There is a vector $v\in\mathbb Q_{>0}^{V(T)}$ with $v^TCv<0$.
For any such vector set
\begin{align}
 y_{ij}&=\frac1{v_iv_j} &&(ij\in E(T)),\label{mts:eq:cert-y}\\
 x_i&=\frac{\deg_T(i)}{v_i^2}-\sum_{j\sim i}\frac1{v_iv_j},
 &s&=0.\label{mts:eq:cert-x}
\end{align}
Writing $c=\prod_i v_i^{-2}$, the exact Rayleigh values are
\begin{equation}
 \del_{s,x_i}F_{T,S}=c^2v_i^2(v^TCv)<0
 \qquad(i\in V(T)).
 \label{mts:eq:certificate}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the connected nonnegative adjacency matrix $A_H$, failure of
$I-A_H/2\succeq0$ means its largest eigenvalue exceeds two. A strictly
positive Perron eigenvector therefore has negative $C_H$ energy. Approximate
it sufficiently closely by positive rational entries; strict negativity
persists. Extend to a positive rational vector on the other vertices of
$T$. Since $C$ is supported on $S$, the energy is unchanged.

At \eqref{mts:eq:cert-y}--\eqref{mts:eq:cert-x}, with $D_v=\diag(v_i)$,
\begin{equation}
 L_0=D_v^{-1}\Lap(T)D_v^{-1}.
 \label{mts:eq:lap-congruence}
\end{equation}
The tree Laplacian has kernel $\R\one$ and adjugate $\one\one^T$: any
cofactor is one, by elimination of leaves or the incidence determinant of
the tree. Adjugate transformation under the invertible diagonal
congruence gives
\[
 \det L_0=0,\qquad \adj(L_0)=c\,vv^T.
\]
Using Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:identity} at $s=0$ yields
$F=0$, $F_s=c\,v^TCv$, and $F_{x_i}=c\,v_i^2$. In the Rayleigh expression
$F_sF_{x_i}-FF_{s,x_i}$, the second term vanishes, proving
\eqref{mts:eq:certificate}. Lemma~\ref{mts:lem:rayleigh} then excludes stability.
\end{proof}

This theorem extends the source's skeleton certificate to the full host
without contracting away its extra vertices. It does not assert that all
negative certificates occur at positive variable values: the $x_i$ may be
negative, which is entirely legitimate for a test of real stability.
[Merge note: ``the source'' is Part~VI; the formulas are those of
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:negative}, equations
\eqref{ade:eq:certy}--\eqref{ade:eq:explicitRayleigh}. On the host tree
this is a second route to the necessity half of
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:subdivision}, which Part~VI proves by matroid minors
(Lemma~\ref{ade:lem:shorten}).]

\begin{example}[A transparent spectral failure]
For the fully marked $K_{1,5}$, take center coordinate $v_0=2$ and all five
leaf coordinates equal to one. Then $v^TCv=-1$, all $y_e=1/2$, the center
$x_0=-5/4$, and each leaf $x_i=1/2$. Thus $c=1/4$ and
$\del_{s,x_0}F=-1/4$. This bare-star certificate is already in the
repository (the example after Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:negative}). Inserting an unmarked subdivision vertex on an arm, and
attaching an unmarked two-edge twig there, preserves the energy: put value
one at all new vertices and use \eqref{mts:eq:cert-x}. The delivered output
checks this nine-vertex extension exactly as well.
[Merge note: both certificates are recorded under
\texttt{rayleigh\_certificates} in
\nolinkurl{data/10-marked-trees-verification.json}.]
\end{example}

\subsection{An elementary form of the classical classification}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.25\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Name & Shape of the terminal skeleton $H$\\
\midrule
$A_r$, $r\ge1$ & A path on $r$ vertices.\\
$D_{c+3}$, $c\ge1$ & One trivalent vertex with arm lengths $(1,1,c)$.\\
$E_6,E_7,E_8$ & One trivalent vertex with arm lengths
$(1,2,2)$, $(1,2,3)$, $(1,2,4)$, respectively.\\
$\widetilde E_6,\widetilde E_7,\widetilde E_8$ & One trivalent vertex with
arm lengths $(2,2,2)$, $(1,3,3)$, $(1,2,5)$, respectively.\\
$\widetilde D_4$ & The four-leaf star $K_{1,4}$.\\
$\widetilde D_{d+4}$, $d\ge1$ & Two trivalent vertices joined by a path of
length $d$, with two additional immediate leaves at each end.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\caption{All trees with adjacency spectral radius at most two. Arm lengths
count edges of the terminal skeleton, not edges of the host tree. The
finite types have $2I-A_H\succ0$; affine types have corank one.}
\label{mts:tab:ADE}
\end{table}

\begin{proposition}[Classical tree criterion]\label{mts:prop:ADE}
A nonempty tree $H$ satisfies $I-A_H/2\succeq0$ if and only if it occurs
in Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
This is Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:ADElist}, and Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE} is its
list (a)--(f) in source~10's layout. Source~10's proof is the same
elementary argument (excluded degrees five and four through $K_{1,5}$ and
the $K_{1,4}$ eigenvector, the double-fork eigenvector, and Schur pivots
along the arms) and is not reprinted. For a skeleton with one trivalent
vertex and arm lengths $a\le b\le c$, the decisive condition is the arm
inequality~\eqref{ade:eq:arms},
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{a+1}+\frac1{b+1}+\frac1{c+1}\ge1,
 \label{mts:eq:arms}
\end{equation}
with equality exactly in the affine cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof of Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main} (source~10, direct)]
The inversion bridge gives (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii). An unmarked hull
branch is excluded by Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:branch}. On every remaining nonempty
marking, Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:identity} and Lemma~\ref{mts:lem:resolvent} give stability when $C_H\succeq0$,
and Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:certificate} excludes it otherwise. The empty case is
$F=\det L$. Finally Proposition~\ref{mts:prop:ADE} identifies the matrix criterion with
(iv). For a nonnegative adjacency matrix its largest eigenvalue is its
spectral radius, giving the stated equivalent numerical criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Positive covariance is also necessary]\label{mts:cor:PSDexistence}
The graph $\calA(T;S)$ is stable if and only if a positive-semidefinite
symmetric matrix satisfying \eqref{mts:eq:energy} exists. Such a matrix is
automatically supported on $S$ and is unique.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Singleton equations make every diagonal outside $S$ zero. A
positive-semidefinite matrix with $C_{ii}=0$ has its entire $i$th row zero,
as follows from its two-by-two principal minors. Now use
Theorems~\ref{mts:thm:covariance} and~\ref{mts:thm:main}.
\end{proof}

\section{Recognition and geometric consequences}\label{mts:sec:recognition}

\begin{theorem}[Linear-time recognition]\label{mts:thm:recognition}
Given a tree by adjacency lists and a marking, stability of $\calA(T;S)$ can
be decided in $O(n)$ combinatorial time, without constructing its support
polynomial and without numerical eigenvalue computation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Handle $S=\varnothing$ separately. Repeatedly remove unmarked leaves,
updating degrees with a queue. Every vertex and edge is processed a
constant number of times, and the remaining graph is $K=\Hull_T(S)$.
Reject if a remaining unmarked vertex has degree at least three.
Suppress the unmarked degree-two vertices, following each path once.
This constructs $H$ in linear time. Its membership in Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE} is
checked from its degrees, the number of branches, and, in the one-branch
case, its three arm lengths. These traversals are linear.
\end{proof}

A geometric rejection can include three explicit first-mark paths, giving
the induced theta certificate. A positive result can include the skeleton
shape and the subdivision paths. A spectral rejection can be supplemented
by the rational vector of Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:certificate}. The theorem's linear-time
claim concerns the structural decision, not an unproved uniform bound on
the bit length of every possible rationalized eigenvector.

\begin{corollary}[Four-leaf bound]\label{mts:cor:leaves}
If $S$ is stable and $|S|\ge2$, then $\Hull_T(S)$ has at most four leaves.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Suppressing degree-two vertices does not change the leaves, and every
ADE tree in Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE} has at most four.
\end{proof}

The bound is on the number of \emph{hull leaves}, not the number of marks:
a path can have all its vertices marked, and a double-fork skeleton can
have arbitrarily many marks along its central path.

\begin{theorem}[A sharp diameter window]\label{mts:thm:diameter}
Let $\alpha_{\mathrm{st}}(T)$ be the largest cardinality of a stable marking.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \diam(T)+1\le\alpha_{\mathrm{st}}(T)
       \le\min\{n,\diam(T)+3\}.
 \label{mts:eq:diameter}
\end{equation}
The offsets one, two, and three are all attained.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Mark all vertices on a longest path. Its hull and skeleton are paths, so
it is stable and has $\diam(T)+1$ vertices. Conversely, every nonempty
stable marking has an ADE skeleton $H$ on $|S|$ vertices. Inspection of
Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE}, or its arm formulas, gives
$|V(H)|\le\diam(H)+3$. Distances between terminals can only increase under
subdivision, so $\diam(H)\le\diam(T)$. Also $|S|\le n$.
Paths attain offset one, $K_{1,3}$ attains offset two, and $K_{1,4}$ attains
offset three.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[No monotonicity under changing the neighborhood]\label{mts:prop:nonmonotone}
The stable markings are in general neither downward closed nor upward
closed under inclusion. Every marking of $T$ is stable if and only if $T$
is a path.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On $K_{1,3}$ the fully marked set has skeleton $D_4$ and is stable, but
deleting its center mark leaves the unstable three-leaf marking. On
$K_{1,5}$, the center together with four leaves is stable, whereas adding
the fifth leaf gives the excluded five-leaf star. Thus neither monotonicity
holds.

If $T$ is a path, every hull and skeleton are paths. If $T$ is not a path,
it has a vertex with at least three neighbors. Mark precisely three of
those neighbors. The hull is a three-leaf star with unmarked center, so
this marking is unstable.
\end{proof}

These examples explain why minimum repair cannot be reduced to a naive
procedure which only deletes marks or only adds missing branch marks.

\section{An exact endpoint formula for all stable neighborhoods}\label{mts:sec:enumeration}

Define the stable-marking family and its enumerators by
\begin{align}
 \Stab(T)&=\{S\subseteq V(T):F_{T,S}\text{ is real stable}\},\notag\\
 \Zpoly_T(z)&=\sum_{S\in\Stab(T)}z^S,
 & Z_T(t;w)&=\Zpoly_T((tw_v)_{v\in V}).
 \label{mts:eq:Z}
\end{align}
Here $z^S=\prod_{v\in S}z_v$. Write $Z_T(t)=Z_T(t;\one)$ for unweighted
size enumeration. This polynomial counts \emph{apex neighborhoods}; it is
not $p_{\calA(T;S)}$, which counts supports for one fixed neighborhood.

For distinct vertices $a,b$, let $\pathin ab$ be the internal vertices of
the unique $a$--$b$ path, and put
\begin{equation}
 P_{ab}(z)=\prod_{v\in\pathin ab}(1+z_v).
 \label{mts:eq:pathproduct}
\end{equation}
For a vertex set $R$ let
\[
 E_k(R)=\sum_{A\subseteq R,\ |A|=k}z^A,
 \qquad E_0(R)=1,
\]
with $E_k(R)=0$ for $k>|R|$.

For $\ell=3,4$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal L_\ell(T)=\{L\subseteq V:|L|=\ell,\ \Leaf(\Hull_T(L))=L\}.
 \label{mts:eq:leafsets}
\end{equation}
Not every three- or four-element set is eligible: an element lying between
two others is not a leaf of their hull and must be excluded. Each pair of
distinct vertices is automatically eligible as a two-leaf hull.

\subsection{The three-leaf factor}

For $L=\{a,b,c\}\in\mathcal L_3(T)$, let $o=o(L)$ be the unique trivalent
vertex of its hull. Its three arms have internal vertex sets
$R_1,R_2,R_3$, excluding $o$ and the corresponding leaf. Let $\mathcal E$
be the set of all \emph{distinct permutations} of the six triples
\begin{equation}
 (0,1,1),\ (0,1,2),\ (0,1,3),\ (1,1,1),\ (0,2,2),\ (0,1,4).
 \label{mts:eq:exceptions}
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}
 Q(R_1,R_2,R_3)
 =1+\sum_{i=1}^3\left(\prod_{v\in R_i}(1+z_v)-1\right)
   +\sum_{(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathcal E}\prod_{i=1}^3E_{k_i}(R_i).
 \label{mts:eq:Q}
\end{equation}
The first part counts choices of internal marks on at most one arm. The
second part contains the six exceptional finite/affine patterns. Repeated
coordinates in a triple do not create extra multiplicities.

\subsection{Four-leaf hulls}

Every four-leaf tree, after degree-two vertices are suppressed, has either
one degree-four vertex or two degree-three vertices. Partition
$\mathcal L_4(T)$ accordingly as $\mathcal L_4^{(4)}(T)$ and
$\mathcal L_4^{(3,3)}(T)$. In the first case denote the branch by $o(L)$;
in the second denote the two branches by $o(L),p(L)$. These are vertices
of the host tree, and may be separated by any positive path length.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted endpoint decomposition]\label{mts:thm:enumerator}
For every nonempty finite tree,
\begin{align}
 \Zpoly_T(z)
 &=1+\sum_{v\in V}z_v
   +\sum_{\{a,b\}\subseteq V}z_a z_b P_{ab}(z)\notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{L\in\mathcal L_3(T)}
            z^{L\cup\{o(L)\}}Q(R_1,R_2,R_3)\notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{L\in\mathcal L_4^{(4)}(T)}z^{L\cup\{o(L)\}}\notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{L\in\mathcal L_4^{(3,3)}(T)}
            z^{L\cup\{o(L),p(L)\}}P_{o(L)p(L)}(z).
 \label{mts:eq:enumerator}
\end{align}
Every monomial on the right occurs once. In particular the expression,
although \eqref{mts:eq:Q} uses a subtraction shorthand, has nonnegative
coefficients after expansion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The empty marking and all singletons give the first two terms. Every
other stable marking has a unique leaf set
$L=\Leaf(\Hull_T(S))$ with $2\le|L|\le4$, by Corollary~\ref{mts:cor:leaves}.
All vertices outside this hull are unmarked. The leaves and all branch
vertices of the hull must be marked; only its degree-two vertices can be
chosen freely subject to the ADE condition. Moreover
$\Hull_T(S)=\Hull_T(L)$, so each outer case in \eqref{mts:eq:enumerator} is
recoverable uniquely from the resulting marking.

If $|L|=2$, the hull is a path. Its endpoints must be marked and any
subset of internal vertices is allowed, giving $z_a z_b P_{ab}$.

If $|L|=3$, its branch $o$ and three leaves are mandatory. If $k_i$
internal marks are chosen on arm $i$, the terminal skeleton has arm
lengths $k_i+1$. By Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE}, it is of $D$ type when at least two of
the $k_i$ vanish, giving the first part of \eqref{mts:eq:Q}. The remaining
allowed unordered triples are exactly \eqref{mts:eq:exceptions}. For a
specified triple, the weighted choices are
$E_{k_1}(R_1)E_{k_2}(R_2)E_{k_3}(R_3)$. These cases are disjoint from the
$D$ cases and from one another.

If $|L|=4$ and there is one degree-four branch, the only allowed skeleton
is $\widetilde D_4$. Hence none of its four pendant arms may contain an
extra mark. If there are two degree-three branches, the only allowed
skeleton is an affine double fork. Again the four pendant arms may have
no extra marks, but every subset of the internal joining path is allowed.
These are precisely the last two lines. No other hull leaf count or branch
type can occur, completing the disjoint decomposition.
\end{proof}

This is a polynomial-size \emph{description}, not a promise to print every
monomial of the multivariate expansion in polynomial time. For example,
$\Zpoly_{P_n}(z)=\prod_v(1+z_v)$ has $2^n$ distinct monomials.

\begin{theorem}[Exact counting in polynomial time]\label{mts:thm:counting}
For rational vertex weights $w_v$, the complete coefficient vector of
$Z_T(t;w)$ can be computed using $O(n^5)$ exact arithmetic operations and
polynomial space. For unit weights, counting stable neighborhoods and
counting those of any prescribed cardinality have polynomial bit
complexity.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate all subsets of at most four endpoints, of which there are
$O(n^4)$. Using unique tree paths, construct their hulls, check that the
chosen vertices are exactly the leaves, and identify the branches in
$O(n)$ time per candidate. Store path polynomials
$\prod_{v\in\pathin ab}(1+w_vt)$ for endpoint pairs. There are $O(n^2)$
such products, each of degree at most $n$; even independent multiplication
for each pair costs at most $O(n^4)$ arithmetic operations and uses
$O(n^3)$ coefficient storage.

After substituting $z_v=tw_v$, each $E_k(R_i)$ is a scalar multiple of
$t^k$, obtained from the appropriate path polynomial. The exceptional
list is fixed and has $k_i\le4$. Thus every endpoint contribution can be
added to the answer in $O(n)$ operations. The total is $O(n^5)$.

For unit weights, every output coefficient is at most $2^n$ and has
$O(n)$ bits. The path products, elementary coefficients, and accumulated
nonnegative contributions have polynomial bit length as well, so exact
integer arithmetic preserves polynomial bit complexity. With rational
weights of total input bit length $B$, all squarefree monomial products
have a common denominator dividing the product of the input denominators;
the coefficient numerators and denominators have $O(B+n)$ bits up to
standard representation constants. The same argument therefore also
supplies polynomial bit complexity in $n+B$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Independent random markings}

For independently marked vertices with probabilities $0<p_v<1$, the exact
probability of obtaining a stable neighborhood is
\begin{equation}
 \Pr(S\in\Stab(T))
 =\left(\prod_{v\in V}(1-p_v)\right)
     Z_T\left(1;\left(\frac{p_v}{1-p_v}\right)_{v\in V}\right).
 \label{mts:eq:probability}
\end{equation}
This follows by factoring the probability of each marking. Values $p_v=0$
or $1$ are handled by the original finite sum, or by continuity. Thus
rational independent marking probabilities also admit exact polynomial-time
stability-probability evaluation, despite the lack of monotonicity.

\section{Maximum-weight choice and minimum-cost repair}\label{mts:sec:optimization}

\begin{theorem}[Exact maximum-weight stable marking]\label{mts:thm:optimization}
Given arbitrary rational scores $c_v$, one can find a set $S\in\Stab(T)$
maximizing $\sum_{v\in S}c_v$ in $O(n^5)$ arithmetic operations and
comparisons. Negative scores are allowed, and an optimizing set, not just
its value, is returned.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the endpoint cases of Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:enumerator}, but maximize rather than
sum. Consider the empty marking and every singleton separately. For each
other case, include its mandatory leaves and branch vertices.

On a two-leaf path, choose exactly the positive-score internal vertices;
zero-score choices can be resolved arbitrarily. For a three-leaf hull,
first consider the $D$ cases: either no internal marks, or positive-score
internal marks on one selected arm only. Take the best of these options.
For each exceptional triple $(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathcal E$, choose the $k_i$
highest-score vertices of arm $i$; reject that triple if an arm is too
short. These selections can include negative scores, because the required
cardinalities are fixed within the case. Only the four largest entries
per arm are needed, and they can be found in a linear scan.

For a four-leaf hull with one degree-four branch, there are no optional
marks. With two trivalent branches, choose all positive-score internal
vertices on their joining path and none on the pendant arms. Compare all
candidate totals and retain their vertex sets. Each endpoint case is
processed in $O(n)$ time and there are $O(n^4)$ cases. Correctness follows
from the exhaustive, disjoint geometric description in
Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:enumerator} and elementary optimization within each free or
fixed-cardinality region.
\end{proof}

This is not a generic theorem about optimizing stable matroids. The host
is a tree and only its single apex neighborhood is changed. The small
number of hull leaves and fixed list of exceptional arm counts are doing
the algorithmic work.

\begin{corollary}[Nearest stable neighborhood]\label{mts:cor:repair}
Given an initial neighborhood $S_0$, a stable neighborhood minimizing
$|S\triangle S_0|$ is computable within the same bound. More generally,
nonnegative rational costs for adding and deleting individual apex edges
can be minimized exactly.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For Hamming distance, assign
$c_v=2\ind_{\{v\in S_0\}}-1$. Then
\[
 |S\triangle S_0|=|S_0|-\sum_{v\in S}c_v.
\]
For weighted repair, let $d_v$ be the deletion cost on $v\in S_0$ and
$a_v$ the addition cost on $v\notin S_0$. The total repair cost is
\[
 \sum_{v\in S_0}d_v
 -\sum_{v\in S\cap S_0}d_v
 +\sum_{v\in S\setminus S_0}a_v.
\]
Use score $d_v$ on the original marks and score $-a_v$ elsewhere, and
apply Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:optimization}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Why additions can be optimal]
On the three-leaf star, start with the three leaves marked. Adding the
center costs one and makes the marking stable. Deleting one leaf also
costs one, but deletion cost two per leaf and center-addition cost one
makes addition uniquely cheaper. Conversely, on a fully marked five-leaf
star, deletion of one leaf repairs the spectral obstruction; adding
marks cannot help because all vertices are already marked.
\end{example}

The implementation exposes four public entrypoints:
\begin{center}\small\ttfamily
\begin{tabular}{ll}
recognize & stable\_polynomial\\
maximum\_weight\_stable & nearest\_stable
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
All use integer or rational arithmetic, never a floating-point spectral tolerance.

\section{Explicit families and a second real-rootedness classification}\label{mts:sec:shape}

\subsection{Paths and stars}

\begin{proposition}[Path and star formulas]\label{mts:prop:star}
For a path,
\begin{equation}
 \Zpoly_{P_n}(z)=\prod_{v\in V(P_n)}(1+z_v),
 \qquad Z_{P_n}(t)=(1+t)^n.
 \label{mts:eq:pathZ}
\end{equation}
For the star $K_{1,m}$, with center $o$ and leaf set $L$,
\begin{align}
 \Zpoly_{K_{1,m}}(z)
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(2,m)}E_k(L)
       +z_o\sum_{k=0}^{\min(4,m)}E_k(L),\label{mts:eq:starZmulti}\\
 Z_{K_{1,m}}(t)
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(2,m)}\binom mk t^k
       +t\sum_{k=0}^{\min(4,m)}\binom mk t^k.
 \label{mts:eq:starZ}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All path markings are stable. For the star with unmarked center, at most
two leaves may be marked, since three create an unmarked hull branch.
With marked center, the skeleton is a star with the selected leaves, and
its covariance is positive semidefinite precisely when at most four
leaves are selected. Count these disjoint alternatives.
\end{proof}

For $m\ge4$ the total number of stable star neighborhoods is
\begin{equation}
 Z_{K_{1,m}}(1)=2+2m+2\binom m2+\binom m3+\binom m4.
 \label{mts:eq:starcount}
\end{equation}
Under uniform independent marking its probability is this count divided
by $2^{m+1}$, asymptotic to $m^4/(24\,2^{m+1})$. Thus paths have stable
probability one, while large stars have exponentially small stable
probability with a polynomial prefactor.

\subsection{Two initial coefficients force complete root rigidity}

The following elementary equality argument is useful beyond this example.
It explains why good root geometry cannot survive the act of counting
stable neighborhoods.

\begin{lemma}[Two-level root rigidity]\label{mts:lem:rigidity}
Let $\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}$ contain every subset of cardinality at
most two, and put $f(t)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal F}t^{|S|}$. Then $f$ has only
real roots if and only if $\mathcal F=2^{[n]}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The assertion is immediate for $n\le1$. Otherwise $f(0)=1$, $[t]f=n$,
and $[t^2]f=\binom n2$. If $f$ has only real roots, its nonnegative
coefficients imply all roots are negative. Writing $d=\deg f\le n$, we
can therefore factor
\[
 f(t)=\prod_{i=1}^d(1+\lambda_i t),\qquad\lambda_i>0.
\]
Comparison of the first two coefficients gives
\[
 \sum_i\lambda_i=n,\qquad
 \sum_i\lambda_i^2=n^2-2\binom n2=n.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz now gives $n^2\le dn$, so $d\ge n$. Thus $d=n$ and
equality holds; all $\lambda_i=1$. Hence $f=(1+t)^n$. Since each
coefficient counts a subcollection of the $\binom nk$ available
$k$-subsets, equality of every coefficient forces every subset to belong
to $\mathcal F$. The reverse implication is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Root classification for the stable-neighborhood enumerator]\label{mts:thm:Zroots}
For every nonempty finite tree $T$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $T$ is a path;
\item every marking of $T$ is stable;
\item the univariate polynomial $Z_T(t)$ has only real roots;
\item the multivariate polynomial $\Zpoly_T(z)$ is real stable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The equivalence of (i) and (ii) is Proposition~\ref{mts:prop:nonmonotone}. A marking of
size at most two always has an empty, singleton, or path skeleton, so
$\Stab(T)$ contains all subsets of those sizes. Lemma~\ref{mts:lem:rigidity} gives
(iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii). If (iv) holds, diagonalizing all variables
gives (iii). If $T$ is a path, \eqref{mts:eq:pathZ} is a product of stable
linear factors, giving (iv).
\end{proof}

This theorem concerns $Z_T$, which varies the apex neighborhood. It does
\emph{not} assert that the support polynomial $p_{\calA(T;S)}$ for an
individual nonpath tree is nonreal-rooted. In particular, the repository
proves real-rootedness for the full-apex star support polynomial for every
$m$, even though $Z_{K_{1,m}}$ is nonreal-rooted for every $m\ge3$
(Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:introbook}: the book $B_m$ is $\calA(K_{1,m})$).

\subsection{Even weaker coefficient-shape properties fail}

Small exact examples from \eqref{mts:eq:starZ} are
\begin{align}
 Z_{K_{1,3}}(t)&=1+4t+6t^2+3t^3+t^4=(1+t)^4-t^3,\label{mts:eq:Z3}\\
 Z_{K_{1,4}}(t)&=1+5t+10t^2+6t^3+4t^4+t^5,\label{mts:eq:Z4}\\
 Z_{K_{1,6}}(t)&=1+7t+21t^2+15t^3+20t^4+15t^5.
 \label{mts:eq:Z6}
\end{align}
The first has no real zeros at all: it is positive for $t\ge0$ by its
coefficients, and for $t<0$ its expression $(1+t)^4-t^3$ is positive.
In the second, $6^2<10\cdot4$, so log-concavity fails. In the third,
$21>15<20$, so unimodality fails.

More generally, for every $m\ge4$, the coefficients at degrees two,
three, and four are respectively $m(m+1)/2$, $\binom m2$, and
$\binom m3$. The log-concavity inequality at degree three fails exactly
when
\[
 3(m-1)<(m+1)(m-2),
\]
which holds for every integer $m\ge4$. For every $m\ge6$, those same three
coefficients have a strict dip, since
$m(m+1)/2>\binom m2<\binom m3$. Thus the exact algorithms do not rely on
unimodality, log-concavity, or a hidden stable-polynomial property of the
marking family.

The distinction between these checks matters. In particular, the
exhaustive counting and optimization comparisons use the structural
classification to identify admissible subsets; they are not independent
analytic tests of stability in every number of variables. The full
coefficient checks \emph{do} independently enumerate matching supports
and compare every coefficient of the determinant formula for the stated
small orders. Neither kind of finite check replaces the general proofs.

\subsection{Independent exact routines}

The matching-support enumerator uses sets of attainable column masks,
not lists of matching witnesses. If $D(I)$ is the collection of column
sets matchable to a row set $I$, then for a chosen row $i\in I$,
\[
 D(I)=\{J\cup\{j\}:J\in D(I\setminus\{i\}),\ j\in N(i)\setminus J\}.
\]
Identical column sets are deduplicated. This is essential: counting
matchings would verify the wrong polynomial.

The covariance test is independent of the ADE shape routine. It constructs
the matrix forced by singleton and consecutive-mark path equations, then
uses exact Schur complements. A negative diagonal rejects positive
semidefiniteness; a zero diagonal must have a zero row; a positive pivot
is eliminated exactly. In particular affine diagrams are not classified
by a floating-point cutoff.

For the connected-set test, every nonempty connected $W\subseteq V(T)$
is enumerated in the stated small orders. The program checks that all
energies \eqref{mts:eq:energy} hold exactly if and only if no unmarked hull
branch exists. The determinant tests use integer incidence cofactors and
the rational quadratic form, not sampled numerical polynomial evaluations.

A formalization could isolate a small finite combinatorial core: hulls,

partition. Separately it would prove the forest-cofactor identity,
resolvent lemma, and exact Rayleigh certificate. The classical stable
minor closure and spectral facts should be explicit dependencies until

\section{Further research questions and topics}\label{mts:sec:questions}

The following questions retain the distinctions exposed by the proofs.
They are not claims established by this article.
[Merge note: source~10's eight questions continue the numbering as
Research questions~\ref{mts:q:diagonal}--\ref{mts:q:compiler}. The first
three restate Part~VI's Research questions~\ref{mts:hq:diagonals},
\ref{mts:hq:apices} and~\ref{mts:hq:cycles} with added detail and are
printed with pointers, because source~10's formulations are broader
(arbitrary markings; a terminal-geometry criterion; unicyclic and cactus
hosts). Research questions~\ref{mts:q:certificates}
and~\ref{mts:q:compiler} overlap Part~VI's Research
questions~\ref{ade:q:first}, \ref{mts:hq:formal} and~\ref{ade:q:last}.
The other three are new.]

\begin{question}[The individual support diagonal]\label{mts:q:diagonal}
Classify real-rootedness of $p_{\calA(T;S)}(t)$ for arbitrary marked trees.
In particular, resolve the repository's question whether the full-apex
diagonal $p_{\calA(T;V(T))}$ is real-rooted for every tree.
\end{question}
Our criterion classifies multivariate stability, not this weaker
property. On branch-complete markings, \eqref{mts:eq:identity} gives a concrete
resolvent formula for investigating residues on Laplacian eigenspaces.
The theorem that $Z_T$ is real-rooted only for paths does not answer this
question, because $Z_T$ varies $S$ rather than counting supports for one $S$.
[Merge note: the full-apex case is Part~VI's Research
question~\ref{mts:hq:diagonals}; its merge note records an exact check of
every tree with $2\le r\le12$ (all real-rooted), which is evidence, not an
answer. For $S=V(T)$, the specialization $x=\one$, $y=t\one$, $s=t$ of
\eqref{mts:eq:identity} is Part~VI's
formula~\eqref{ade:eq:treeunivariatequestion}.]

\begin{question}[More than one apex]\label{mts:q:apices}
For two or more separately selectable apex elements with specified
neighborhoods, characterize when the canonical support polynomial is
stable. Is there a finite terminal-geometry criterion analogous to
branch-completeness?
\end{question}
One apex leaves precisely one unrooted incidence component. Several apices
must coordinate several components while removing multiplicities of their
assignments. Simply multiplying the one-apex formulas, or replacing the
rank-one term by $\det(L+sC)$, counts the wrong objects.
[Merge note: this is Part~VI's Research question~\ref{mts:hq:apices},
asked there with prescribed terminal neighbourhoods; source~10 adds the
request for a criterion analogous to branch-completeness.]

\begin{question}[Cycle-space corrections]\label{mts:q:cycles}
Extend the covariance-existence and stability dichotomies when the host
is unicyclic, a cactus, or has bounded cycle rank.
\end{question}
The present proof uses unique paths twice: to create the unmarked-branch
obstruction and to make every relevant selected incidence component a
tree with one-dimensional cofactor direction. Cycles change both the
connected-set energy and the multiplicities of incidence determinants.
A useful first goal is an exact analogue of Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:covariance} for one
cycle, before attempting a general stable representation.
[Merge note: this is Part~VI's Research question~\ref{mts:hq:cycles}, with
the covariance-existence dichotomy added as a target.]

\begin{question}[Faster exact enumeration and repair]\label{mts:q:faster}
Can the $O(n^5)$ endpoint algorithms be replaced by quadratic or near-linear
tree dynamic programs, retaining exact weighted coefficients or optimal
signed-score repair?
\end{question}
The finite arm-pattern list suggests a bounded set of states, but the
unbounded $A$, $D$, and affine-$D$ path lengths must be compressed without
counting the same hull repeatedly. The formulas here give an exact
baseline for validating such a faster implementation.

\begin{question}[Coefficient shape after real-rootedness fails]\label{mts:q:shape}
Characterize the trees whose stable-neighborhood size sequence is
log-concave or unimodal. Find structural explanations for the number and
location of its modes, rather than expecting a universal positive answer.
\end{question}
Stars already disprove universal log-concavity and unimodality. Any useful
positive theorem must impose a genuine structural restriction. The
path-only real-rootedness theorem settles the strongest version entirely;
it should not be reposed as an open question.

\begin{question}[Random trees and asymptotic stable probabilities]\label{mts:q:random}
For random labelled trees, or deterministic families with growing branching
complexity, determine the asymptotic probability that an independent
random marking is stable.
\end{question}
The exact formula \eqref{mts:eq:probability} reduces the problem to counts of
small-leaf hulls and their allowable marked paths. Paths and stars show
that no universal order of magnitude is possible without hypotheses.
A meaningful analysis must specify both the host-tree model and the
marking probabilities.
[Added 30 September 2026, batch 66: answered in Part~X for uniform
labelled trees with independent marks of one common probability $p$,
in every regime of $p$ (Theorems~\ref{rts:thm:jointcount},
\ref{rts:thm:poisson}, \ref{rts:thm:rare}, \ref{rts:thm:sparse}
and~\ref{rts:thm:critical}): for instance the probability is asymptotic
to $\frac98\sqrt{2\pi}\,p^3n^{5/2}e^{-pn}$ whenever $p\sqrt n\to\infty$.
For deterministic families Part~X gives the probability only within a
polynomial factor, from the diameter (Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:quenched});
an asymptotic equivalent there, other random-tree laws and
vertex-dependent markings remain open (Research
questions~\ref{rts:q:quenched}, \ref{rts:q:models}
and~\ref{rts:q:inhomogeneous}). See Section~\ref{rts:sec:answers}.]

\begin{question}[Restricted obstruction certificates]\label{mts:q:certificates}
Within this family, identify economical canonical-matroid certificates
for the spectral failures and compare them with the geometric odd-theta
certificate. Which different marked trees yield the same excluded matroid
minor?
\end{question}
The existing theory of small half-plane-property matroids
\cite{KummerSert} and cyclotomic spectral obstructions \cite{McKeeSmythIMRN}
must be consulted before claiming a new minimal-obstruction list. Our
criterion gives a recognition theorem, not such a minimality classification.
[Merge note: compare Part~VI's Research questions~\ref{ade:q:first}
(forbidden canonical matroid minors) and~\ref{ade:q:last} (minimal induced
obstructions), and Section~\ref{ade:sec:inducedminimal}: the unstable
bipartite graphs have no finite set of induced-minimal obstructions.]

\begin{question}[A small verified compiler from trees to proofs]\label{mts:q:compiler}
Formalize the endpoint partition and construct a checker that accepts
an ADE skeleton certificate or a negative obstruction certificate and
returns a theorem about the original support polynomial.
\end{question}
The input should include the actual marking and host-tree paths, not
just an abstract diagram. Correctness of the compiler must connect the
combinatorial certificate to the determinant or minor semantics. Checking
an isolated rational inequality is insufficient without that bridge.
[Merge note: compare Part~VI's Research question~\ref{mts:hq:formal}
(formal integration of the cofactor lemma, covariance rigidity and the
Rayleigh certificate compiler).]

\section{Conclusion}

The full-apex ADE theorem leaves a geometric issue when the neighborhood
is arbitrary: an unmarked branch connecting several marks is not an
innocent subdivision vertex. It simultaneously destroys the connected-set
covariance interpolation and creates a persistent odd-theta obstruction.
Once those branches are marked, the terminal-supported covariance is
forced, and its positive semidefiniteness is both sufficient and necessary.
This gives a complete classification for all markings of all finite trees.

The classification does more than decide one instance. The marked hull
has at most four leaves, producing a disjoint weighted endpoint formula,
exact counting, and exact signed-score selection and repair. The sharp
diameter window limits the maximum cardinality, while the two-level
rigidity argument determines the real-rootedness of the neighborhood
counting polynomial completely. These conclusions remain meaningful even
though that enumerator can fail both log-concavity and unimodality.

The general bipartite stability problem and the individual tree-support
diagonal problem remain distinct further targets. The present contribution
is a proved and executable completion of one structural family, with its
new enumeration and optimization consequences, rather than an unsupported
claim about all half-plane-property matroids.

\needspace{10\baselineskip}
\section{A compact proof certificate for the main results}
\label{mts:app:certificate}

\noindent\emph{(Appendix~B of source~10.)}
The classification can be audited in the following order.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If a hull branch is unmarked, select three first-mark paths. Their
incidence--apex graph is induced, and legitimate matroid path shortening
reduces it to the credited quartic obstruction.
\item Otherwise the terminal skeleton is a tree. Its zero-extended
$C_H=I-A_H/2$ has connected-set energy exactly the indicator of meeting
$S$, and singleton/path equations force this matrix uniquely.
\item Forest cofactors turn those energies into the Boolean support
identity $F=\det L+s\tr(\adj(L)C)$.
\item Positive semidefiniteness gives stability through the sign of
$\im\tr(CL^{-1})$. Indefiniteness gives a rational negative Rayleigh
value through a diagonally rescaled tree Laplacian.
\item The classical tree spectrum calculation identifies the ADE list.
Its at-most-four-leaf property partitions every stable marking by a unique
endpoint hull. The allowed arm counts yield \eqref{mts:eq:enumerator}; free
choices and fixed-cardinality choices yield the optimization algorithm.
\item Every one- and two-element marking is stable. If $Z_T$ were
real-rooted, its first two coefficients would force all its factors to be
$1+t$, hence every marking would be stable, forcing $T$ to be a path.
\end{enumerate}

This certificate lists logical dependencies. It is not machine-checked
formal proof syntax, and the accompanying finite tests should not be
substituted for any of its all-size steps.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~11 (as delivered).}
For a bipartite graph $H=(X\sqcup Y,E)$, let $\cD_H$ consist of the
nonnegative integral demand vectors $c$ satisfying
$c(A)\le |N_H(A)|$ for all $A\subseteq Y$. A classical correspondence of
Suho Oh identifies the vectors with a fixed positive support $J$ with the
supplier sets $I$ matchable to $J$. We give an explicit algorithmic
realization using two integer-margin minimum-cost transportation problems,
each of total flow $|X|(|J|+1)$. A fixed cycle-generic cost system forces
both optimal supports to be the same spanning tree. The supplier degrees
recover $I$, while the supplier leaves recover every coordinate of $c$.
We prove the inverse identities directly, without enumerating a mixed
subdivision, and obtain polynomial bit complexity and short exact
primal--dual certificates. A core factorization reduces the forward flow
to $|J|(|J|+1)$, followed by independent supplier attachments.

The construction closes the full-coordinate sampling gap recorded in the
pinned ProveIt report on preorder root polytopes. Composing it with the
established matroid basis walk gives almost-uniform samples of actual
lattice points, not merely their supports; total-variation error is
preserved exactly. We also prove support restrictions, unused-supplier
deletion laws, perturbation invariance, and an obstruction to fully
symmetry-natural deterministic bijections. The results apply to every
finite preorder. An executable standard-library implementation is checked
exhaustively on $4{,}785$ bipartite graphs and on all $390$ labeled
preorders of order at most four.
\end{tcolorbox}
\noindent The abstract is reproduced as delivered, with source~11's
$\mathcal D_H$ printed $\cD_H$. Its ``pinned ProveIt report'' is this
report, and the gap is Part~V's sampling boundary.

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Contribution and status (source~11, as delivered).} The
existence of the demand/base correspondence, its counting consequences,
and rapid mixing on matroid bases are prior results. The contribution
developed here is the explicit two-flow realization, its proofs and
certificates, its compatibility laws, and the resulting full-coordinate
sampler for the repository's problem. The manuscript does not assert
first priority over all possible algorithmic realizations of Oh's
construction. The proofs below are ordinary mathematical proofs; the
implementation has been run and tested, but neither has been checked by
Lean or Rocq or independently refereed.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{What Part~IX answers}
\label{tf:sec:answers}
Status after Part~IX, as of 30 September 2026:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item \textbf{Part~V's ``Sampling boundary'' is answered.} Its samplers
return support sets or support pairs; Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:sampler} and
Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:preordersampler} return almost-uniform actual
vectors of $\cD_H$ and of $\Qt\cap\Z^V$, with every coordinate value, and
Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:tv} transfers the total-variation error exactly. The
bijection is restriction-compatible in two stated senses: for receivers
outside the support (Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:receivers}) and for suppliers
outside the selected set (Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:deletion}); arbitrary
minors are not covered. The approximate, not exact, sense of
``almost-uniform'' is that of Part~V's support samplers. The same answers
Part~V's ``Precisely what is sampled for a preorder'' and its two
unnumbered questions ``An effective demand/support bijection (source~06)''
and ``A direct demand/support bijection (source~07)''
(Section~\ref{lor:sec:oldquestions}): the tree is extracted from an
optimum, so no noncanonical chosen matching enters, as source~07's test
demands.
\item \textbf{The bijection of Research questions~\ref{gam:q:bridge}
and~\ref{gam:q:bijection} is constructed}, explicitly, in polynomial time,
preserving the exact receiver support, and with an elementary proof that
imports no Ehrhart theory (Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:main} and the merge note
after Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:count}). Their compatibility clauses are
answered only in part: the cost system is a controlled ordering of the
augmented edges, positive support weights are preserved
(Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:tv}), and deletion laws hold outside $I$ and $J$;
Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:symmetry} shows that no deterministic
support-preserving rule is equivariant under all graph automorphisms, so
full naturality is impossible. The rest is Research
question~\ref{tf:q:functoriality}.
\item \textbf{Part~VII's ``Direct lattice-point bijections
(source~09)''} is answered in its support-resolved part; a
\emph{canonical} bijection, and compatibility with the paired clone
action, are not obtained (the maps depend on the cost chamber,
Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:chambers}; symmetry is restored only in law, by
a random cost order).
\item \textbf{Not answered:} Part~V's Research
question~\ref{tf:hq:capacities} (binary capacities), which
Research question~\ref{tf:q:capacities} extends; Part~V's Research
question~\ref{lor:q:last} (formalization), which Research
question~\ref{tf:q:formal} overlaps. No other numbered research question
of Parts~I--VIII is affected, and Conjectures~5.1(d) and~5.3

\section{The question answered and the relation to prior work}
\label{tf:sec:target}

\subsection{The question left by Part~V}
\label{tf:sec:gap}
Parts~II, IV and~V of this report develop support enumerators, matroid
models, and approximate counting for bipartite demand vectors. Part~V
ends its sampling discussion (Section~\ref{lor:sec:algorithms}) with an
explicit boundary, the ``Sampling boundary'' box after ``Sampling after
fixing the support size'': the algorithms produce support sets or
matchable support pairs, not the coordinate values of a uniform lattice
point (see also ``Precisely what is sampled for a preorder'' in the same
section). It asks for an efficiently invertible, restriction-compatible
demand/support correspondence.

[Merge note: source~11 identifies this passage by the pinned commit, the
path and blob of this report's \texttt{article.tex}, and the line
interval 9510--9555 of that blob (Section~\ref{tf:sec:source}); those
line numbers refer to Parts~I--VII as printed before Part~VIII and no
longer apply. Source~11 calls it ``a dated, identified question, not an
inference from a missing theorem in a summary.'' Parts~II and~IV asked
the same bijective question earlier, as Research
questions~\ref{gam:q:bridge} and~\ref{gam:q:bijection}; Part~V repeats it
in Section~\ref{lor:sec:oldquestions}, and Part~VII in its questions
(``Direct lattice-point bijections (source~09)''). What Part~IX answers of
each is stated in Section~\ref{tf:sec:answers}.]

The distinction matters. Suppose a probability measure has the right
support-size distribution. This does not specify the individual positive
coordinates. Even knowing every fibre cardinality does not provide a
polynomial-time decoder from a uniformly chosen object of an equinumerous
family. The algorithm below supplies precisely that decoder and its inverse.

\subsection{What is already known}
Oh constructs a correspondence between bases of a transversal matroid and
positive-coordinate lattice points of an associated generalized
permutohedron \cite{Oh}. In the arXiv version inspected here,
Section~4, Remark~4.4 and Proposition~4.5 describe the relevant
zonotopal-cell correspondence and its leaf-count formula. Thus an
abstract demand/base bijection is not a new theorem of this manuscript.
Ohsugi--Tsuchiya use the same correspondence in the graph-polynomial
setting \cite{OT20}. Loho--Smith study closely related degree-vector and
lattice-point bijections for matching fields and triangulations
\cite{LohoSmith}. Those works are important context for the present use of
coherent spanning trees.

The rapid-mixing theorem used later is due to Anari, Liu, Oveis Gharan,
and Vinzant \cite{ALOV}. Their theorem gives polynomial-time approximate
sampling of matroid bases. We do not prove a new general matroid mixing
theorem. Likewise, the definition and lattice-point study of preorder
polytopes originate in the work of Athanasiadis--Chapoton \cite{AC}.
[Merge note: source~11 prints the author order ``Chapoton--Athanasiadis''
here and in its bibliography; this report's entry~\cite{AC} and Part~I
use the order of the arXiv record, Athanasiadis and Chapoton.]

Our approach locates the relevant coherent tree with one min-cost flow in
each direction. The important extra information is the explicit margins,
finite perturbation sizes, bit bounds, independently checkable optimality
certificate, and exact compatibility statements. No list of cells in a
triangulation is an input. No numerical infinitesimal is required.
