\section{Demand vectors and matchable support pairs}
\label{tf:sec:definitions}
Let $H=(X\sqcup Y,E)$ be a finite simple bipartite graph, with
$m=|X|$ suppliers and $n=|Y|$ receivers. For $A\subseteq Y$ put
\[
 N_H(A)=\{x\in X:\text{some }y\in A\text{ satisfies }xy\in E\},
 \qquad c(A)=\sum_{y\in A}c_y.
\]
We study the finite set
\begin{equation}
 \cD_H=\{c\in\N^Y:c(A)\le |N_H(A)|\text{ for every }A\subseteq Y\}.
 \label{tf:eq:demand}
\end{equation}
In particular, $\sum_yc_y\le m$. For $J\subseteq Y$, write
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \cD_H(J)&=\{c\in\cD_H:\supp(c)=J\},\\
 \PM_J(H)&=\{I\subseteq X:|I|=|J|,\ H[I,J]\text{ has a perfect matching}\}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{tf:eq:fibres}
\end{equation}
A member of $\PM_J(H)$ is a supplier \emph{set}, not a perfect matching.
Multiple perfect matchings on the same pair $(I,J)$ are counted once.
We also use the disjoint union
\[
 \PM(H)=\{(I,J):J\subseteq Y,\ I\in\PM_J(H)\}.
\]
There is one empty pair, corresponding to the zero vector.
[Merge note: $\cD_H$ is Part~V's demand set~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:hall} and
Parts~II and~IV's $\mathcal R_H$; $\PM(H)$ is Part~V's set of matchable
support pairs (written $U\sim_H S$ there, and $\mathcal M(H)$ in
Part~IV). Source~11 writes $\mathcal B_H(J)$ and $\mathcal B_H$ for
$\PM_J(H)$ and $\PM(H)$; they are renamed because Part~V's $\cB_H$ is the
basis polynomial~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:basis} (Section~\ref{tf:sec:notation}).]

\begin{lemma}[Integral allocation]
\label{tf:lem:hall}
A vector $c\in\N^Y$ belongs to $\cD_H$ if and only if there is a partial
assignment of suppliers to adjacent receivers in which each supplier is
used at most once and receiver $y$ receives exactly $c_y$ suppliers.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An assignment immediately proves all the inequalities in
\eqref{tf:eq:demand}. Conversely, replace receiver $y$ by $c_y$ identical
copies. For a set $U$ of copies, let $A$ be the original receivers
represented in $U$. Then
$|U|\le c(A)\le |N_H(A)|=|N(U)|$.
These inequalities imply a matching saturating every copy. To recall the
augmenting-path argument, take a maximum matching. If a copy is unmatched,
follow alternating paths from all unmatched copies. Every reachable
supplier must be matched, or an augmenting path exists. Its matched copy
is reachable too. The reachable copies therefore outnumber their entire
supplier neighbourhood, contradicting the displayed inequality. The
saturating matching is the required assignment.
\end{proof}
[Merge note: this is the clone-and-Hall argument of Part~II
(Section~\ref{htwo:sec:count}) and Part~V's
Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:hallmodel}, with the augmenting-path step spelled out
as in Part~IV's manuscript~01 (after Lemma~\ref{gam:lem:count}).]

For $J\ne\varnothing$ write $r=|J|$ and add a dummy receiver $0$ adjacent to
every supplier. We use $0$ as a separate symbol, not as a member of $Y$.
Let
\begin{equation}
 G_J=(X\sqcup(\{0\}\cup J),\ E_J),\qquad
 E_J=\{xy\in E:y\in J\}\cup\{x0:x\in X\}.
 \label{tf:eq:augmentation}
\end{equation}
An assignment may send an unused supplier to the dummy. For a demand
vector define
\begin{equation}
 c_0=m-\sum_{y\in J}c_y.
 \label{tf:eq:c0}
\end{equation}
This number is nonnegative. An empty fibre is detected by asking whether
$J$ can be saturated by a matching; if it cannot, neither side of
\eqref{tf:eq:fibres} has an element.

\section{The two-flow theorem}
\label{tf:sec:main}
We first state the complete construction. Its proof occupies the next
four sections.

\begin{definition}[Cycle-generic costs]
A real edge-cost assignment $w$ on the full dummy-augmented graph is
\emph{cycle-generic} if the alternating sum of its costs around every
simple even cycle is nonzero. All restrictions to $G_J$ use the same costs.
\end{definition}

For an explicit integral choice, order all $q=|E|+m$ augmented edges as
$e_0,\ldots,e_{q-1}$ and set
\begin{equation}
 w(e_i)=2^i.
 \label{tf:eq:costs}
\end{equation}
The largest power in a cycle sum exceeds the sum of all the smaller
powers, so this choice is cycle-generic. Each cost has at most $q$ bits.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit two-flow correspondence]
\label{tf:thm:main}
Fix cycle-generic costs $w$. For each nonempty $J$ with $r=|J|$,
the following maps are well-defined inverse bijections
\[
 \Phi_w:\PM_J(H)\longrightarrow\cD_H(J),\qquad
 \Psi_w:\cD_H(J)\longrightarrow\PM_J(H).
\]

\emph{Forward map.} Given $I\in\PM_J(H)$, minimize
$\sum_{xy\in E_J}w_{xy}F_{xy}$ over nonnegative flows with margins
\begingroup\renewcommand{\theHequation}{tf.two-flow.A}% unique PDF anchor for a tagged display (merge)
\begin{equation}
 \sum_y F_{xy}=m\one_{x\in I}+1\quad(x\in X),\qquad
 \sum_x F_{xy}=m\quad(y\in\{0\}\cup J).
 \tag{A}\label{tf:eq:A}
\end{equation}\endgroup
The positive-flow support is a unique spanning tree $T$. A supplier in
$I$ has degree two and any other supplier has degree one. Set
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_w(I)_y=
 \begin{cases}
 1+\#\{x\in X\setminus I:xy\in T\},&y\in J,\\
 0,&y\notin J.
 \end{cases}
 \label{tf:eq:leaf}
\end{equation}

\emph{Inverse map.} Given $c\in\cD_H(J)$, put $L=r+1$ and use
\eqref{tf:eq:c0}. Minimize the same objective with margins
\begingroup\renewcommand{\theHequation}{tf.two-flow.B}% unique PDF anchor for a tagged display (merge)
\begin{equation}
 \sum_y F_{xy}=L\quad(x\in X),\qquad
 \sum_xF_{x0}=Lc_0+r,\qquad
 \sum_xF_{xy}=Lc_y-1\quad(y\in J).
 \tag{B}\label{tf:eq:B}
\end{equation}\endgroup
Again the support is a unique spanning tree $T$, every supplier has
degree one or two, and
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_w(c)=\{x\in X:\deg_T(x)=2\}.
 \label{tf:eq:inverse}
\end{equation}
If $c=\Phi_w(I)$, the two optimal trees in (A) and (B) are identical.
Each optimization has integral optimal flow and total flow $m(r+1)$.
For the costs \eqref{tf:eq:costs}, both maps are computable in polynomial bit
time and admit exact certificates of polynomial length.
\end{theorem}

For $J=\varnothing$ the maps send $\varnothing$ to the zero vector and
back. This convention covers $m=0$, $n=0$, and graphs with no ordinary
edges. The theorem concerns \emph{one} optimization per direction, not
an alternating iterative process between (A) and (B).

\section{Why generic optimal supports are trees}
\label{tf:sec:transport}
For a bipartite graph $G=(X\sqcup C,E_G)$ and positive margins $a_x,b_y$
with equal sums, a transportation flow is a family $F_{xy}\ge0$ on its
edges satisfying the row and column sums. A feasible set is compact:
every flow coordinate lies between zero and the total margin. Thus a
linear cost has a minimum whenever the set is nonempty.

\begin{lemma}[Acyclicity, uniqueness, and integrality]
\label{tf:lem:forest}
Under cycle-generic costs, every minimum-cost flow has an acyclic positive
support, and the minimum-cost flow is unique. If its margins are integral,
its positive flow values are integral.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose an optimal positive support contains a cycle. Add a sufficiently
small $\eta$ to the alternate edges and subtract $\eta$ from the other
edges. Both signs of $\eta$ preserve nonnegativity for sufficiently small
$|\eta|$, and all margins are unchanged. The objective varies by a
nonzero multiple of $\eta$, so one sign improves the cost. This is a
contradiction.

If $F$ and $F'$ were distinct optima, their average would also be optimal
and its positive support would be the union of their supports. That union
is therefore a forest. But $F-F'$ has zero row and column sums. Repeatedly
remove a leaf of the forest: the difference on its sole edge must be zero.
This removes every edge and shows $F=F'$.

For integral margins, the same leaf elimination proves integrality of the
unique feasible flow on its support forest. The sole edge at a leaf has
its integral residual margin; subtracting that value leaves integral
margins on the remaining forest.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Strict tree certificates]
\label{tf:lem:dual}
Suppose a minimum-cost flow is positive on a spanning tree $T$. There
are potentials $u_x,v_y$, unique after fixing one of them, such that
\begin{equation}
 u_x+v_y=w_{xy}\quad(xy\in T),\qquad
 u_x+v_y<w_{xy}\quad(xy\in E_G\setminus T).
 \label{tf:eq:dual}
\end{equation}
Consequently, every other positive flow on $T$, for any other margins,
is the unique minimum-cost flow for those margins.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix one potential and propagate the equations along the tree. For an
off-tree edge $xy$, its reduced cost
$s_{xy}=w_{xy}-u_x-v_y$ is the alternating cost of the fundamental cycle
formed by adding $xy$ to $T$. If $s_{xy}<0$, add a small positive flow on
$xy$ and alternate along the tree path. All edges from which flow is
subtracted are positive. The margins stay fixed and the cost decreases.
Thus $s_{xy}\ge0$, and cycle-genericity excludes equality.

For any flow $G$ of the new margins $a',b'$, one has
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{xy}w_{xy}G_{xy}
 =\sum_xu_xa'_x+\sum_yv_yb'_y+
   \sum_{xy\notin T}s_{xy}G_{xy}.
 \label{tf:eq:dualgap}
\end{equation}
A flow on $T$ attains the first two terms. Strict positivity of the slacks
forces every other optimum to be supported on $T$; leaf elimination then
forces equality of the flows. This proves the assertion without requiring
a separate appeal to a linear-programming duality theorem.
\end{proof}

These lemmas separate two issues. Genericity gives a forest, but not
necessarily a connected support for arbitrary margins. The particular
congruences in (A) and (B) supply connectedness. Once a tree is known,
\eqref{tf:eq:dualgap} transfers its optimality between margin systems.

\section{The forward optimization and the leaf decoder}
\label{tf:sec:forward}
Assume $I\in\PM_J(H)$, $r=|J|>0$. Choose any perfect matching between
$I$ and $J$. Send $m$ units along every matching edge and one unit from
every supplier to the dummy. This is a feasible flow for (A). In
particular, all margins are strictly positive.

\begin{lemma}[Connectedness from the forward margins]
\label{tf:lem:Aconnected}
The unique optimizer of (A) has connected support.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take a component of its positive-support forest, with supplier set $A$
and receiver set $C\subseteq\{0\}\cup J$. Positive margins imply that
every vertex is incident to a positive edge, so the component contains at
least one supplier. Balancing its total margins gives
\[
 m|I\cap A|+|A|=m|C|.
\]
Hence $m$ divides $|A|$. Since $1\le |A|\le m$, the component contains all
suppliers. There can be no second component, again because every component
has a supplier.
\end{proof}

The optimizer is therefore a spanning tree with $m+r$ edges. Each
supplier in $I$ has row sum $m+1$, larger than the column sum $m$ of any
single receiver. Its degree is at least two. Every other supplier has
degree at least one. The sum of these lower bounds is
$2r+(m-r)=m+r$, exactly the number of tree edges. Thus all the degree
bounds are equalities.

Root the tree at the dummy $0$. A supplier in $I$ has one parent receiver
and one child receiver; a supplier outside $I$ is a leaf. Conversely,
every nonroot receiver has a parent supplier, and that supplier must have
degree two. Consequently the parent--child edges from $I$ to $J$ form a
perfect matching. This matching is extracted from the tree, and need not
be the matching used to establish feasibility of (A).

Assign each supplier in $I$ to its child receiver, and every supplier
outside $I$ to its sole neighbour. Ignore assignments to $0$. Every
receiver in $J$ gets one supplier from $I$, together with precisely its
supplier leaves. It follows from Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:hall} that the vector
in \eqref{tf:eq:leaf} lies in $\cD_H(J)$. This proves well-definedness of
the forward map, including all coordinate values, rather than only its
support.

\section{The inverse optimization and its degree bound}
\label{tf:sec:backward}
Now let $c\in\cD_H(J)$ with $r>0$, and put $L=r+1$. By
Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:hall}, allocate suppliers to realize $c$, sending unused
ones to $0$. Scale that assignment by $L$. For each $y\in J$, choose one
supplier assigned to $y$ and divert one unit of its flow from $y$ to the
dummy. These chosen suppliers are distinct. This gives exactly the margins
(B). All receiver margins are positive, including the dummy margin
$Lc_0+r$.

\begin{lemma}[Connectedness from the inverse margins]
\label{tf:lem:Bconnected}
The unique optimizer of (B) has connected support.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If a positive-support component does not contain $0$, let its receiver
set be $S\subseteq J$ and its supplier set be $A$. Positive margins imply
$1\le |S|\le r$. The margin equality is
\[
 L|A|=L c(S)-|S|,
\]
which says that $L=r+1$ divides $|S|$. This is impossible. Hence every
component contains the same vertex $0$, and there is only one.
\end{proof}

Root the resulting spanning tree at $0$. For a receiver $y\in J$, let
$S_y$ denote the \emph{number} of receiver vertices from $J$ in the
subtree rooted at $y$; let $A_y$ denote the set of suppliers in that
subtree. Its parent supplier $x$ lies outside this subtree. Summing flow
balances over the subtree yields
\begin{equation}
 F_{xy}=L\left(\sum_{z\text{ in the receiver subtree of }y}c_z-|A_y|\right)-S_y.
 \label{tf:eq:cutB}
\end{equation}
The left side is positive and at most the whole row supply $L$ of $x$.
The quantity in parentheses is an integer, and $1\le S_y\le r=L-1$.
The only possible integer is therefore one. We have proved
\begin{equation}
 F_{xy}=L-S_y\qquad\text{for every supplier-to-child-receiver edge.}
 \label{tf:eq:childB}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[No branching at a supplier]
\label{tf:lem:degreeB}
Every supplier in the optimal tree of (B) has degree at most two.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If a supplier had two distinct child receivers $y,z$, their subtrees
would be disjoint, so $S_y+S_z\le r$. By \eqref{tf:eq:childB}, the sum of
its flows to just those two children would be
\[
 2L-(S_y+S_z)\ge 2L-r=L+1,
\]
exceeding its entire row supply $L$. Thus a supplier has at most one child
receiver, in addition to its parent receiver.
\end{proof}

All supplier degrees are one or two. Since the tree has $m+r$ edges,
exactly $r$ suppliers have degree two. Denote their set by $I$. The
parent--child construction from the preceding section again gives a
perfect matching between $I$ and $J$. It remains to check that the leaf
formula recovers the original vector, not merely some demand vector.

For $y\in J$, let $\ell_y$ be its number of supplier-leaf children. If a
nonleaf supplier child of $y$ has child receiver $z$, its flow to $y$ is
$L-(L-S_z)=S_z$. The flow into $y$ from its parent supplier is $L-S_y$.
Since
\[
 S_y=1+\sum_{z}S_z,
\]
where the sum runs over these grandchildren, its column balance becomes
\[
 Lc_y-1=(L-S_y)+L\ell_y+\sum_z S_z=L(1+\ell_y)-1.
\]
Thus $c_y=1+\ell_y$, exactly \eqref{tf:eq:leaf}. At the dummy, the analogous
identity gives $c_0=\ell_0$. This proves the local recovery assertion.

\section{Why the two trees are identical: the inverse proof}
\label{tf:sec:inverse}
It is not enough to establish that the formulas have the right codomains.
We must show that an optimal tree for one flow is optimal for the other.
The strict tree certificate makes this possible.

Call a rooted spanning tree of $G_J$ \emph{admissible} if every supplier
has degree one or two. Write $I(T)$ for its degree-two suppliers and
$c(T)$ for its leaf vector in \eqref{tf:eq:leaf}. For a receiver $y\in J$,
write $S_y$ for its subtree's number of ordinary receivers and $a_y$ for
its subtree's number of suppliers. The parent supplier of $y$ is outside
that subtree. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 1\le S_y\le r,\qquad 0\le a_y\le m-1.
 \label{tf:eq:subbounds}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Two positive flows on every admissible tree]
\label{tf:lem:twoflows}
Every admissible tree supports a strictly positive flow for (A) with
$I=I(T)$ and a strictly positive flow for (B) with $c=c(T)$. The flows
are as follows. A supplier leaf sends $1$ in (A) and $L$ in (B) to its
parent. If a degree-two supplier $x$ has child receiver $y$, then
\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &x\longrightarrow y&x\longrightarrow\text{parent}(x)\\\hline
 \text{flow (A)}&m-a_y&a_y+1\\
 \text{flow (B)}&L-S_y&S_y
\end{array}
\label{tf:eq:twoflowtable}
\end{equation}
All entries are strictly positive integers.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Positivity follows from \eqref{tf:eq:subbounds}. Row sums are immediate.
For a nonroot receiver $y$, its supplier subtree consists of its supplier
leaves and its nonleaf supplier children, together with the subtrees of
their child receivers. Thus
\[
 a_y=\ell_y+\sum_z(1+a_z).
\]
Its column sum in (A) is therefore
\[
 (m-a_y)+\ell_y+\sum_z(a_z+1)=m.
\]
At $0$, every supplier is in one of the attached subtrees or is a leaf
there, so the same identity gives column sum $m$.

For (B), the column computation in Section~\ref{tf:sec:backward} gives
$L(1+\ell_y)-1=Lc_y-1$ for $y\in J$. The dummy receives
$L\ell_0+\sum_zS_z=Lc_0+r$. This is the required margin.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:main}]
The preceding sections prove feasibility, uniqueness, connectedness,
integrality, the supplier degree pattern, and both decoding formulas.
Let $T$ be the optimizer of (A) for $I$, and set $c=c(T)$. By
Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:twoflows}, $T$ supports a positive flow with margins (B).
Its strict potentials from Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:dual} prove that this is the
unique optimizer of (B). Therefore $\Psi_w(\Phi_w(I))=I$.

Conversely, let $T$ be the optimizer of (B) for $c$ and let $I=I(T)$.
Section~\ref{tf:sec:backward} proves $c(T)=c$ and $I\in\PM_J(H)$.
Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:twoflows} puts a positive (A)-flow on $T$, and the same
strict potentials make it the unique (A)-optimizer. Thus
$\Phi_w(\Psi_w(c))=c$. The total margin in each case is $m(r+1)$.
The polynomial complexity and certificate claims are proved in
Section~\ref{tf:sec:algorithms}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Supportwise counting identity]
\label{tf:cor:count}
For every bipartite graph $H$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{c\in\cD_H}\prod_{y\in\supp(c)}z_y
 =\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(H)}\prod_{y\in J}z_y.
 \label{tf:eq:supportidentity}
\end{equation}
In particular, $|\cD_H(J)|=|\PM_J(H)|$ for every $J$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take the disjoint union of the support-preserving bijections, including
the empty fibre.
\end{proof}
The identity is a known consequence of the Oh correspondence, not a new
counting formula claimed here. The theorem supplies an explicit decoder
for each term on its right-hand side.

[Merge note (second route): Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:count} is Part~V's

every $z_y=1$ gives Part~II's Lemma~\ref{htwo:lem:count}. Its proof above
is therefore a further proof of those three statements, and the only one

Research questions~\ref{gam:q:bridge} and~\ref{gam:q:bijection} ask for,

and R\"ohrle--Ulirsch inputs) are untouched, and, as source~11 says, the

\section{A smaller core flow and independent supplier attachments}
\label{tf:sec:core}
The forward optimization can be made substantially smaller when $m$ is
large and the requested support has size $r$. Its essential tree is
already determined by the $r$ selected suppliers.

\begin{theorem}[Core-tree factorization]
\label{tf:thm:core}
Fix $I\in\PM_J(H)$ with $r=|I|=|J|>0$. Restrict the augmented graph to
$I\sqcup(\{0\}\cup J)$, keeping the original costs. Solve its forward
problem with $m$ replaced by $r$:
\begin{equation}
 \sum_y K_{xy}=r+1\quad(x\in I),\qquad
 \sum_{x\in I}K_{xy}=r\quad(y\in\{0\}\cup J).
 \label{tf:eq:coreflow}
\end{equation}
Let $T_I$ be its optimal tree and let $v_y$ be its receiver potentials,
normalized by $v_0=0$. For every unselected supplier define
\begin{equation}
 a_I(x)=\underset{y\in (N_H(x)\cap J)\cup\{0\}}{\arg\min}
              (w_{xy}-v_y),\qquad x\in X\setminus I.
 \label{tf:eq:attach}
\end{equation}
Each minimizer is unique. The full optimal tree of (A) is
\begin{equation}
 T=T_I\cup\{x a_I(x):x\in X\setminus I\},
 \label{tf:eq:coretree}
\end{equation}
and its demand vector is
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_w(I)_y=1+\#\{x\notin I:a_I(x)=y\}\quad(y\in J).
 \label{tf:eq:coredecode}
\end{equation}
Thus the forward map needs a flow of total value $r(r+1)$ on only $r$
supplier vertices, followed by independent reduced-cost comparisons for
the other suppliers.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The restriction has a perfect matching from $I$ to $J$, so the earlier
forward argument applies. All its suppliers have degree two. Its strict
potentials satisfy \eqref{tf:eq:dual} on the restricted graph.

If two distinct receivers $y,z$ tied in \eqref{tf:eq:attach}, the path from
$y$ to $z$ in $T_I$, together with $xy$ and $xz$, would form a simple
cycle of alternating cost zero. This contradicts cycle-genericity.
Define the new supplier potential by
$u_x=w_{x,a_I(x)}-v_{a_I(x)}$. All its other incident edges then have
strictly positive reduced cost.

The graph \eqref{tf:eq:coretree} is an admissible spanning tree: it is
obtained by attaching supplier leaves to $T_I$. The old potentials and
the new $u_x$ satisfy the strict certificate on the entire graph. By
Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:twoflows}, the tree supports a positive flow with the full
margins (A), and \eqref{tf:eq:dualgap} proves it uniquely optimal. The leaf
decoder is exactly \eqref{tf:eq:coredecode}.
\end{proof}

This factorization supplies a useful interpretation. The chosen supplier
set determines a small price system $v$. Every other supplier chooses the
unique cheapest receiver after subtracting that receiver's price, or
chooses the dummy. Its contribution to the demand vector is independently
one unit at the chosen ordinary receiver, or zero at the dummy. The
independence here is \emph{deterministic additivity}, not a probabilistic
independence assertion about a random supplier set.

\begin{corollary}[Unused-supplier deletion and insertion]
\label{tf:cor:deletion}
Keep $I,J$ and inherited costs fixed, and replace $X$ by any subset
$X'\supseteq I$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \Phi^{X'}_w(I)_y
 =1+\#\{x\in X'\setminus I:a_I(x)=y\}\quad(y\in J).
 \label{tf:eq:restriction}
\end{equation}
In particular, deleting one supplier outside $I$ subtracts one unit at
its chosen receiver, or subtracts nothing if it chooses the dummy.
All such deletions commute. If $I\subseteq X'\subseteq X''$, then
\begin{equation}
 \Phi^{X'}_w(I)\le\Phi^{X''}_w(I)\quad\text{coordinatewise},\qquad
 \|\Phi^{X''}_w(I)-\Phi^{X'}_w(I)\|_1\le |X''\setminus X'|.
 \label{tf:eq:monotone}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The core tree, its receiver potentials, and the minimizer for any
remaining supplier do not change when another unselected supplier is
deleted. Apply Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:core}. Every ordinary coordinate stays
positive because of its initial contribution one.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Support restriction]
\label{tf:cor:receivers}
Deleting or adding receivers outside the fixed support $J$, together
with their incident edges, does not change either map when the costs on
the retained augmented edges are unchanged.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Both optimizations are performed on exactly $G_J$, and the core
construction uses only the same receivers.
\end{proof}

These are precise senses in which the correspondence is restriction
compatible. Deleting a supplier \emph{inside} $I$, deleting a positive
receiver, or changing the cost choices is a different operation and is
not covered by these statements.

\section{Finite perturbations and stability of the construction}
\label{tf:sec:perturbations}

\subsection{No infinitesimals are needed}
The integral margins are normalized versions of two finite perturbations.
They can be varied over explicit open ranges without changing the tree.

\begin{proposition}[Margin invariance]
\label{tf:prop:margins}
Let $T$ be the common optimal tree corresponding to $(I,c)$. Both of the
following transportation problems have the same optimal support $T$:
\begin{align}
 a_x&=\one_{x\in I}+\delta_x,& b_y&=1\quad(y\in\{0\}\cup J),
 &\delta_x&>0,\quad\sum_x\delta_x=1; \label{tf:eq:delta}\\
 a_x&=1,& b_0&=c_0+r\varepsilon,
 & b_y&=c_y-\varepsilon\quad(y\in J),\quad 0<\varepsilon<1/r.
 \label{tf:eq:epsilon}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the notation of Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:twoflows}. In \eqref{tf:eq:delta}, a
supplier leaf sends $\delta_x$ to its parent. A selected supplier $x$
with child receiver $y$ sends
\[
 1-\sum_{z\in A_y}\delta_z\quad\text{to }y,
 \qquad \delta_x+\sum_{z\in A_y}\delta_z\quad\text{to its parent},
\]
where $A_y$ is the supplier subtree of $y$. These quantities are strictly
positive because $x\notin A_y$ and all $\delta$ are positive. The row
sums are as required; partitioning supplier subtrees verifies that every
column sum is one.

For \eqref{tf:eq:epsilon}, a supplier leaf sends one. A selected supplier
with child $y$ sends $1-\varepsilon S_y$ to $y$ and
$\varepsilon S_y$ to its parent. These values are positive in the stated
range. The calculation used for (B) gives the desired column sums.
The strict potentials of $T$ prove optimality for both families by
Lemma~\ref{tf:lem:dual}.
\end{proof}

Taking $\delta_x=1/m$ and multiplying by $m$ gives (A). Taking
$\varepsilon=1/(r+1)$ and multiplying by $r+1$ gives (B). These choices
have small exact denominators. The upper bound on $\varepsilon$ cannot be
replaced uniformly by a non-strict bound: when a receiver subtree contains
all $r$ ordinary receivers, the corresponding edge becomes zero at
$\varepsilon=1/r$.

\subsection{Cost chambers and gauge invariance}

\begin{proposition}[Dependence only on cycle signs]
\label{tf:prop:chambers}
Two cycle-generic cost assignments with the same signs on every oriented
alternating cycle induce the same maps. In particular, the maps are
constant on each chamber of the finite arrangement of cycle-cost
hyperplanes. Replacing $w_{xy}$ by $w_{xy}+\alpha_x+\beta_y$ leaves the
maps unchanged.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A positive feasible tree is optimal precisely when all its off-tree
reduced costs are positive. Each is an oriented fundamental-cycle sum.
Its feasibility depends on the margins, not on the costs. Thus the same
trees are selected whenever all cycle signs agree. For the gauge change,
every fixed-margin objective changes by the same constant
$\sum_x\alpha_xa_x+\sum_y\beta_yb_y$, or equivalently every alternating
cycle sum is unchanged.
\end{proof}

For the integral costs \eqref{tf:eq:costs}, every nonzero cycle sum has
absolute value at least one. A simple cycle has at most $m+n+1$ edges.
Consequently any perturbation satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \max_e|\widetilde w_e-w_e|<\frac{1}{m+n+1}
 \label{tf:eq:costradius}
\end{equation}
preserves every cycle sign, hence all maps simultaneously. This is a
mathematical robustness estimate, not a recommendation to replace exact
arithmetic by unvalidated floating-point optimization.

\section{Algorithms, bit complexity, and exact certificates}
\label{tf:sec:algorithms}

\subsection{Explicit complexity bounds}
Let $q_J=|E_J|\le q=|E|+m$. With costs \eqref{tf:eq:costs}, either full
flow problem is a network with $O(m+r)$ vertices, $O(q_J+m+r)$ arcs,
and total integral flow
\[
 F=m(r+1)\le m(m+1).
\]
A successive shortest augmenting-path implementation makes at most $F$
augmentations because each augmentation increases the sent flow by at
least one. Reduced-cost potentials permit Dijkstra's algorithm at each
iteration. This gives the conservative arithmetic-operation bound
\begin{equation}
 O\bigl(m(r+1)(q_J+m+r)\log(m+r+2)\bigr).
 \label{tf:eq:complexity}
\end{equation}
The bit length of costs, distances, and potentials is
$O(q+\log(m+r+2))$: initial costs have $q$ bits, and the algorithm uses
shortest residual paths and tree-potential sums of polynomial length.
Flow values have $O(\log(m+r+2))$ bits. Thus \eqref{tf:eq:complexity} is a
polynomial bit-time bound as well, with the usual cost of operations on
these integers included. It is not a unit-cost claim for exponentially
large numbers. Reading the graph, constructing the globally ordered cost
system, and writing the $n$ output coordinates add input-processing work;
a canonical sorted edge order takes $O(q\log(q+2)+n)$ elementary operations.
These costs are separate from the flow bound.

The core version improves the forward bound. If $q_I$ is the number of
augmented edges incident to $I$ and ending in $\{0\}\cup J$, its flow
uses only $2r+1$ bipartite vertices, total flow $r(r+1)$, and then a
linear scan of the remaining incident edges. A corresponding bound is
\begin{equation}
 O\bigl(r(r+1)(q_I+r)\log(r+2)+q_J+n\bigr)
 \label{tf:eq:corecomplexity}
\end{equation}
on integers of the same polynomial bit length. This bound explains why
it is useful to separate selected suppliers from unused suppliers.
This is the mathematical flow-and-scan bound after the input representation
has been prepared. The reference code favors a simple, checkable interface
and may rebuild restricted graph data rather than cache it.

The shipped optimizer starts with zero flow and nonnegative integral edge
costs. It repeatedly uses a shortest residual augmenting path, increases
flow by its bottleneck, and updates vertex potentials. It then derives a
new set of row/column potentials directly from the final support tree and
checks the certificate below. The correctness theorem does not require
trusting the optimizer's internal floating-point tolerances: there are
none. A different exact or numerical solver may be substituted, but its
output must pass the same exact certificate checks.

\subsection{A small trusted checker}
For a claimed optimum on $G_J$, supply the following data: the $m+r$
positive tree edges with their integral flows, $m$ row potentials, and
$r+1$ column potentials. A checker verifies that the edges form a
spanning tree, that all flows are positive, that the required margins
hold, that every tree edge has reduced cost zero, and that every other
allowed edge has strictly positive reduced cost.

\begin{theorem}[Soundness of the certificate]
\label{tf:thm:certificate}
If these checks pass, the supplied flow is the unique minimum-cost flow
for the stated margins. Checking the expected margins (A) or (B) and the
appropriate degree/leaf decoder then certifies the corresponding map
value. The certificate has $O(m+r)$ integer entries apart from endpoint
labels, and can be verified with $O(q_J+m+r)$ elementary graph and
arithmetic operations, up to the usual near-linear disjoint-set overhead.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The objective-gap identity \eqref{tf:eq:dualgap} is valid for every competing
feasible flow. All off-tree terms are nonnegative and have strictly
positive coefficients. An optimum must therefore be supported on the
claimed tree. Zero-margin differences on a tree vanish by leaf
elimination. The remaining assertions follow from counting the listed
entries and scanning the edges and margins.
\end{proof}

For the core algorithm, only the $2r$ core-tree edges and the core
potentials need a transportation certificate. For each of the $m-r$
remaining suppliers, the checker verifies the unique minimum in
\eqref{tf:eq:attach}, then counts its contribution. This checks the
smaller computation directly. It does not have to re-run the full flow.

\subsection{Reproducible interface}
The standard-library module
\nolinkurl{code/11-two-flow-transport_bijection.py} (delivered as
\nolinkurl{code/transport_bijection.py}) exposes the full forward map,
the faster core forward map, the inverse map, both certificate checkers,
and a basis-walk sampler. Suppliers and ordinary receivers use zero-based
indices; the dummy is represented by $-1$. The mathematical $0$ denoting
the dummy should not be confused with ordinary receiver index $0$ in the
program.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
from transport_bijection import BipartiteDemand

H = BipartiteDemand(4, 3,
    [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2)])
I, J = (0, 1, 3), (0, 1, 2)

c, cert = H.basis_to_demand_core(I, J, certificate=True)
H.verify_core_certificate(c, cert)
assert c == (1, 1, 2)
assert H.demand_to_basis(c) == (I, J)
assert H.basis_to_demand(I, J) == c
\end{lstlisting}
[Merge note: the import uses the delivered module name
\texttt{transport\_bijection}; with the shipped file name it works only in
a copy that restores the delivered layout, as the report's
\texttt{README.md} describes.]
The inverse rejects nonintegral, negative, overlarge, or infeasible
inputs. Matching routines use iterative augmenting paths, so their graph
size is not limited by Python's recursion depth. Enumeration routines
occur only in the verifier, not in the production maps.

\section{A complete worked certificate}
\label{tf:sec:example}
For readability this section numbers the suppliers $1,2,3,4$ and the
ordinary receivers $1,2,3$. Take edges
\[
 11,\quad21,\quad22,\quad32,\quad33,\quad43
\]
and choose $I=\{1,2,4\}$, $J=\{1,2,3\}$. Add all four dummy edges and
assign powers-of-two costs in the following order:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{c|rrrrrrrrrr}
edge&$10$&$11$&$20$&$21$&$22$&$30$&$32$&$33$&$40$&$43$\\\hline
cost&1&2&4&8&16&32&64&128&256&512
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The full forward margins are $(5,5,1,5)$ on suppliers and $(4,4,4,4)$
on receivers $(0,1,2,3)$. The inverse margins for the decoded vector
$c=(1,1,2)$ are $(4,4,4,4)$ on suppliers and $(3,3,3,7)$ on receivers.
Both positive supports are the tree in Figure~\ref{tf:fig:tree}.

The row and column potentials are
\begin{equation}
 u=(1,4,-128,256),\qquad v=(0,1,12,256).
 \label{tf:eq:examplepotentials}
\end{equation}
Every tree edge satisfies $u_x+v_y=w_{xy}$. The three off-tree edges
$21,30,32$ have positive slacks $3,160,180$, respectively. The exact
primal costs are $2253$ for (A) and $2363$ for (B); substituting the
respective margins in $u\cdot a+v\cdot b$ gives those same values.
These equalities and strict slacks certify both optima.

Deleting supplier $3$ leaves the core tree. Its receiver potentials are
still $v$. Supplier $3$ compares its three available reduced costs:
\[
 w_{30}-v_0=32,\qquad w_{32}-v_2=52,\qquad w_{33}-v_3=-128.
\]
It chooses receiver $3$. The core contributes $(1,1,1)$, and that single
leaf contributes $(0,0,1)$, producing $(1,1,2)$. The core transport sends
only $r(r+1)=12$ units, rather than the full transport's $m(r+1)=16$.
The complete machine-readable certificates appear in

\section{What compatibility can and cannot mean}
\label{tf:sec:limits}

\subsection{Equivariance with specified costs}
A graph isomorphism which also transports the cost assignment takes
feasible flows to feasible flows with the same objective. Uniqueness then
transports the selected tree, and the degree and leaf formulas commute
with the isomorphism. The correspondence is therefore natural for
\emph{cost-labelled} graphs. The auxiliary costs cannot in general be
removed while keeping a deterministic equivariant bijection.

\begin{proposition}[A symmetry obstruction]
\label{tf:prop:symmetry}
There is no rule assigning to every unlabelled bipartite graph a
support-preserving bijection $\PM(H)\to\cD_H$ that is equivariant under
all graph automorphisms.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take two suppliers $x_1,x_2$, one receiver $y$, and both ordinary edges.
In the positive-support fibre the two supplier sets are $\{x_1\}$ and
$\{x_2\}$. The two demand vectors are $c_y=1$ and $c_y=2$.
The automorphism swapping $x_1,x_2$ exchanges the supplier sets but fixes
each demand vector. An equivariant map would have to give the exchanged
sets the same image, contradicting injectivity.
\end{proof}

There is nevertheless an equivariant \emph{randomized} correspondence:
choose a uniformly random ordering of all augmented edges, use
\eqref{tf:eq:costs}, and apply the deterministic map for that order. A graph
isomorphism transports the uniform distribution on orders to the uniform
distribution on orders. This construction restores symmetry in law, not
as a single deterministic bijection.

\subsection{Basis locality does not imply coordinate locality}

\begin{proposition}[Unavoidable large jumps]
\label{tf:prop:jumps}
There is no constant $C$, independent of the graph, such that a bijection
from lifted matroid bases to full demand vectors always sends every basis
exchange to a coordinate change of $\ell_1$-size at most $C$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take $H=K_{m,1}$. Its demand vectors are the integers $0,1,\ldots,m$.
The lifted matroid defined in the next section is the uniform matroid of
rank $m$ on $m+1$ elements: omitting the receiver gives the empty support,
and omitting any supplier gives a matchable singleton support. Its basis
exchange graph is complete. Under any bijection, the bases mapped to $0$
and $m$ are adjacent, so an exchange has coordinate displacement $m$.
\end{proof}

Thus the transported rapidly mixing chain is an exact chain on lattice
points, but it need not be a nearest-neighbour lattice walk. This prevents
an unwarranted local-move interpretation of the sampling theorem. It does
not contradict the one-unit supplier-insertion law
\eqref{tf:eq:monotone}, which changes the graph while keeping the selected
supplier set fixed.

\section{From matroid samples to full-coordinate samples}
\label{tf:sec:sampling}

\subsection{The lifted transversal matroid}
Construct a transversal matroid $\mathsf M_H$ on the disjoint ground set
$X\sqcup Y$ using a separate set of $m$ slots indexed by $X$. The ground
element $x\in X$ can occupy only its own slot; the ground element $y\in Y$
can occupy any slot in $N_H(y)$. The supplier elements themselves occupy
all slots, so the matroid has rank $m$.

A size-$m$ ground set $B$ is a basis exactly when
\begin{equation}
 B=(X\setminus I)\cup J\quad\text{for some }(I,J)\in\PM(H).
 \label{tf:eq:lift}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the supplier elements in $B$ consume their own slots, leaving
exactly $I$ available for the receiver elements $J$. These receivers fill
those slots exactly when $I$ is matchable to $J$. This is a polynomial-time
basis oracle using ordinary bipartite matching.
[Merge note: this is Part~V's private-copy matroid $\mathsf M_H$ and its
basis correspondence, Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bases} (sources~06
and~07, the same forced-slot argument), with the private elements
identified with $X$ as in source~07; its basis polynomial is
$\cB_H$ in~\eqref{lor:sp:eq:basis}. It is the dual of Part~VII's matroid
(Section~\ref{mat:sec:prov}).]

Taking the disjoint union of Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:main} gives an explicit
bijection
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\Phi_w:\{\text{bases of }\mathsf M_H\}\longrightarrow\cD_H,
 \qquad (X\setminus I)\cup J\longmapsto\Phi_w(I,J).
 \label{tf:eq:liftedbijection}
\end{equation}
The faster core decoder from Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:core} may be used on the
right. No perfect matching is included in the state, so matching
multiplicity does not bias this correspondence.

\subsection{The exact target measure}
Give each receiver a positive rational activity $\theta_y$ and set the
supplier activity to one. For a basis $B$, its weight is
$\prod_{y\in B\cap Y}\theta_y$. The corresponding demand law is
\begin{equation}
 \mu_\theta(c)=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}
       \prod_{y\in\supp(c)}\theta_y,
 \qquad
 Z_\theta=\sum_{c\in\cD_H}\prod_{y\in\supp(c)}\theta_y.
 \label{tf:eq:measure}
\end{equation}
For $\theta_y=1$, this is the uniform distribution on individual demand
vectors. It is not the distribution obtained by assigning suppliers
independently and then recording their loads; the latter would weight a
vector by the number of assignments realizing it.

\begin{theorem}[Exact error transfer]
\label{tf:thm:tv}
Let $\pi_\theta$ be the weighted basis distribution on $\mathsf M_H$, and let
$\nu$ be any probability distribution on its bases. Then
\begin{equation}
 (\widehat\Phi_w)_*\pi_\theta=\mu_\theta,
 \qquad
 \TV\bigl((\widehat\Phi_w)_*\nu,\mu_\theta\bigr)
 =\TV(\nu,\pi_\theta).
 \label{tf:eq:tv}
\end{equation}
In particular, decoding loses no accuracy and requires no fibre-size
correction or rejection step.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The bijection preserves the support, hence the weight of each individual
state. For the second assertion, the sum
$\frac12\sum_B|\nu(B)-\pi_\theta(B)|$ is merely reindexed by the
bijection. This proves equality, rather than only the general
non-increase under a pushforward.
\end{proof}

The exact target law is independent of the cost system used for decoding.
A random independent choice of a cycle-generic cost system can therefore
also be used: conditioning on that choice gives the same exact target
law, and averaging preserves a uniform error bound.

\subsection{A fully specified almost-uniform sampler}
Use the weighted down-up walk on bases. From $B$, remove a uniformly
chosen element, obtaining $A$. Among elements $e$ with $A\cup\{e\}$ a
basis, choose $e$ with probability proportional to its activity and add
it. The general matroid theorem gives spectral gap at least $1/m$ and a
polynomial mixing bound for this walk \cite{ALOV}. Its applicability to
positive product activities follows from the weighted basis-polynomial
form of that theorem.

For completeness, the quantities needed to turn the theorem into an
explicit input-size bound are elementary. Put
\[
 N=m+n,\qquad W=\max(1,\max_y\theta_y).
\]
Start at $B_0=X$, which is always a basis of weight one. Its inverse
stationary mass obeys
\begin{equation}
 \pi_\theta(B_0)^{-1}=Z_\theta
 \le \binom NmW^m\le 2^N W^m.
 \label{tf:eq:startmass}
\end{equation}
For $0<\eta<1$ and $m>0$, the conservative budget
\begin{equation}
 t=\left\lceil m\left(N\log2+m\log W
                  +2\log(1/\eta)+2\right)\right\rceil
 \label{tf:eq:budget}
\end{equation}
is sufficient for total-variation error at most $\eta$. For example, the
usual reversible-chain estimate gives
\[
 \TV(P^t(B_0,\cdot),\pi_\theta)
 \le\tfrac12\pi_\theta(B_0)^{-1/2}e^{-t/m},
\]
using the nonnegative spectrum of the down-up operator. Substituting
\eqref{tf:eq:startmass} proves the claim with room to spare. Equivalently one
can use the direct mixing-time bound in \cite[Theorem~1.1]{ALOV}.

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-time full-vector sampling]
\label{tf:thm:sampler}
Given an explicit bipartite graph, positive rational support activities,
and $0<\eta<1$, one can sample a full vector whose distribution is within
$\eta$ in total variation of \eqref{tf:eq:measure}, in time polynomial in
the graph size, the activity bit lengths, and $\log(1/\eta)$.
In the unit-activity case this is an almost-uniform sampler for $\cD_H$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Run the basis walk for \eqref{tf:eq:budget} steps and decode once at the end.
At a step, list at most $N$ possible additions and test them by the
matching oracle from \eqref{tf:eq:lift}. Positive rational choices can be
made exactly using integer random choices after clearing denominators;
the bit lengths remain polynomial. The mixing budget is polynomial in the
claimed parameters. Apply the core decoder and Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:tv}.
The cases $m=0$ or empty ground set return the unique zero vector.
Exact bounded-integer draws give expected polynomial bit time. A worst-case
polynomial-time approximate version runs the chain to error $\eta/2$ and
caps each random-integer rejection routine, allocating total failure
probability at most $\eta/2$ across all draws. Binary rejection has
success probability at least $1/2$ at each attempt, so logarithmically
many attempts per draw suffice; on failure one may return a fixed valid
vector. This preserves the claimed total error and polynomial bound.
\end{proof}

The theorem uses ideal independent random bits. The shipped reference
sampler uses Python's pseudorandom generator, with an optional seed for
reproducibility, and implements positive \emph{integer} receiver
activities directly. It uses an integer upper bound on
\eqref{tf:eq:budget}, replacing natural logarithms by binary bit-length
bounds, so a rounded logarithm cannot shorten its budget. The maps and
certificate checkers themselves are
fully exact and deterministic. An exact rational-activity implementation
requires only replacing the weighted discrete choice, not a new
mathematical argument. A deliberately shortened user-specified walk does
not carry the stated mixing guarantee.
[Merge note: the walk is the one of Part~V's
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:FPRASpartition} (both import~\cite{ALOV}); there a
sample is a support pair, here it is decoded once, at the end, into the
full vector.]

\subsection{Conditioning on support information}
For a fixed exact support $J$, the domain is the set of bases of the
rank-$r$ transversal matroid on suppliers $X$ presented by slots $J$.
A maximum matching either detects an empty fibre or supplies a starting
basis. Sampling that matroid and applying $\Phi_w$ gives an almost-uniform
\emph{full vector} conditioned on $\supp(c)=J$. Its internal coordinate
values, not just the support, are sampled.

More generally, prescribe disjoint sets $J_+$ and $J_-$ of receivers
which must be positive and zero, respectively. In the lifted matroid,
these are the conditions $J_+\subseteq B$ and $B\cap J_-=\varnothing$.
If feasible, contracting $J_+$ and deleting $J_-$ gives a matroid whose
bases, after adjoining $J_+$, are exactly the allowed bases. Feasibility
requires that $J_+$ be independent in the deletion and that the deletion
retain rank $m$; both are matching tests. The weighted basis sampler on
this minor, followed by the same decoder, gives the corresponding
conditioned full-vector law. General minor oracles are implemented by
adjoining the contracted set before the original oracle query.
[Merge note: the minor is Part~V's Proposition~\ref{lor:sp:prop:conditioning};
what is new here is the decoding of its bases into full vectors.]

The repository also provides a log-concave tilting and rejection method
for a prescribed support \emph{size} (Part~V, ``Sampling after fixing the
support size'' in Section~\ref{lor:sec:algorithms}, with
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:coefficients}). Composing its resulting
basis distribution with \eqref{tf:eq:liftedbijection} supplies full vectors
with no further loss of total-variation accuracy. This last assertion is
a composition with the report's stated method; it is not a new proof of
its coefficient-approximation theorem.

Activities depending on coordinate magnitudes, such as
$\prod_yq_y^{c_y}$, are not covered by the support-product theorem. Nor is
an exact independent uniform sampler claimed. These are distinct problems.

\section{Preorder polytopes and integral dilations}
\label{tf:sec:preorders}
Let $\tau$ be a preorder on a finite set $V$: the relation is reflexive
and transitive, but need not be antisymmetric. A lower ideal is a set
$A\subseteq V$ such that $y\in A$ and $x\le_\tau y$ imply $x\in A$.
The associated preorder polytope is
\begin{equation}
 \Qt=\{c\in\R_{\ge0}^{V}:c(A)\le |A|
                  \text{ for every lower ideal }A\}.
 \label{tf:eq:preorderpolytope}
\end{equation}
This is the family studied in \cite{AC} and in this report
(Part~I's~\eqref{eq:Q}; the lower ideals are Part~I's order ideals $\J$).

Use one supplier and one receiver for each element of $V$, and define
\begin{equation}
 x\text{ supplies }y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\le_\tau y.
 \label{tf:eq:orientation}
\end{equation}
The orientation is explicit because the output coordinates are labelled:
reversing the preorder is not silently the same operation on those
coordinates.

\begin{proposition}[Exact demand realization]
\label{tf:prop:preorder}
For the bipartite graph $H_\tau$ in \eqref{tf:eq:orientation},
\begin{equation}
 \cD_{H_\tau}=\Qt\cap\Z^V.
 \label{tf:eq:preorderequality}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
This is Part~V's Lemma~\ref{lor:lem:preorderreduction}, with the same
orientation (an edge $i\to j$ exactly when $i\le_\tau j$, diagonal edges
included) and the same lower-closure proof, which source~11 gives again:
the neighbourhood of a receiver set $S$ is $\mathord\downarrow S$, so
$c(S)\le c(\mathord\downarrow S)\le|\mathord\downarrow S|=|N_{H_\tau}(S)|$
for $c\in\Qt\cap\Z^V$; conversely $N_{H_\tau}(A)=A$ for a lower ideal
$A$, and the demand inequality for $A$ is the ideal inequality
in~\eqref{tf:eq:preorderpolytope}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Full lattice-point sampling for every finite preorder]
\label{tf:cor:preordersampler}
Every finite preorder admits an explicit invertible support-preserving
encoding of the integer points of $\Qt$ by bases of a transversal
matroid. The encoding and decoding are polynomial-time and admit the
certificates above. In particular, there is a polynomial-time
almost-uniform sampler of the actual integer points of $\Qt$, including
their coordinate values, and corresponding samplers with positive support
activities or prescribed zero/nonzero coordinates.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:preorder}, Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:main},
\eqref{tf:eq:lift}, and Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:sampler} and its support-conditioning
construction.
\end{proof}

No bound on the height of the preorder is imposed, and equivalence
classes can have any size. The result does not rely on any of the
repository's unformalized gamma-positivity or polytopal-realization
arguments; its preorder specialization is the direct equality
\eqref{tf:eq:preorderequality}.

\subsection{Dilations and the encoding-size boundary}
For a positive integer $q$, replace each supplier of $H_\tau$ by $q$
distinguishable copies with the same neighbours. The neighbourhood of $S$
then has size $q|\mathord\downarrow S|$, so its demand set is exactly
$q\Qt\cap\Z^V$. The construction and sampler therefore apply to all
positive integral dilations as well.

This is polynomial in the \emph{expanded} input size $q|V|$, not a claim
of polynomial complexity in $\log q$. When capacities are given in binary,
explicit cloning may be exponentially expensive. Distinguishable clones
also inherit distinct costs; their exchange symmetry is not used to
identify bases. The symmetry obstruction in
Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:symmetry} explains why careless quotienting can
lose an injective correspondence.
[Merge note: the cloned graph and its pseudopolynomial boundary are
Part~V's capacity extension, Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:capacity} and the
remark after it; Part~V's Research question~\ref{tf:hq:capacities} asks
for the binary-capacity algorithm, and Research
question~\ref{tf:q:capacities} below asks it again for the bijection and
the sampler.]

\section{Computational verification and the formal proof boundary}
\label{tf:sec:formal}

\subsection{Independent finite checks}
The package includes a deterministic exact verifier using independent
matching-permutation tests and demand-inequality enumeration. On every
exhaustive graph instance it enumerates all matchable support pairs,
checks both inverse identities, checks equality of the two optimal tree
supports, checks the full and core forward implementations against each
other, verifies the exact certificates, and compares the entire image
with an independently enumerated demand set.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.42\textwidth}rY@{}}\toprule
Suite & Instances & Coverage\\\midrule
All bipartite graphs with $0\le m,n\le3$ & 689 & 5,880 support pairs;
all demand vectors.\\
All bipartite graphs with $(m,n)=(4,3)$ & 4,096 & 68,832 support pairs;
all demand vectors.\\
All labeled preorders with $0\le |V|\le4$ & 390 & 12,709 lattice points;
ideal inequalities checked against demand inequalities.\\
Seeded random graph and cost-order trials & 250 & 4,256 feasible-pair
trials, 9,427 restriction/deletion checks, 8,512 chamber/gauge checks.\\
Exact rational Markov chains & 2 & 17 states each; row sums, detailed
balance, target point weights, and finite-time distances.\\\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\caption{Executed verification. Counts refer to the reported suites;
random trials can revisit a pair, and the preorder suite can overlap the
small graph suite.}
\label{tf:tab:verification}
\end{table}

The $4{,}785$ exhaustive bipartite graphs contain $74{,}712$ matchable
support pairs in total. The preorder counts by order are
$1,1,4,29,355$, including the empty preorder. The random seed is
$20260930$. The tests also replace powers of two by powers of three,
which preserve all alternating-cycle signs, and add nonnegative row and
column gauges. Three deliberately corrupted primal/dual certificates are
rejected.

For the two exact Markov-chain tests, the target partition functions are
$17$ in the uniform case and $144$ with receiver activities $(2,3,5)$.
Starting from the supplier basis, the exact total-variation distances
after eight steps are approximately $0.00875421$ and $0.00833044$,
respectively. These numbers are exact rational computations rounded for
display, not statistical estimates or a proof of the general mixing
bound. Their full fractions appear in
\nolinkurl{data/11-two-flow-chain.json} (delivered as
\nolinkurl{data/chain.json}).

The verifier may be run, in the delivered layout, with
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
python code/verify.py --suite all
\end{lstlisting}
It writes fresh JSON reports under \texttt{data/}; run it on a copy to
preserve the delivered records. [Merge note: the shipped files are
\nolinkurl{code/11-two-flow-verify.py}, which imports
\texttt{transport\_bijection} by its delivered name, and
\nolinkurl{data/11-two-flow-*.json}; the report's \texttt{README.md} gives
a recipe that restores the delivered names in a copy.] No external Python package is required.
Elapsed times are environment-dependent and are not mathematical claims.

\subsection{What has and has not been certified}
There are three distinct levels of assurance. First, the article proves
the general theorems for arbitrary finite graphs. Second, the program
emits exact arithmetic certificates whose mathematical soundness is
Theorem~\ref{tf:thm:certificate}. Third, the exhaustive tests check many
finite inputs with independent combinatorial predicates. None of these
is a Lean or Rocq kernel check. The implementation and tests could still
contain errors not found in the tested cases; the mathematical proofs
remain the general justification.

The supplied sampler implements the unconditioned law with integer
support activities. The conditional samplers and rational-activity
extension are specified and proved above, but are not separate packaged
API wrappers. The package does not include an exact uniform sampler,
a theorem-prover build, or a new implementation of the general matroid
counting FPRAS.

\subsection{A concrete formalization plan}
A useful first milestone for ProveIt is a small certificate checker rather
than a monolithic formalization of an optimization library. Represent a
finite graph, flow, and potential by finite arrays of integers. Prove the
margin-summation identity \eqref{tf:eq:dualgap}, then prove that a zero-margin
flow supported on a finite tree vanishes. These two lemmas suffice for
unique-optimality certificates.

Next formalize the two component-balance congruences and the inverse
subtree estimate \eqref{tf:eq:childB}. These establish connectedness and the
degree-two condition. The leaf formula and the two explicit positive
flows in \eqref{tf:eq:twoflowtable} then prove inverse correctness. The core
factorization needs only the unique reduced-cost minimizer and the same
certificate identity. The preorder specialization is the elementary
lower-closure argument in Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:preorder}.

An external optimizer can remain outside the trusted boundary for
\emph{concrete} checked examples. A universal existence theorem for all
inputs requires more: either a verified terminating min-cost-flow
algorithm, or a formal proof that a feasible transportation polytope has
an optimal vertex followed by the forest argument. Checking certificates
alone does not prove that a solver always produces one. The general
matroid mixing theorem is a separate, substantial dependency; it should
be imported explicitly or formalized separately, not hidden behind a
certificate for a single sample.

\section{Further research questions and an actionable programme}
\label{tf:sec:questions}
The following questions are proposed continuations of this work. They
are not assertions that each formulation is a recognized unsolved
problem in the published literature.

\begin{question}[A direct inverse price algorithm]\label{tf:q:prices}
Can the unique inverse price vector described in
Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:prices} below be computed by a substantially faster
combinatorial procedure than a full transportation solve? The forward
map already isolates a small core. An inverse method that discovers its
$r$ indifferent suppliers without processing $m(r+1)$ units of flow
would give a symmetric improvement. A useful first target is sparse
incidence graphs of bounded treewidth.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Cost compression]\label{tf:q:compression}
For which graph classes can a cycle-generic cost system be chosen with
polynomially bounded \emph{magnitudes}, rather than merely polynomial bit
length? Independently, can the required comparisons be implemented
lexicographically without manipulating the powers of two explicitly?
The distinction is important: the current algorithm is already polynomial
in bit complexity, but its constants and integer arithmetic can still be
improved.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Binary-encoded capacities]\label{tf:q:capacities}
Can cloning be replaced by a compressed correspondence and sampler whose
running time is polynomial in capacity bit lengths? One must preserve
unit weight per demand vector rather than introduce the binomial
multiplicities of identical supplier copies. A precise first case is a
fixed small number of receiver types with large supplier capacities.
\end{question}
[Merge note: this extends Part~V's Research
question~\ref{tf:hq:capacities} (``Binary capacities and approximation
complexity''), which asks for the same compression for partition
functions and support coefficients, from counting to the bijection and
the sampler.]

\begin{question}[Updating the selected core]\label{tf:q:core}
Supplier insertions outside $I$ are independent leaf attachments. What is
the cheapest update when a basis exchange changes $I$ itself? A dynamic
algorithm should reuse old potentials and identify the changed tight
edges. Proposition~\ref{tf:prop:jumps} rules out uniformly bounded coordinate
movement, but not an efficient update of a possibly large movement.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Magnitude-sensitive probability measures]\label{tf:q:magnitude}
Which coordinate-dependent weights on $\cD_H$ become tractable weights on
the lifted bases? In particular, determine useful conditions under which
$\prod_yq_y^{c_y}$ or conditioning on a prescribed coordinate sum admits
a rapid sampler through this correspondence. Support-product weights are
already handled; arbitrary magnitude weights need a new argument.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Stronger functoriality]\label{tf:q:functoriality}
Characterize the receiver deletions or selected-supplier operations for
which a meaningful commuting diagram survives, possibly after changing
the support fibre. The existing results cover receiver operations outside
$J$ and supplier operations outside $I$. Any stronger naturality theorem
must respect the explicit symmetry obstruction.
\end{question}
[Merge note: this is what remains of the compatibility clauses of
Research questions~\ref{gam:q:bridge} (induced subgraphs, vertex
deletion) and~\ref{gam:q:bijection} (induced subgraphs, a controlled
vertex ordering), and of source~09's ``Direct lattice-point bijections''
(deletion, the paired clone action; Part~VII's questions); see
Section~\ref{tf:sec:answers}.]

\begin{question}[Geometric cells and chamber crossings]\label{tf:q:chambers}
Describe how the decoded demand vector changes when the cost system
crosses a single cycle-cost hyperplane. The chamber theorem proves
constancy away from the walls but does not classify the corresponding
bijection permutation across a wall. Such a description could connect
local tree changes, mixed-subdivision flips, and coupling constructions.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Certified implementation and formal extraction]\label{tf:q:formal}
Implement the certificate checker in Lean or Rocq and prove its soundness,
then formalize the two-flow inverse theorem. A practical intermediate
deliverable is a verified core certificate with an external optimizer:
it would certify full coordinate values with a small trusted checker
before a full min-cost-flow algorithm or a matroid mixing theorem is
formalized.
\end{question}
[Merge note: this overlaps Part~V's Research question~\ref{lor:q:last}
(``Formalization in layers''), whose first layer is the private-copy basis
correspondence and the preorder reduction; with
Corollary~\ref{tf:cor:count} the finite support-fibre count of that
question's second layer also has an elementary proof to formalize.]

For an immediate continuation, the strongest sequence is: certify the
small checker; benchmark and optimize the selected-core routine; then
investigate dynamic core updates and binary capacities. This sequence
produces useful artifacts at each stage and separates easy verification
work from the genuinely new algorithmic questions.

\section{Conclusion}
The repository's missing step is not another equality of enumerators.
It is a way to turn one sampled combinatorial state into a specified
integer vector, with the right multiplicity and an efficiently checkable
inverse. The two-flow construction supplies that step.

A single generic cost system chooses an admissible tree. Two deliberately
chosen margin systems recover that same tree from opposite sides of the
correspondence. Supplier degrees encode the selected basis; supplier
leaves encode the full coordinates. The smaller core formulation goes
further: after one flow on the selected suppliers, every other supplier
contributes by a separate reduced-cost minimum. The full-vector sampler
then follows by a literal change of coordinates on the known matroid
basis walk, preserving total-variation error exactly.

These are constructive refinements of an existing geometric
correspondence, not a replacement of the prior literature. They provide a
complete answer to the identified full-coordinate sampling gap at the
pinned repository snapshot, with precise restriction laws, counterexamples
to stronger interpretations, explicit code, and a feasible route to
formal verification.

\section{The unique dual price vector}
\label{tf:app:prices}
\noindent\emph{(Source~11's Appendix~A.)}
The core construction has a concise dual interpretation which also
suggests an inverse algorithm. For $c\in\cD_H(J)$, $r>0$, and
$\varepsilon=1/(r+1)$, set $v_0=0$ and consider the concave piecewise-linear
function
\begin{equation}
 f_c(v)=\sum_{x\in X}\min_{y\in (N_H(x)\cap J)\cup\{0\}}
                         (w_{xy}-v_y)
              +\sum_{y\in J}(c_y-\varepsilon)v_y.
 \label{tf:eq:priceobjective}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Unique inverse prices]
\label{tf:prop:prices}
Under cycle-generic costs, \eqref{tf:eq:priceobjective} has a unique
maximizer. It is the receiver-potential vector of the optimal tree for
(B), normalized by $v_0=0$. At this price vector, precisely the suppliers
in $\Psi_w(c)$ have two minimizing receivers; every other supplier has a
unique minimizing receiver. No supplier has three minimizing receivers.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For any $v$, put $u_x=\min_y(w_{xy}-v_y)$. Then
$u_x+v_y\le w_{xy}$ on every edge. Applying the objective-gap identity
to the flow (B) divided by $L=r+1$ shows that $f_c(v)$ is bounded above
by that flow's cost. The optimal tree potentials attain this bound,
because every positive-flow edge is tight and every row has positive
flow. Thus the maximum exists.

If another $v$ attained the same bound, every positive-flow edge of the
optimal tree would also have to be tight, since the objective gap is a
sum of nonnegative edge slacks weighted by positive flow. Together with
$v_0=0$, the tree equalities determine every potential uniquely.
Finally, the strict off-tree slacks show that the minimizing edges at a
supplier are exactly its incident tree edges. Their numbers are one or
two, and the degree-two suppliers are precisely $\Psi_w(c)$.
\end{proof}

For the graph $K_{m,1}$ this interpretation becomes an ordinary ranking.
Write $d_x=w_{xy}-w_{x0}$. Cycle-genericity makes these numbers distinct.
For the singleton selected set $I=\{i\}$, the core price is $v_y=d_i$,
and an unselected supplier chooses $y$ precisely when $d_x<d_i$.
Therefore
\[
 \Phi_w(\{i\})_y=1+\#\{x:d_x<d_i\}.
\]
The positive demand values $1,\ldots,m$ are exactly the ranks of the
supplier differences. The empty support gives zero. This simplest case
already exhibits the role of costs, the impossibility of a completely
symmetry-natural deterministic rule, and the difference between sampling
supplier sets and sampling assignments.

\section{Algorithm summary and delivered files}
\label{tf:app:algorithms}
\noindent\emph{(Source~11's Appendix~B.)}
\begin{statusbox}
\textbf{Forward, full form.} Validate the matchable pair $(I,J)$. Return
zero if $J$ is empty. Otherwise solve (A), verify its strict tree
certificate, and output one on every receiver in $J$ plus its number of
unselected supplier leaves.

\medskip
\textbf{Forward, core form.} Solve \eqref{tf:eq:coreflow} on the selected
suppliers only. Verify its certificate and extract $v$. For each
unselected supplier, find the unique minimum \eqref{tf:eq:attach}; add one
at its chosen receiver unless it chooses the dummy.

\medskip
\textbf{Inverse.} Set $J=\supp(c)$ and $c_0=m-\sum c_y$. Return the empty
pair for zero. Otherwise solve (B), verify its strict tree certificate,
and select exactly the suppliers of degree two.

\medskip
\textbf{Sampling.} Walk on lifted matroid bases for the explicit mixing
budget, then run the core decoder once. No transportation optimization is
needed during an ordinary basis-walk step.
\end{statusbox}

Source~12 continues Part~VIII only. It imports Part~VIII's classification

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~12 (as delivered).}
A research question in ProveIt's marked-tree stability report asks for the
probability that an independently marked random tree has a real-stable
incidence--apex matching-support polynomial. We answer it for uniform
labelled trees. Using the report's credited ADE-skeleton classification,
we derive an exact exponential generating function and an exact joint
count by the number of marks and the marked-hull size. For Bernoulli
marking with probability $p$, the annealed stability probability satisfies
\[
 \pi_n(p)\sim \frac98\sqrt{2\pi}\,p^3n^{5/2}e^{-pn}
\]
whenever $p\sqrt n\to\infty$, including every fixed $p>0$. An exact
finite-correction Poisson identity makes this statement uniform up to
$p=1$. In the critical window $p\sqrt n\to\lambda$, an explicit entire
function describes the crossover, the limiting number of marks, and a
mixture of chi-distributed hull sizes. Below that window, stability is
asymptotically equivalent to having at most two marks.

For fixed $0<p<1$, conditioning on stability produces $np^2+O_{\PP}(\sqrt n)$
marks and a hull of size $np+O_{\PP}(\sqrt n)$, with an explicit joint
Gaussian law and constant-order moment corrections. The host diameter
differs from the hull size by $O_{\PP}(\log n)$. In contrast, for every
fixed host tree the stability probability is determined, up to a
polynomial factor, by its diameter. This yields a strict separation
between the typical-host exponential rate $\log(1-p)$ and the annealed
rate $-p$. Exact finite checks and a dependency ledger accompany the proofs.
\end{tcolorbox}
\noindent The abstract is reproduced as delivered. Its ``marked-tree
stability report'' is Part~VIII of this report, and ``the report's
credited ADE-skeleton classification'' is Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main}.

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Status and scope (source~12, as delivered).} The ADE
characterization is an imported repository theorem, not a new result of
this article. The enumerative and probabilistic results below are proved
here for the precisely specified model. The proofs and programs are not
Lean- or Rocq-verified, and have not been independently refereed. Global
publication priority is not asserted. No repository file was modified.
\end{statusbox}

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Priority and prior work (merge).}
The stability classification is Part~VIII's Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main}
(itself a corollary of Part~VI), imported and not re-proved: every
probability in Part~X is a probability of Part~VIII's branch-complete ADE
markings, and Part~X's finite checks test that combinatorial class, not
polynomial stability. The ADE list is classical and is Part~VI's
Theorem~\ref{ade:thm:ADElist}; its spectral context is credited to
McKee--Smyth~\cite{McKeeSmythJA}, a different paper from the two
McKee--Smyth papers already cited (\cite{McKeeSmyth}
and~\cite{McKeeSmythIMRN}). The half-plane-property framework is
Choe--Oxley--Sokal--Wagner's~\cite{COSW}. The labelled-tree and
rooted-forest counts, the matrix-tree expansion, Pr\"ufer codes, Lagrange
inversion, Cauchy coefficient bounds, Stirling's formula, Poisson central
limits, Chernoff bounds and the characteristic-function method are
classical (Flajolet--Sedgewick~\cite{FS}); the long-path calculation
behind the diameter rate~\eqref{rts:eq:diamLD} is included with its proof
and is not claimed as new. The model of Section~\ref{rts:sec:model}
restates Part~VIII's, and Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:almostpath} sharpens the
inspection behind Part~VIII's Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:diameter} (merge note
after it). New relative to Parts~I--IX: the skeleton series and its
eventual constant $\frac98$ (Proposition~\ref{rts:prop:constant}, with
the automorphism column of Table~\ref{rts:tab:ADE}), the joint count, the
generating functions and the Poisson identity
(Sections~\ref{rts:sec:counts}--\ref{rts:sec:poisson}), the fixed-$k$,
supercritical, sparse and critical limits
(Sections~\ref{rts:sec:fixedk}, \ref{rts:sec:rare}--\ref{rts:sec:critical}),
the conditional Gaussian laws and family weights
(Section~\ref{rts:sec:Gaussian}), the conditioned diameter
(Section~\ref{rts:sec:geometry}), the quenched sandwich and the
annealed--quenched gap (Section~\ref{rts:sec:quenched}), and the
universality theorem (Section~\ref{rts:sec:universality}). Source~12's
audit was focused and found no prior publication of these formulas,
which is not evidence of first priority; no worldwide priority is claimed
for any result of Part~X.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{What Part~X answers}
\label{rts:sec:answers}
Status after Part~X, as of 30 September 2026:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item \textbf{Part~VIII's Research question~\ref{mts:q:random} is answered
for random labelled trees} under independent marking with one common
probability $p$, in every regime of $p$: the probability is exact
(Theorems~\ref{rts:thm:jointcount}, \ref{rts:thm:GF}
and~\ref{rts:thm:poisson}) and asymptotically determined below, in and
above the window $p\asymp n^{-1/2}$ (Theorems~\ref{rts:thm:sparse},
\ref{rts:thm:critical} and~\ref{rts:thm:rare},
Corollary~\ref{rts:cor:sparse}), and Section~\ref{rts:app:regimes}
summarizes the regimes. The question's
second half, \emph{deterministic families with growing branching
complexity}, is answered only on the exponential scale:
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:quenched} determines the stability probability of
every host within a polynomial factor from its diameter, without an
asymptotic equivalent (Research question~\ref{rts:q:quenched}). Other
random-tree laws and vertex-dependent or correlated markings remain open
(Research questions~\ref{rts:q:models} and~\ref{rts:q:inhomogeneous}).
Part~VIII's remark that a meaningful analysis must specify the host model
and the marking law is borne out: the constant $\frac98$ and the rate
$-p$ belong to this model (Research question~\ref{rts:q:models}).
\item \textbf{No other numbered research question of Parts~I--IX is
answered.} Part~VIII's Research question~\ref{mts:q:apices} is posed again,
with a random-tree layer, as Research question~\ref{rts:q:apices}, and
Part~VIII's Research question~\ref{mts:q:compiler} is overlapped by
Research question~\ref{rts:q:sampling}.
\end{itemize}
Part~X refutes no statement of Parts~I--IX, and nothing is retracted.
Part~VIII gains a dated pointer after Research
question~\ref{mts:q:random}; the title block, the abstract, the scope box
and the reading route gain dated sentences.

\section{The question answered and the contribution boundary}
\label{rts:sec:intro}

\subsection{An explicit repository question}
\label{rts:sec:question}
Part~VIII of this report asks for asymptotic stable-marking probabilities
for random labelled trees, while emphasizing that the tree model and
marking law must be specified (Research question~\ref{mts:q:random}). The
source label is \texttt{mts:q:random}. This is a repository research
question, not a claim that a named conjecture in the published literature
is being settled.
We choose the uniform Cayley tree and independent Bernoulli marking,
and determine the probability throughout its principal scaling regimes.
We also obtain a deterministic estimate that applies to every host tree.

The source has already classified all markings on all finite trees
(Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main}) and already proved that the
stable-neighbourhood counting polynomial is real-rooted exactly when the
host is a path (Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:Zroots}). Neither statement is posed
as an open question here. Nor do we reclaim the source's deterministic
endpoint enumerator (Theorems~\ref{mts:thm:enumerator}
and~\ref{mts:thm:counting}), optimal-repair algorithm
(Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:optimization}, Corollary~\ref{mts:cor:repair}), or
ADE spectral test.

\subsection{What is proved here}
Let $T_n$ be uniform among the $n^{n-2}$ trees on $[n]$, and mark each
vertex independently with probability $p$. Write $\st_n$ for stability,
$K_n$ for the number of marks, and $H_n$ for the number of vertices of
their hull, with $H_n=0$ for no marks. The main conclusions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=3pt]
\item An exact labelled decomposition and a finite joint counting formula
for $(K_n,H_n)$ on $\st_n$; an exact Poisson-tail formula with only eight
exceptional coefficient corrections.
\item A three-regime probability theory: at most two marks dominate below
$p\asymp n^{-1/2}$; an explicit crossover function governs that window;
and $\frac98\sqrt{2\pi}p^3n^{5/2}e^{-pn}$ is an equivalent throughout
$p\sqrt n\to\infty$.
\item At fixed marking density, explicit conditional Gaussian laws and
constant-order moment corrections, limiting skeleton-family weights,
and a linear-diameter conditioned geometry.
\item A diameter-based, polynomial-factor estimate for every host, and
therefore an annealed--quenched exponential-rate separation.
\end{enumerate}
The factor $9/8$ has a transparent source: the three infinite families of
allowed labelled skeletons contribute $1/2$, $1/2$, and $1/8$ to the
exponential generating-function coefficients. The probabilistic conclusions
are not numerical extrapolations; they follow from exact identities.

\subsection{Prior methods and limits of the audit}
The general relation between stable multiaffine polynomials and matroids
belongs to the established half-plane-property literature \cite{COSW}.
The spectral setting of the ADE list is classical \cite{McKeeSmythJA}.
Labelled substitution, Lagrange inversion, and meromorphic coefficient
asymptotics are standard methods of analytic combinatorics \cite{FS}.
We use these methods with their usual credit and supply the needed
calculations. The continuum-random-tree literature \cite{Aldous} provides
natural context for later quenched fluctuation questions, but no continuum
limit theorem is needed for our proofs.

The source audit was focused, not an exhaustive reading of the entire
repository or all random-tree literature. It did not establish a prior
publication containing these precise stable-marking formulas. That
negative search outcome is not evidence of first priority. The defensible
claim is an explicit mathematical continuation of the pinned question,
with an auditable separation of imported and newly derived statements.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The model and the imported structural theorem}
\label{rts:sec:model}

All trees are finite, simple, undirected, and nonempty. A marking is a
subset $S$ of the vertex set of a tree $T=(V,E)$. Form a bipartite graph
$\calA(T;S)$ with left shore $V$ and right shore
$E\sqcup\{\star\}$. An edge-element $e=ab$ is adjacent to $a,b$; the
apex element $\star$ is adjacent precisely to $S$.

For $I\subseteq V$ and $J\subseteq E\sqcup\{\star\}$, write $I\sim J$
when $|I|=|J|$ and there is a perfect matching between them. The canonical
basis polynomial is
\begin{equation}
 F_{T,S}(x;y,s)=\sum_{I\sim J}
       \prod_{v\in V\setminus I}x_v
       \prod_{e\in J\cap E}y_e\ s^{\ind_{\{\star\in J\}}}.
 \label{rts:eq:basis}
\end{equation}
A feasible support contributes once, even if several matchings realize
it. This distinction is essential. A real polynomial is \emph{real stable}
when it is nonzero whenever every variable has positive imaginary part.

For $S\ne\varnothing$, the marked hull $\Hull_T(S)$ is the least connected
subtree containing $S$. Every leaf of this hull belongs to $S$. A marking
is \emph{branch-complete} when every vertex of degree at least three in
its hull is marked. Suppressing the unmarked degree-two hull vertices
then produces a tree on $S$, the \emph{terminal skeleton}.
[Merge note: this is Part~VIII's model (Section~\ref{mts:sec:main}),
restated by source~12: $\calA(T;S)$ is Part~VIII's incidence--apex graph,
\eqref{rts:eq:basis} is~\eqref{mts:eq:F}, the hull is Part~VIII's
$K=\Hull_T(S)$ and the terminal skeleton is Part~VIII's $H(T,S)$. In
Part~X the letters $K$ and $H$ denote the \emph{numbers} $K_n=|S|$ and
$H_n=|\Hull_T(S)|$ instead (Table~\ref{rts:tab:notation}).]

\begin{theorem}[Imported marked-tree classification, Part~VIII]
\label{rts:thm:imported}
The polynomial \eqref{rts:eq:basis} is real stable if and only if either
$S=\varnothing$, or $S$ is branch-complete and the adjacency matrix of
its terminal skeleton has spectral radius at most two. Equivalently,
the skeleton belongs to Table~\ref{rts:tab:ADE}.
\end{theorem}
This is the pinned source's theorem \texttt{mts:thm:main}, with its
spectral list \texttt{mts:tab:ADE}: Part~VIII's
Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:main}, (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv),
with Table~\ref{mts:tab:ADE}. It is used as a dependency,
not silently reproved or declared formally verified by this article.
All subsequent combinatorics can alternatively be read as unconditional
statements about the explicitly defined class of ADE-admissible markings.
