\begin{definition}[Annealed and quenched probabilities]
Fix $n\ge1$. Let $T_n$ be uniform among labelled trees on $[n]$,
independently of Bernoulli marks with parameter $p$. Put
\[
 \pi_n(p)=\PP(\st_n),\qquad
 \pi_p(T)=\PP(S\text{ is stable}\mid T).
\]
The first averages over both sources of randomness (\emph{annealed}); the
second holds the tree fixed (\emph{quenched}). We use $q=1-p$ and,
when $q>0$, $r=p/q$. The hull size counts vertices; diameter counts edges.
\end{definition}

For $n=1$, the number of trees is one and both markings are stable.
For $p=0$, $\pi_n(0)=1$. For $p=1$, stability means that the entire tree
is an ADE tree. Statements involving $r$ or $\log q$ exclude $p=1$.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The skeleton generating function}
\label{rts:sec:skeleton}
Let $a_k$ be the number of allowed skeletons on a prescribed $k$-element
label set, and put $c_k=a_k/k!$. Relabelling a fixed unlabelled tree
produces $k!/|\Aut|$ labelled trees. Consequently Table~\ref{rts:tab:ADE} gives
\begin{align}
 A(y):=\sum_{k\ge1}c_ky^k
 ={}&y+\frac{y^2}{2(1-y)}+\frac{y^4}{6}
       +\frac{y^5}{2(1-y)}+\frac{y^5}{24}
       +\frac{y^6}{8(1-y)} \notag\\
   &+\frac{y^6}{2}+\frac{7y^7}{6}
       +\frac{3y^8}{2}+y^9.
 \label{rts:eq:A}
\end{align}
For example, at seven vertices the exceptional contributions are
$E_7$ and $\widetilde E_6$, of weights $1$ and $1/6$. At eight vertices
they are $E_8$ and $\widetilde E_7$, of weights $1$ and $1/2$.

\begin{proposition}[Eventual coefficient constancy]
\label{rts:prop:constant}
With $\cst=9/8$, one has
\begin{equation}
 A(y)=y+\cst\frac{y^2}{1-y}+\sum_{k=2}^9\delta_ky^k,
 \qquad c_k=\cst\quad(k\ge10),
 \label{rts:eq:delta}
\end{equation}
where Table~\ref{rts:tab:coeff} gives the complete exceptional prefix.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Expand the three geometric series in \eqref{rts:eq:A}. Their eventual
coefficients are $1/2+1/2+1/8=9/8$; every other summand is a polynomial.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}crrrrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & 1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8&9\\
\midrule
$c_k$ & $1$&$\frac12$&$\frac12$&$\frac23$&$\frac{25}{24}$&$\frac{13}{8}$&$\frac{55}{24}$&$\frac{21}{8}$&$\frac{17}{8}$\\[2pt]
$\delta_k$ & --&$-\frac58$&$-\frac58$&$-\frac{11}{24}$&$-\frac1{12}$&$\frac12$&$\frac76$&$\frac32$&$1$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Skeleton coefficients and finite corrections to $9/8$.}
\label{rts:tab:coeff}
\end{table}

The constant coefficients are not a statement about uniform unlabelled
random trees. The factorial normalization comes from labelled enumeration,
and changing the random-tree model changes the analysis.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Exact joint enumeration by marks and hull size}
\label{rts:sec:counts}

\subsection{A rooted-forest counting lemma}
We use the falling factorial $\fall nk=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$.

\begin{lemma}[Prescribed roots]
\label{rts:lem:forest}
For a prescribed root set of size $\ell$ in $[n]$, the number of forests
whose components each contain exactly one root is
\begin{equation}
 f_{n,\ell}=\ell n^{n-\ell-1}\quad(1\le\ell\le n),
 \label{rts:eq:forest}
\end{equation}
with value one when $\ell=n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Orient every edge toward its component root. The directed forest
matrix-tree expansion reduces the count to the determinant of
$nI_m-J_m$, where $m=n-\ell$ indexes the nonroots. To recall the
combinatorics of this expansion, choose one outgoing edge from each
nonroot; the alternating terms in the determinant cancel exactly the
choices containing a directed cycle among nonroots. The remaining
functional digraphs all reach a root and are precisely the desired
forests. The matrix has eigenvalues $n$ with multiplicity $m-1$ and
$n-m=\ell$ with multiplicity one, giving \eqref{rts:eq:forest}. If $m=0$,
the empty determinant is one, also the value of $\ell n^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact joint count]
\label{rts:thm:jointcount}
Let $C_{n,k,\ell}$ count pairs $(T,S)$ with stable marking, $|S|=k$,
and $|\Hull_T(S)|=\ell$. For $2\le k\le\ell\le n$,
\begin{equation}
 C_{n,k,\ell}=
 \binom nk a_k\fall{n-k}{\ell-k}
 \binom{\ell-2}{k-2}f_{n,\ell}.
 \label{rts:eq:jointcount}
\end{equation}
The remaining nonzero entries are
$C_{n,0,0}=n^{n-2}$ and $C_{n,1,1}=n^{n-1}$, with the single-vertex
convention already stated. Thus
\begin{equation}
 \pi_n(p)=\frac1{n^{n-2}}\sum_{k,\ell}C_{n,k,\ell}p^kq^{n-k}.
 \label{rts:eq:probcount}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose the $k$ marked labels and one of their $a_k$ allowed skeletons.
Set $j=\ell-k$. On the $k-1$ skeleton edges, insert ordered lists of
$j$ distinct unmarked labels. Orient each skeleton edge by any fixed
label-dependent convention; this avoids introducing a spurious factor
of two. The list lengths form a weak composition of $j$ into $k-1$
parts, of which there are $\binom{j+k-2}{k-2}$. Choosing and ordering
the subdivision labels gives $\fall{n-k}j$ possibilities.

The resulting subdivided skeleton is exactly the hull. Attach the
remaining vertices by a rooted forest whose roots are the $\ell$ hull
vertices; Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:forest} counts these attachments. Every attached
vertex is unmarked. Conversely, pruning all unmarked fringe and
suppressing the unmarked degree-two hull vertices recovers each choice
uniquely. This proves the product formula. Zero and one mark are always
stable and give the two remaining entries.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A fixed marked set]
\label{rts:cor:R}
For a prescribed $k$-element marked set, $k\ge2$, write
$b_{n,k}=\PP(\st_n\mid S=[k])$. Then
\begin{align}
 b_{n,k}&=a_k R_{n,k},\notag\\
 R_{n,k}&=n^{1-k}\sum_{j=0}^{n-k}
 \frac{\fall{n-k}j}{n^j}\binom{k+j-2}{k-2}(k+j).
 \label{rts:eq:R}
\end{align}
Conditional on stability and this marked set, the labelled terminal
skeleton is exactly uniform among its $a_k$ possibilities, for every
finite $n\ge k$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Divide \eqref{rts:eq:jointcount} by $\binom nk n^{n-2}$ and sum over $\ell$.
The attachment factor does not depend on the shape of the skeleton.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A nonnegative one-dimensional kernel}
Substituting $a_k=k!c_k$ into \eqref{rts:eq:jointcount} and collecting by
$\ell$ gives the useful exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\pi_n(p)}{q^n}=1+nr+
 n\sum_{\ell=2}^n\frac{\fall n\ell}{n^\ell}\,\ell
       \sum_{k=2}^{\ell}c_k\binom{\ell-2}{k-2}r^k.
 \label{rts:eq:kernel}
\end{equation}
Every summand here is nonnegative. Since $c_k=\cst$ after $k=9$, the
inner sum has the computationally economical form
\begin{equation}
 \cst r^2(1+r)^{\ell-2}
 +\sum_{k=2}^{\min(9,\ell)}\delta_k\binom{\ell-2}{k-2}r^k.
 \label{rts:eq:kernelinner}
\end{equation}
This evaluates the probability in $O(n)$ arithmetic operations after
updating the falling-factorial ratio recursively. It is an arithmetic
operation count, not a claim of linear bit complexity at arbitrary
precision. The correction form can exhibit cancellation; the nonnegative
form remains available for independent exact verification.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The labelled generating function and its deformations}
\label{rts:sec:GF}
Let $U(x)$ be the exponential generating function for rooted labelled
trees:
\begin{equation}
 U(x)=xe^{U(x)},\qquad
 U(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n^{n-1}}{n!}x^n.
 \label{rts:eq:tree}
\end{equation}
Its unrooted counterpart is $U-U^2/2$. For completeness,
$x\frac{d}{dx}(U-U^2/2)=U$, so the latter has coefficient
$n^{n-2}/n!$ and zero constant term. The rooted equation follows by
removing the root and obtaining a labelled set of rooted trees, or by
Lagrange inversion \cite{FS}.

\begin{theorem}[Exact two-colour generating function]
\label{rts:thm:GF}
Let $x$ count unmarked vertices and $z$ marked vertices in the labelled
exponential convention. Stable marked trees have generating function
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F(x,z)=U(x)-\frac{U(x)^2}{2}
 +(1-U(x))A\left(\frac{ze^{U(x)}}{1-U(x)}\right).
 \label{rts:eq:GF}
\end{equation}
For $0<p<1$, put $s=U(qt)$. Then
\begin{align}
 \mathcal F_p(t)&=s-\frac{s^2}{2}
 +(1-s)A\left(\frac{ps}{q(1-s)}\right),\label{rts:eq:GFp}\\
 \pi_n(p)&=B_n[t^n]\mathcal F_p(t),
 \qquad B_n=\frac{n!}{n^{n-2}}.\label{rts:eq:Bn}
\end{align}
More generally, marking fugacity $u$ and hull-size fugacity $v$ give
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal F_p(t;u,v)=s-\frac{s^2}{2}
 +(1-vs)A\left(\frac{vpu\,s}{q(1-vs)}\right),
 \label{rts:eq:GFuv}
\end{equation}
and $B_n[t^n]\mathcal F_p(t;u,v)=\EE[u^{K_n}v^{H_n}\ind_{\st_n}]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At each marked skeleton vertex, attach an arbitrary labelled set of
rooted unmarked trees, giving the factor $ze^U$. Each unmarked vertex
inserted along a skeleton edge, together with its own fringe, has weight
$xe^U=U$. An ordered sequence of such vertices has weight $(1-U)^{-1}$.
Thus a skeleton with $k$ vertices and $k-1$ edges contributes
$c_k(ze^U)^k(1-U)^{-(k-1)}$. Summing gives the last term of
\eqref{rts:eq:GF}; the first two terms count the empty marking.
This decomposition is the labelled version of Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:jointcount}.

Substitute $x=qt$, $z=pt$ and use $te^s=s/q$. For the refinement, each
marked vertex acquires $uv$, every subdivision vertex acquires $v$,
and no fringe vertex acquires $v$. Replacing $ze^U$ by $uvpt e^s$ and
$U$ along edges by $vs$ gives \eqref{rts:eq:GFuv}. In particular, $v$ counts
hull vertices, not the total size of the attached rooted trees.
\end{proof}

The rational skeleton function has its only pole at $y=1$. For fixed
$0<p<1$, this produces a pole at $s=q$, hence at
\begin{equation}
 t_0=e^{-q}.
 \label{rts:eq:t0}
\end{equation}
The rooted-tree branch point is at $t=1/(eq)$, and
$t_0<1/(eq)$ because $q e^{1-q}<1$ for $0<q<1$. The collision of these
two singularities as $p\downarrow0$ explains why a separate critical
analysis is needed; the fixed-$p$ pole argument alone is not a uniform
proof in that limit.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{A fixed number of marks: chi hulls and uniform subdivisions}
\label{rts:sec:fixedk}
Define
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_k=\frac{2^{k/2-1}\Gamma(k/2)}{(k-2)!}
 =\frac{\sqrt\pi\,2^{1-k/2}}{\Gamma((k-1)/2)}
 \qquad(k\ge2).
 \label{rts:eq:alpha}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-$k$ asymptotics]
\label{rts:thm:fixedk}
For every fixed $k\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 R_{n,k}\sim\alpha_kn^{1-k/2},\qquad
 b_{n,k}\sim a_k\alpha_kn^{1-k/2}.
 \label{rts:eq:fixedk}
\end{equation}
There is a constant $M_k$ with $R_{n,k}\le M_kn^{1-k/2}$ for all $n\ge k$.
Given stability and $K_n=k$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{H_n}{\sqrt n}\dto\chi_k,
 \label{rts:eq:chi}
\end{equation}
where $\chi_k$ has density
$x^{k-1}e^{-x^2/2}/(2^{k/2-1}\Gamma(k/2))$ on $x>0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $j/\sqrt n$ in a fixed compact interval,
\[
 \frac{\fall{n-k}j}{n^j}
 =\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\left(1-\frac{k+i}{n}\right)
 =e^{-j^2/(2n)+o(1)},
\]
uniformly in that interval. Also
$\binom{k+j-2}{k-2}(k+j)\sim j^{k-1}/(k-2)!$ as $j\to\infty$.
The Riemann sum in \eqref{rts:eq:R} therefore yields
\[
 n^{k/2-1}R_{n,k}\longrightarrow
 \frac1{(k-2)!}\int_0^\infty x^{k-1}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\alpha_k.
\]
To justify tails and obtain the stated upper bound, use
\[
 \frac{\fall{n-k}j}{n^j}
 \le \exp\left(-\frac{kj+j(j-1)/2}{n}\right)
\]
and bound the remaining factor by a constant depending on $k$ times
$(j+1)^{k-1}$. Comparison with a Gaussian integral is uniform in $n$;
the finitely many small $n$ can be absorbed into $M_k$.

The exact joint count assigns to $j=H_n-k$ precisely the normalized
summands of \eqref{rts:eq:R}. Applying the same Riemann-sum argument to
bounded continuous test functions proves the chi limit.
\end{proof}

For $k=2$, $a_2=\alpha_2=1$, and in fact stability has probability one.
For $k=3$, $a_3=3$ and
\begin{equation}
 b_{n,3}\sim 3\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,n^{-1/2}.
 \label{rts:eq:k3}
\end{equation}
Three marks fail generically because the branching point of their hull
need not itself be marked; \eqref{rts:eq:k3} quantifies the exceptional event.

\begin{corollary}[Limiting metric skeleton at fixed $k$]
\label{rts:cor:dirichlet}
Given stability and $K_n=k\ge2$, the labelled skeleton is exactly uniform
among the $a_k$ possibilities. Conditional on $H_n=k+j$, its subdivision
counts are uniform among weak compositions of $j$ into $k-1$ parts.
As $n\to\infty$, the normalized edge-length vector converges to
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1)$, independently of the uniform
skeleton and the limiting chi radius $H_n/\sqrt n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed composition, the ordered subdivision labels and the attached
forests have counts independent of that composition and of the skeleton.
Uniform lattice points in the dilated simplex, divided by $j$, converge
by elementary Riemann sums to uniform simplex measure, namely the stated
Dirichlet law. By Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:fixedk}, $j\to\infty$ in probability.
Conditioning on $j$ and then using bounded test functions proves joint
convergence and independence. Replacing subdivision counts by edge lengths
adds one to each coordinate and does not alter the limit.
\end{proof}

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{An exact Poisson identity with finite corrections}
\label{rts:sec:poisson}
For $2\le k\le n$ put
\begin{equation}
 W_{n,k}(p)=\fall nk p^kq^{n-k}R_{n,k}.
 \label{rts:eq:W}
\end{equation}
This is the probability contribution that a skeleton coefficient equal
to one would give at size $k$; the actual contribution is $c_kW_{n,k}$.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-correction Poisson formula]
\label{rts:thm:poisson}
For $n\ge2$ and $0<p<1$, if $X\sim\Pois(nq)$, then
\begin{align}
 \pi_n(p)={}&q^n+npq^{n-1}
 +\cst p^3B_ne^{nq}\PP(X\le n-2)\notag\\
 &+\cst p^2n(n-1)q^{n-1}
 +\sum_{k=2}^{\min(9,n)}\delta_k W_{n,k}(p).
 \label{rts:eq:poisson}
\end{align}
The formula is exact, not asymptotic. The exponential and the Poisson
probability may be replaced together by their finite sum.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The singleton and empty terms in \eqref{rts:eq:delta} give the first two
terms of \eqref{rts:eq:poisson}; its finite polynomial gives the last sum by
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:jointcount}. For the geometric tail, set
$y=ps/[q(1-s)]$ and calculate
\begin{equation}
 (1-s)\cst\frac{y^2}{1-y}
 =\cst p^2\left(\frac q{q-s}-1-\frac sq\right).
 \label{rts:eq:tailalgebra}
\end{equation}
Lagrange inversion for $s=qt e^s$ gives
\begin{equation}
 [t^n]\frac q{q-s}
 =\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac in\right)\frac{(nq)^i}{i!}.
 \label{rts:eq:Lagrange}
\end{equation}
Indeed, apply $[t^n]g(s)=q^n[n^{-1}z^{n-1}]g'(z)e^{nz}$,
expand $g'(z)=q/(q-z)^2$, and change the summation index.
Since $[t^n]s/q=(nq)^{n-1}/n!$, subtraction and the identity
$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i(nq)^i/i!=nq\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(nq)^i/i!$ yield
\begin{align*}
 [t^n]\left(\frac q{q-s}-1-\frac sq\right)
 =p\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}\frac{(nq)^i}{i!}
   +\left(1-\frac1n\right)\frac{(nq)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}.
\end{align*}
Multiplying by $\cst p^2B_n$ gives the middle two terms of
\eqref{rts:eq:poisson}.
\end{proof}

A useful exact interpretation is that every departure from the universal
geometric skeleton tail is confined to the eight sizes $2,\ldots,9$.
The negative corrections in Table~\ref{rts:tab:coeff} are algebraic correction
terms, not probabilities. Their signed appearance must not be used to
infer a probabilistic mixture.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The rare-event equivalent above the critical window}
\label{rts:sec:rare}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform supercritical equivalent]
\label{rts:thm:rare}
For any sequence $0<p_n\le1$ with $p_n\sqrt n\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \pi_n(p_n)\sim\cst p_n^3 B_n e^{n(1-p_n)}
 \sim\frac98\sqrt{2\pi}\,p_n^3n^{5/2}e^{-np_n}.
 \label{rts:eq:rare}
\end{equation}
In particular, for every fixed $0<p\le1$,
$n^{-1}\log\pi_n(p)\to-p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First suppose $0<p\le1/2$, set $x=p\sqrt n$, and assume $x\ge2$.
Define the positive rate gap
\begin{equation}
 I(p)=-p-\log(1-p)\ge p^2/2.
 \label{rts:eq:I}
\end{equation}
Let $M_n=\cst p^3B_ne^{nq}$. Stirling's lower bound gives
$M_n\ge C p^3n^{5/2}e^{-np}$ with an absolute $C>0$.
For each fixed $2\le k\le9$, Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:fixedk} implies
\begin{equation}
 \frac{|\delta_k|W_{n,k}}{M_n}
 \le C_k x^{k-3}q^{-k}e^{-nI(p)}.
 \label{rts:eq:corrbound}
\end{equation}
The zero- and one-mark terms, and the extra boundary term in
\eqref{rts:eq:poisson}, are bounded similarly; the latter has ratio at most
$C x^{-1}q^{-1}e^{-nI(p)}$.

For the Poisson tail use the Chernoff bound at $n-1>nq$:
\[
 \PP(X\ge n-1)\le
 \exp\left(-(n-1)\log\frac{n-1}{nq}+n-1-nq\right)
 \le C e^{-nI(p)}.
\]
The last constant is absolute because $q\ge1/2$; the difference between
the two exponents is
$\log(1/q)-(n-1)\log(1-1/n)-1$, which is bounded.
Thus, uniformly in this range,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\pi_n(p)}{M_n}
 =1+O\left((1+x^6)e^{-nI(p)}\right).
 \label{rts:eq:uniformsmallp}
\end{equation}
It tends to one whenever $x\to\infty$.

For $1/2\le p<1$, set $J_0=\log2-1/2>0$. For every fixed
$k\le9$ and $n\ge18$, the function
$q^{n-k}e^{n(1-q)}$ is increasing on $0<q\le1/2$, so it is at most
$2^ke^{-nJ_0}$. The same bounds as above, now retaining this expression
instead of $q^{-k}e^{-nI(p)}$, show that all correction ratios are
$O(n^3e^{-nJ_0})$. The Poisson-tail ratio is bounded uniformly by its
value at mean $n/2$, with the same exponential rate. The remaining
terms are smaller. Hence $\pi_n/M_n\to1$ uniformly in this second range.

At $p=1$ and $n\ge10$, \eqref{rts:eq:probcount} reduces exactly to
$\pi_n(1)=a_n/n^{n-2}=\cst B_n$. Finally,
$B_n\sim\sqrt{2\pi}n^{5/2}e^{-n}$ proves the second equivalent.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Fixed-density meromorphic strengthening]
\label{rts:prop:pole}
For fixed $0<p<1$, there is $0<\theta_p<1$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \pi_n(p)=\cst p^3B_ne^{nq}(1+O(\theta_p^n)).
 \label{rts:eq:fixedpole}
\end{equation}
Consequently the expansion from Stirling, beginning with the factor
$1+1/(12n)+O(n^{-2})$, may be appended to \eqref{rts:eq:rare}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The same conclusion follows from \eqref{rts:eq:poisson}, or directly from
\eqref{rts:eq:GFp}. Near $t_0=e^{-q}$,
$s'=s/[t(1-s)]$ implies
\[
 \mathcal F_p(t)=\frac{\cst p^3}{1-t/t_0}+\text{an analytic remainder}.
\]
Choose $R$ strictly between $t_0$ and $1/(eq)$. The principal rooted-tree
branch is analytic in $|t|<1/(eq)$; the equation $s=q$ has the unique
solution $t=t_0$ there. After subtracting the displayed pole, all other
terms are analytic on a slightly larger disc than $|t|\le R$.
Cauchy's coefficient bound gives an error $O(R^{-n})$, proving the result.
\end{proof}

The exponential factor is $e^{-pn}$, not $(1-p)^n$. Replacing the former
by the latter loses an exponentially significant factor when $p$ is
fixed. Section~\ref{rts:sec:quenched} explains why the latter nevertheless
appears naturally when the host tree is held fixed.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Below the window: at most two marks dominate}
\label{rts:sec:sparse}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform sparse comparison]
\label{rts:thm:sparse}
As $p\sqrt n\to0$, with $0\le p<1$,
\begin{equation}
 \pi_n(p)=q^n\left(1+nr+\binom n2r^2\right)
                 (1+O(r\sqrt n)).
 \label{rts:eq:sparse}
\end{equation}
At $p=0$ interpret the formula exactly. In particular, stability and the
event $K_n\le2$ have asymptotically equal probabilities.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every zero-, one-, or two-mark set is stable, so the displayed main term
is a lower bound. By \eqref{rts:eq:kernel} and $c_k\le21/8$, the contribution
of $k\ge3$, divided by $q^n$, is at most
\begin{align*}
 Cn r^2\sum_{\ell=2}^n\ell\frac{\fall n\ell}{n^\ell}
             \big((1+r)^{\ell-2}-1\big)
 &\le Cn r^3\sum_{\ell=2}^n\ell^2
        \exp\left(-\frac{\ell(\ell-1)}{2n}+r\ell\right).
\end{align*}
When $r\sqrt n\le1/4$, Gaussian integral comparison bounds the sum by
$C'n^{3/2}$. The remainder is therefore at most
$C''n^{5/2}r^3$. For $n\ge2$, divide by the two-mark main term
$\binom n2r^2$ to obtain $O(r\sqrt n)$; the zero case is immediate.
Since $p\sqrt n\to0$ also implies $r\sqrt n\to0$, the claim follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two sparse subregimes]
\label{rts:cor:sparse}
If $np\to\mu\in[0,\infty)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \pi_n(p)\longrightarrow e^{-\mu}(1+\mu+\mu^2/2).
 \label{rts:eq:poissontruncated}
\end{equation}
For $\mu>0$, the conditional mark count tends to a Poisson random variable
of mean $\mu$ conditioned to be at most two; for $\mu=0$ it tends to zero.
If instead $np\to\infty$ and $p\sqrt n\to0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \pi_n(p)\sim\binom n2p^2q^{n-2},\qquad
 \PP(K_n=2\mid\st_n)\longrightarrow1.
 \label{rts:eq:twomarks}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the elementary binomial-to-Poisson limit in the first case. In the
second case the two-mark term dominates the zero- and one-mark terms.
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:sparse} shows that stable configurations with three or
more marks have negligible mass in both cases.
\end{proof}

In the second regime the original, unconditioned expected number of marks
$np$ diverges, but stability selects just two. This selection changes in
the window $p\asymp n^{-1/2}$, not when $np$ first becomes large.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The critical crossover and its limiting distributions}
\label{rts:sec:critical}
Define the entire function
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(\lambda)=\sum_{k\ge2}c_k\alpha_k\lambda^k.
 \label{rts:eq:psi-series}
\end{equation}
The gamma denominator in \eqref{rts:eq:alpha} and boundedness of $c_k$ give
infinite radius of convergence. For real $\lambda>0$ it is strictly
positive. A form involving just eight correction terms is
\begin{align}
 \Psi(\lambda)={}&\cst\left[\lambda^2+
 \sqrt{\frac\pi2}\lambda^3e^{\lambda^2/2}
       \left(1+\operatorname{erf}\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt2}\right)\right]
 +\sum_{k=2}^9\delta_k\alpha_k\lambda^k.
 \label{rts:eq:psi-closed}
\end{align}

\begin{lemma}[Integral form]
\label{rts:lem:psi}
For real $\lambda\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(\lambda)=\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2/2}
       \sum_{k\ge2}\frac{c_k\lambda^kx^{k-1}}{(k-2)!}\,dx.
 \label{rts:eq:psi-int}
\end{equation}
This identity gives \eqref{rts:eq:psi-closed}. It also yields
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(\lambda)\sim\tfrac12\lambda^2\quad(\lambda\downarrow0),
 \qquad
 \Psi(\lambda)\sim\cst\sqrt{2\pi}\lambda^3e^{\lambda^2/2}
       \quad(\lambda\to\infty).
 \label{rts:eq:psiasympt}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Integrate each monomial using \eqref{rts:eq:alpha}; nonnegativity justifies
interchange for real $\lambda\ge0$. For the constant tail the inner
sum is $\cst\lambda^2x e^{\lambda x}$. Completing the square and
integrating by parts gives
\[
 \int_0^\infty x e^{-x^2/2+\lambda x}\,dx
 =1+\lambda\sqrt{\frac\pi2}e^{\lambda^2/2}
           \left(1+\operatorname{erf}\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt2}\right).
\]
The finite corrections are immediate. The first nonzero series coefficient
is $c_2\alpha_2=1/2$; at infinity the finite polynomial is negligible
beside the positive exponential term.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Critical probability]
\label{rts:thm:critical}
If $p_n\sqrt n\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\pi_n(p_n)}{nq_n^n}\longrightarrow\Psi(\lambda).
 \label{rts:eq:critical}
\end{equation}
The normalization uses the actual $q_n^n$; replacing it merely by
$e^{-\lambda\sqrt n}$ can lose a constant or a larger factor for general
sequences approaching the same $\lambda$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the exact formula \eqref{rts:eq:poisson}. For $X\sim\Pois(nq_n)$,
the centered standardized threshold tends to $\lambda$, so
$\PP(X\le n-2)\to\Phi(\lambda)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal
CDF. This Poisson central limit follows, for example, by expanding its
characteristic function
$\exp(m(e^{it/\sqrt m}-1-it/\sqrt m))$ as $m\to\infty$.
Also $nI(p_n)\to\lambda^2/2$. Thus the main Poisson term, divided by
$nq_n^n$, tends to
$\cst\sqrt{2\pi}\lambda^3e^{\lambda^2/2}\Phi(\lambda)$.
The boundary term tends to $\cst\lambda^2$.
For each fixed $k$, Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:fixedk} gives
\[
 \frac{W_{n,k}(p_n)}{nq_n^n}
 =\frac{\fall nk r_n^kR_{n,k}}n\longrightarrow\alpha_k\lambda^k.
\]
The zero- and one-mark terms vanish after normalization. Since
$2\Phi(\lambda)=1+\operatorname{erf}(\lambda/\sqrt2)$, these limits
are exactly \eqref{rts:eq:psi-closed}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Critical mark count and hull mixture]
\label{rts:thm:critical-law}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:critical}, conditional on
stability,
\begin{equation}
 \PP(K_n=k\mid\st_n)\longrightarrow
 w_k(\lambda):=\frac{c_k\alpha_k\lambda^k}{\Psi(\lambda)}
 \quad(k\ge2).
 \label{rts:eq:criticalweights}
\end{equation}
These limits sum to one. The limiting probability generating function
is $\Psi(\lambda u)/\Psi(\lambda)$, with convergence of every fixed
moment. Jointly with this discrete limit, $H_n/\sqrt n$ tends to the
mixture that, given $K=k$, has law $\chi_k$. Equivalently, the limiting pair $(K_\lambda,X_\lambda)$ has joint
mass--density
\begin{equation}
 \PP(K_\lambda=k,\ X_\lambda\in dx)=
 \frac{c_k\lambda^k}{(k-2)!\Psi(\lambda)}
       x^{k-1}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx,\qquad x>0.
 \label{rts:eq:criticaldensity}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The exact probability contribution for $K_n=k$ is $c_kW_{n,k}$.
The calculation in the preceding proof gives \eqref{rts:eq:criticalweights},
and \eqref{rts:eq:psi-series} shows that no probability escapes to infinity.
The chi mixture follows from Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:fixedk} and truncating the
mark count at a large fixed value.

For moment convergence, let $u>0$ be fixed and put $d=q+pu$,
$p'=pu/d$, $q'=q/d$. Tilting the independent mark law gives exactly
\begin{equation}
 \EE[u^{K_n}\ind_{\st_n}]=d^n\pi_n(p').
 \label{rts:eq:tilt}
\end{equation}
Now $p'\sqrt n\to\lambda u$ and $d^n(q')^n=q^n$. The critical
probability theorem yields the asserted generating-function limit for
every fixed positive $u$. Taking some $u>1$ bounds exponential moments
and gives uniform integrability of every fixed power of $K_n$.
\end{proof}

Conditional on the limiting value $K=k$, the skeleton and edge proportions
retain the independent uniform and Dirichlet laws of
Corollary~\ref{rts:cor:dirichlet}. Formula~\eqref{rts:eq:criticaldensity} describes
the marked hull, not the full host diameter: in this sparse window the
unmarked fringe need not have logarithmic height.

The large-$\lambda$ asymptotic in \eqref{rts:eq:psiasympt} agrees with
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:rare}, because
$q^n=e^{-np-np^2/2+O(np^3)}$ when the expansion is applicable. This is a
consistency check of the overlap of the two descriptions; the uniform
supercritical theorem itself was proved without extrapolating a
fixed-$\lambda$ limit.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Fixed-density conditional Gaussian laws}
\label{rts:sec:Gaussian}
Throughout this section $0<p<1$ is fixed. Introduce complex fugacities
$u,v$ near one, and define
\begin{align}
 d(u)&=q+pu,\notag\\
 s_0(u,v)&=\frac{q}{v d(u)},\notag\\
 \tau(u,v)&=\frac1{v d(u)}\exp\left(-\frac q{v d(u)}\right),\label{rts:eq:tau}\\
 C(u,v)&=\cst\left(\frac{pu}{d(u)}\right)^2
                    \left(1-\frac q{v d(u)}\right).
 \label{rts:eq:amplitude}
\end{align}
At $u=v=1$, $\tau=e^{-q}$ and $C=\cst p^3$.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform moving-pole estimate]
\label{rts:lem:movingpole}
In a complex neighbourhood of $(1,1)$,
\begin{equation}
 \EE[u^{K_n}v^{H_n}\mid\st_n]
 =\frac{C(u,v)}{\cst p^3}
    \left(\frac{e^{-q}}{\tau(u,v)}\right)^n
       (1+O(\theta^n)),
 \label{rts:eq:quasipowers}
\end{equation}
for some $\theta<1$, uniformly in that neighbourhood. Derivatives of
any fixed order satisfy the corresponding exponentially small error.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{rts:eq:GFuv}, the equation making the skeleton argument equal to
one is $s=s_0(u,v)$. Invert $s=qt e^s$ to obtain \eqref{rts:eq:tau}.
The singular summand of $A$ is $\cst/(1-y)$; consequently the singular
part of the last term of \eqref{rts:eq:GFuv} is
\[
 \frac{\cst q(1-vs)^2}{q-vd(u)s}.
\]
Since $t s'=s/(1-s)$, its coefficient in front of
$(1-t/\tau)^{-1}$ is
$\cst(1-vs_0)^2(1-s_0)=C(u,v)$.
Choose a radius strictly between $e^{-q}$ and $1/(eq)$. For $u,v$
sufficiently close to one, this remains a disc with exactly that pole;
potential poles at $s=1/v$ and the tree branch point stay outside a
slightly larger circle. Subtract the moving pole and apply Cauchy's
bound uniformly on the circle. Divide by the estimate at $(1,1)$.
Cauchy's formula in the parameter variables controls the derivatives.
\end{proof}

Put $u=e^a,v=e^b$. The logarithm of the exponential factor is
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda(a,b)=b+\log(q+pe^a)+\frac{qe^{-b}}{q+pe^a}-q.
 \label{rts:eq:Lambda}
\end{equation}
Its gradient and Hessian at zero are
\begin{equation}
 \nabla\Lambda(0,0)=(p^2,p),\qquad
 \Sigma_p=\begin{pmatrix}2p^2q&pq\\pq&q\end{pmatrix}.
 \label{rts:eq:Sigma}
\end{equation}
The determinant is $p^2q^2>0$.

\begin{theorem}[Joint central limit and moment corrections]
\label{rts:thm:CLT}
Conditional on $\st_n$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{\sqrt n}\begin{pmatrix}K_n-np^2\\H_n-np\end{pmatrix}
 \dto N(0,\Sigma_p).
 \label{rts:eq:CLT}
\end{equation}
For a suitable $\theta_p<1$, the conditional moments satisfy
\begin{align}
 \EE K_n&=np^2+3q+O(\theta_p^n),&
 \EE H_n&=np+q/p+O(\theta_p^n),\label{rts:eq:means}\\
 \Var K_n&=2np^2q-3pq+O(\theta_p^n),&
 \Var H_n&=nq-q/p^2+O(\theta_p^n),\label{rts:eq:variances}\\
 \Cov(K_n,H_n)&=npq-q/p+O(\theta_p^n).&&\label{rts:eq:cov}
\end{align}
All expectations in these displays are conditional on stability.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Insert $a=i\xi/\sqrt n$, $b=i\eta/\sqrt n$ into
\eqref{rts:eq:quasipowers} and expand \eqref{rts:eq:Lambda} to second order.
After centering, the logarithm of the characteristic function tends to
$-\frac12(\xi,\eta)\Sigma_p(\xi,\eta)^T$. The amplitude tends to one.
The continuity theorem proves \eqref{rts:eq:CLT}.

For the refined moments, differentiate the logarithm of
\eqref{rts:eq:quasipowers}. The first derivatives of
$\log C(e^a,e^b)$ at zero are $3q$ and $q/p$; its second derivatives
in $(a,a),(b,b),(a,b)$ are respectively $-3pq,-q/p^2,-q/p$.
Combining these with \eqref{rts:eq:Sigma} proves the formulas. The uniform
analytic estimate justifies the exponentially small differentiated errors.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Three limiting skeleton families]
\label{rts:cor:families}
At fixed $0<p<1$, conditional on stability, the skeleton lies asymptotically
in the path, long-$D$, and double-fork affine-$D$ families with probabilities
\begin{equation}
 \frac49,\qquad\frac49,\qquad\frac19,
 \label{rts:eq:families}
\end{equation}
respectively. Every other family has exponentially small conditional
probability. The limiting family is independent of the Gaussian vector
in \eqref{rts:eq:CLT}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The three family generating functions have residues $1/2$, $1/2$, and
$1/8$ at $y=1$; their finite exceptional terms have no such pole.
Repeat Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:movingpole} separately for each family. The moving
pole and its exponential factor are unchanged; the amplitude is merely
multiplied by its residue divided by $9/8$. This proves both the family
probabilities and independence from the limiting Gaussian fluctuations.
\end{proof}

These statements require fixed $p$ for their present uniformity. They do
not assert a triangular-array central limit theorem throughout the full
supercritical range of Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:rare}.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The conditioned host has linear diameter}
\label{rts:sec:geometry}
The hull-size law alone does not determine the host diameter: fringe
might be tall, or a hull might branch too much. The next two estimates
control these issues in the fixed-density conditional model.

\begin{lemma}[Height of a uniform rooted forest]
\label{rts:lem:height}
Let a forest on $[n]$ be uniform among forests rooted at a prescribed set
of $\ell$ vertices, and write $m=n-\ell$. For $1\le h\le m$, the expected
number of vertices at distance exactly $h$ from the root set is
\begin{equation}
 (\ell+h)\frac{\fall mh}{n^h}.
 \label{rts:eq:forestheight}
\end{equation}
If $\ell\ge\varepsilon n$ for a fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the maximum
root distance is $O_{\PP}(\log n)$, uniformly in the root set and $\ell$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose a root and an ordered list of $h$ distinct nonroots, prescribing
a directed path to that root. There are $\ell\fall mh$ choices.
The probability that a fixed such path occurs is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{(\ell+h)n^{m-h-1}}{\ell n^{m-1}}.
 \label{rts:eq:pathforest}
\end{equation}
To see the numerator, contract the fixed path to its root. An edge from
an outside nonroot into the contracted component has $h+1$ possible
original targets; edges to each other root have one. The directed forest
matrix on the remaining $m-h$ nonroots is again $nI-J$, whose determinant
is $(\ell+h)n^{m-h-1}$. When $m=h$, it is the empty determinant, and the
same formula is one. The denominator is Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:forest}.
Each vertex at distance $h$ has exactly one path to its root, so multiplying
\eqref{rts:eq:pathforest} by the number of choices proves
\eqref{rts:eq:forestheight}.

A forest reaching depth at least $h$ has a vertex at depth $h$. Markov's
inequality gives probability at most
$(\ell+h)(m/n)^h\le2n(1-\varepsilon)^h$. Take a sufficiently large
constant times $\log n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Longest subdivision chain]
\label{rts:lem:composition}
If $(J_1,\ldots,J_d)$ is uniform among weak compositions of $j$ into
$d\ge2$ parts, then
\begin{equation}
 \PP(J_i\ge a)=\frac{\binom{j-a+d-1}{d-1}}{\binom{j+d-1}{d-1}}
 \le\left(\frac{j}{j+d-1}\right)^a
 \quad(0\le a\le j).
 \label{rts:eq:compositiontail}
\end{equation}
If $d/(j+d)$ is bounded below by a positive constant, the maximum part
is $O_{\PP}(\log(j+d+1))$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Subtract $a$ from the chosen part and count compositions. The ratio is
$\fall ja/\fall{j+d-1}a$, whose successive factors are bounded by the
first one. A union bound over the $d$ parts proves the second assertion.
The case $j=0$ is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Diameter and joint fluctuations]
\label{rts:thm:diameter}
For fixed $0<p<1$, conditional on stability,
\begin{equation}
 \diam(T_n)=H_n+O_{\PP}(\log n),\qquad
 \frac{\diam(T_n)}n\pto p.
 \label{rts:eq:diamlinear}
\end{equation}
The joint central limit theorem \eqref{rts:eq:CLT} remains valid if $H_n$ is
replaced by $\diam(T_n)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:CLT} gives $K_n/n\to p^2$ and $H_n/n\to p$ in
conditional probability. Given $n,k,\ell$, the skeleton, and the
subdivision data, the fringe forest is uniform on the prescribed $\ell$
roots by the exact counting construction. Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:height} therefore
makes its height $O_{\PP}(\log n)$.

Given the skeleton and hull size, its $j=\ell-k$ subdivision vertices
are distributed uniformly among the $d=k-1$ edge lists. Since
$d/(j+d)\to p$, Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:composition} bounds every subdivided
edge length by $O_{\PP}(\log n)$.

By Corollary~\ref{rts:cor:families}, with probability tending to one the
skeleton is a path, a long $D$ tree, or a double fork. In these cases it
has a path omitting at most two pendant edges and their leaf endpoints.
After subdivision, the hull has a path containing all but at most twice
the maximum edge length of its vertices. Its diameter consequently
differs from $\ell$ by $O_{\PP}(\log n)$. Attaching a forest can increase
the diameter by at most twice its maximum root distance. This proves
\eqref{rts:eq:diamlinear}; since $\log n=o(\sqrt n)$, Slutsky's theorem
gives the final assertion.
\end{proof}

The error estimate in \eqref{rts:eq:diamlinear} is probabilistic. It does not
claim a constant-order expansion for the mean diameter, nor replace the
exact constant corrections for $H_n$ in \eqref{rts:eq:means} by unproved
corrections for diameter. It also does not extend automatically to the
critical window, where $H_n$ is only of order $\sqrt n$ and the root
fraction in Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:height} vanishes.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{A deterministic diameter estimate and annealed--quenched separation}
\label{rts:sec:quenched}

\begin{lemma}[Two marks away from a path]
\label{rts:lem:almostpath}
For every stable marking $S$ on any finite tree $T$, there is a host path
$P$ such that $|S\setminus P|\le2$. Conversely, every marking contained
in a path is stable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The empty marking is immediate. Inspection of Table~\ref{rts:tab:ADE} shows
that each allowed skeleton has a path omitting at most two vertices.
For a one-branch skeleton, choose the two longest arms; the third arm has
length at most two in every listed case. For the four-leaf star, choose
two leaves; for a double fork, choose one leaf at each end. The lifted
path in the hull omits precisely those marked skeleton vertices, regardless
of how long the unmarked subdivisions are. This proves the first claim.
A marking contained in a host path has a path hull and path skeleton,
so Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:imported} proves the converse.
\end{proof}
\noindent[Merge note: the converse is the lower-bound half of the proof
of Part~VIII's Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:diameter}, and the first claim
refines its upper-bound inspection $|V(H)|\le\diam(H)+3$: Part~VIII
bounds the \emph{number} of marks by the diameter, Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:almostpath}
places all but two of them on one host path. It is kept as a second,
stronger route, because Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:quenched} needs the path.]

\begin{theorem}[Quenched probability within a polynomial factor]
\label{rts:thm:quenched}
Let $T$ be any tree on $n$ vertices, with diameter $d$, and let $0<p<1$.
Then
\begin{align}
 q^{n-d-1}\le\pi_p(T)
 \le\min\left\{1,
 \frac{n(n+1)}2\left(1+nr+\binom n2r^2\right)q^{n-d-1}\right\}.
 \label{rts:eq:sandwich}
\end{align}
Consequently, for fixed $p$,
\begin{equation}
 \log\pi_p(T)=(n-d-1)\log q+O_p(\log(n+1)),
 \label{rts:eq:quenchedlog}
\end{equation}
uniformly over all host trees. The subscript on $O_p$ here denotes
dependence on the fixed parameter $p$, not stochastic order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose a longest path. The event that all marks lie on it has probability
$q^{n-d-1}$, with no restriction on marks along the path, and is stable.
This proves the lower bound.

There are exactly $n(n+1)/2$ unoriented nonempty paths, allowing a single
vertex. By Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:almostpath}, stability implies that at least
one such path has at most two marks outside it. If that path has $a$
vertices, this event has probability
\[
 q^{n-a}\left(1+(n-a)r+\binom{n-a}{2}r^2\right).
\]
Since $a\le d+1$, this is at most
$q^{n-d-1}(1+nr+\binom n2r^2)$. The union bound proves
\eqref{rts:eq:sandwich}. Its multiplicative factor grows at most polynomially
in $n$ at fixed $p$, proving \eqref{rts:eq:quenchedlog}.
\end{proof}

This bound holds for paths, stars, balanced trees, and arbitrary labelled
or unlabelled hosts. It supplies an exponential-scale description without
running the source's exact endpoint algorithm. It is not a relative-error
approximation scheme: the uncontrolled factor can still be polynomially
large.
[Merge note: ``the source's exact endpoint algorithm'' is Part~VIII's
formula~\eqref{mts:eq:probability} with Theorem~\ref{mts:thm:counting},
which evaluates $\pi_p(T)$ exactly for one given host in $O(n^5)$
arithmetic operations but gives no asymptotics;
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:quenched} gives its exponential order for every host
without evaluating it.]

\subsection{An elementary diameter large-deviation calculation}
The following standard Cayley-forest calculation is included as an
independent check of the exponential rate; first priority for this
random-tree diameter rate is not claimed.

\begin{lemma}[Counting long paths]
\label{rts:lem:longpaths}
Let $N_d(T_n)$ be the number of unoriented paths of length $d\ge1$ in a
uniform Cayley tree. Then
\begin{equation}
 \EE N_d(T_n)=\frac{\fall n{d+1}(d+1)}{2n^d}.
 \label{rts:eq:pathcount}
\end{equation}
For any fixed $0<\delta<1$ and integers $d_n/n\to\delta$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac1n\log\PP(\diam(T_n)\ge d_n)\longrightarrow-J(\delta),
 \quad
 J(\delta)=\delta+(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta).
 \label{rts:eq:diamLD}
\end{equation}
In particular $\diam(T_n)/n\to0$ in probability.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A fixed length-$d$ labelled path is contained in
$(d+1)n^{n-d-2}$ Cayley trees: contract the path to a component of weight
$d+1$, keeping all other vertices as weight-one components, and use the
weighted tree identity. This identity follows directly from a Pr\"ufer
code: for component weights $w_i$, summing edge-target choices gives
$(\prod_iw_i)(\sum_iw_i)^{m-2}$ for $m$ components. Thus the probability
of the fixed path is $(d+1)/n^d$. There are $\fall n{d+1}/2$ candidate
unoriented paths, proving \eqref{rts:eq:pathcount}.

A tree has diameter at least $d$ exactly when $N_d\ge1$, and
$N_d\le n(n-1)/2$. Hence its probability is between
$\EE N_d/n^2$ and $\EE N_d$. The logarithm of the factorial ratio in
\eqref{rts:eq:pathcount}, divided by $n$, tends to
\[
 \int_0^\delta\log(1-x)\,dx
 =-\delta-(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta).
\]
All other factors have logarithm $O(\log n)$. Since $J(\delta)>0$ for
$\delta>0$, the last assertion follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict annealed--quenched gap]
\label{rts:thm:gap}
For fixed $0<p<1$ and a uniform Cayley host,
\begin{equation}
 \frac1n\log\pi_p(T_n)\pto\log(1-p),
 \qquad
 \frac1n\log\EE[\pi_p(T_n)]\longrightarrow-p.
 \label{rts:eq:gap}
\end{equation}
These rates differ strictly, since $\log(1-p)<-p$.
More precisely, uniformly over hosts,
\begin{equation}
 \log\pi_p(T)-n\log q=-(\diam(T)+1)\log q+O_p(\log(n+1)).
 \label{rts:eq:quenchedfluct}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:quenched} with
$\diam(T_n)/n\to0$ for the first limit. The second follows from
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:rare} and $\EE\pi_p(T_n)=\pi_n(p)$.
The inequality follows from the power series of $\log(1-p)$ or its
strict concavity. Equation~\eqref{rts:eq:quenchedfluct} is a rearrangement
of \eqref{rts:eq:quenchedlog}.
\end{proof}

There is also a variational explanation. The polynomial-factor sandwich
reduces the annealed exponential rate to the exponential moment of the
diameter. The tail estimate \eqref{rts:eq:diamLD}, upper bounds on a finite
mesh, and the lower bound from any one tail event give
\begin{align}
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\pi_n(p)
 &=\log q+\sup_{0\le\delta\le1}
       \{-\delta\log q-J(\delta)\}\notag\\
 &=-p.
 \label{rts:eq:variational}
\end{align}
Here $J(0)=0,J(1)=1$ by continuity. To justify the upper bound, partition
$D/n$ into mesh intervals, bound the increasing weight $q^{-D}$ by its
right endpoint and the probability by the left-endpoint tail, then let
the mesh tend to zero. For the lower bound, on $D\ge\delta n$ the
weight is at least $q^{-\delta n}$. Polynomial factors disappear after
dividing logarithms by $n$.

Differentiation gives the unique maximizing diameter fraction
$\delta=p$. Substitution gives
$\log q-p\log q-p-q\log q=-p$.
Thus the exponential gain in the average is supplied by atypically long
trees, consistent with the stronger conditioned-diameter theorem. This
argument recovers the exponential rate but neither the factor
$\frac98\sqrt{2\pi}p^3n^{5/2}$ nor the Gaussian covariance.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{A general eventual-coefficient universality principle}
\label{rts:sec:universality}
The calculation is not tied to the names of the ADE diagrams. It uses
an invariant class of terminal skeletons whose labelled coefficients
are eventually constant.

\begin{theorem}[Constant-tail skeleton universality]
\label{rts:thm:universal}
Let $\mathscr H$ be an isomorphism-invariant class of finite trees, with
$c_k^{\mathscr H}$ equal to its number of labelled $k$-vertex members
divided by $k!$. Suppose $c_k^{\mathscr H}=c>0$ for all sufficiently
large $k$. Define admissible markings by requiring a branch-complete
hull and a terminal skeleton in $\mathscr H$, allowing the empty marking.
Then for $p\sqrt n\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \PP(\mathscr H\text{-admissible})
 \sim c\sqrt{2\pi}p^3n^{5/2}e^{-pn}.
 \label{rts:eq:universal}
\end{equation}
At fixed $0<p<1$, the conditional joint Gaussian law for marks and hull
size has exactly the covariance \eqref{rts:eq:Sigma}, and the constant-order
moment corrections \eqref{rts:eq:means}--\eqref{rts:eq:cov} are unchanged.
In the critical window, replace $c_k$ by $c_k^{\mathscr H}$ in
\eqref{rts:eq:psi-series}; the resulting function gives the same type of
critical limit.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The exact skeleton decomposition remains valid with
$A_{\mathscr H}(y)=\sum c_k^{\mathscr H}y^k$. Write it as
$c y^2/(1-y)$ plus a polynomial (allowing the singleton coefficient to
differ). The Poisson formula then has finitely many fixed-$k$ corrections;
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:fixedk} bounds each one. The proof of
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:rare} applies with a finite, possibly larger polynomial
in $p\sqrt n$ multiplying $e^{-nI(p)}$.

At fixed density the moving pole is unchanged, and the amplitude is
\eqref{rts:eq:amplitude} with $\cst$ replaced by $c$. Its constant multiplier
cancels in the conditional generating function. In the critical window,
the same finite-correction argument or the nonnegative kernel gives the
stated replacement of $\Psi$. Possible changes to the singleton term
vanish after normalization by $nq^n$.
\end{proof}

The geometric results do \emph{not} follow merely from eventual
coefficient constancy. The diameter theorem used the concrete path-like
shape of the three infinite ADE families; the deterministic sandwich used
the stronger fact that every allowed skeleton is within two vertices of
a path. These hypotheses must not be dropped when transferring the
probabilistic algebra to another skeleton class.

\section{Computational verification and reproducibility}
\label{rts:sec:verification}

\subsection{Exact checks and their scope}
[Merge note: source~12's programs and records are shipped with the prefix
\texttt{12-random-trees-}: \texttt{code/verify.py} and
\texttt{code/extra\_checks.py} are
\nolinkurl{code/12-random-trees-verify.py} and
\nolinkurl{code/12-random-trees-extra_checks.py}; every file of its
\nolinkurl{data/} directory keeps its name behind the same prefix in
\nolinkurl{data/}; and its \texttt{requirements.txt} and
\texttt{build.sh} are \nolinkurl{data/12-random-trees-requirements.txt}
and \nolinkurl{code/12-random-trees-build.sh}. The text below keeps the
delivered names.]
The accompanying program \texttt{code/verify.py} independently generates
labelled trees by Pr\"ufer codes, enumerates all markings, prunes unmarked
leaves to obtain their hulls, rejects unmarked hull branches, and tests
the explicit ADE shape list. Its resulting histogram of $(K,H)$ is
compared to \eqref{rts:eq:jointcount} using exact integers.

The completed exhaustive run covers all $18{,}249$ labelled trees of
orders one through seven and all $2{,}238{,}526$ marked-tree pairs. Every
one of the 70 nonzero joint bins agrees. It also checks 306 high-precision
probability and conditional-moment identities against exact rational
histograms at orders two through eighteen and three rational marking
probabilities. These tests exercise enumeration, not a numerical
stable-polynomial oracle.

The independent \texttt{code/extra\_checks.py} performs 170 exact rational
checks of \eqref{rts:eq:poisson}, at orders two through thirty-five and five
marking probabilities. It enumerates all 435 nonisomorphic trees of
orders two through eleven, compares the shape criterion with an exact
positive-semidefiniteness test for $2I-A$, and sums inverse automorphism
orders to recover Table~\ref{rts:tab:coeff} and the $9/8$ tail at orders ten
and eleven. The spectral test uses exact characteristic-polynomial
coefficients, not floating-point eigenvalues. Since the matrix is real
symmetric, all coefficients of $\det(tI+2I-A)$ are nonnegative exactly
when it has no positive root, equivalently when $2I-A\succeq0$.
Ten symbolic derivatives check the Gaussian covariance and the
constant-order cumulant corrections.

None of these finite tests proves the imported all-size equivalence
between polynomial stability and the ADE criterion. They also do not
replace the analytic arguments for limits. Their role is to detect

and algebraic errors in identities derived in the manuscript.

\subsection{How to reproduce the package}
The main verifier needs Python 3.10 or later and \texttt{mpmath} for
high-precision evaluations. The extra verifier also uses \texttt{networkx}
and \texttt{sympy}. From the package directory run
\begin{quote}\ttfamily\small
python code/verify.py -{}-max-n 7 -{}-tables\\
python code/extra\_checks.py
\end{quote}
The first script's work grows rapidly with the exhaustive order; its
finite scope should not be increased inadvertently. Both scripts write
machine-readable records in \texttt{data/}. The shipped scripts and
results were actually run for the bounds reported above. Rebuilding the
PDF uses \texttt{build.sh}, which invokes \texttt{pdflatex} twice. No
external figures or bibliography database are required.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Further research questions and proposed approaches}
\label{rts:sec:questions}
The source question is now answered for the uniform labelled host and
independent common-parameter marking law, with precise scaling limits.
The following questions concern genuinely additional conclusions rather
than restatements of the proved results.
[Merge note: ``the source question'' is Part~VIII's Research
question~\ref{mts:q:random}. Source~12's ten questions continue the
report's numbering as Research
questions~\ref{rts:q:quenched}--\ref{rts:q:sampling}; source~12 did not
label them, and the labels are new. Research question~\ref{rts:q:apices}
restates Part~VIII's Research question~\ref{mts:q:apices} (itself Part~VI's
Research question~\ref{mts:hq:apices}) and adds a random-tree layer;
Research question~\ref{rts:q:sampling} overlaps Part~VIII's Research
question~\ref{mts:q:compiler}. Both are numbered, with pointers, because
their formulations are broader. The other eight are new.]

\begin{question}[The polynomial factor in the quenched estimate]\label{rts:q:quenched}
Determine an asymptotic equivalent for $\pi_p(T_n)$ conditional on a
Cayley host, beyond the diameter-based estimate
\eqref{rts:eq:quenchedlog}. Which combination of near-diameter path
multiplicities and allowed one- or two-mark exceptions supplies the
prefactor?
\end{question}
The exact endpoint formulas in the source
(Section~\ref{mts:sec:enumeration}) and
Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:almostpath} suggest grouping stable markings by a canonical
near-longest path. A naive union bound over all paths overcounts heavily;
a canonical decomposition is the missing step.

\begin{question}[Quenched fluctuations from continuum diameter]\label{rts:q:crt}
Use \eqref{rts:eq:quenchedfluct} with a precisely normalized continuum-random-tree
diameter theorem to identify the limit law of
$(\log\pi_p(T_n)-n\log q)/\sqrt n$.
\end{question}
The error in our deterministic estimate is negligible on this scale.
The substantive task is an accurate comparison of normalization
conventions in the continuum-tree literature \cite{Aldous}, followed by
any desired stronger coupling or tail refinement. No unexplained factor
of two should be inserted into such a transfer.

\begin{question}[Uniform conditional limits when $p\downarrow0$]\label{rts:q:uniform}
Extend the fixed-density conditional Gaussian laws to sequences
$p\to0$ with $p\sqrt n\to\infty$. Determine the correct centering,
scaling, and uniform remainder across the overlap with the critical law.
\end{question}
The moving pole approaches the rooted-tree branch point, so the fixed
complex neighbourhood in Lemma~\ref{rts:lem:movingpole} collapses. The exact
Poisson identity already controls the probability; derivatives of a
suitable uniformly deformed identity are a concrete route to the
conditional laws.

\begin{question}[Critical corrections and local limits]\label{rts:q:critical}
Compute the first $n^{-1/2}$ correction to \eqref{rts:eq:critical} for a
specified expansion of $p_n$, and prove a local limit theorem for the
joint discrete pair $(K_n,H_n)$ in the window.
\end{question}
Expand the falling factorial in \eqref{rts:eq:kernel} or use an Edgeworth
expansion of the Poisson term together with the finite fixed-$k$
corrections. The dependence on the second term of $p_n$ must be retained;
Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:critical} deliberately avoids hiding it in the normalization.

\begin{question}[Fringe structure and extreme heights under stability]\label{rts:q:fringe}
Identify the empirical distribution of fringe components in the
fixed-density conditioned model, and sharpen the $O_{\PP}(\log n)$
bounds for the tallest fringe and longest subdivision chain.
\end{question}
The exact conditional forest law and uniform compositions reduce these
to classical-looking occupancy and branching calculations, but their
conditioning and dependence must be tracked. This would also refine the
difference $\diam(T_n)-H_n$ beyond our logarithmic bound.

\begin{question}[Other random-tree laws]\label{rts:q:models}
Determine counterparts for simply generated trees, conditioned
Galton--Watson trees, uniform unlabelled trees, and random trees with a
prescribed degree sequence.
\end{question}
The structural classification still applies to each host. The attachment
count and the relative weights of skeletons change, however; the factor
$9/8$ and the exponent $-p$ should not be presumed universal across these
models. A first tractable case is a degree-weighted labelled tree family
with an analytic rooted-tree equation.

\begin{question}[Inhomogeneous and dependent markings]\label{rts:q:inhomogeneous}
Replace the common Bernoulli parameter by vertex-dependent activities or
by marks correlated through a tree-indexed process. Determine which
parts of the diameter sandwich and critical scaling survive.
\end{question}
The event that all marks lie on a path remains a useful lower bound,
and the two-outside-marks necessity remains deterministic. Their
probabilities no longer reduce to a function of path length alone;
weighted path optimization becomes part of the problem.
[Merge note: for independent vertex-dependent probabilities $p_v$ on one
given host, Part~VIII's formula~\eqref{mts:eq:probability} already
evaluates the stability probability exactly; the question asks for the
asymptotic laws.]

\begin{question}[Several apices]\label{rts:q:apices}
For two or more independently marked apex elements over the same tree
incidence graph, obtain a structural stability criterion and then a
random-tree probability theory.
\end{question}
This is not covered by the single-apex covariance or skeleton theorem.
It requires a new stability analysis before enumerative substitutions
are justified. Small exact Rayleigh certificates and covariance-rank
constraints are plausible initial probes.
[Merge note: the structural half is Part~VIII's Research
question~\ref{mts:q:apices}, which is Part~VI's Research
question~\ref{mts:hq:apices} with a request for a terminal-geometry
criterion; source~12 adds the random-tree probability theory.]

\begin{question}[More general skeleton singularities]\label{rts:q:singularities}
Classify attainable labelled skeleton coefficient sequences and derive
probability laws when their generating functions have a higher-order
pole or a non-polar dominant singularity.
\end{question}
The substitution in Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:GF} remains valid for a specified
class. Its singularity controls both the prefactor and the conditional
parameter laws. Theorem~\ref{rts:thm:universal} settles only the eventual
constant-coefficient case; geometric consequences need separate shape
hypotheses.

\begin{question}[Exact conditioned sampling and formal verification]\label{rts:q:sampling}
Build an exact sampler for stable marked Cayley trees, and a
proof-assistant verification of the decomposition and its connection to
polynomial stability.
\end{question}
The joint counts choose $(k,\ell)$; then choose an allowed labelled
skeleton, a uniform weak composition, subdivision labels, and a rooted
forest. Correctness follows from the bijection once the component samplers
are verified. A formal development should separate the imported analytic
stability theorem, the finite combinatorial bijection, and the later
asymptotic analysis; accepting a tested shape classifier alone would not
prove the polynomial statement.
[Merge note: the formal half overlaps Part~VIII's Research
question~\ref{mts:q:compiler} (a verified compiler from trees to
stability certificates); the exact sampler is new.]

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Conclusion}
The marked-tree classification turns a multivariate zero-free condition
into a finite list of terminal shapes. Labelled decomposition then turns
that list into a rational skeleton series. Its eventual coefficient
$9/8$ produces both an exact Poisson-tail identity and a uniform rare-event
equivalent. The critical window retains all finite skeleton sizes through
one explicit entire function, while fixed-density conditioning selects
three long, path-like families with Gaussian fluctuations.

The geometric conclusion is sharper than a probability estimate:
stability at positive density is realized by host trees with diameter
asymptotic to $pn$. A typical unconditioned host has sublinear diameter
and a different exponential stability rate. The deterministic
polynomial-factor sandwich identifies diameter as the quantity that
separates the two perspectives. Together these results answer the pinned
random-tree question for a concrete model and expose several precise
next problems, without confusing an ordinary mathematical proof with a
formal proof certificate or a priority claim.

\section{A compact map of parameter regimes}
\label{rts:app:regimes}
\noindent\emph{(Source~12's Appendix~B.)}
For $q_n=1-p_n$, the following summary keeps the normalizations distinct.

\toprule
Regime & Proved conclusion\\
\midrule
$np_n\to\mu<\infty$
 & $\pi_n\to e^{-\mu}(1+\mu+\mu^2/2)$; conditional marks are
 Poisson truncated to $0,1,2$.\\
$np_n\to\infty$, $p_n\sqrt n\to0$
 & $\pi_n\sim\binom n2p_n^2q_n^{n-2}$; conditional mark count tends to two.\\
$p_n\sqrt n\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)$
 & $\pi_n\sim nq_n^n\Psi(\lambda)$; discrete mark-count law

 & $\pi_n\sim\frac98\sqrt{2\pi}p_n^3n^{5/2}e^{-np_n}$,

 explicit joint Gaussian law.\\

 & $n^{-1}\log\pi_p(T_n)\to\log(1-p)$ in probability.\\

 & Exact identity $\pi_n(1)=\frac98\,n!/n^{n-2}$.\\

\phantomsection\part*{Part XI.\quad Hall bottlenecks and the limits of rank normalization}
\addcontentsline{toc}{part}{Part XI.\texorpdfstring{\quad}{ } Hall bottlenecks and rank normalization}

\noindent\emph{Part~XI was added on 30 September 2026 in batch~68 of
ProveIt's incoming-report intake, from one manuscript. It answers Part~V's
Research question~\ref{lor:q:first} (``Normalization by the matching
number'') negatively in the version with positive weights on both shores:
a bipartite graph with 30 vertices, 104 edges and matching number eight,
with vertex weights in $\{1,500\}$, has a weighted support polynomial that
is not ultra-log-concave of order eight, by an exact integer certificate,
although Part~V's Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC} makes it
ultra-log-concave of order fifteen. A symmetric Hall-bottleneck family
gives a complete rank-six phase diagram, the endpoint threshold for every
core size, and a lower bound asymptotic to $\frac43\nu(H)$ along even ranks
for any normalization depending on the matching number alone. In the
positive direction the first rank-normalized inequality holds for every
positively weighted graph, with a defect identity and its equality cases,
and the support polynomial is computed exactly by an algorithm
parameterized by the matching number. The unit-weight and one-shore
versions of the question remain open. Parts~I--X are unchanged except for
dated pointers. Section~\ref{hb:sec:prov} records the provenance, fixes
the notation and states what is answered.}

\section{Provenance, conventions and what Part~XI answers}
\label{hb:sec:prov}

\subsection{The manuscript}
\label{hb:sec:source}
Part~XI is printed from batch-68 manuscript~03, called \emph{source~13}
here after its file prefix: \emph{Hall Bottlenecks and the Limits of Rank
Normalization: Exact counterexamples, a complete rank-six phase diagram,
and fixed-parameter counting of matching supports}, dated 30 September

\texttt{a866ff9a2} and was placed in \texttt{29e52fcdf}. It is pinned to

report's \texttt{article.tex} as blob
\texttt{ba1cc4a6c99abd5ff808\allowbreak aae97df75efe434833e9}: Parts~I--IX
exactly as printed (the same blob as source~12's pin; it did not see

Source~13 continues Part~V. Its baseline, the smaller-shore inequality
\eqref{hb:eq:baseline}, is Part~V's Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC}
(R\"ohrle--Ulirsch's Theorem~A for unit weights), which it credits and
does not claim. It uses the transversal-matroid presentation of Part~V
(the private-copy matroid $\mathsf M_H$, whose dual is Part~VII's $M_G$),

It cites only Part~V; its provenance record says that the README and

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=Pale,arc=1mm]
\small\textbf{Abstract of source~13 (as delivered).}
The matching-support polynomial of a bipartite graph counts pairs of equally
sized vertex sets admitting a perfect matching, with each pair counted once.
Its known ultra-log-concavity uses the smaller shore size, not necessarily the
maximum matching size. We resolve the universal \emph{positively weighted,
two-shore} rank-normalization strengthening negatively. A graph with 30
vertices, 104 edges, matching rank eight, and vertex weights in
$\{1,500\}$ violates the final rank-normalized inequality by an exact integer
certificate. A symmetric Hall-bottleneck family yields a complete rank-six
phase diagram: for outer size $n\le32$ every positive core activity works,
whereas for $n\ge33$ a single explicit quadratic gives the exact failure
threshold. For arbitrary core size we determine the endpoint obstruction and
prove that any universal rank-only normalization must be at least
$\frac43r-O(1)$ along even ranks. In the positive direction, every graph
satisfies the first rank-normalized inequality, with a defect identity and an
exact equality classification. Finally, neighborhood types relative to a
minimum vertex cover give an exact weighted counting algorithm in
$2^{r^2+O(r)}\operatorname{poly}(|V|+|E|)$ time. Complete proofs, finite
positive-coefficient certificates, executable code, and further questions are
provided.
\end{tcolorbox}
\noindent The abstract is reproduced as delivered. Its $r$ is the matching
number $\nu(H)$, as everywhere in Part~XI.

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Scope and status (source~13, as delivered).}
The counterexamples concern arbitrary positive weights on \emph{both} shores.
They do not settle the unit-weight or one-shore-only rank-normalization
questions. The results below are proved in ordinary mathematics and checked
by exact computations, not verified in Lean. They are newly derived for this
article; global priority is not certified by the targeted literature review.
No published smaller-shore theorem is contradicted.
\end{statusbox}

\begin{statusbox}
\small\textbf{Priority and prior work (merge).}
The smaller-shore inequality~\eqref{hb:eq:baseline} is not new: it is
Part~V's Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC}, and for unit weights it is
Theorem~A of R\"ohrle and Ulirsch~\cite{RU} for the relation bimatroid of
their Example~2.4; the Lorentzian inputs (matroid basis polynomials,
nonnegative linear substitutions, the bivariate criterion) are
Br\"and\'en--Huh's~\cite{BH}, exactly as in Part~V. Source~13's
re-derivation of the baseline (its Section~2.1) is Part~V's proof and is
not reprinted (Section~\ref{hb:sec:baseline}). K\H{o}nig's theorem
(Lemma~\ref{hb:lem:konig}, proved with its classical alternating-path
argument), elementary symmetric functions, augmenting-path matching tests
and exact rational arithmetic are classical. New relative to Parts~I--X:
the Hall family and its support criterion and coefficient formula
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:family}), the 30-vertex counterexample and its
corollaries (Section~\ref{hb:sec:witness}), the rank-six phase diagram
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:rank6}), the endpoint threshold
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:general}), the forced-core limiting order and the
lower bound for rank-only normalizations (Section~\ref{hb:sec:limit}), the
first-margin defect identity and its equality cases
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:first}) and the cover-type counting algorithm
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:algorithm}). Source~13's source review was targeted,
not a comprehensive priority search; no worldwide priority is claimed for
any result of Part~XI.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{What Part~XI answers}
\label{hb:sec:answers}
Status after Part~XI, as of 30 September 2026:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em]
\item \textbf{Part~V's Research question~\ref{lor:q:first} is answered
negatively in its weighted version.} Source~07's formulation there asks to
prove the replacement of $\binom dk$ by $\binom{\nu(H)}k$ ``or find a
smallest counterexample, including positive vertex weights as a separate
version''. With positive weights on both shores the replacement fails
(Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness}), already at matching number six
(Section~\ref{hb:sec:rank6}), and every normalization depending only on
the matching number must be at least $\frac43\nu(H)-\frac{17}9+o(1)$
along even ranks (Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:universalorder}). A
smallest counterexample is not determined: the least possible matching
number of a weighted counterexample is three, four, five or six (Research
question~\ref{hb:q:rank}), and the 30-vertex example is not claimed to be
smallest. The unit-weight version and the version with weights on one
shore stay open (Research questions~\ref{hb:q:unit}
and~\ref{hb:q:oneshore}); the core-three family is
$\ULC_{\nu(H)}$ at unit weight (Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:asymptoticweight}),
which is consistent with the batch-55 unit-weight search recorded after
Research question~\ref{lor:q:first}. As subclasses, every positively
weighted graph of matching number at most two satisfies the
rank-normalized inequalities (Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:smallrank}), and every
graph satisfies the first one (Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:firstidentity}).
[Merge observation, not in source~13: for a preorder the question has no
content, since the graph of Part~V's Section~\ref{lor:sec:preorders}
contains its diagonal perfect matching, so $\nu(H_\tau)=n$ is the shore
size and Corollary~\ref{lor:cor:preorderintro} is unaffected.]
\item \textbf{Part~V's division caveat} (after Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:CLC} and
after Research question~\ref{lor:q:first}) gains an instance inside the
class: Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:division} is a Lorentzian polynomial of the
form~\eqref{lor:eq:weightedhom} whose quotient by the seventh power of the
homogenizing variable is not Lorentzian.
\item \textbf{Part~V's Research question~\ref{lor:q:equality}} (equality at
a single index under positive weights) \textbf{is answered at the first
index} for the normalization by $\nu(H)$
(Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:equality}: disjoint unions of $\nu(H)$ stars with
equal edge-weight sums). [Merge observation, not in source~13: the
threshold $(D-1)/(2D)$ of the first order-$D$ inequality increases with
$D$, so Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:firstidentity} makes the first inequality
strict for every order $D>\nu(H)$; equality at the first index of Part~V's
inequality~\eqref{lor:eq:mainULC}, with or without positive weights,
therefore holds exactly when the normalizing shore size equals $\nu(H)$
and the nonisolated graph is such a union of stars. For a preorder, in the
unweighted inequality~\eqref{lor:eq:preorderULC}, it holds exactly for the
antichain, since each of the $n$ disjoint stars must then consist of one
diagonal edge; this answers the first index of Part~VII's restatement in
Section~\ref{mat:sec:oldquestions}.] Equality at other
indices and the null directions of the covariance bound stay open.
\item \textbf{Part~IV's Research questions~\ref{lor:hq:param}
and~\ref{lor:hq:countcx}, and Part~V's Research
question~\ref{hb:hq:algorithms}, gain one parameterized class.}
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:FPT} computes every weighted support polynomial exactly
in $2^{\nu(H)^2+O(\nu(H))}$ times a polynomial; through Part~II's
Theorem~\ref{htwo:thm:main} this computes $h_{P_G}$ and the height-two
gamma polynomial $p_G$ exactly with the matching number of the
comparability graph as parameter (merge observation). The widths and
treewidths those questions name are a different parameter and remain open.
The $\#\mathrm P$-hardness of Theorem~\ref{lor:sp:thm:preorderhard}
concerns unrestricted matching numbers; for bounded matching number
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:FPT} is polynomial. The algorithm groups outside vertices by their neighbourhoods in
a minimum cover, one form of the ``repeated neighborhoods'' that Research
question~\ref{hb:hq:algorithms} names.
\item \textbf{No other numbered research question of Parts~I--X is
answered.} Part~IX samples demand vectors and lattice points; Part~XI
counts support pairs exactly and is not a sampler. Part~VII's preorder
matroid is not used beyond the duality noted in Section~\ref{hb:sec:source}.
\end{itemize}
Part~XI refutes no statement of Parts~I--X, and nothing is retracted:
Part~V proves only the smaller-shore normalization and says that the
replacement by $\nu(H)$ is not proved there. Part~V gains dated pointers
