\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The question and its exact scope}
\label{hb:sec:intro}

A normalization parameter can carry genuine structural information. For a
polynomial of degree $r$, it is tempting to assume that every binomially
normalized coefficient inequality should use $\binom rk$. Matching-support
polynomials show why this temptation requires a proof: their natural
homogeneous realization remembers unused vertices on a shore, even when
those vertices do not increase the largest possible matching.

This article studies that issue in a concrete family. The main negative
result is not merely a failure of a proposed proof technique. It is an exact
counterexample to the strengthened inequality itself. The accompanying
positive results isolate what survives, explain a mechanism for failure,
and supply a counting procedure suitable for further investigations.

\subsection{Repository target and published baseline}
\label{hb:sec:repotarget}

The repository target is Part~V of this report, at the fixed ProveIt
snapshot recorded in Section~\ref{hb:app:provenance}. Its discussion of
homogenization (after Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:CLC}) explicitly distinguishes
the shore size from the actual matching rank. Its subsection on the
smaller active shore (in Section~\ref{lor:sec:sp:ulc}) states that
replacement by maximum matching size would be stronger and is not proved
there; the question is its Research question~\ref{lor:q:first}.
[Merge note: source~13 names this report by its title, \emph{A Reflexive
Root-Polytope Model for Preorder $h$-Polynomials}, ``especially its
Part~V'', and cites it as a repository reference; the citation is
replaced by references to Part~V's statements, and the parenthetical
pointers and the last clause were added. ``ProveIt'' and ``the
repository'' in Part~XI mean Parts~I--IX of this report at the pin.]

R\"ohrle and Ulirsch's Theorem A gives smaller-shore ultra-log-concavity for
bimatroid regular-minor counts; their relation example includes the
matching-support counts considered here \cite{RU}. The homogeneous
polynomial tools used in the baseline are those of Br\"and\'en and Huh
\cite{BH}. We retain that baseline, rather than presenting it as a new
result, and ask whether the stronger normalization persists with arbitrary
positive vertex weights.

There are three different questions:
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:threequestions}
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{unit-weight:} & u_x=v_y=1,\\
\text{one-shore weighted:} & u_x=1,\quad v_y>0,\\
\text{two-shore weighted:} & u_x>0,\quad v_y>0.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
A counterexample to the third question need not answer either of the first
two. All claims in this article respect this distinction.

\subsection{Results and proof architecture}

The central family is obtained by deleting one rectangular block from a
complete bipartite graph. Small core sets on both shores form a minimum
vertex cover; many outer vertices compete for these cores. Giving the core
vertices a common activity $w$ produces an explicitly computable polynomial.

The proof of the 30-vertex counterexample is in
Section~\ref{hb:sec:witness}. The full rank-six classification is in
Section~\ref{hb:sec:rank6}; its only substantial polynomial expansions are
certified by positive coefficient tables in Section~\ref{hb:app:positive}.
Section~\ref{hb:sec:general} treats the last inequality for every core size.
Section~\ref{hb:sec:limit} identifies the exact normalization threshold for the
forced-core limiting family and extracts a universal lower bound.
Section~\ref{hb:sec:first} proves the first rank-normalized inequality for
arbitrary graphs and explains equality. Section~\ref{hb:sec:algorithm} gives
an exact algorithm parameterized by matching rank.

The counterexample, phase diagram, endpoint calculation, limiting threshold,
and elementary defect identity do not depend on any unrefereed assertion in
ProveIt. The repository motivates the question. The Lorentzian corollary uses
the established homogeneous polynomial results explicitly identified below.
[Merge note: in this report the support criterion
(Lemma~\ref{hb:lem:criterion}) is the only ingredient the counterexample
needs; Part~V's theorems enter only through the baseline it is compared
with.]

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Supports, weights, and normalization}
\label{hb:sec:definitions}

Let $H=(X,Y;E)$ be a finite simple bipartite graph. Isolated vertices may be
removed whenever shore sizes are used. Write $m=|X|$, $n=|Y|$ after this
removal, and let $r=\nu(H)$ be the maximum matching size.

\begin{definition}
A \emph{matchable support pair} is a pair $(I,J)$ with $I\subseteq X$,
$J\subseteq Y$, $|I|=|J|$, such that $H[I,J]$ has a perfect matching.
For positive vertex weights $u=(u_x)_{x\in X}$ and $v=(v_y)_{y\in Y}$, set
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:supportpoly}
 p_H(t;u,v)=\sum_{(I,J)\in\PM(H)}u_Iv_Jt^{|I|}
          =\sum_{k=0}^{r}a_k t^k,
 \qquad u_I=\prod_{x\in I}u_x,\quad v_J=\prod_{y\in J}v_y.
\end{equation}
The empty support has weight one. Each support pair occurs exactly once,
regardless of the number of its perfect matchings.
\end{definition}

For example, the unit-weight polynomial of $K_{2,2}$ is
$1+4t+t^2$, not $1+4t+2t^2$. The distinction between a support and a
witnessing matching is essential both to the counterexamples and to the
algorithm. A matching of size $r$ has submatchings of every size from zero
to $r$, so all $a_0,\ldots,a_r$ are strictly positive.

\begin{definition}
For an integer $D\ge r$, the sequence $(a_k)_{k=0}^{r}$ is
\emph{ultra-log-concave of order $D$}, abbreviated $\ULC_D$, when the
zero-padded sequence $a_k/\binom Dk$, $0\le k\le D$, has no internal zeros
and is log-concave. Define its margins by
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:margin}
 \Delta_k^{(D)}
 =k(D-k)a_k^2-(k+1)(D-k+1)a_{k-1}a_{k+1},
 \qquad 1\le k<D.
\end{equation}
Then $\ULC_D$ is equivalent to $\Delta_k^{(D)}\ge0$ for every such $k$.
\end{definition}

The formula follows by dividing consecutive binomial coefficients. At an
index with three positive coefficients it is equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:ratioULC}
 \frac{a_k^2}{a_{k-1}a_{k+1}}
 \ge \frac{k+1}{k}\frac{D-k+1}{D-k}.
\end{equation}
The right side decreases as $D$ increases. Thus $\ULC_{D_0}$ implies
$\ULC_D$ for $D\ge D_0$. Replacing the smaller shore size by $r$ genuinely
strengthens the assertion when $r<\min(m,n)$.

\subsection{The established smaller-shore theorem}
\label{hb:sec:baseline}

[Merge note: source~13 here spells out, ``for reference'', the short
specialization argument behind Part~V's
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC}: the transversal matroid with one private
element $\bar x$ for each $x\in X$, of rank $m$ (Part~V's $\mathsf M_H$),
whose bases are exactly $\{\bar x:x\in X\setminus I\}\sqcup J$ for
$(I,J)\in\PM(H)$, because the private elements occupy $X\setminus I$ and
leave the vertices of $I$ to match $J$ (Part~V's
Proposition~\ref{lor:prop:bases}, by the same forced-slot argument), and
the substitution below, which is Part~V's display~\eqref{lor:eq:weightedhom}
with its homogenizing variable $s$ printed $\sigma$. That is Part~V's proof
and is not reprinted in full; the display and the conclusion are kept,
because Part~XI cites them.]
Let $\mathcal B_H(a,z)$ be the basis polynomial of this matroid,
Part~V's~\eqref{lor:eq:basispoly}. Substitution gives
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:matroidspecialization}
 \left(\prod_{x\in X}u_x\right)
 \mathcal B_H\bigl((\sigma/u_x)_{x\in X},(t v_y)_{y\in Y}\bigr)
 =\sum_{k=0}^{r}a_k \sigma^{m-k}t^k.
\end{equation}
Matroid basis polynomials are Lorentzian, nonnegative linear substitutions
preserve that property, and in two variables the degree-$D$ criterion is
precisely $\ULC_D$ \cite{BH}. Applying these facts to
\eqref{hb:eq:matroidspecialization}, and then transposing the graph, yields
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:baseline}
 p_H(t;u,v)\text{ is }\ULC_{\min(m,n)}.
\end{equation}
This is the weighted baseline already used in the repository (Part~V's
Theorem~\ref{lor:thm:weightedULC}). For unit
weights it also follows from the relation-bimatroid case of
\cite[Theorem A and Example 2.4]{RU}.

The polynomial in \eqref{hb:eq:matroidspecialization} has a factor $\sigma^{m-r}$.
Deleting this factor changes the homogeneous degree. Nothing in the
specialization argument permits one to delete it while retaining the
Lorentzian property. Section~\ref{hb:sec:witness} shows that this is a real
obstruction within these very specializations.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{A Hall-bottleneck family with an exact support formula}
\label{hb:sec:family}

Fix integers $n\ge s\ge1$. Partition the two shores into outer and core
sets:
\[
 X=L\sqcup A,\qquad Y=R\sqcup B,
 \qquad |L|=|R|=n,\quad |A|=|B|=s.
\]
Define $H_{s,n}$ by
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:edges}
 E=(L\times B)\cup(A\times R)\cup(A\times B).
\end{equation}
Every possible edge is present except those from $L$ to $R$. The core
vertices in $A\sqcup B$ have weight $w>0$, and the outer vertices have
weight one. We write $a_k^{s,n}(w)$, or simply $a_k(w)$, for its coefficients.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\small},
 box/.style={draw,rounded corners=2pt,minimum width=36mm,minimum height=12mm,align=center}]
\node[box] (L) at (0,1.6) {$L$: $n$ outer vertices\\weight $1$};
\node[box] (A) at (0,-0.5) {$A$: $s$ core vertices\\weight $w$};
\node[box] (R) at (7,1.6) {$R$: $n$ outer vertices\\weight $1$};
\node[box] (B) at (7,-0.5) {$B$: $s$ core vertices\\weight $w$};
\draw[thick] (L.east)--(B.west);
\draw[thick] (A.east)--(R.west);
\draw[thick] (A.east)--(B.west);
\node at (3.5,2.75) {No edges between $L$ and $R$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Each drawn connection denotes all edges between the indicated
blocks. The core is a vertex cover of size $2s$.}
\label{hb:fig:family}
\end{figure}

\begin{lemma}\label{hb:lem:rank}
The graph $H_{s,n}$ has $2(n+s)$ vertices, $2ns+s^2$ edges, and matching
rank $2s$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The vertex and edge counts follow from the disjoint blocks in
\eqref{hb:eq:edges}. Every edge meets $A\sqcup B$, so a matching has at most
$2s$ edges. Because $n\ge s$, we can match all of $B$ to $s$ distinct
vertices of $L$, and all of $A$ to $s$ distinct vertices of $R$. The union
has $2s$ edges, attaining the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact support criterion]\label{hb:lem:criterion}
Suppose a pair of supports of size $k$ selects $i$ vertices of $A$ and $j$
vertices of $B$. It is matchable if and only if $i+j\ge k$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are $k-i$ selected vertices of $L$, each of which must be matched to a
selected vertex of $B$. Hence $k-i\le j$ is necessary. The symmetric
condition $k-j\le i$ is the same inequality.

Conversely, when $i+j\ge k$, match the $k-i$ selected vertices of $L$ to
that many selected vertices of $B$, and match the $k-j$ selected vertices
of $R$ to that many selected vertices of $A$. The unused selected core
sets on the two shores both have size $i+j-k$. Match them to each other.
Every required edge is present, and the three matchings are vertex-disjoint.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact coefficient formula]\label{hb:thm:coefficients}
With binomial coefficients interpreted as zero outside their usual range,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:familycoeff}
 a_k^{s,n}(w)=
 \sum_{\substack{0\le i,j\le s\\i+j\ge k}}
 \binom si\binom sj\binom n{k-i}\binom n{k-j}w^{i+j},
 \qquad 0\le k\le2s.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose the two core subsets and the two outer subsets. Their counts are the
four binomial coefficients in the summand, and their weight is $w^{i+j}$.
Lemma~\ref{hb:lem:criterion} is exactly the condition for retaining that
summand. No choice of a perfect matching appears in the count.
\end{proof}

The formula already reduces a potentially enormous support enumeration to
$(s+1)^2$ terms per coefficient. Its utility is not merely numerical: only a
few core choices can contribute to the highest three coefficients, allowing
an exact obstruction analysis.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{An exact 30-vertex counterexample}
\label{hb:sec:witness}

\begin{theorem}[Failure of weighted rank normalization]\label{hb:thm:witness}
Let $H=H_{4,11}$, with weight $500$ on its eight core vertices and weight
one on its 22 outer vertices. Then $H$ has 30 vertices, 104 edges, and
maximum matching size eight. Its support polynomial is not $\ULC_8$.
Consequently the universal positively weighted, two-shore replacement of
smaller-shore normalization by matching rank is false.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{hb:lem:rank} gives the graph parameters. Keeping $w$ symbolic,
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:coefficients} gives
\begin{align}
 a_6(w)&=3025w^6(w^2+24w+216),\label{hb:eq:witnessa6}\\
 a_7(w)&=27225w^7(w+16),\label{hb:eq:witnessa7}\\
 a_8(w)&=108900w^8.\label{hb:eq:witnessa8}
\end{align}
Here $3025=\binom{11}{2}^2$, $27225=\binom{11}{3}^2$, and
$108900=\binom{11}{4}^2$. Substitution gives the identity
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:witnessmargin}
 7a_7(w)^2-16a_6(w)a_8(w)
 =9\cdot3025^2w^{14}(-w^2+480w+2304).
\end{equation}
At $w=500$ the quadratic on the right is $-7696$. The other factors are
strictly positive. Thus $\Delta_7^{(8)}<0$, which violates the definition
of $\ULC_8$.
\end{proof}

This is a short exact certificate: the graph definition, three polynomial
coefficients, and the negative value of a quadratic suffice. Floating-point
root finding, exhaustive enumeration, and an asymptotic limit are not
needed for the proof.

The first integer activity for which the \emph{last} inequality fails in
this particular graph is $485$, since the reduced quadratic is $368$ at
$484$ and $-121$ at $485$. We use $500$ for a simpler stated weight and a
larger margin. This is not a claim that 30 is the smallest possible number
of vertices in a counterexample.

\begin{corollary}[A concrete failed degree reduction]\label{hb:cor:division}
There is a bivariate Lorentzian polynomial of degree 15 arising from a
positive specialization of a transversal-matroid basis polynomial such
that division by its factor $\sigma^7$ is not Lorentzian.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For the graph and weights of Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness}, let
\[
 F(\sigma,t)=\sum_{k=0}^8a_k \sigma^{15-k}t^k.
\]
Equation~\eqref{hb:eq:matroidspecialization} proves that $F$ is Lorentzian.
The polynomial $F/\sigma^7$ has degree eight and the same coefficient sequence.
The bivariate criterion would make that sequence $\ULC_8$ if the quotient
were Lorentzian, contrary to Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness}.
\end{proof}

In particular, the failure does not depend on leaving the transversal
setting or introducing coefficients of mixed sign. The coefficients of
$p_H$ are positive, and its correct smaller-shore normalization is 15.
The exact check in the accompanying data confirms all order-15 inequalities
and the positivity of the first six order-eight margins. The proof of the
counterexample itself only needs the seventh margin.

\subsection{Nonreal zeros and robustness}

\begin{corollary}\label{hb:cor:nonreal}
The polynomial in Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:witness} has a nonreal zero. Its failure
of rank-normalized ultra-log-concavity persists on an open neighborhood of
the stated positive vertex weights.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If all zeros were real, positivity of all coefficients and of the constant
term would make them strictly negative. Write
$p_H(t)=a_8\prod_{i=1}^8(t+\lambda_i)$ with $\lambda_i>0$, and put
$S=\sum_i\lambda_i$. Then $a_7=a_8S$ and
$a_6=a_8(S^2-\sum_i\lambda_i^2)/2$. The inequality
$\sum_i\lambda_i^2\ge S^2/8$ would imply
$7a_7^2-16a_6a_8\ge0$, contradicting \eqref{hb:eq:witnessmargin}.
For robustness, every coefficient and every margin is a polynomial in the
vertex weights. A strict negative value of one margin persists under
sufficiently small perturbations.
\end{proof}

One can make the second assertion quantitative. Suppose
$a_k^2/(a_{k-1}a_{k+1})=R_0$ violates the required ratio $R_*$, so
$R_0<R_*$. If each individual vertex weight is multiplied by a number in
$[\mathrm e^{-\eta},\mathrm e^\eta]$, then each monomial of $a_j$ changes by a factor in
$[\mathrm e^{-2j\eta},\mathrm e^{2j\eta}]$. Positivity gives the same bounds for $a_j$.
The perturbed ratio at $k$ is at most $\mathrm e^{8k\eta}R_0$. Therefore any
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:robustness}
 0<\eta<\frac1{8k}\log\frac{R_*}{R_0}
\end{equation}
preserves the violation. For the lead example $k=7$ and $R_*=16/7$.
Thus the obstruction is not an isolated equality accident.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{A complete rank-six phase diagram}
\label{hb:sec:rank6}

The rank-eight example is small in vertex count. Taking core size three
instead gives a complete description of \emph{all} rank-normalized
inequalities in the symmetric family, not just the last one.

Let $n\ge3$, let $H=H_{3,n}$, and abbreviate
$A=\binom n3$ and $B=\binom n2$. Formula~\eqref{hb:eq:familycoeff} becomes
\begin{align}
 a_0={}&1,\notag\\
 a_1={}&9w^2+6nw,\notag\\
 a_2={}&(6B+9n^2)w^2+18nw^3+9w^4,\notag\\
 a_3={}&(2A+18nB)w^3+(6B+9n^2)w^4+6nw^5+w^6,\label{hb:eq:rank6coeffs}\\
 a_4={}&(6nA+9B^2)w^4+6nBw^5+n^2w^6,\notag\\
 a_5={}&6ABw^5+B^2w^6,\notag\\
 a_6={}&A^2w^6.\notag
\end{align}
Define
\begin{align}
 Q_n(w)={}&(-n^2+34n-49)w^2\notag\\
 &+12(n-1)(n-2)(n+3)w
   +8(n-1)(n-2)^2(n+1).\label{hb:eq:Q}
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[Complete classification in the core-three family]
\label{hb:thm:rank6phase}
For every integer $n\ge3$ and every real $w>0$, the first four
order-six margins of $H_{3,n}$ are strictly positive. The fifth satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:rank6last}
 \Delta_5^{(6)}
 =5a_5^2-12a_4a_6
 =\frac{n^4(n-1)^2w^{10}}{48}Q_n(w).
\end{equation}
Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\alph*)}]
\item If $3\le n\le32$, the polynomial is $\ULC_6$ for every $w>0$.
\item If $n\ge33$, put
\begin{align*}
 a&=n^2-34n+49,\\
 b&=12(n-1)(n-2)(n+3),\\
 c&=8(n-1)(n-2)^2(n+1),
\end{align*}
and define
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:criticalweight}
 w_c(n)=\frac{b+\sqrt{b^2+4ac}}{2a}.
\end{equation}
Then $p_{H_{3,n}}(t;w)$ is $\ULC_6$ exactly for $0<w\le w_c(n)$.
For $w>w_c(n)$, precisely the last of its five order-six margins is
negative.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Insert \eqref{hb:eq:rank6coeffs} in \eqref{hb:eq:margin}. For the first four
margins one obtains
\begin{align}
 \Delta_1^{(6)}&=9w^2P_1(n-2,w),&
 \Delta_2^{(6)}&=3w^4P_2(n-2,w),\notag\\
 \Delta_3^{(6)}&=w^6P_3(n-2,w),&
 \Delta_4^{(6)}&=\frac{n^2w^8}{4}P_4(n-2,w),\label{hb:eq:positivefactors}
\end{align}
where all coefficients of the four polynomials $P_i(x,w)$ are
nonnegative and their constant terms are positive. Their complete
coefficient lists are in Section~\ref{hb:app:positive}; those lists, together
with \eqref{hb:eq:rank6coeffs}, are finite algebraic certificates of
\eqref{hb:eq:positivefactors}. Since $n-2\ge1$ and $w>0$, the four margins are
strictly positive. Direct substitution for $a_4,a_5,a_6$ gives
\eqref{hb:eq:rank6last}.

The coefficient of $w^2$ in $Q_n$ changes sign between $n=32$ and $n=33$:
its real roots as a polynomial in $n$ are $17\pm4\sqrt{15}$. The linear
and constant coefficients in $Q_n$ are strictly positive for $n\ge3$.
Thus $Q_n(w)>0$ for every positive $w$ when $3\le n\le32$.

For $n\ge33$, write $Q_n(w)=-aw^2+bw+c$ with $a,b,c>0$. This quadratic
has exactly one positive root, the value in \eqref{hb:eq:criticalweight}.
It is nonnegative on $0<w\le w_c(n)$ and negative above that threshold.
Equation~\eqref{hb:eq:rank6last} and the already established positivity of the
other margins prove all assertions.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact witnesses and threshold values}

At $n=33$ the obstruction simplifies to
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:rank6example}
 Q_{33}(w)=16(-w^2+26784w+522784).
\end{equation}
It is nonnegative at the integer $26803$ and negative at $26804$; more
precisely, $Q_{33}(26804)=-212736$. Hence $H_{3,33}$ with core weight
$26804$ is an exact rank-six counterexample on 72 vertices and 207 edges.
The minimum matching rank of a two-shore weighted counterexample is
therefore at most six. Section~\ref{hb:sec:first} shows it is at least three;
we do not determine which of ranks three through six is the first possible.

\centering
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
Outer size $n$ & Vertices & First integer failure & $Q_n$ at that integer\\
\midrule
33 & 72 & 26804 & $-212736$\\
34 & 74 & 9589 & $-98473$\\
36 & 78 & 4625 & $-534465$\\
40 & 86 & 2671 & $-778249$\\
48 & 102 & 1865 & $-1151481$\\
50 & 106 & 1793 & $-1246737$\\
64 & 134 & 1635 & $-3057345$\\
100 & 206 & 1866 & $-6822324$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exact integer thresholds in the rank-six family. Each row is
certified by evaluating the quadratic at the listed integer and its
predecessor, not by rounding a floating-point root.}
\label{hb:tab:rank6}
\end{table}

The activity threshold is not monotone in outer size. Adding vertices can
initially make failure easier because it changes the high-degree balance,
while eventually the activity must scale linearly with the outer size.
The following asymptotic statement makes the latter assertion precise.

\begin{corollary}\label{hb:cor:asymptoticweight}
As $n\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:weightasymptotic}
 \frac{w_c(n)}{n}\longrightarrow 6+2\sqrt{11}.
\end{equation}
Every unit-weight member $H_{3,n}$, $n\ge3$, is nevertheless $\ULC_6$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{hb:eq:criticalweight}, $a/n^2\to1$, $b/n^3\to12$, and
$c/n^4\to8$. Divide the numerator and denominator by the corresponding
powers of $n$ to obtain
$(12+\sqrt{144+32})/2=6+2\sqrt{11}$.

At $w=1$,
\[
 Q_n(1)=8n^4-20n^3+23n^2-18n-9.
\]
Writing $n=x+3$ gives
\[
 Q_{x+3}(1)=8x^4+76x^3+275x^2+444x+252,
\]
which is positive for $x\ge0$. Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:rank6phase} proves the
unit-weight assertion.
\end{proof}

This family therefore supplies a useful warning about experiments: a
search restricted to unit weights would miss its entire rank-six
obstruction, no matter how many outer vertices it considered.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{The endpoint obstruction for every core size}
\label{hb:sec:general}

The previous computation is part of a general phenomenon. Fix $s\ge2$,
$n\ge s$, let $R=2s$, and abbreviate
\[
 A=\binom ns,\qquad B=\binom n{s-1},\qquad C=\binom n{s-2}.
\]
These three letters denote numbers in this section, not the vertex blocks.

\begin{proposition}[The last three coefficients]\label{hb:prop:tail}
The coefficients of $H_{s,n}$ satisfy
\begin{align}
 a_R={}&A^2w^{2s},\notag\\
 a_{R-1}={}&2sABw^{2s-1}+B^2w^{2s},\label{hb:eq:tail}\\
 a_{R-2}={}&\bigl(s(s-1)AC+s^2B^2\bigr)w^{2s-2}
            +2sBCw^{2s-1}+C^2w^{2s}.\notag
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $k=2s$, the condition $i+j\ge k$ forces $i=j=s$. For $k=2s-1$,
the allowed pairs are $(s,s)$, $(s-1,s)$, and $(s,s-1)$. For
$k=2s-2$, one adds $(s-1,s-1)$, $(s-2,s)$, and $(s,s-2)$.
Substituting these choices in \eqref{hb:eq:familycoeff} gives
\eqref{hb:eq:tail}. The two choices omitting two core vertices on the same
shore contribute $2\binom s2 AC=s(s-1)AC$.
\end{proof}

Define
\begin{align}
 \alpha&=(2s-1)B^4-4sA^2C^2,\notag\\
 \beta&=4sAB\bigl((2s-1)B^2-2sAC\bigr),\label{hb:eq:abcgeneral}\\
 \gamma&=4s^2(s-1)A^2(B^2-AC).\notag
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[Exact endpoint threshold]\label{hb:thm:endpoint}
For $s\ge2$ and $n\ge s$,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:endpoint}
 \Delta_{2s-1}^{(2s)}
 =w^{4s-2}(\alpha w^2+\beta w+\gamma),
\end{equation}
where $\beta,\gamma>0$. Thus some positive activity makes the last
rank-normalized inequality fail if and only if $\alpha<0$.

For $s=2$ this never happens. For every $s\ge3$, put
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:Ts}
 T_s=\frac{2(s-1)}{\sqrt{s(2s-1)}}>1.
\end{equation}
Then the equivalent condition is
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:ncondition}
 n-s+1>\frac1{T_s-1}.
\end{equation}
In particular the smallest integer outer size with a possible endpoint
failure is
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:nmin}
 n_{\min}(s)=s+\left\lfloor\frac1{T_s-1}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
For such an $n$, failure occurs exactly above the unique positive root of
$\alpha w^2+\beta w+\gamma$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expanding $(2s-1)a_{2s-1}^2-4s a_{2s-2}a_{2s}$ using
\eqref{hb:eq:tail}, and removing $w^{4s-2}$, gives
\eqref{hb:eq:abcgeneral}. The elementary ratio
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:binomialratio}
 \frac{B^2}{AC}
 =\frac{s}{s-1}\frac{n-s+2}{n-s+1}
\end{equation}
is greater than $s/(s-1)$. Consequently $B^2>AC$ and
$(2s-1)B^2>2sAC$, proving $\beta,\gamma>0$.

If $\alpha\ge0$, the quadratic is positive for every $w>0$. If
$\alpha<0$, its constant term is positive and it tends to $-\infty$;
its two roots have opposite signs. This proves the first assertions.

Using \eqref{hb:eq:binomialratio}, the condition $\alpha<0$ becomes
\[
 \frac{n-s+2}{n-s+1}<\frac{2(s-1)}{\sqrt{s(2s-1)}}.
\]
For $s=2$ the right side is less than one, so the inequality is impossible.
For $s\ge3$ the right side is greater than one, and rearrangement gives
\eqref{hb:eq:ncondition}. The least integer $n$ satisfying that strict
inequality is \eqref{hb:eq:nmin}.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{rrrrl}
\toprule
$s$ & $n_{\min}(s)$ & Vertices & First integer failure & Reduced quadratic\\
\midrule
3 & 33 & 72 & 26804 & $-w^2+26784w+522784$\\
4 & 11 & 30 & 485 & $-w^2+480w+2304$\\
5 & 10 & 30 & 131 & $-11w^2+1400w+4928$\\
6 & 10 & 32 & 96 & $-31w^2+2880w+8250$\\

The word ``endpoint'' is important. The positivity certificates in
Section~\ref{hb:sec:rank6} establish a full phase diagram when $s=3$.
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:endpoint} alone does not rule out earlier-index failures
for a larger core size or assert that the endpoint is always the first
inequality to fail as $w$ increases.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Forced cores and a universal normalization lower bound}
\label{hb:sec:limit}

For very large activity, supports containing every core vertex dominate.
This limit separates a geometric shift in degree from the combinatorics of
choosing outer vertices.

\begin{lemma}[Forced-core limit]\label{hb:lem:limit}
For fixed $s,n$ with $n\ge s$,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:limit}
 w^{-2s}p_{H_{s,n}}(t;w)
 \longrightarrow L_{s,n}(t)
 :=t^s\sum_{j=0}^{s}\binom nj^2t^j
 \qquad(w\to\infty)
\end{equation}
coefficientwise.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{hb:eq:familycoeff}, the largest possible power of $w$ is $2s$,
and only $i=j=s$ contributes to that power. The corresponding support size
is $k=s+j'$ with $0\le j'\le s$, and the coefficient is
$\binom n{j'}^2$. All other terms vanish after division by $w^{2s}$.
\end{proof}

The coefficients of $L_{s,n}$ have leading zeros below degree $s$, but no
internal zeros. Thus $\ULC_D$ is still meaningful for $D\ge2s$.
Only the inequalities at $k=s+j$, $1\le j\le s-1$, are nontrivial ratios
of three positive coefficients.

\begin{lemma}\label{hb:lem:thresholdD}
For $1\le j\le s-1$, set
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:Rjn}
 R_j(n)=\left(\frac{j+1}{j}\frac{n-j+1}{n-j}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
The order-$D$ inequality of $L_{s,n}$ at $k=s+j$ holds if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:finiteDthreshold}
 D\ge F_{s,j}(n):=s+j+
 \frac{s+j+1}{(s+j)R_j(n)-(s+j+1)}.
\end{equation}
The denominator is positive. Moreover $F_{s,j}(n)$ increases with $n$ and
converges to
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:limitDthreshold}
 F_{s,j}(\infty)=s+j+
 \frac{j^2(s+j+1)}{s(2j+1)+j(j+1)}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The ratio of consecutive positive coefficients of $L_{s,n}$ is
\eqref{hb:eq:Rjn}. Substitute it into \eqref{hb:eq:ratioULC} with $k=s+j$.
Since
$R_j(n)>((j+1)/j)^2>(s+j+1)/(s+j)$, rearranging the inequality is valid
and gives \eqref{hb:eq:finiteDthreshold}. The factor
$(n-j+1)/(n-j)$ decreases with $n$, so $R_j(n)$ decreases and the
threshold increases. Taking its limit and simplifying the denominator
proves \eqref{hb:eq:limitDthreshold}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp uniform order for the limiting family]
\label{hb:thm:limitingorder}
Let $s\ge2$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:criticalD}
 D_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)=\frac{8s^2-11s+4}{3s-2},\qquad
 D_s=\max\left\{2s,\left\lceil D_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)\right\rceil\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then $D_s$ is the least integer $D\ge2s$ for which \emph{every}
$L_{s,n}$, $n\ge s$, is $\ULC_D$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The fraction in \eqref{hb:eq:limitDthreshold} is increasing in $j>0$.
For an explicit verification write
\[
 N(j)=j^2(s+j+1),\qquad D(j)=s(2j+1)+j(j+1).
\]
The numerator of the derivative of $N/D$ is
\begin{align*}
 N'D-ND'={}&j^4+4sj^3+2j^3+2s^2j^2+6sj^2+j^2\\
          &+2s^2j+2sj,
\end{align*}
which is positive for $j,s>0$. Therefore
$F_{s,j}(\infty)=s+j+N(j)/D(j)$ is increasing, and its maximum over
$j=1,\ldots,s-1$ occurs at $j=s-1$. Substitution yields
\[
 F_{s,s-1}(\infty)=\frac{8s^2-11s+4}{3s-2}.
\]
Every finite-$n$ threshold is below its limit, so any integer $D\ge2s$
with $D\ge D_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)$ works for every $n$.

Conversely, if $2s\le D<D_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)$, the increasing thresholds
$F_{s,s-1}(n)$ eventually exceed $D$. The final interior inequality then
fails for a sufficiently large $n$. Taking the smallest permitted integer
$D$ proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Necessary size of any universal rank-only order]
\label{hb:cor:universalorder}
Suppose an integer-valued function $\mathcal D(r)\ge r$ has the property
that every bipartite graph of matching rank $r$, with arbitrary positive
weights on both shores, has a $\ULC_{\mathcal D(r)}$ support polynomial.
Then for every $s\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:universalorder}
 \mathcal D(2s)\ge D_s.
\end{equation}
In particular, along even ranks,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:fourthirds}
 \mathcal D(r)\ge\frac43r-\frac{17}{9}+o(1).
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If an admissible integer $D$ is smaller than $D_s$,
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:limitingorder} supplies an $n$ and a strict negative
order-$D$ margin of $L_{s,n}$. Coefficientwise convergence in
\eqref{hb:eq:limit} implies convergence of each margin after multiplication by
$w^{-4s}$. The same margin of $p_{H_{s,n}}$ is therefore negative for a
sufficiently large but finite positive $w$. That graph has matching rank
$2s$, contradicting universality of $D$.

Polynomial division gives
\[
 D_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)
 =\frac83s-\frac{17}{9}+\frac{2}{9(3s-2)}.
\]
Since $r=2s$, this proves \eqref{hb:eq:fourthirds}.
\end{proof}

For example, the limiting family requires orders at least $7$, $9$, and
$12$ at matching ranks $6$, $8$, and $10$, respectively. These are lower
bounds for the general weighted problem, not universal upper bounds.
We have not proved that $D_s$ works for every finite-activity member of the
Hall family, much less for every rank-$2s$ bipartite graph.

\subsection{What drives the obstruction}

The shift $t^s$ in \eqref{hb:eq:limit} is the decisive feature. Once all cores
are forced, adding $j$ outer vertices on each shore gives squared binomial
coefficients, but those coefficients occur at degrees $s+j$, not $j$.
The binomial factors appropriate to an unshifted count no longer match the
factor required at the upper end of a degree-$2s$ polynomial.

This explanation also clarifies why a small rank does not mean a small
homogeneous realization. A large reservoir of outer choices survives even
though the core bounds every matching. The forced-core limit captures this
reservoir while retaining the degree shift caused by the compulsory cores.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{A universal positive result at the first inequality}
\label{hb:sec:first}

The counterexamples leave room for genuine rank-sensitive inequalities.
The first one always holds, and its equality cases have a particularly
simple structure.

\begin{lemma}[Minimum vertex cover]\label{hb:lem:konig}
A bipartite graph of matching rank $r$ has a vertex cover of size $r$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take a maximum matching $M$. Starting from the unmatched left vertices,
follow alternating paths, using unmatched edges from left to right and
matched edges from right to left. Let $Z_X,Z_Y$ be the reachable vertices
on the two shores. No unmatched right vertex is reachable, since that
would give an augmenting path.

The set $C=(X\setminus Z_X)\sqcup Z_Y$ covers every edge. Indeed, an
uncovered edge would run from a reachable left vertex to a nonreachable
right vertex. An unmatched such edge would make the latter reachable; if
the edge is matched, its right endpoint is the predecessor by which the
matched left endpoint became reachable. Both alternatives are impossible.
Every matched edge has exactly one endpoint in $C$: its endpoints are
either both reachable or both nonreachable. Unmatched left vertices are
reachable and unmatched right vertices are nonreachable. Thus $C$ has
exactly $r$ vertices.
\end{proof}

Fix a minimum cover $C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_r\}$. Assign each edge to one of its
incident cover vertices, choosing arbitrarily for edges with both endpoints
in $C$. This partitions the edge set into star classes
$E_1,\ldots,E_r$. Write
\[
 z_{xy}=u_xv_y,\qquad W_i=\sum_{e\in E_i}z_e,
 \qquad a_1=\sum_{i=1}^r W_i.
\]
Let $K$ be the sum of $z_ez_f$ over pairs of edges assigned to different
classes that meet at a vertex. Let $B_4$ be the sum of $u_Iv_J$ over all
support pairs with $|I|=|J|=2$ for which all four possible edges are
present. The symbols $K$ and $B_4$ are nonnegative weighted counts.

\begin{theorem}[Exact first-margin defect identity]\label{hb:thm:firstidentity}
For every positively weighted bipartite graph with matching rank $r\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:defectidentity}
 \frac{r-1}{2r}a_1^2-a_2
 =\frac1{2r}\sum_{i<j}(W_i-W_j)^2+K+B_4.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:firstineq}
 a_1^2\ge\frac{2r}{r-1}a_2,
\end{equation}
which is exactly the first $\ULC_r$ inequality because $a_0=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $m_2$ be the weighted number of individual two-edge matchings, where a
matching has weight equal to the product of the weights of its four covered
vertices. A two-edge matching cannot have both its edges assigned to the
same cover vertex. Consequently
\[
 \sum_{i<j}W_iW_j=m_2+K.
\]
For a given support pair of size two, the number of perfect matchings is
one or two. It is two exactly when its induced bipartite graph is $K_{2,2}$.
Both matchings have the same support weight. Therefore $m_2=a_2+B_4$.
Finally,
\[
 \frac{r-1}{2r}\left(\sum_iW_i\right)^2-\sum_{i<j}W_iW_j
 =\frac1{2r}\sum_{i<j}(W_i-W_j)^2.
\]
Adding these identities proves \eqref{hb:eq:defectidentity}; every term on
the right is nonnegative.
\end{proof}

The identity separates three sources of slack: unequal total weights of
cover-centered star classes, overlap between different such classes, and
multiple witnessing matchings on the same four-vertex support. The last
term would be invisible if supports were mistakenly counted with matching
multiplicity.

\begin{corollary}[Equality classification]\label{hb:cor:equality}
For positive vertex weights and $r\ge2$, equality holds in
\eqref{hb:eq:firstineq} if and only if, after deleting isolated vertices, the
graph is a disjoint union of $r$ stars whose edge-weight sums are equal.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Equality in \eqref{hb:eq:defectidentity} implies $W_1=\cdots=W_r$. Since
$a_1>0$, all these values are positive, so every class is nonempty.
It also gives $K=0$. Positive weights then imply that any edge in one
class is disjoint from any edge in a different class. Thus the vertex
sets of the nonempty classes are disjoint. Each class is a star centered
at its assigned cover vertex, so the nonisolated graph is a disjoint union
of exactly $r$ stars, with equal edge-weight sums.

Conversely, for disjoint stars with common edge-weight sum $W$, a matchable
support chooses either no edge support or one edge support in each star.
The support polynomial is $(1+Wt)^r$. Its first normalized inequality is
an equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{hb:cor:smallrank}
Every positively weighted bipartite graph with matching rank at most two
has a rank-normalized ultra-log-concave support polynomial.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Ranks zero and one have no nontrivial interior inequality. In rank two,
\eqref{hb:eq:firstineq} is the only one.
\end{proof}

The defect identity also gives a quantitative statement without any
structural approximation theorem. If its left side is at most
$\varepsilon a_1^2$, then
\[
 \sum_{i<j}(W_i-W_j)^2\le2r\varepsilon a_1^2,
 \qquad K+B_4\le\varepsilon a_1^2.
\]
Small defect therefore forces the star-class weights to be nearly equal
and the total weighted overlap and multiplicity to be small. Turning this
weighted conclusion into a graph-edit theorem would require additional
lower bounds on individual vertex weights.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Exact counting parameterized by matching rank}
\label{hb:sec:algorithm}

The bottleneck viewpoint has an algorithmic benefit beyond the special
family. A small maximum matching yields a small vertex cover, and outside
vertices can be grouped by their neighborhoods in that cover. We give a
formula that handles arbitrary positive rational weights without counting
the same support repeatedly.

\subsection{Neighborhood types and elementary symmetric weights}

Let a minimum cover be $C=C_X\sqcup C_Y$ with
\[
 p=|C_X|,\qquad q=|C_Y|,\qquad p+q=r.
\]
There are no edges between $X\setminus C_X$ and $Y\setminus C_Y$.
Every nonisolated outside left vertex has a nonempty neighborhood
$T\subseteq C_Y$; let $X_T$ be the vertices of that type. Likewise let
$Y_S$ be the outside right vertices with nonempty neighborhood
$S\subseteq C_X$. There are at most $2^q-1$ left types and $2^p-1$ right
types.

For a finite collection of weights $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_h)$, write
\[
 e_j(z)=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_j\le h}z_{i_1}\cdots z_{i_j},
 \qquad e_0(z)=1.
\]
Set $e_j(z)=0$ for $j>h$. These elementary symmetric functions are the
correct weights for choosing an \emph{unordered subset} of $j$ vertices
of the same type.

\begin{definition}
A cover-type profile consists of selected core subsets
$U\subseteq C_X$, $V\subseteq C_Y$, together with nonnegative integer
multiplicities $\alpha_T$ and $\beta_S$ for the outside left and right
types. It has size $k$ if
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:profilesize}
 |U|+\sum_T\alpha_T=|V|+\sum_S\beta_S=k.
\end{equation}
Its compressed graph contains the selected core vertices and exactly the
specified number of indistinguishable copies of each outside type, with
edges prescribed by the original neighborhoods and the core-induced graph.
\end{definition}

A feasible profile must satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:profilecaps}
 \sum_T\alpha_T\le q,\qquad \sum_S\beta_S\le p.
\end{equation}
Indeed, all selected outside left vertices must match into $V$, and all
selected outside right vertices into $U$. We may use the weaker bounds
$q,p$ for enumeration, and let the matching test enforce the stronger
bounds involving $|V|,|U|$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact cover-type formula]\label{hb:thm:algorithmformula}
For every $k$, the coefficient $a_k$ is the sum, over the profiles satisfying
\eqref{hb:eq:profilesize} and \eqref{hb:eq:profilecaps} whose compressed graph
has a perfect matching, of
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:profileweight}
 u_Uv_V
 \prod_T e_{\alpha_T}\bigl((u_x)_{x\in X_T}\bigr)
 \prod_S e_{\beta_S}\bigl((v_y)_{y\in Y_S}\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every support pair determines a unique profile by intersection with the
cover and by counting its selected vertices of each outside type. Two
actual support pairs with the same profile have isomorphic induced
bipartite graphs under a map fixing the selected core vertices. Thus
matchability depends only on the profile.

Within a matchable profile, the sum of weights of all choices of outside
vertices factors independently across types. The factor for selecting
$\alpha_T$ vertices from $X_T$ is exactly the first elementary symmetric
factor in \eqref{hb:eq:profileweight}, and similarly on the right. The selected
core contributes $u_Uv_V$. Summing over profiles counts every support once
and only once, regardless of the number of perfect matchings in its
compressed graph.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A fixed-parameter bound}

Let $N=|X|+|Y|$ and $M=|E|$. For $t$ types the number of nonnegative
multiplicity vectors with total at most $q$ is $\binom{t+q}{q}$. Therefore
the number of enumerated profiles is at most
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:profilebound}
 B_{p,q}=
 2^r\binom{2^q+q-1}{q}\binom{2^p+p-1}{p}.
\end{equation}
When $p=0$ or $q=0$, the corresponding binomial factor is interpreted as
$\binom00=1$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact fixed-parameter counting]\label{hb:thm:FPT}
All coefficients of a positively rationally weighted matching-support
polynomial can be computed exactly using
\begin{equation}\label{hb:eq:time}
 O\bigl((N+M)r+Nr+r^3 B_{p,q}\bigr)
\end{equation}
arithmetic operations, for $r\ge1$. In particular, the problem has a
$2^{r^2+O(r)}\operatorname{poly}(N+M)$ algorithm parameterized by maximum
matching size. Rank zero is immediate.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A maximum matching and the cover in Lemma~\ref{hb:lem:konig} can be found
with at most $r$ augmentations, each requiring $O(N+M)$ work. Group outside
vertices by their cover neighborhoods. Compute the elementary symmetric
functions in each left group up to degree $q$ and in each right group up
to degree $p$, using the update
\[
 e_j\leftarrow e_j+z e_{j-1}
\]
in descending order of $j$ for each new weight $z$. The total cost is
$O(Nr)$.

Enumerate the profiles in \eqref{hb:eq:profilebound}. Discard those failing
\eqref{hb:eq:profilesize}. Their compressed graphs have $k\le r$ vertices on
each shore, so a simple augmenting-path perfect-matching test takes
$O(r^3)$ operations. For every successful test add
\eqref{hb:eq:profileweight} to $a_k$. Products and graph construction fit into
the same bound.

Finally, $2^q+q-1\le2^{q+1}$ for $q\ge1$, and similarly for $p$. Bounding
$\binom{h}{j}$ by $h^j$ gives
\[
 B_{p,q}\le 2^{r+q(q+1)+p(p+1)}\le2^{r^2+2r}.
\]
This proves the fixed-parameter bound.
\end{proof}

The arithmetic model does not hide an uncontrolled coefficient-size issue.
For rational input weights, a common denominator formed from the input
denominators has bit length at most the sum of their bit lengths. Every
support product has degree at most $2r$, and there are at most
$\sum_{k\le r}\binom{|X|}{k}\binom{|Y|}{k}$ terms. Standard exact rational
arithmetic therefore adds only a polynomial bit-complexity overhead in the
input size and $r$. The reference implementation uses Python's
\texttt{Fraction} for this reason.

This algorithm is deliberately explicit rather than optimized. For dense
graphs of large rank its parameter dependence is prohibitive. For a small
cover with few realized neighborhood types, however, the actual profile
count can be much smaller than the worst-case bound. The Hall family has
only one outside type on each shore, which is why the 30-vertex example is
especially easy to verify by an independent cover-type computation.

\subsection{Implementation contract and example}

The file \texttt{code/support\_count.py} accepts a list of right-neighbor
indices for each left vertex, the right shore size, and optional positive
integer or rational weights. It returns the exact coefficient list. The
following uses the supplied API:
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
from support_count import hall_graph, support_polynomial, ulc_margins

s, n, w = 4, 11, 500
adj = hall_graph(s, n)
weights = [1] * n + [w] * s
coefficients = support_polynomial(adj, n + s, weights, weights)
assert ulc_margins(coefficients, 8)[-1] < 0
assert all(d >= 0 for d in ulc_margins(coefficients, 15))
\end{lstlisting}
Invalid neighbor indices, nonpositive weights, and inexact floating-point
weights are rejected. Isolated vertices are allowed and do not change the
returned polynomial. The independent \texttt{brute\_force} function uses
reachable right-support sets for each left subset; it is intended only for
small cross-checks, not as the fixed-parameter method.
[Merge note: the module is shipped as
\nolinkurl{code/13-hall-bottlenecks-support_count.py}. A file name with
hyphens cannot be imported by name, so the example above runs only on a
copy saved as \texttt{support\_count.py}, as the report's README
describes.]

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Verification, reproducibility, and limits}
\label{hb:sec:verification}

The accompanying program \texttt{code/verify.py} runs the exact checks
below and writes its transcript and certificates to \texttt{data/}.
No mathematical assertion about an infinite family rests solely on these
tests; the proofs are given in the preceding sections.

\paragraph{Independent counting checks.}
The cover-type implementation was compared with the subset dynamic program
on every one of the 512 labeled $3\times3$ bipartite graphs, both at unit
weights and at the unequal weights $(2,3,5)$ and $(7,11,13)$. These are
1,024 exact comparisons. An additional 200 seeded graphs with shore sizes
from one to six and positive rational weights were checked. Thirty-six
small Hall-family instances were compared simultaneously by the closed
formula, the cover-type algorithm, and the subset dynamic program.
The first-margin defect identity was also checked exactly on every
rank-at-least-two instance in the $3\times3$ suite.

\paragraph{Counterexample and symbolic checks.}
The 30-vertex witness was counted by the Hall formula, the general
cover-type algorithm, and full independent enumeration of its supports.
All three coefficient lists agree. Its exact coefficients and margins are
in \nolinkurl{data/rank8_witness.json}, together with an explicit maximum
matching and minimum cover. The symbolic checks verify all rank-six coefficient
formulas, all four positive-coefficient certificates, the final quadratic,
and the general endpoint identity in independent symbols. The general
tail formulas are also checked against the support sum for core sizes two
through six. Integer threshold tables are obtained by exact evaluation and
binary search, not numerical root rounding.

\paragraph{Environment and reproducibility.}
The delivered transcript records Python 3.13.5 and SymPy 1.14.0. The counting
module itself has no third-party dependency; SymPy is used only by the
symbolic verification driver. Running
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
python code/verify.py
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
from the package root regenerates the data and PDF. The included build
script automates the last two commands.
[Merge note: in this report the verifier is
\nolinkurl{code/13-hall-bottlenecks-verify.py}; it imports
\nolinkurl{code/13-hall-bottlenecks-support_count.py} under its delivery
name \texttt{support\_count}, and the records named in this section are
shipped as \nolinkurl{data/13-hall-bottlenecks-<name>}. Besides
\texttt{data/}, the verifier writes \texttt{tex/positivity\_tables.tex}
(shipped as \nolinkurl{data/13-hall-bottlenecks-positivity_tables.tex}),
reads the table block of the main article between the two comment
markers of Section~\ref{hb:app:positive}, and fails without it; it
rewrites its outputs in place. Run it only on a copy restored to the
delivered layout, as the report's README describes. The build script,
shipped as \nolinkurl{code/13-hall-bottlenecks-build.sh}, changes to its
own directory and would compile a nonexistent \texttt{code/article.tex};
this report is built with \texttt{latexmk}. The ``unequal weights
$(2,3,5)$ and $(7,11,13)$'' of the first paragraph are the left and the
right weights of \emph{one} weighting (the transcript says ``one positive
unequal weight vector''): the 1,024 comparisons are 512 graphs at two
weightings.]

\paragraph{What was not verified.}
There is no Lean formalization in this package, no proof-assistant kernel
check, and no claim of exhaustive classification of all graphs of rank
three through six. The 30-vertex example is not asserted to be smallest.
The full phase diagram applies only to the explicitly defined symmetric
core-three family. The endpoint classification for larger cores is not a
classification of all inequalities. The exact limiting-family order is
not a universal upper bound for arbitrary graphs.

\paragraph{Novelty assessment.}
The targeted source review establishes that the smaller-shore result is
already published and that the cited ProveIt snapshot does not prove its
rank replacement. The proofs here resolve the universally two-shore
weighted strengthening and derive the associated structural and
algorithmic results. They should be independently reviewed before any
claim of publication priority. We do not describe the result as resolving
a famous named conjecture or as refuting a theorem in the cited literature.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Further research questions}
\label{hb:sec:questions}

The following questions are formulated to distinguish global classification
from properties of the particular family. They are not used as premises
in any proof above.

\begin{question}[Unit weights]\label{hb:q:unit}
Is every unit-weight matching-support polynomial $\ULC_r$, where
$r=\nu(H)$? If not, what is the smallest-rank counterexample?
\end{question}
The core-three family cannot answer this negatively, by
Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:asymptoticweight}. The cover-type formula provides an
exact search framework that is better aligned with the rank parameter
than enumeration by total vertex count. A proof would need to use the
absence of external fields in an essential way.
[Merge note: this is the unit-weight half of Part~V's Research
question~\ref{lor:q:first}; the batch-55 search recorded after that
question found no unit-weight counterexample in its finite families.]

\begin{question}[One-shore external fields]\label{hb:q:oneshore}
Does $\ULC_r$ hold when $u_x=1$ for every left vertex and the right weights
$v_y$ are arbitrary positive numbers?
\end{question}
The counterexample forces cores on both shores, so it does not settle this
version. One can first analyze a two-activity Hall family and specialize
one activity to one. A general positive theorem here would sharply
separate one-shore support weighting from two-shore weighting.
[Merge note: with Research question~\ref{hb:q:unit}, this is what remains
open of the weighted version of Research question~\ref{lor:q:first}.]

\begin{question}[First possible weighted rank]\label{hb:q:rank}
Do all positively weighted support polynomials of matching ranks three,
four, or five satisfy rank-normalized ultra-log-concavity?
\end{question}
Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:smallrank} and the rank-six example leave the smallest
possible rank in $\{3,4,5,6\}$. A promising approach is to enumerate
cover-type structures, derive symbolic coefficient inequalities, and look
for positive-coefficient or sum-of-squares certificates after reducing
symmetries. Numerical sampling alone would be a poor substitute for these
certificates because the known rank-six threshold can be large.

\begin{question}[A universal rank-only order]\label{hb:q:order}
Does there exist a finite function $\mathcal D(r)$ such that all positively
weighted rank-$r$ support polynomials are $\ULC_{\mathcal D(r)}$?
If so, what is its optimal growth and exact small-rank behavior?
\end{question}
Corollary~\ref{hb:cor:universalorder} rules out $\mathcal D(r)=r$ and any
asymptotic slope below $4/3$ along even ranks. It does not prove existence
of a rank-only order. The possibilities include a larger linear bound,
a nonlinear bound, or failure of every finite uniform order at some rank.

\begin{question}[Full Hall-family phase diagrams]\label{hb:q:phase}
For $s\ge4$, is the endpoint always the first rank-normalized inequality
to fail as the common activity $w$ increases? What is the exact smallest
order that works for every finite activity and outer size at fixed $s$?
\end{question}
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:endpoint} gives a necessary failure region, and
Theorem~\ref{hb:thm:limitingorder} gives the exact limiting answer. The missing
step is a uniform analysis of all intermediate margins. The positive
coefficient method used at $s=3$ is one concrete candidate, but it must be
proved rather than extrapolated from small cases.

\begin{question}[Asymmetric bottlenecks]\label{hb:q:asymmetry}
What happens when the two cores have different sizes, the outer blocks
have different sizes, or the two cores have different activities?
Can such asymmetry lower the first counterexample rank or the vertex count?
\end{question}
The support criterion still reduces to $i+j\ge k$, while the four
binomial factors and the activity weights become asymmetric. The parameter space is larger, but
endpoint coefficients still involve only a few core choices. This is a
natural route to smaller certificates without asserting that the present
symmetric witness is extremal.

\begin{question}[Higher-index defect identities]\label{hb:q:defects}
Is there a higher-degree analogue of \eqref{hb:eq:defectidentity} in which a
rank-normalized margin decomposes into nonnegative terms plus an explicit
Hall-bottleneck obstruction?
\end{question}
Such an identity could explain exactly why the first inequality is
universal and higher ones fail. It might also isolate graph classes where
all obstruction terms vanish, producing structural sufficient conditions
for rank normalization rather than a new numerical bound alone.

\begin{question}[Faster exact counting]\label{hb:q:algorithm}
Can the $2^{r^2+O(r)}$ profile enumeration be reduced to a singly
exponential dependence on $r$, or to a substantially better dependence on
the number of realized neighborhood types?
\end{question}
The current procedure repeats matching tests for many profiles with shared
structure. Dynamic programming over subsets of the cover, representative
profile classes, or algebraic compression could help. Any improvement must
preserve support counting, not silently replace it by the easier-to-write
sum over individual matchings.
[Merge note: compare Part~V's Research question~\ref{hb:hq:algorithms},
which asks for exact algorithms depending on repeated neighbourhoods, and
Part~IV's Research question~\ref{lor:hq:countcx}.]

\begin{question}[Formal proof and certificate interfaces]\label{hb:q:formal}
What is the smallest reusable formal interface that proves the support
formula, certifies the counterexample, and verifies the cover-type count?
\end{question}
A first stage needs only finite bipartite matchings, binomial counting,
exact polynomial identities, and ordered-field inequalities. The
Lorentzian corollary can be separated as a later stage depending on the
published homogeneous theorem. This separation would allow a short
kernel-checked certificate of the negative answer without first
formalizing the entire surrounding theory.
[Merge note: Part~V's Research question~\ref{lor:q:last} asks for a
layered formalization of Part~V's theorems; this question concerns
Part~XI's finite certificate and its cover-type count. Nothing of either
is formalized.]

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
\section{Conclusion}
\label{hb:sec:conclusion}

The difference between shore size and matching rank is substantive for
positively weighted matching supports. A simple missing rectangular block,
together with a core activity, already defeats the rank-normalized
inequality. The resulting obstruction is exact, robust, and visible in a
single quadratic; at rank six it admits a complete phase diagram.

At the same time, rank remains useful. It controls a universal first
inequality with a transparent equality theory, provides a parameter for
exact support counting, and constrains any possible replacement
normalization. The next decisive questions are therefore not whether the
published smaller-shore theorem is valid---it is retained throughout---but
which restrictions restore rank normalization and whether a universal
rank-only order exists beyond the lower bound proved here.

\section{A hypertree proof of the known root identity}\label{app:hypertrees}

This appendix reconstructs Proposition~\ref{prop:known} without using the
support-enumerator theorem of~\cite{DHLTW}. It is included for conceptual
clarity and as an independent route to the same normalization. Its one
substantial imported result is the K\'alm\'an--Postnikov theorem~\cite{KP}.

\subsection{Hypertrees and internal inactivity}

For a connected bipartite graph with left shore $L$, a left hypertree is a
vector $a\in\N^L$ realized by a spanning tree $T$ through
$a_i=\deg_T(i_L)-1$. Distinct trees realizing the same vector contribute only
one hypertree. Order the left shore. A coordinate $i$ is internally inactive
when there is a smaller coordinate $j$ such that replacing $a$ by
$a-\ee_i+\ee_j$ gives another hypertree. The interior polynomial is the sum
of $t^{\text{number of internally inactive coordinates}}$ over hypertrees.

The K\'alm\'an--Postnikov theorem identifies this interior polynomial with the
Ehrhart numerator of the bipartite root polytope. Their paper uses a reversed
convention for the triangulation $h$-polynomial in its Theorem~1.1; the
Ehrhart-basis formulation immediately following that theorem, equation (1.2),
identifies the coefficients with the usual $h^*$-numerator used here. Thus
there is no additional reversal of $t$ in the statement we apply.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:hypertrees}
The left hypertrees of $\widehat G_\tau$ are exactly
\begin{equation}
 a=(n-x(E),x_1,\ldots,x_n),\qquad x\in P_\tau.\label{eq:hypertree}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A spanning tree of $\widehat G_\tau$ has $2n+1$ edges, so the sum of its left
degree-minus-one vector is $(2n+1)-(n+1)=n$. For a nonempty
$A\subseteq[n]$, the tree edges incident with $A_L$ form a forest on
$A_L\cup N(A)$. Their number is $a(A)+|A|$, and a forest on this nonempty
vertex set has at most $|A|+|N(A)|-1$ edges. Hence
\[
 a(A)\leq |N(A)|-1=|\down A|.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:draconian} now shows that $x=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ belongs to
$P_\tau$, and the sum condition determines $a_0$.

Conversely, let $x\in P_\tau$. Replace the left element $i$ by $x_i$ distinct
clones, each adjacent to the right set $\down i\subseteq[n]$. A set of clones
whose labels lie in $A$ has at most $x(A)\leq|\down A|$ members. Thus Hall's
matching condition holds, and all clones can be matched to distinct right
vertices. This is also a constructive statement: if an augmenting-path
matching leaves a clone unmatched, the alternating paths reachable from it
produce a set of clones with fewer neighbors, contradicting Hall's condition.

Build a tree by first taking all edges $i_L0_R$ for $0\leq i\leq n$. Each
right vertex $j_R$, $j>0$, is then attached to the left label of its matched
clone, or to $0_L$ if it is unmatched. The first edges form a star; every
subsequent edge attaches a new leaf. Hence the result is a spanning tree.
Its left degrees are $x_i+1$ for $i>0$ and $n-x(E)+1$ for $i=0$, exactly
as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:activity}
Order the left vertices with $0$ first. For the hypertree in
\eqref{eq:hypertree}, internal inactivity is $|\supp(x)|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first coordinate is never internally inactive. A zero coordinate cannot
transfer a unit, so it is also not internally inactive. If $x_i>0$, then
$x-\ee_i\in P_\tau$ because all the defining inequalities are upper bounds
and the coordinates remain nonnegative. By Lemma~\ref{lem:hypertrees}, the
vector obtained by transferring one unit from coordinate $i$ to coordinate
$0$ is another hypertree. Thus every positive nonzero-index coordinate is
internally inactive, and there are no others.
\end{proof}

Summing over~\eqref{eq:hypertree} gives an interior polynomial equal to
$h_\tau(t)$. The K\'alm\'an--Postnikov theorem identifies it with
$h^*(B_\tau,t)$, proving Proposition~\ref{prop:known} by this second route.
Notice that the argument counts hypertree \emph{vectors}, not spanning trees;
counting all realizing trees would introduce incorrect multiplicities.

\section{Proof dependencies and normalization audit}\label{app:audit}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{0.29\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Claim or input & Where it comes from\\
\midrule
$h^*(B_\tau)=h_\tau$ & Known: \cite[Theorem~1.2]{DHLTW}, specialized using
Lemma~\ref{lem:draconian}. Alternatively Appendix~\ref{app:hypertrees} plus
\cite{KP}.\\[3pt]
Ideal Hall presentation & Proposition~\ref{prop:inequalities}; transitivity is
used explicitly.\\[3pt]
Integer fiber factorization & Theorem~\ref{thm:fibers}; all coordinates and
inverse parameters are displayed.\\[3pt]
$h^*(C_\tau)=h_\tau$ & Corollary~\ref{cor:numerators}; a consequence of the
fiber factorization and the known root identity.\\[3pt]
Unimodularity & Leaf elimination in Lemma~\ref{lem:determinant}, followed by
Proposition~\ref{prop:startriangulation}.\\[3pt]
Polytopal pulling boundary & The established pulling lemma
\cite[Lemma~2.1]{AthSpecial}.\\[3pt]
Palindromicity, unimodality & Dehn--Sommerville and the $g$-theorem applied to
the constructed simplicial polytope; an independent reciprocity proof of
palindromicity is in Section~\ref{sec:second}.\\[3pt]
Alternative polytopal route & The explicit special simplex and
\cite[Theorem~3.5]{AthSpecial}.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

There are several easy places to make an otherwise plausible argument wrong.
The support polynomial of $Q_\tau$ is not asserted to be $h^*(Q_\tau)$.
It is the numerator of the different polytopes $B_\tau$ and $C_\tau$.
The larger denominator has exponent $2n+1$ and the smaller one exponent $n+1$.
Both auxiliary vertices, and the edge between them, are required. The edge
orientation convention is $j\leq_\tau i\iff i_Lj_R$ is present. The
integer-fiber parameters consist of $n+1$ nonnegative entries; the exponent
$n$ in~\eqref{eq:seriesfactor} results only after dividing by the additional
slack factor in the Ehrhart series of $C_\tau$.

No argument substitutes a rational equivalence for an integral one. The
fiber base is integral because $a_\tau(y)$ is an integer for integral $y$.
The determinant statements refer to the full relevant lattices. Finally,
regularity or shellability alone is not used to claim that a sphere is
polytopal: the specific pulling-boundary theorem supplies that step.

\section{Reproducing the accompanying computations}\label{app:reproduce}

The archive contains \texttt{article.tex}, \texttt{article.pdf}, a build script,
\texttt{code/verify.py}, the full CSV enumeration, a JSON result report, and
status notes. From the extracted directory, run
\begin{lstlisting}
python3 code/verify.py --output data
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The verifier requires Python 3.10 or later and no third-party Python packages.
Do not use Python's \texttt{-O} option, since assertions are part of the checks.
The LaTeX document uses standard TeX Live packages, including
\texttt{newpxtext}, \texttt{newpxmath}, \texttt{tcolorbox}, and \texttt{hyperref}.

The CSV uses zero-based bit positions: the row value $5$ represents the set
$\{0,2\}$. Row $i$ records the principal ideal of element $i$, not its filter.
A polynomial is stored as coefficients from degree zero upward. The JSON
report also records explicit edge sets for matching certificates and complete
Ehrhart counts for the independently tested instances.

[Added 28 September 2026, batch 39: this appendix describes Part~I's
package; Part~II's programs and how to rerun them are in
Section~\ref{htwo:sec:build}.]

The calculations in the supplied report completed without failed assertions.
Their runtime is recorded separately as an observation from this environment,
not as a performance guarantee. No claim of formal verification is made.
